title: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
text:
He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.
At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.
A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.
She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."
In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.
"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.
She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power.
"We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."
She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail.
Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.
Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.
But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves.
"In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."
He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.
As the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs.
This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.
The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.
The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom.
"Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.
Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."
description: Thailand has prosecuted 294 people since 2020 under its lèse majesté law, with sentences going up to 50 years.

title: ICE agent charged for allegedly striking a Mexican national with his car
text:
ICE agent charged for hitting Texas immigrant with vehicle during pursuit
A US immigration agent has been charged with felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle earlier this month in Texas, a prosecutor announced.
The prosecutor said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Morales is accused of running over a Mexican national who was living in the US without legal documentation, leaving him with multiple leg fractures and a hip injury.
An ICE spokesperson dismissed the indictment as "nothing more than a political stunt" and described the allegations as "reckless and false".
The indictment comes amid the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration and a series of violent incidents involving federal agents that have resulted in injuries and deaths.
If convicted, Morales faces between two to 20 years in prison for the second-degree felony, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.
Teare said Morales pursued a vehicle driven by Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national who has lived in Texas for more than 30 years without legal documentation, on the morning of 10 October.
Parra-Hernandez and another occupant fled the vehicle on foot before Morales "aggressively steered his vehicle" into the Mexican national, Teare said at a news conference in Houston on Friday.
He said Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record and was not subject to a deportation order.
"Not only did he hit Mr Hernandez, he ran over both of his legs, leaving him seriously injured and hospitalised to this day," Teare said.
Morales then called 911 to report that Parra-Hernandez had hit his car.
Teare said that ICE was allegedly pursuing a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant, who has apparently been dead for nine years.
Immediately after the incident, an ICE spokesperson told the BBC's US media partner CBS News that Parra-Hernandez had run in front of the immigration agent's vehicle.
Following the indictment, ICE rejected the allegations brought by the grand jury - a panel of citizens empowered to determine whether there was sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges.
"This is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.
"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the spokesperson said, adding that the men and women of ICE "are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct".
The statement added that federal officers acting in the course of their duties could only be investigated by other federal agencies. The spokesperson insisted that local governments did not have the authority to run such an investigation.
District Attorney Teare stressed that he had the utmost respect for law enforcement and believed that undocumented individuals who were violent felons should be deported.
He said he hoped the prosecution would not only deliver justice for Parra-Hernandez and his family but also send "a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels that they have a free pass to terrorise our streets".
description: The Mexican national, who was living in the US without legal documentation, suffered multiple leg fractures and a hip injury, prosecutors said.

title: Scottish councils want a rethink on reform plans - is there a way forward?
text:
Scottish councils want a rethink on reform plans - is there a way forward?
Council leaders have called for the Scottish government to "rethink" its proposals for local government reforms.
Ministers have proposed replacing existing councils with six to 10 large regional authorities and more than a hundred smaller local bodies.
Following a meeting of the 32 council leaders, umbrella body Cosla said a change of structure alone is not the answer.
It has now set out its own vision for reform - with more powers being devolved to a local level and a review of funding arrangements, including council tax.
Cosla president Shona Morrison acknowledged public services did need to change but said the Scottish government's proposals and approach to engagement "need a rethink".
What has the government proposed?
The Scottish government has made "public service reform" a key goal in this new term of parliament.
Plans for a wholescale redrawing of local government weren't mentioned in the SNP manifesto, but after councils asked what ministers actually wanted, a vision was swiftly drawn up.
The new political map of Scotland would include six to ten large regional authorities, in charge of key services like education, bin collection, economic development and major planning decisions.
There would also be 120 to 160 smaller community authorities which would deal with local issues, such as licensing and town centre improvements.
Separate arrangements would be put in place for island communities.
Every bit as ambitious as the vision itself was the timescale proposed, with the government aiming to secure a broad agreement about a way forward inside just three months.
How have councils responded?
Cosla says this should not just be a conversation about the structure of local government, but the outcomes it provides for communities.
Their proposals on governance arrangements look quite different to the Scottish government one, though.
Cosla said plans should start with the 32 existing councils, building in better "regional collaboration and shared capacity".
They said that would involve services being joined up across wider areas "without automatically assuming a new regional authority is needed".
There could be "voluntary consolidation of councils" where that is supported locally, but only "subject to democratic agreement".
Cosla also said it was "unclear what the proposal for 130+ community authorities will add".
They are instead pushing for a "whole-system" review of where powers lie - right across Holyrood, the NHS, national agencies and public bodies as well as councils - to get them as close to communities as possible.
That part is not a million miles away from John Swinney's vision, which involves cutting the number of health boards on the mainland to two and merging a clutch of public sector bodies and agencies.
But it underlines the scale of the task involved - it is nothing less than a total rewiring of how Scotland is run.
Could council tax be reformed?
When you talk to people in local government, what tends to come across is that their most pressing concern is not about structure – it is about finance.
We are approaching the traditional season of bickering over the settlement local government gets to deliver services in the Holyrood budget.
Cosla wants "funding guarantees" to be a core part of talks from the outset - including council tax reform.
The SNP has famously been talking about scrapping the council tax since 2003, but tends to talk about changes as a longer-term project.
Last summer it said reforms "will not be possible this decade" because the complex process of thrashing out an agreement about revaluing properties would require an electoral mandate in 2031.
With the current system based on property values in 1991, someone is going to have to bite the bullet on that eventually.
Council tax isn't the end of the story on funding, though, as we have seen with innovations like visitor levies.
The "roadmap" for fiscal devolution just announced for councils in England raises some interesting possibilities too.
Chancellor John Healey has proposed assigning some income tax revenues directly to local authorities - an idea we know the SNP like, because they included it in their 2016 election manifesto.
Andy Burnham talks about Scotland as "one of the most centralised nations in Europe" - so could his devolution talks with John Swinney result in more powers being pushed down to a local level, beyond Holyrood?
What happens next?
Cosla bosses are due to meet the first minister next week for talks now that both sides have their cards on the table.
Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth is due to attend the meeting too and may end up playing a key role given she is also the finance secretary who will be setting the government's budget plans out at the start of December.
Cosla say reform plans "cannot be separated" from the upcoming budget, which is looking perilously tight.
The Scottish government's own medium-term financial strategy projects a £4.8bn shortfall between spending plans and expected income by 2029-30.
Is there realistically going to be a bumper payout for councils, at a pivotal moment for these talks? Yet another row over funding would create little goodwill for reform negotiations.
The same is true of public sector pay plans - there is precious little wiggle room left in the three-year envelope agreed two years ago.
Unless extra cash is found from somewhere, there could well be a scrap with unions over pay deals - the same unions which will have a say in these local reform plans.
There are also council elections looming next May.
Ministers insist those can go ahead because the new system could keep existing ward boundaries, meaning the 1,226 councillors elected in May could simply shift to the new authorities, sitting on both the regional and community authorities.
That raises a whole series of questions, though.
A region spanning Glasgow and the surrounding area could end up with more than 350 councillors.
Meanwhile some community authorities could end up with just two or three councillors on them, representing either tiny pockets of cities or large swathes of more rural areas.
Given turnout at council elections is frequently poor - a by-election in Aberdeen over the summer saw just 13.3% of people bother - voters will need a clear idea in their heads of exactly what the choice on offer is.
Are reforms going to happen?
Now that both central and local government has outlined a vision, we can start to get an idea of whether there is a way forward.
The notion of it being settled in a matter of months can probably be put to bed already - this is the sort of process that will take years, if it gets off the ground at all.
As we've just seen with the question of councillors and wards there are dozens of issues to be worked through, from council property holdings to debts to pensions, before we even get to carving up the many responsibilities of local government.
There may well be red lines among those responsibilities too - the government is has openly talked about shifting social care responsibility to health boards, which councils will be loathe to relinquish.
Talking of social care, reform legislation would need to be passed at Holyrood, and consensus built to avoid a repeat of the collapse of the National Care Service.
That was an ambitious project which was bogged down by a lack of a clear vision from government and any agreement with local government and unions - surely a cautionary tale.
There is a will on all sides for something to be done to reform public services - to get them running as efficiently as possible, both for the benefit of communities and to balance the books.
Ministers attempted to inject a bit of urgency with the tight timescale for initial consultation.
But there is no escaping that this is a vast and complicated enterprise - combined with the redrawing of health boards, it would be the biggest thing Holyrood has ever done in one go.
The concern is that all of this focus on reform creates uncertainty in the short term, which means other endeavours grind to a halt.
Councils have plenty to get on with - from national projects like reform of compulsory purchase rules to things like local development plans, which sound boring but are critical in whether things like new housing developments can go ahead.
So the negotiations which take place over the coming weeks could be critical in everything from the housing emergency to the state of the high street, to the running of local schools and care services, and to your local tax bill and your bin collections.
description: Council leaders have called for the Scottish government to reconsider a planned reorganisation of local authorities.

title: Why does the legend of Sawney Bean and Scotland's cannibal clan persist?
text:
Why does the legend of Sawney Bean and Scotland's cannibal clan persist?
A clan of cannibals preying on unwary travellers brings to mind horror films like The Texas Chainsaw Massacre or The Hills Have Eyes.
However hundreds of years before Leatherface ever revved up his chainsaw, similar gruesome tales were being spoken of in Scotland.
The legend of Sawney Bean and his family has chilled generations, telling of a murderous family who attacked and then devoured people passing near a hidden cave on the South Ayrshire coast.
Whether Bean and his relatives ever actually existed is another matter, and still provokes different opinions to this day.
"The first records of the Sawney Bean we know came in the 18th Century and originated in England," says Dr Gordon McKelvie, a lecturer in history at the University of Winchester who has written about the subject.
"I'm not saying there were never any cannibals in Scotland, but all these stories are written years after the alleged events happened and it feels almost safe, because 'oh, this all happened years in the past' not the here and now.
"The stories probably come from various local legends being repackaged and it was like fan fiction, where people added their own details as it went along."
The most common version of the legend has Bean born and growing up in East Lothian, but deciding to shun an honest living and moving to South Ayrshire with a woman.
Using a well-hidden cave on the coast, Bean and his family - which in some accounts of the tale number dozens - murdered passing travellers using the highway between Girvan and Ballantrae, before eating them. It was something described luridly in old tales.
However one day a man was able to use a pistol and sword to fend off an attack, although not before his unfortunate wife met a hideous end at the clan's hands.
The authorities were summoned, and King James himself led 400 men to hunt for the killers.
Upon being captured, the cannibals were taken to Leith and executed in a manner as horrible as they gave to their victims, by being dismembered or set on fire.
Hundreds of years on, and the location itself - dark and hidden - can still be unsettling, even to modern eyes.
Chris Campbell lives in Girvan and is interested in the area's myths and legends.
This led him to explore along the coast, eventually discovering one of the alleged locations for Bean and his clan.
"There was a part that was pitch black and there were three or four of us standing there in the cave, unable to see a thing," he says.
"It was unsettling. There are all these wee nooks and crannies, so you could imagine living there a bit of time before anyone would know."
Unlike McKelvie, Campbell believes there is enough published material surrounding Bean to suggest he existed in some form - but not in Ayrshire.
He believes the actual location would be in Galloway.
However the caves Campbell visited were used for illegal activity - though of a more prosaic kind than Bean's crimes.
"The myth is that it was on the Ayrshire coast, it was actually Galloway where Bean would be," he says.
"The Ayrshire myth played into the hands of smugglers, who would ship contraband to the coast. All the rumours about the caves would help keep other people away.
"But you can read enough descriptions of the trial, and the history of it, that I think he did exist."
Many of those descriptions came from publications like the Newgate Calendar, which carried sensationalist stories about crime that were often heavily embellished.
At the time of publication anti-Scottish sentiment was also high in England, while the name Sawney was considered a jibe at Scottish people, in the way "jock" would later become.
Some historians have previously said the entire legend was intended to degenerate Scots, suggesting they were so barbaric they would eat human flesh - including the claim that Bean killed 1,000 people.
Miles away from the alleged crimes, a version of the story remains a popular attraction at the Edinburgh Dungeon, where visitors are surrounded by alleged descendants of Bean who tell his story.
"It is such a good story so it has been a part of the Dungeon since we opened 25 years ago, " says Lyndsay Hebert, the venue's performance manager.
"We put you in the centre of the cave, with a person telling you exactly how they hunt people down, exactly how they will capture you and dissect you - it brings the guest into the nest of the cannibal."
The influence of Sawney Bean has since travelled far beyond Scotland.
Horror film director Wes Craven was allegedly inspired by the tales when he penned The Hills Have Eyes - about a cannibal family attacking people in the Nevada desert.
References to the legend have popped up in everything from manga series Attack on Titan to a story by science fiction writer Harlan Ellison and songs by various death metal and punk bands.
Closer to home it inspired Scottish slasher film Sawney: Flesh of Man - with David Hayman picking up victims in a taxi cab for a modern version of the tale - and Ayrshire band Junkman's Choir have a song about him.
Hebert believes the stories endure because it is still frightening to think of what humans are capable of.
"There is a primal fear there in the story that a human being is doing this to another person. It's not a monster or a creature but another human being."
That sentiment is something McKelvie agrees with, as well as its appeal to the darker part of human nature.
"Sex and violence always get an audience. As much as we balk at lurid tales in reality, we will still want to read them or watch them."
description: The legend of Sawney Bean and his family has chilled generations, telling of a murderous family who devoured people in South Ayrshire.

title: Love, luck and magic: Why are young people turning to online witches?
text:
Love, luck and magic: Why are young people turning to online witches?
Love or luck, take your pick. All yours with a simple click.
Or at least that's the promise being made by so-called "Etsy witches", who claim to cast spells for everything from good fortune to good weather.
And it seems there's a growing appetite for a little magic. Online retailer Etsy says searches for weather spells and witches have significantly increased this year.
But what are people hoping to get from these online witches, and why are young people turning to them for a helping hand?
For one 'Etsy witch', there's certainly no shortage of people looking for some extra luck.
Ellecia Cahill, from Erskine, describes herself as a "mystic" and has clocked up more than 2,000 sales online from readings and channelled letters - messages which claim to be from loved ones - as well as selling crystals and amulets.
And while you might expect love spells to top the shopping list, she says there's something else her customers are particularly keen on.
Abundance spells - in other words, a little help attracting money, success and opportunities.
She claims one customer - a tech investor from the wealthy Mediterranean principality of Monaco - had seen a "significant increase" in his net worth since he bought an abundance talisman.
A scroll through similar online retailers reveals a spell for every occasion, including spells promising to keep the rain away on your wedding day or to help you get tickets to a sold-out concert.
A spokesperson for Etsy told BBC Scotland they have seen "growing interest" in "magical touches" for occasions like weddings.
They said searches for spells for people trying to ensure sunshine on their big day have grown by 206% while general searches for wedding related-spells and witches are up 105%.
Whether they can actually deliver is another question entirely - in fact, Etsy rules say spells must be marketed as for entertainment purposes only.
For Cahill, it's not all about doing business.
The 24-year-old says that young people - though they are very used to thinking logically - are looking to believe in something magical.
She says that a lot of younger people feel lonely, and she wants to be a "safe space" for people, and to give them comfort.
"As humans we need to believe in something that is bigger than ourselves," she said. "Curiosity is natural.
"I think a lot of the time people know the answer they want, but are just looking for a bit of reassurance.
"Even if magic isn't real, if it helps someone feel more confident what is the harm?"
Actress Laura Blair, from Glasgow, bought a spell to help her with a specific job goal.
The 29-year-old told BBC Scotland: "I paid for a job spell, and they then allocated me to a witch. I had to send them my full names and more specifics and then she sent me a video of her doing the spell."
While the purchase didn't work out exactly as she'd hoped, she has noticed a positive impact on her acting career generally.
"Since I cast the spells I've had multiple acting roles, its actually the busiest I've ever been in my career," she said.
Another user, Chloe, also from Glasgow, wasn't so happy with her results.
"It was a waste of time and money. What I asked for didn't happen but it is a funny story, I suppose," the 22-year-old said.
"I had just gone through a break-up and wanted my ex back - but in hindsight maybe it is just as well it didn't work."
'Commodification of spirituality'
Researcher Alexandria Arthur-Hastie is a sociologist of religion at Leeds Beckett University. She believes the rise of online witches is part of a broader shift away from traditional religion and towards more "personalised forms of spirituality".
Hastie said it was unsurprising that witchcraft had expanded online, just like other aspects of modern life which have moved onto digital platforms.
"It's really just the latest step in the commodification of spirituality," she told BBC Scotland.
She said shows likes Sabrina the Teenage Witch and Charmed brought magic into the mainstream and these days, people can discover witchcraft through social media.
But the academic says there's something deeper behind the appeal.
For some young people, she said turning to witchcraft can be a way of finding support when life feels uncertain - be it relationships, careers or worries about the future.
"People go online, they're looking for solutions to these life problems, they're looking for a balm to soothe, really," she said.
Hastie said many contemporary witches see themselves not as mystical figures but as healers, focused on helping themselves, others and wider society.
"They really see it almost as a caring profession, something akin to maybe counselling," she said.
description: One online retailer has reported a sharp rise in the amount of people buying spells to help with luck.

title: Ballet Cymru marks 40 years of dance in Newport
text:
The childhood promise that brought professional ballet to a post-industrial town
Darius James remembers sitting before Gwent County Council at 10 years old and being asked the question: "Why should we give you money?"
He had earned a place at the Royal Ballet School, but his parents could not afford the school fees.
In response, he told the council he would go away and develop his skills and use them to help his community in Newport.
As James' Newport-based dance company Ballet Cymru marks its 40th anniversary, he hopes he has fulfilled that promise.
Growing up in Newport in the 1970s, James said it was "really, really unusual" for a boy to be doing ballet and that he was grateful for the support of his parents.
He said his father, a keen footballer who spent his life working at the Alcan aluminium factory in Newport, particularly embraced something that was so new to him.
"He didn't really understand at the beginning, but he loved it. And we work with a lot of young people now whose parents are not quite as understanding, even 40 years later, which is a bit depressing."
After years of training at the Royal Ballet School and dancing professionally, James returned to Newport and founded Ballet Cymru, originally called Gwent Ballet Theatre, in 1986.
He said the idea to start a ballet company in a post-industrial town was "totally crazy, but totally needed and logical".
"There is so much talent in Newport, so many brilliant, brilliant young people, and there's not the outlets you have in London or Cardiff."
After some initial backing from the Arts Council of Wales, he said Ballet Cymru went 13 years without any funding at all and 28 years without its own dedicated studio.
To help finance the company, James toured with other ballet troupes including Northern Ballet.
Amy Doughty, the company's co-artistic director and James' wife, joined Ballet Cymru as a dancer in 1996, and said they would rehearse wherever they could find space.
"We'd have to carry in all the ballet bars, all the equipment that we use, all the dance floors," she said.
However, with National Lottery funding in 2014, the company was able to renovate a warehouse into its current studio.
It sits on the same industrial estate James' father walked through to work each day.
In the early years, James said he would cover the word "ballet" on the van they took to do community workshops because he feared it would put people off before trying.
Doughty believes attitudes have changed since then, adding: "I think we've worked really hard in Newport to go into schools, to do shows here, to really develop people who understand what we're about."
However, James believes some barriers to participation in dance remain.
The directors identified seven boys through the company's Duets scheme who they believed showed talent, only to face reluctance from some parents.
"The dads will come in and say my son doesn't dance, he doesn't want to do ballet," Doughty said.
But the pair said the children had "absolutely loved it".
Established in 2012, the scheme runs workshops in Welsh schools where the company identifies children it believes have natural ability in dance but are not in any formal training.
Ballet Cymru then provides them with two years of free tuition. For Doughty, the financial aspect is particularly important.
She grew up in Australia as one of four children and said without scholarships, she would not have enjoyed the same career in dance.
Doughty feels that not being familiar with ballet can stop people from engaging with the art form.
"The reality is, we've got to take it to them. They're not going to seek us out, why would they?"
She said one way they try to do this is by giving free show tickets to children participating in the Duets programme and their families.
For some, she said, it can be their first time seeing live ballet.
Ballet Cymru marked its anniversary with shows at the Riverfront theatre in Newport on Thursday and Friday, before a tour to Leeds and Bangor.
Doughty said her hope was that she and James had built something that would last and grow beyond them.
Looking back at the council's decision to support him, James said: "They believed in me.
"If in the last 40 years we've reached one kid and inspired them to be better than they would have been otherwise, then surely that's worth it.
"I'm sure it's more, but just one would be worth it."
description: Ballet Cymru's founder reflects on the path that led to 40 years of the professional dance company.

title: Pontypool boy to go to US for cancer vaccine after drug withdrawn
text:
Toddler heads to US for cancer treatment as family given 'glimmer of hope'
A mother who is preparing to take her three-year-old son to the US for a vaccine trial says it has given her family a "glimmer of hope" for his future.
Almost a year ago, doctors warned Teddy Sloman's parents that he might not survive life-saving surgery after being diagnosed with high-risk neuroblastoma, a rare, aggressive childhood cancer.
But recent scans showed no active disease, and the family are preparing to fly to New York next month for what his mum Sarah hopes will be "the final chapter" of his treatment and "the end of this ridiculous nightmare".
"We've now given him the absolute best chance that we could possibly have in the world of medical science," she said.
Sarah, from Pontypool, Torfaen, said the process since Teddy's diagnosis had been "incredibly difficult" as they were often dealing with problems they could not have anticipated.
As a paediatric nurse herself, she previously said her medical knowledge had been both "a blessing and a curse".
An experimental treatment aimed at preventing the return of the type of cancer Teddy has was no longer available in the UK, so his family raised £250,000 to access the vaccine trial in New York.
Sarah said the scan results felt like "Christmas came early" after months of fearing Teddy would relapse, and they were finally "moving forward to the next step".
But she added they had to "mentally navigate all of these things" when all they "really want to do is stay at home and enjoy being a family for once".
The Welsh government said improving cancer care was a top priority and it was "acutely aware" how much it meant to people.
Teddy was diagnosed in July 2025 after months of symptoms that were initially thought to be teething, illness and constipation.
He stopped eating and drinking, was sleeping for hours in the day and night, and began vomiting.
Sarah felt a mass in his abdomen and was first told "it was just faeces".
With Teddy still feeling unwell, Sarah took him back to The Grange Hospital in Cwmbran in July.
A locum doctor in charge of the children's assessment unit said it was "not normal" for Teddy to have these symptoms and ordered a scan, later finding out that the mass was "actually a significant tumour".
Sarah said hearing the diagnosis was "surreal".
"I, as a student nurse, had been in that exact situation sort of 20 years ago... and it just felt so surreal, like an out-of-body experience.
"This is my work world. This is not supposed to be my personal life."
Teddy's tumour was so large it filled his entire abdomen, pressing on his organs and making it hard for him to eat or even breathe, and the cancer had spread to his bone marrow.
Sarah said: "Everything that we didn't want it to be, it was. So it's the most aggressive, the most rare, the most everything else."
Aneurin Bevan University Health Board said it recognised how "distressing it can be for parents when their child is seriously unwell, particularly when symptoms are complex and difficult to diagnose".
It added that it welcomed the family to contact them to discuss any concerns so they could be "reviewed fully".
The family spent 10 months in Noah's Ark Children's Hospital for Wales and also had to travel to Birmingham and London for specialist treatment.
This led to long-term implications, and Teddy now receives his food entirely through a tube and has to learn how to eat and drink again after already having to learn to walk three times due to being in bed for long periods.
Sarah said she felt "mum guilt" as her youngest son Joey, who is nearly two, spent most of his time with grandparents and relatives while Teddy was in hospital.
"We started running on fumes a long time ago, but you just do what needs to be done," she said.
Sarah said due to a measles outbreak in New York, they had made the "heartbreaking decision" to leave Joey in the UK during their first trip.
Over the past few months at home, the pair had been playing together and telling each other "they love each other", she said.
"It's those little things that you don't want to lose, you don't want to let go of.
"You want them to grow up together, looking out for each other and doing all the things that all the siblings [do]."
She added: "All of those things now feel like they're possible, whereas this time last year they didn't."
In June, the family found out that maintenance drug difluoromethylornithine (DFMO), which could prevent Teddy relapsing, had been withdrawn from the NHS, by the US-based company which owns it following a clinical trial.
Those who were already receiving the drug were allowed to continue for two years, but it was not available to new patients, such as Teddy.
Sarah said they were the only family they knew of going through the private treatment process.
To get an official referral for the clinical vaccine trial, Teddy's family had to send a urine sample, get a bone marrow aspirate and for his scans to declare "no active disease".
"To have the results come back... and for them to say that there's no active neuroblastoma cells, it was Christmas come early. It was everything that we'd hoped for for so long," said Sarah.
Teddy has officially been accepted as a patient for the vaccine trial in New York, and will have his initial appointment in November - but it comes at a hefty price.
"If he relapses the survival rates drop to single figures. So if there's a tiny chance that this vaccine can do some good [it's worth it]," Sarah said.
"At one point we were looking at selling the house and getting loans and all sorts because we just didn't see [another option].
"There's nothing in the world you wouldn't do for your children."
Friends launched a campaign to raise £250,000 and reached their target in 12 weeks, with Sarah admitting she thought "we'd never make it in a million years".
The fundraiser has since been increased to £350,000 to help with ongoing costs, and more than £300,000 has been raised so far.
She added: "It's absolutely incredible and there are not enough words in the world to thank people."
Despite everything, Sarah described Teddy as a cheerful "social butterfly" who had remained positive throughout.
"His friends are learning how to jump in muddy puddles and do climbing frames and Teddy's learning how to take blood pressures and use a stethoscope."
Sarah said more focus, support and research was needed for childhood cancers and that funding was "harrowing" compared to adult cancers.
"We shouldn't need to be raising all this money to fly the other side of the world for drugs," she said.
"I just want Teddy's story to be known so that the next person coming behind us doesn't have to go through this excruciating journey that we have."
The Welsh government said improving cancer care was a "top priority", with a 10-year strategy focused on better prevention, diagnosis and treatment aimed at improving services and outcomes for patients of all ages.
It added that, through Health and Care Research Wales, there was funding for "early stage clinical trials for children and young people" through a partnership with Cancer Research UK.
description: Teddy Sloman was diagnosed with high-risk neuroblastoma, a rare and aggressive childhood cancer.

title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
text:
US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots – the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
In an update on Saturday morning, Zelensky said around 200,000 households in the Dnipro region were left without electricity as well as at least 80,000 households in the Kyiv region following Russian strikes on Friday night.
He accused Russia of "deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure every day".
The US approved sale of Patriot missiles comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies that the country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
Additional reporting by Victoria Bourne
description: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.

title: Manhunt under way after Toronto CEO and family violently attacked in home invasion
text:
Manhunt under way after Toronto CEO and family violently attacked in home invasion
Police are searching for suspects after a Canadian real estate executive and his two daughters were shot, while his wife was attacked with a hammer, during an early morning home invasion in a wealthy Toronto neighbourhood.
David Morton, chief executive of the Mac Group, confirmed the attack in a statement, saying: "No family should ever have to experience this."
Morton said his family was reeling from "the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home".
The suspects demanded valuables before assaulting the family and fleeing in a car, Toronto Police said. Authorities have not released the identities of the suspects.
The home invasion took place in the Bridle Path, one of Canada's wealthiest neighbourhoods, whose residents have included music stars Drake and Celine Dion.
The area is known for its large mansions behind high walls and iron gates, with hired security often seen patrolling the area.
Police said the incident happened around 03:44 EST (07:00 GMT) on Thursday morning, when the suspects entered the property through a rear door.
The suspects then confronted the family and fired their guns multiple times, wounding the father and his two daughters, and hitting the wife on the head with a hammer.
"Three masked individuals forcibly entered our residence, armed with handguns and a hammer," Morton confirmed in a statement on Friday.
"During the attack, three members of our family were shot and are currently recovering in hospital. All four members of our family were also attacked with a hammer, leaving everyone injured and requiring emergency medical attention."
Morton did not name the family members, but media reports indicate that his two adult daughters Cristina and Maggie were shot, and his wife Doriana Zohil-Morton was struck in the head with a hammer.
Two of the victims remain in hospital, police said.
Police did not identify the victims, but listed their ages as 75, 64, 28 and 26. Police said the three suspects are believed to be men in their 20s.
The police believe the family was targeted solely because they lived in an affluent area.
“Typically, in an affluent neighbourhood comes nice things – and there’s always people out there that want to acquire nice things,” Inspector Kristy Smith of the Toronto Police Service told reporters.
Smith added that police do not yet know whether the suspects took anything from the home and are working to recover bullet casings that could help identify them.
Police figures show that home invasions are on the rise in Toronto, and some residents say they are taking steps to upgrade home security.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow, who was recently elected to a second term, said she was "deeply troubled" by the home invasion.
"This attack has understandably shaken the neighbourhood and many residents across Toronto," Chow wrote on X. "This violence is not acceptable in our city. People must be safe in their own homes."
Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre called it a "horrific" incident in a separate post on X.
"These criminals must be apprehended and held accountable for their actions before the justice system," he said.
Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said that Bridle Path residents should expect to see increased police patrols over the coming days.
"We also continue to make strategic decisions and dedicate additional resources to address this concerning trend of home invasions and to keep our communities safe," he said.
description: The real estate mogul and his two daughters were shot, while his wife was assaulted with a hammer, in an attack that has shocked the city.

title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
text:
Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
- Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final
We've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.
The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.
They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.
The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.
The finale drew an average audience of 11.2 million live viewers, and that number will rise when catch-up is included. Other recent episodes have been watched by more than 15 million, including catch-up.
Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.
Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the climax of the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.
When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful.
"Absolutely devastated. Almost scraped it," Kenny seethed. "I was so close, I smelled the victory."
However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.
In a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing.
"This might actually be the best day of my life," said 24-year-old Bash through tears of joy.
He, too, can expect a major career boost.
Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."
The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.
Earlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."
When it came to the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her.
"I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged.
"But I'm walking away feeling super proud and like I've really accomplished something here."
Meanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but valiant catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.
The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.
James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he too could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish.
"I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."
Celebrities who departed earlier in the series included ex-EastEnders actor Ross Kemp, model Jerry Hall, sitcom star Miranda Hart, comedian Joe Lycett, presenter Hannah Fry and former BBC journalist Amol Rajan.
This series is also likely to be remembered for the two contestants who made the unorthodox decision to reveal themselves as traitors, before being summarily dispatched by their fellow players.
First, actor Richard E Grant was so giddy to have received the tap on the shoulder that he blurted out his supposedly secret status in episode two.
Comedian James Acaster, meanwhile, was the most reluctant traitor in the history of The Traitors, and unexpectedly gave himself up when he came under pressure at the round table in Thursday's penultimate episode.
Aftermath of Acaster's admission
There have been reports that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.
Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".
Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.
In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.
Acaster did not take part in Friday's edition of spin-off show Uncloaked, which reunited some of the celebrity contestants following the final.
'A bit dull?'
The comedian's bombshell the previous night did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.
On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"
Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.
And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.
The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.
description: The second series of the hit show reached its climax on Friday after attracting 15 million viewers.

title: Jersey poppy seller moved by Remembrance Day campaign
text:
Poppy seller moved by Remembrance Day campaign
A poppy seller has described taking part in a Remembrance Day campaign as "very moving".
The Royal British Legion Jersey branch What Remembrance Means to Me video campaign involves islanders sharing experiences, including poppy seller John Pallot-Brown.
Pallot-Brown, the branch's standard bearer, said he wanted to remember his granddad and dad, who served served in World War One and World War Two respectively.
Lieutenant Governor of Jersey Sir Jerry Kyd said the appeal was important to remember those who "sacrificed themselves for our freedom".
In the video, Pallot-Brown said neither his father and grandfather spoke much about their service but he remembered being taken to the cenotaph as a child.
"There's a saying I'm quite fond of, all gave some and some gave all," he said in the video.
"At the end we must remember them."
Sir Kyd said the poppy appeal was not only about past wars but also about "today".

title: Soaring cost of Halloween treats spooks shoppers
text:
Soaring cost of Halloween treats spooks shoppers
Halloween shoppers in the US seeking sweet relief this spooky season have instead been shocked by the high price of seasonal treats, as cost of living pressures continue to bite.
Demetrio Beltres, a 33-year-old financial adviser searching for Halloween bargains for trick or treaters said he was spending more than his usual $15 (£11) to $20 this year because prices were much higher.
"I'm trying to spend at least $20 to $30 just to make sure that I get the kids something," he said, while browsing the rows of colour options at a Target in Manhattan.
A lot of people are finding they are in the same boat as Demetrio this year.
Stephen Zagor, adjunct associate professor at Columbia Business School, said people have only so much to spend, and when everyday essentials are costing more, people may feel less inclined to make this the most extravagant Halloween.
"I think the holiday's gotten scary, more from an economic [perspective], than it might be for scaring people at the door," he said.
Analysis from left-leaning non-profit Groundwork Collaborative and the Century Foundation found the cost of popular Halloween chocolates and confectionery was 15.3% higher this year than in 2025.
Separate research from personal finance firm Finance Buzz found prices for Halloween treats have soared by 71% over the past five years - a much bigger increase than the general pace of price rises over the same period.
The price of confectionery generally has been pushed up thanks to higher cocoa prices.
The cost of a tonne of cocoa skyrocketed to a high of more than $10,700 in January 2025, according to figures from the International Monetary Fund via the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis, as climate change contributed to severe weather which affected supplies.
"The cocoa that is now being consumed was bought when the prices were high," said Zagor, who specialises in food businesses.
Cost of living pressures have also increased, with inflation running at 3.7%, and fuel prices remain high. Diesel, at $6.32 a gallon, is only 20 cents below the record reached in September.
People shopping for Halloween treats in New York were noticing the price pressures.
"Everything is expensive, so it does not surprise me that Halloween candy is expensive too," said Mallory, who declined to give her last name.
The combined cost of living pressures have affected how much people are buying in the run up to the holiday, according to consumer and market research company Nielsen IQ. It found Halloween treat sales were down 11.7% by the middle of September, and by the middle of October sales were down 6.7%.
Chris Costagli, NielsenIQ's vice-president of US food thought leadership, said shoppers appeared more willing to spend as Halloween neared, but remained cautious.
"Sales have improved considerably from where we started in September, with smaller packs gaining ground while larger sizes continue to struggle," he said.
"This feels like a consumer who still wants the occasion, but is paying much closer attention to what goes into the basket."
How to make Halloween feel special without blowing the budget
Zagor, who is a fan of Halloween as well as traditional Halloween treats, said cutting back on costs, could present a good opportunity to offer trick or treaters a different kind of experience when they come to your door.
"It could be how you present the candy when kids come to your house as much as the one piece of candy that you're going to give," he said.
Options could include using a spooky fake skeleton hand to share out treats, rather than letting children reach into a bowl, or dressing up to meet trick or treaters.
Zagor said making your own treats is another option, inviting people over to make them together.
"You could certainly do something slightly magical, slightly interesting," he suggested.
"The trick literally could be as important as the treat."
description: The price of candy, especially chocolate, is up, and Halloween bargain hunters are searching for deals and ways to cut costs.

title: Judge to investigate whether Trump administration lied in golf course renovation case
text:
Judge investigating whether Trump administration lied about golf course renovations
A US judge said on Friday that she will launch an investigation into whether justice department lawyers deceived her about President Donald Trump's plans for renovating a golf course.
Trump has posted on social media that the East Potomac Golf Course would be closed in November for several months for the renovations, despite an ongoing legal challenge.
The judge is looking into whether the administration's last-minute notification to her about removing trees from the course was made in bad faith, and if government lawyers misrepresented Trump's renovation plans.
Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".
He has called the 106-year-old course "Trash Island", saying it will be renovated over the course of 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".
The legal dispute goes back to February, when the DC Preservation League and others sued over redevelopment plans for the park.
It escalated this month when the National Park Service began to cut down hundreds of trees without notifying the judge presiding over the lawsuit, US District Judge Ana Reyes, until 15 hours before work was set to begin on a holiday weekend.
After the trees were cut, Reyes ordered the Trump administration to stop tree removal until at least 26 October and give her three business days' notice about making any other permanent changes.
In a 70-page ruling this week, she extended that order and also barred the administration from making further alterations to the course without ten days' notice while the lawsuit proceeds. The administration has notified the court it intends to appeal that ruling, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
Despite the court-ordered block, Trump had recently announced that the course would be closed for 15 months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.
Government lawyers this week confirmed to Reyes that the course would be closed for renovations, after telling her earlier there were no plans to shutter it.
Reyes took a harsh tone with the lawyers at Friday's hearing, repeatedly questioning when they had knowledge of the plan to close the golf course.
At one point, she asked whether the Secretary of the Interior was involved in the project.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward - the number three official at the justice department - responded by asking what she meant by "involved".
Reyes then read the definition of the word from a dictionary.
At the end of the hearing, Reyes said she would be investigating whether the justice department attorneys "have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules".
That included whether giving late notice to the court about the renovation plans was "done in bad faith" and whether the attorneys failed to correct previously false statements or withheld information.
She said she would carry out the inquiry with a special master, an independent third party. In the US, judges appoint special master to carry out investigations or other provide other legal work related to cases and disputes.
description: A judge grilled Trump lawyers about what they knew of plans to close the golf course next month and said .

title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
text:
Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.
Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

title: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
text:
King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
The King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.
He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people.
Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.
Above the King was a sign that he took time to read.
"This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."
The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.
In 2022, the King described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda.
Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.
Outside one of the King's engagements later in the day, a small but noisy group of protesters gathered.
Many held placards saying "no apology will return what was stolen, reparations now" and "justice must not depend on wealth status and connections".
"This great wealth was built on the backs of slavery," said protester, Guyanese politician, Terrence Campbell.
"I do not want the British public to think that by me saying reparations can take various forms, it means that they do not have responsibility for reparations. They do, because the United Kingdom benefited tremendously from slavery."
The King will not be apologising for the UK involvement in the slave trade during the visit, nor will he offer reparations - compensation from those countries who benefited from the slave trade - in line with the position of the UK government.
This tour has seen a number of demonstrations so far but none have seriously disrupted the King's programme.
Royal tours often include cultural exchanges and the King's trip to Guyana saw an unusual mix up of musical styles.
On the bandstand of Promenade Gardens in Georgetown, the bagpipes of the National Piping Centre could be heard alongside traditional Guyanese drummers in a collaboration of musical styles.
Seven pipers from the National Piping Centre have been touring Guyana over the past week to learn more about the Guyanese musical traditions.
As part of his visit on Friday, the King also shared a moment with a veterans from Guyana who fought for Britain in the Second World War during an event at the Commonwealth War Graves in the capital Georgetown.
King Charles met Donald Grant, 99, who will celebrate his 100th birthday next week on November 3.
He also spoke to James Samuel, 100, who is in a wheelchair, with the the King hearing how aged 19 he enlisted in the British Guiana Volunteer Force in 1943.
"What a great pleasure it is to see you on this occasion," the King told him.
The King was waved off at the end of his state visit by Britain's High Commissioner to Guyana, Joseph Fisher, Guyana's Prime Minister Mark Phillips and a number of other dignitaries.
His departure had a small ceremonial element with the Guyana Defence Force providing a guard of honour at Cheddi Jagan International Airport.
