title: Reform councillor sanctioned for multiple conduct breaches
text:
Councillor sanctioned for multiple conduct breaches
A Reform UK councillor at Leicestershire County Council has been sanctioned for multiple code of conduct breaches.
Member conduct panel hearings, held at County Hall on Friday, considered two complaints against Joseph Boam, one lodged by a former senior council officer and the other by a Conservative councillor.
Boam was publicly censured by the panels, told to apologise to the complainants, and could be removed from the council committees on which he sits.
The councillor did not attend the panel meetings and the hearings were told he did not give any reasons for his absence.
Boam has previously denied breaching the code of conduct and called the complaint process "a ridiculous waste of taxpayer money".
The panel heard the former deputy council leader had refused to co-operate with investigations into the allegations against him.
One complaint, from November 2025, was made by Lauren Haslam, the council's former monitoring officer, in response to a clip of a council meeting which Boam published on a Facebook account he runs.
Haslam alleged the clip had been selectively edited to give "a misleading and inaccurate impression of her response" in a way that was disrespectful to her as a professional officer of the council.
During the meeting, Boam had asked Haslam if she thought that a rise in complaints against elected members was "from far-left activists trying to cancel and silence Reform UK councillors", to which she replied: "No, I wouldn't agree with that statement, thank you."
However, investigators found Boam chose to only publish her initial three-second reply and deliberately omitted a further explanation that followed.
As a result, the panel judged that the post led to her being accused of bias and of being a "nasty piece of work", according to the comments that followed.
Haslam later asked Boam to remove the post, but he did not acknowledge or respond to the email, nor did he remove the post.
Haslam, who worked for the council for over 25 years, told investigators she "could not bear to view his Facebook post" and the replies to it.
"I knew there would be unfounded negative comments about me posted on it by members of the public," she said.
Boam posted: "She is meant to [be] impartial. I speak for many [councillors] in Leicestershire when I say that is most definitely not the case."
'Significant distress'
Boam denied this breached the code, claiming his comment reflected "a legitimate, shared concern among colleagues".
The panel was told that Boam had not provided any evidence to support his claim about Haslam's impartiality, which she said had caused her "significant distress and reputational damage".
Haslam added the complaint "contributed to [her] decision to resign employment with Leicestershire County Council and seek employment elsewhere".
Alex Oram, an investigator who looked into the complaints, said Boam's omission of Haslam's full response to his question created "a misleading narrative that appeared to present the complainant as unreasonably dismissive" of his concerns.
Oram said Boam had exposed Haslam to public derision, adding that there were legitimate ways for councillors to pursue concerns of political bias but he had not used them.
The investigator said publicly declaring on social media that the monitoring officer was biased represented an "insidious form of public pressure" capable of undermining her professional independence.
The panel, made up of two Reform councillors, two Conservatives and a Liberal Democrat, unanimously upheld Haslam's complaint.
The second complaint against Boam, who represents Whitwick, was made by Ozzy O'Shea, who was the Conservative cabinet member for highways and transport before Reform took control of the council in May 2025.
O'Shea alleged Boam "unfairly and inaccurately" blamed him for the rerouting of bus services down Church Lane in Whitwick in Facebook posts, which included an AI-generated caricature of the Tory councillor.
The meeting was told O'Shea had nothing to do with the decision, which emerged after the election and was a commercial decision by bus firm Arriva.
The panel concluded Boam knew, or should have known, that was the case.
Boam told council officials he did not knowingly publish false information or act in bad faith and said his comments reflected his "genuinely held understanding of political responsibility" for the circumstances leading to the rerouting of the buses.
However, Oram said Boam had gone beyond expressing opinions and had claimed anyone who challenged him was lying.
Boam had tried to misdirect public anger for political advantage, Oram said, and had never accepted what he posted was inaccurate.
The panel dismissed an allegation Boam had harassed O'Shea but ruled he had failed to treat him with respect, and also had brought the council into disrepute.
It also said Boam's failure to cooperate with the investigations and non-attendance at the panels were a breach of the code that had "contributed to a waste of public resources".
The panel unanimously censured Boam and said he should make written apologies to both Haslam and O'Shea within 14 days.
The panel has also recommended that Reform UK council leader Dan Harrison and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray remove Boam from two committees on which he sits until May 2027.
The BBC understands Harrison will consider what steps to take at a Reform Group meeting on Tuesday.

title: Aberfan man found with 'homemade petrol bomb' charged
text:
Man, 38, found with 'homemade petrol bomb' charged
A man alleged to have made a "homemade petrol bomb" has been charged with making an explosive device after suspicious items were found in Aberfan.
South Wales Police said the 38-year-old man, from Aberfan, Merthyr Tydfil, has been charged with making an explosive substance with intent to endanger life or injure property.
The force said the find was made on the Taff Trail in the town on 17 October.
The man appeared before magistrates in Merthyr Tydfil, accused of making a "homemade petrol bomb".
He has been held in custody ahead of his next court appearance on 5 November.

title: Major changes confirmed for Manchester's Bee Network
text:
Major changes confirmed for Bee Network
Greater Manchester's Bee Network has announced a series of changes that will be rolled out across its services.
The measures include free bus travel for 11 to 16-year-olds, rail integration and longer-term plans for daily fare caps.
The changes are expected to begin in the coming months and build on the franchising of the region's bus network, which was brought back under local control by former mayor Andy Burnham.
Here is a look at the plans set to affect passengers over the coming months.
Railway integration
Train stations across the region will begin joining Greater Manchester's Bee Network from December, with work continuing in phases until 2030.
Under plans announced by Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM), the integration aims to improve rail services, reliability, infrastructure and the overall passenger experience.
In December, a new ticketing system covering train, tram and bus travel will be introduced.
It is designed to make it easier for passengers to switch between different forms of public transport across Greater Manchester.
Longer-term plans include an integrated Bee Network payment system with daily and weekly fare caps, which is due to be introduced by the end of 2028.
Mandie Shilton Godwin, councillor for Chorlton Park, said: "I've heard people say they drive into Manchester because they're not confident in using the train."
Free bus travel
Free bus travel for all 11 to 16-year-olds with a bus pass will be rolled out across the region from January 2027. Applications for the passes will open on 8 December 2026.
Up to 200,000 young people are expected to benefit from the scheme.
The move, which is expected to cost up to £20m a year, was one of Mayor Bev Craig's first pledges after she was elected Mayor of Greater Manchester in July.
Councillor Mike McCusker said the plans meant "all school-aged children should be able to travel for free, as they do in London".
Piccadilly underground plans
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has also provided an update on proposals for an underground station at Piccadilly after Mayor Bev Craig said she wanted a decision on the scheme by Christmas.
The plans form part of the £45bn Northern Powerhouse Rail project to improve east-west travel across northern England. Manchester's civic leaders have also set out ambitions for Piccadilly station to become the "King's Cross of the North".
TfGM said it was reviewing the options for Piccadilly station and would present its preferred plan and funding proposals to the government.

title: Government approves Sea Link cable between Kent and Suffolk
text:
Sea Link cable project approved by government
A major new undersea electricity cable linking Kent and Suffolk has been approved by the government.
The Sea Link project will help carry electricity generated by offshore wind farms, interconnectors and nuclear power stations to strengthen the grid.
The 138km cable will run beneath the North Sea between Pegwell Bay in Kent and the Suffolk coast near Aldeburgh and Thorpeness.
Conservationists have raised concerns that the plans could impact wildlife, sensitive coastal habitats and the wider landscape.
National Grid said the scheme would be capable of carrying enough electricity to power the equivalent of two million homes.
The project is designed to transport up to 2GW of low-carbon electricity from where it is generated to homes and businesses elsewhere in the country.
The government said the scheme would help ease pressure on the electricity network and reduce the need to pay generators to switch off power that cannot be carried on the grid.
It said the project would support efforts to improve energy security and cut reliance on fossil fuels.
'Deeply disappointed'
Kent Wildlife Trust said it was "deeply disappointed" by the decision.
"We recognise the need to upgrade the electricity network to support the transition to a low-carbon future," a spokesperson said.
"However, there is a profound irony in destroying or degrading the very natural habitats that help us tackle climate change and protect us from its impacts."
The Planning Inspectorate said it had listened to local views and fully considered the evidence gathered before making its recommendation.
Kent Wildlife Trust said it would "continue to challenge the project and hold those responsible to account".
"We owe it to future generations to ensure that the consequences of this decision are not overlooked."

title: Children's authors to donate to Sally Rooney amid Palestine Action row
text:
Children's laureates to donate to Sally Rooney after UK sales halted over Palestine Action support
The children's laureates for Wales and Ireland are to give their book royalties to Sally Rooney after she halted UK sales because of her support for Palestine Action.
Nicola Davies and her Irish counterpart Chris Haughton made the decision after she stopped supplying her novels to booksellers in the UK because of fears her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence".
The Normal People author said in 2025 she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, despite it being a proscribed a terrorist organisation in the UK.
Davies said: "I don't think I can say I'm standing up for children in Wales without standing up for children in Palestine."
Speaking about the war in Gaza, Wales' children's literature laureate added: "They are children, they are innocent children. Caught up in something absolutely horrible.
She said she's in no way antisemitic but she cannot "stand by and watch this happen."
Davies said she would donate her royalties from The Day War Came to Rooney - the book tells the story of a young girl forced to flee her home after war destroys her town.
The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage.
It came after the group claimed responsibility for breaking into RAF Brize Norton last year where two military aircrafts were damaged.
Palestine Action has engaged in activities that have predominantly targeted arms companies since the start of the war in Gaza.
There are 84 organisations proscribed under the Terrorism Act 2000, including al-Qaeda, a jihadist network founded by the late Osama Bin Laden, as well as neo-Nazi group National Action and private Russian military company the Wagner Group.
"It's a ridiculous situation... the British government have dug themselves into a very big hole," said Davies about the Palestine Action ban.
"It's not about politics, belief systems, it's about humanity."
Davies said Gaza was half the size of the Welsh county of Flintshire and compared the war there between Israel and Hamas to Wales having all of its children located there and being bombed.
"The population of Palestine has a very high proportion of children, they have been disproportionally impacted... there are tens of thousands of amputees under the age of 10."
Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza in response to the Hamas-led attack on the country on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, including at least 21,976 children, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The UN says another 10,000 children in Gaza have sustained life-changing injuries, including permanent disabilities.
Asked if she was concerned about any potential repercussions for donating her royalties to Rooney, Davies said: "Of course - but the repercussions for those in Gaza are horrific."
She said she understood Palestine Action was a proscribed group, but added: "As far as British law is concerned, I'm not doing anything illegal.
"I'm not donating to Palestine Action, I'm donating to Sally Rooney as an act of solidarity."
Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData.
Normal People was published in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones.
Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You.
Ebook editions of her books have been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock.
In a previous statement, regarding her decision to stop supplying UK booksellers as a result of her support for Palestine Action, Rooney said: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
In 2025, Haughton co-wrote a statement in support of ending arms sales to Israel and in support of Palestine Action.
He said he would donate the proceeds from his UK book sales to Rooney and "it's up to her what she does with it".
"As a children's author I cannot work while these atrocities continue," he added, in a statement.
Labour called for a ceasefire for the first time in February 2024 and the UK voted in favour of UN Security Council resolution for a ceasefire in March 2024.
Speaking in July ahead of his appointment as prime minister, Andy Burnham apologised for Labour's initial response to Israel's military action in Gaza, saying the party "didn't get it right".
But, when responding at Prime Minister's Questions on 21 October, he said the proscription of Palestine Action by the previous Labour government "followed a rigorous and evidence-based process that came before this house, endorsed by Parliament".
In a statement, the Home Office said: "The Court of Appeal found that Palestine Action carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence."
"Support for the organisation and financial support to benefit it is against the law."
It added: "The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right."

title: Former homeless woman and her toddler's dinosaur walk for charity
text:
Woman dresses up as dinosaur for 30-day challenge
A woman has walked a mile a day for 30 days in a green inflatable dinosaur suit to give back to the people who supported her when she was homeless.
When 27-year-old Aimee and her seven-month-old son, from Swindon in Wiltshire, became homeless in 2025 she vlogged about their experience on TikTok, gaining "lots of followers" and plenty of support as a result.
Aimee then decided to "give back to the community" by taking on the walking challenge in order to raise £1,600 for Swindon neonatal charity Tiny But Mighty.
"I was super nervous going out in the costume but once I had it on I was absolutely fine," she said. "We had lots of beepers and so many people cheering us on - it was very emotional."
Aimee said she ended up living in temporary accommodation after becoming homeless.
But after vlogging about her day-to-day experiences on TikTok and getting lots of "great support and love from everyone", she was able to "turn a bad situation into a good one".
She said: "If it wasn't for everyone who supported and followed my journey - me and my little boy wouldn't be where we are now.
"[But] so many people reached out and really wanted to help and I said, 'I'll let people help and then, whenever I can, I'll give it back to the people' which is exactly what I did."
At the beginning of October, she began the month-long challenge with her son in his pushchair.
Aimee, who said her dinosaur was called "Rory", was also joined by friend Maria who dressed as a unicorn nicknamed "Sparkles".
Aimee said: "To begin with [my son] was a bit on the unsure side but I popped it on at home and we ran up and down the flat with me wearing it.
"He was giggling his little head off and yesterday he didn't bat an eyelid."
She said some people thought she was "mad" but that passing schoolchildren and families said they loved her "amazing" dinosaur suit.
"We had lots of beepers and a fair few donations," she said.
Chloe Kirwan, who founded the charity, said she had been "blown away" by Aimee's fundraiser.
"We're a tiny, not-for-profit charity in Swindon and when I asked Aimee for a bit of social media support, I wasn't expecting this," she said.
"She's raised awareness of the charity not only in Swindon but across the country.
"We couldn't have done it without her."

title: Basildon council warned about 'unlawfully' withdrawing local plan
text:
Government warned council over 'unlawful' housing vote
The government warned a local authority in Essex hours before a vote that it would consider legal action if it withdrew plans for about 28,000 new homes.
The Conservative-led Basildon Borough Council has been directed by government to submit its local plan by the end of the year.
"Any decision to take steps to withdraw the plan in defiance of the direction would be unlawful," Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook wrote to the council leader.
A council meeting on Monday was delayed by 45 minutes while the motion, which was proposed by the Reform UK Mayor of Basildon Sam Journet, was amended.
'Height of irresponsibility'
Labour's Gavin Callaghan said the handling of the motion was "absolute chaos, a complete mess" and told fellow councillors that voting to withdraw the local plan was "the height of irresponsibility".
Conservative council leader Andy Barnes said: "It is not a motion to withdraw the local plan. We are some way away from that in terms of that being an option."
The original motion called on the council "to withdraw the current local plan from further progression".
It was amended to say it would be withdrawn "if the forthcoming judicial review is not successful, as a last resort".
Journet, who is the Reform group's leader as well as mayor of the district, told councillors that if the judicial review legal action "failed", then the motion stated that "the council should push the nuclear button and withdraw the current local plan from further progression. That is the fall-back position".
Basildon's local plan, which has been worked on for years by different political parties, was put out for a consultation that closed last month.
The council last produced a new local plan, which outlines where housing and development should take place, in 1998.
Barnes told councillors that Essex County Council had found the plan for thousands of new homes to be built up to 2043 to be "unworkable" because of infrastructure.
A county council spokesperson said: "Parts of the draft plan do not yet provide enough evidence that the infrastructure needed to support growth can be delivered.
"In particular, more work is needed to realise the impact of growth on local roads and transport networks. There needs to be a clear and fully costed plan for delivering the required infrastructure."
Basildon Council raised concerns that some local infrastructure projects like improving the A127 had recently been scrapped by the government.
'Need a sound plan'
"We need a sound local plan supported by credible evidence about the infrastructure needed to deliver it. That means taking Essex County Council and the NHS seriously," Barnes told councillors.
The Conservatives currently run Basildon Council as a minority administration, following big gains by Reform in the 2026 local elections. The Conservatives have asked the government to extend its deadline for the submission of a local plan from the end of December to the end of March.
In his letter on Monday, Pennycook said the extension "request will be considered carefully".
Labour and Independent councillors had left the chamber and did not vote on the motion.
Before walking out, Independent Kerry Smith told councillors: "It's there - the threat of legal action. This has been rushed and we've not had the opportunity as opposition members to get legal advice from a barrister."
Conservative, Reform UK and Wickford Independent councillors voted for the motion and for an extraordinary meeting to discuss "the future of the emerging local plan".

title: Abuse claim at former children's home Forhill House investigated
text:
Abuse claim at former children's home investigated
An investigation into historic sexual abuse at a former children's home has been launched by police.
A man has reported physical and sexual abuse by male staff members at Forhill House, on Lea End Lane, Alvechurch, Worcestershire, when he was a teenage boy.
The offences allegedly took place between 1970 and 1985, West Mercia Police said.
The force has asked anyone who lived at, or was involved with, the children's home in the 1970s or early 1980s to come forward.
Det Con Caitlin Allen said: "We commend the victim in coming forward, and we will carry out a full and thorough investigation to establish what happened.
"We are appealing for anyone who may have witnessed the abuse or have information to assist with our enquiries to please get in touch.
"These people are now likely to be in their 50s or 60s. Please be assured that you will be supported."

A man has died after he was hit by a lorry in west Belfast.

title: Jersey gas firm guilty of safety breaches after house explosion
text:
Gas firm guilty of safety breaches after explosion
A gas company has been found guilty of breaching health and safety law after an explosion in a family home in 2024.
Island Energy was charged for failing to ensure the health and safety of people not in its employment, including the public.
The five-day trial at Jersey's Royal Court followed an investigation by the Health and Safety Inspectorate into the explosion at the property on Le Mont Pinel on 26 June 2024.
The case concluded in June 2026 but the media was unable to report any details until the end of a separate trial against the company for another explosion in 2022 which killed 10 people.
The verdict was delivered on the second anniversary of the 2024 explosion.
During the trial, the court heard how residents Lawrence and Cynthia Musikavanhu were sat in their lounge when there was an explosion inside their home at about 22:50.
The prosecution described how Cynthia was sitting on the sofa, using her phone, when "everything went dark".
She did not know what was happening until she saw her husband and the damage to the wall behind him.
Lawrence only remembered being handed a torch by their neighbour then going to check on their children who were asleep in bedrooms upstairs.
The couple and their children were subsequently rescued by emergency services.
Lawrence and Cynthia were admitted to hospital for 11 days with several injuries, with Lawrence requiring ankle surgery. Their children were not injured.
The court heard about the "destruction and damage" caused by the explosion, including pieces of laminate flooring being projected into the ceiling and the front facade of the property collapsing in the early hours.
The couple and their neighbours at Elizabeth Villas were in court for the duration of the trial.
The court heard the explosion was caused by a gas leak from a corroded steel service pipe running inside the property.
The pipe was redundant because the house had its gas meter removed in December 2021 but was still connected to the mains supply, the trial heard.
Prosecutors argued although the corrosion was not the fault of the gas company, and the pipe may have corroded at any time, Island Energy did not take all reasonable steps to disconnect the service pipe by the time of the explosion.
This was despite the company setting itself a target to disconnect service pipes within a year of the meter being removed.
Prosecuting, Advocate Paul Lee said the explosion at Elizabeth Villas "was not a minor incident".
"It could very easily have been fatal to the occupants... sat downstairs as the floor beneath them exploded... from gas in a pipe that should not have been there," he said.
He said Island Energy "stepped over safety... repeatedly over a significant period of time".
The jurats found the company guilty on the basis it "failed to carry out a procedure they themselves had set up".
The court also heard the company identified the failure of redundant service pipes as the highest health and safety risk to the organisation in 2020, 2021 and 2022.
In 2024, it launched a project to identify all properties where a gas meter had been removed but the service pipe had not yet been cut off and it employed contractors from the UK to reduce the backlog, the court heard.
Representing Island Energy, Advocate Mike Preston cited the impacts of the Covid pandemic and the Haut du Mont explosion in 2022 on resourcing level and workload as mitigating factors.
He argued the company was making progress on disconnecting redundant services but the impact of the Haut du Mont explosion "changed everything", affecting the company's ability to deal with operations.
He said the company conceded it was not perfect but maintained it did everything possible to ensure safety, adding the law "does not require safety guaranteed at all costs".

title: 'Surreal' for Dorset's Lloren to hear songs on Celebrity Traitors
text:
'Surreal' for singer to hear songs on Celebrity Traitors
"I love murder mystery and binge watched with my partner and I'm absolutely hooked, I love it."
The latest series of Celebrity Traitors had its fair share of dramatic moments and shock reveals, but its soundtrack has done much to create the moody atmosphere, with its brooding covers and cinematic compositions.
Dorset singer-songwriter Lloren, real name Lauren Bannon, has had three of her songs featured during some of series two's most explosive moments.
"It was only this series that I was like 'Do you know what, I need to watch this' because... I thought this, this sounds like a bit of me," she said in the countdown to the show's explosive finale on Friday evening.
Lloren studied music production at Southampton Solent University, with her influences including Lana del Rey, Taylor Swift, and Sigrid.
She first came to the nation's attention in 2018 when she reached The Voice UK final, and released her debut album It's Always Sunny in LA last year.
The songwriter has had her music featured in shows ranging from Grey's Anatomy and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here, to Love Island.
Lloren's songs on Celebrity Traitors were made with Power-Haus Creative, a company that works with composers and recording artists, often on music for programmes and trailer music.
Remember My Name, also produced and composed by Berlin Aires and Jonathon Deering, featured during the pivotal moment when mathematician and celebrity faithful Hannah Fry was given an ultimatum to join the traitors.
"Sometimes [songs] just come because you're just feeling a certain way," Lloren told BBC Dorset Breakfast show presenter Steve Harris.
"Then other times, like at a songwriting camp that I did, we were given briefs and told 'make things that may be dark or a bit sinister' and so I just channelled my inner diva and thought, you know, 'they'll remember my name'.
"So that specific song was written with the idea in mind. It needed to be moody and that it would probably land on something.
"I didn't know what it would land on, didn't know it would be Traitors, but I knew it's got to be a dark scene, I've got to channel this sort of energy."
Allow Google YouTube content?
The song's use on the programme, which this year had its biggest launch yet, still came as a pleasant surprise.
"They don't warn me beforehand - with a lot of ITV and BBC stuff it's called blanket cover, and quite often you get no indication that you're going to be on it, and I must have a fan in the music supervisor realm."
She added: "I hadn't really watched The Traitors until this series which is crazy to me because I love murder mystery. I'm a big murder mystery fan.
"I just hadn't got round to do it. And I've been hooked.
"Also my friend Sean Stealth, he had one as well and I recognised the track instantly and I was like, 'Oh I think this is my friend', and then me and my partner were watching and I was like, 'Do you know what? I did backing vocals for this'.
"Actually, me and a group of us that were at a songwriting camp in France had done the backing vocals for it so that was quite a surreal moment.
"Anytime I see my song on TV it's surreal and I have to pinch myself."
Lloren's new single Take Me Away is out now, ahead of her new album Love is Alien to Me.

title: Potholed A143 in Suffolk to close overnight for repairs
text:
Potholed road to close at night for temporary fixes
A busy road plagued by potholes will close overnight for repairs.
The A143 between Stanton and Ixworth in Suffolk has had ongoing issues since it was resurfaced in September 2025.
The county council's Suffolk Highways team said it would close the road on Saturday at 20:00 GMT until 05:00 on Sunday "to undertake temporary repairs to the most severely affected sections of the carriageway".
The authority said it would carry out tests "to establish why the road surface continues to deteriorate and to identify the most effective long-term solution".
The road, between Bury St Edmunds and Diss, underwent repairs on a number of occasions during the summer, when hot weather appeared to melt some of the surface.
Suffolk Highways said: "We recognise the continued frustration and inconvenience that the ongoing road surface issues on the A143 at Stanton are causing for motorists, local residents and businesses, and we understand the concerns that have been raised."
Suffolk Highways said details about further works needed on the stretch, "including timings and any traffic management arrangements," would be shared once investigations were completed.
"The findings from these investigations will then be used to develop a future programme of further works," it added.
"Once arrangements and dates have been confirmed, we will ensure local communities, elected members and road users are kept informed."

title: Engineer shortage blamed for new delay for Turkish-built CalMac ferry
text:
Engineer shortage blamed for new delay for Turkish-built CalMac ferry
The handover of a new CalMac ferry being built in Turkey faces another short delay due to a shortage of engineers.
MV Loch Indaal was expected to be ready by the end of October, but ferries agency CMAL said the ship had still not secured final regulator approval.
In a letter to MSPs, it said the handover was now expected by mid-November and would be followed by up to 10 days preparation for the ship's voyage to Scotland.
The ship, which was already 20 months behind schedule, will eventually enter service on CalMac's Islay route.
The delay is the second to be announced in 24 hours, after it was confirmed that handover of another new CalMac ferry MV Loch Rosa would be put back to February to allow for re-designed propellers to be fitted prior to handover.
MV Loch Indaal is the second of four identical ferries ordered from the large Cemre shipyard.
In June CMAL revealed it had paid in-full for all four of the ships, thought to be about £200m in total, despite only one of them, MV Isle of Islay, having been completed.
CMAL said this would help the Turkish firm cope with financial challenges and would secure its legal ownership of the ferries.
Since then the Scottish government has agreed to pay an extra £20m to cover extra project costs.
In its latest update to Holyrood's transport committee, CMAL said inspectors for the UK's Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) had visited the shipyard during October but there were some unresolved issues with the ship.
The letter continued: "The shipyard has experienced challenges securing the availability of specialist engineers from Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs), which will extend delivery beyond the end of October.
"While this is disappointing, the matter is outside the shipyard's control."
CMAL said the MCA inspectors would return in the week beginning 9 November.
Work is also continuing at the Cemre shipyard on MV Lochmor and MV Claymore which are due to serve Little Minch routes from Skye to Harris and North Uist.

title: Jack Grealish donates £10k towards dad-of-three's cancer trial
text:
'Jack Grealish put £10k towards my husband's cancer treatment'
A mother of three said she was left "frozen in shock" after discovering footballer Jack Grealish had donated £10,000 towards her husband's cancer treatment.
Crystal Duffey, from Southport, launched a fundraising appeal after her husband, Leon Skapars, 36, was diagnosed with a rare kidney cancer and told he had between 12 months and three years to live.
She said Grealish's contribution could help fund clinical trials and give Leon more time with their three children.
"We had a cry when we saw it," she said. "£10,000 is a lot of money. But for our family, this could change our future."
Leon was diagnosed with sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma in August 2025, after five months of thinking he had kidney stones.
"Leon had been in and out of hospital since March," said Crystal, 31.
"He had blood in his urine and bad lower back pain, but we had felt reassured.
"We were told it was nothing to worry about, that he was too young to have cancer, that it was kidney stones and it would pass."
Crystal said Leon's diagnosis had come as a complete shock.
"We were completely devastated and blown away when they actually said they'd found an 8cm tumour," she said.
"We were still hoping it was just a benign tumour, but they told us that it was a very rare, aggressive form of cancer."
After immunotherapy in December and having a kidney removed, Leon was told in April that the cancer had spread to both lungs and the lymph nodes in his chest.
He had stage four cancer and was put onto the NHS palliative care pathway.
"Everything just came crashing down on us," Crystal said.
A clinical trial Leon was due to start in Manchester fell through, meaning the family had his tumour tested privately.
He was found to be eligible for a clinical trial at the MD Anderson Cancer Centre in Texas in the United States, where the cost for a place is $200,000 (£179,110).
"We knew it would take a lot to fundraise that sort of money," Crystal said.
"But we wanted to do everything we could to ensure he has access to the best possible care - and we can keep our family together."
Despite some steady progress, Crystal said she was worried they would never get close to their target.
But everything changed on Thursday, when Crystal saw the generous donation from Jack Grealish.
"Someone shared a video from Leon's Instagram page and put it on their story and Jack Grealish, the footballer, saw it and he donated £10,000," Crystal said.
"I was really shocked. I thought it must be a glitch or something.
"When I scrolled down to see the name I couldn't believe what I was seeing."
For the Everton-supporting family, the donation has been "incredibly emotional", Crystal said.
"I froze for a minute in shock," Crystal continued. "I woke Leon up and I really struggled to get the words out.
"We were both dead excited and smiling and then we just hugged and both had a little cry together because it's just so special."
She also said many fans from the Everton community had reached out with messages of support since the donation.
Cyrstal said: "Everyone who has messaged said, 'You're not fighting this alone, we are the people's team and we're all here with you'.
"We have got so much love and support around us.
"Now it feels like the trial is within reach and he is going to have that fair chance and opportunity to be here for the kids. We really needed this."

title: Ministers vow online safety action after 18-year-old sextortion victim took own life
text:
Ministers vow online safety action after teen sextortion victim took own life
The UK government has said it remains committed to making the online world as safe as possible for young people following the death of a teenager who took his own life after he fell victim to an online sextortion scam.
Cai Davies, 18, died in June 2025 after he had sent messages to a woman he believed had a romantic interest in him.
South Wales Central Coroner's Court heard he had been targeted by scammers operating from Africa, who demanded money from him and said intimate photos would be sent to his friends and posted on YouTube.
The coroner addressed a Regulation 28 preventing future deaths report to the UK and Welsh government with her concerns about how Cai had fallen victim to the scam.
Assistant coroner Rachel Knight recorded a conclusion of suicide after Davies, from Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, died.
Knight said it was "more likely than not" that personal stresses in his life together with falling victim to the sextortion scam "more than minimally contributed" to his death.
She wrote of the scammers: "Conversation quickly turned sexual and she asked him for intimate images, which were then used to blackmail him for money by threatening to send the images to his family and friends, and to upload them to a YouTube channel.
"The images were indeed sent to at least one of Cai's Facebook friends by the scammer.
"Cai was bombarded with video calls and messages via Facebook Messenger and WhatsApp over a very short period of time making demands for money."
'Profoundly troubling'
Online Safety Minister Ian Murray set out several recent measures the UK government had taken to protect children and young people.
These included criminalising the taking of intimate images without consent, a requirement for online platforms to remove those images, and the introduction of the Online Safety Act.
Murray wrote: "The circumstances surrounding Cai's death are profoundly troubling and I am grateful to you for drawing these matters to my attention.
"As the minister responsible, the government and I are fully committed to making the online world as safe as it can be for everyone, especially children and young people."
The Welsh government said issues around telecommunications and internet services were reserved to Westminster but Senedd ministers were committed to reducing online harm in Wales.
Education Minister Anna Brychan and Culture Minister Heledd Fychan said: "The Welsh government will continue to engage with the UK government and Ofcom on current and emerging online safety risks and their implications for devolved responsibilities.
"We are considering the implications for devolved responsibilities of legislative proposals by the UK government relating to children and young people's access to social media and certain high-risk online features."
They added the Welsh government would "continue to consider emerging evidence, including about the potential effects of online safety measures on suicide prevention and self harm and the risks of unintended consequences".
Brychan and Fychan said the Welsh government would be reviewing existing guidance as well as developing fresh online safety guidance for schools and a new national online safety programme.
"These actions will form part of the Welsh government's wider commitment to strengthening digital resilience, preventing harm and helping people affected by online exploitation to access appropriate support.
"We will continue to review our approach as the evidence and nature of online risks develop," they added.

title: Video describing attack not true, says Guildford murder accused
text:
Video describing murder not true, says accused
A teenager made a video "in desperation" describing the moment a 15-year-old boy was stabbed to try to "placate" his "bully boy" co-defendant, a court has heard.
Luis Guembes died after he was stabbed in the head, shoulder and lower back in Guildford's Stoke Park in January.
The murder trial of two teenage boys at Guildford Crown Court has previously heard they deny attacking Guembes in a row over money.
One defendant testified on Friday that some details heard in the video, such as an apparent admission to stabbing Guembes, were not true.
The teenager told the court he thought there would be "repercussions" if he did not make the video and the other defendant would be angry.
He said part of the video, which was made shortly after Guembes was attacked, were false, including the line: "I stabbed him, bro".
The court heard the teenager thought he had deleted the Snapchat video but it had actually only moved to another part of the app.
Roderick Johnson KC, for the defendant, asked him what the point was of making the video if the co-defendant did not receive it.
The teenager replied: "I got home and realised it wasn't in any way true and [the other defendant] wouldn't believe it, so I deleted it."
The teenagers, aged 15 and 16 at the time but now both 16, cannot be named because of their age.
'Going to chef him'
Earlier the court heard the other defendant got "extremely frustrated" as he tried to get the contact details for Guembes from a friend to receive compensation for breaking his phone.
The teenager said he felt "frightened" when the other defendant said the friend, who seemed not to be co-operating, was "wet" and he was "going to chef him".
He told the court he understood the term "chef" to mean slash.
"I thought if I didn't co-operate the same might apply to me", he said.
The teenager told the court he attempted to contact Guembes himself to "speed things up" because he was waiting to go into town.
Cross-examining the teenager, Tim Forte KC, for the other defendant, argued the threat to the friend was untrue, and questioned why he hadn't raised it earlier.
The barrister asked if it was "something you made up now to explain your defence".
The teenager replied: "That's incorrect".
Earlier the teenager told the court that shortly after the incident he and the other defendant were communicating via the Discord app.
"He seemed frustrated, almost angry with me, that I hadn't done what he wanted me to and I was worried what had happened to Guembes," he said.
He denies stabbing Guembes or intending to hurt him.
The defence case for the other defendant is expected to begin when the trial continues on Monday.

title: City of London leader named 'most influential black Briton'
text:
City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
Ian Thomas, chief executive of the City of London Corporation, has been named the UK's most influential Black Briton in this year's Black Powerlist awards.
The 57-year old is the first Black person to oversee the Square Mile's governing body in its more than 900-year history.
The City of London Corporation is an administrative body with responsibility for London's central financial district, headed by its own Lord Mayor.
Thomas tops the 2027 Black Powerlist, which recognises the most powerful people of African and Caribbean heritage in the UK.
The award body said he was "a respected public-service leader with over 30 years' experience in local government".
Other influential names in this year's top ten include entrepreneurs Emma Grede and Steven Bartlett, as well as actor and filmmaker Sir Idris Elba.
Comedian Sir Lenny Henry has also been recognised, with a Lifetime Achievement award, for co-founding Comic Relief, which has raised over £1.6bn since 1985.
Now in its 21st year, the Black Powerlist celebrates people who have broken through barriers to reach leadership roles, thereby inspiring future generations.
"It exists to show young people of African and Caribbean heritage what is possible, in fields they might never have considered," said Michael Eboda, the list's publisher.
Thomas said he secured the role at the head of the City of London Corporation in 2022 only following seven interviews and an election.
'When I started my journey in public service, I never, ever thought, [not] in a million years, that I'd be recognised in this way," he told the BBC.
'Discipline and respect'
As chief executive, he oversees around 5,000 staff with responsibilities including the City of London Police, 11,000 acres of open spaces such as Epping Forest and Hampstead Heath, and advocacy for the UK's financial and professional services sector.
Thomas was born in Sheffield to parents who made the city their home after leaving Jamaica as part of the Windrush generation.
"They worked incredibly hard and instilled that sense of discipline and respect, and that's the core of how I do business," he said of his upbringing.
Growing up, Thomas aspired to be a footballer and took part in trials alongside Alan Shearer.
Reflecting on his own change of direction, Thomas joked it was about "following dreams and if they don't come true… there's always something else".
Before joining the City of London Corporation, Thomas served as chief executive of the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames where he oversaw public services and a £1.2bn regeneration programme.
He was appointed a CBE in the 2019 New Year Honours in the wake of the Rotherham Abuse scandal for transforming children's services during his time as strategic director for children and young people at Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council.
Thomas replaces last year's incumbent, Afua Kyei, the Bank of England's chief financial officer and executive director, and is joined on this year's list by Comfort Ero, the President and chief executive of the International Crisis Group, who takes second place.

title: Party Rock Anthem singer Lauren Bennett struggled with mental health, inquest finds
text:
Party Rock Anthem singer struggled with mental health before death
A British singer who was a member of the girl group G.R.L took her own life, an inquest has found.
Lauren Bennett, 36, who also featured on LMFAO's 2011 hit Party Rock Anthem, was found dead in Kent on 29 May.
In a statement read out by an assistant coroner on Friday, her husband Kenny Wormald said she had been struggling with severe mental health issues before her death.
The court heard she told him she was going out for a walk on the morning of her death while he remained in bed half asleep.
When she did not return for a few hours and did not answer calls or texts from him and multiple other family members, Wormald and her father went looking for her.
- If you have been affected by this story, you can find organisations which offer help and information at the BBC Action Line
He went to a rural location using Find My iPhone for Bennett's device where he found her body.
The professional dancer said the pair talked about everything and there was no indication she was going to end her life.
Her father, Richard Bennett, said his daughter had lived an "amazing life" in a statement read out by assistant coroner Jyoti Gill.
He said she signed a record deal at just 17 and moved to the US on her own.
Pages of farewell notes were later found at her home, Kent and Medway Coroners' Court heard.
Bennett had previously been diagnosed with Fragile X syndrome, a genetic disorder that can cause anxiety, mood instability and depression, it was also told.
In the January before her death, the musician did not sleep for a number of days and was admitted to hospital under a mental health section.
She had experienced "substantial psychological suffering" since this point, Gill noted.
Bennett was in the care of "special mental health services" at the time of her death.
She had reacted poorly to medication and did not think she was going to get better, the court was told.
No alcohol or illicit drugs were found in Bennett's system when she died.
Bennett's former musical group G.R.L. shared the news of her death on its Instagram account in July.
"Our hearts are broken, and we cannot begin to express how much she meant to us," they said.
Party Rock Anthem has been named the fifth most successful song of all time by Billboard after spending six weeks as the number one song on its Hot 100 in 2011.
Bennett also featured alongside LMFAO members in the song's music video, which has more than 2.5bn views on YouTube.
Aria Crescendo, who Bennett performed with in the band Paradiso Girls prior to G.R.L., told the BBC: "She was super talented, super beautiful and super funny.
"We're so in shock that this happened, honestly."

title: Pulp's star plaque honours legendary Sheffield band
text:
Pulp's star plaque honours legendary city band
Sheffield indie-rockers Pulp have been officially honoured as legends of their home city with the unveiling of a walk of fame star plaque outside the town hall.
Past and present members of the band, including singer Jarvis Cocker, gathered for the celebration and held a pop-up event at a nearby pub.
They join Gordon Banks, Dame Jessica Ennis, Michael Palin and others in receiving the accolade, which was unveiled by the band and the Lord Mayor of Sheffield.
Speaking to a crowd watching the ceremony, Cocker said: "It's nice to get a legend star and I'll walk past it at some point, I'm sure, but the thing that's great about being in a band is inventing things and making up stuff for yourself."
He added: "Pulp is a group that started when I was at school in 1978. There was no musical accomplishment required.
"It was just, have you got some time on Friday evening, and would you come to my mother's house while she's at the pub so we can make some noise?
"People came and did that, and over the years the noise became more palatable."
Dozens of fans cheered as Cocker and Lord Mayor Andrew Sangar pulled back a red cloth to reveal the plaque.
Fran Belbin, leader of Sheffield Council, said: "What I always think about Pulp, though, is they did 15 years of relative obscurity and they really persevered and they really stuck at it.
"I think that's a really important message as well to all those people who are making music in their bedrooms or creating art in other ways: stick at it, keep going - and I feel that's a really strong message."
Pulp achieved critical success in the mid-1990s with the release of their album Different Class and their hit single Common People, which a teenage band performed for gathering fans shortly before the unveiling ceremony in Sheffield.
Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Pulp guitarist Mark Webber described it as "a very strange and unexpected day".
"I guess no one would have ever thought we would be embalmed on the pavement outside of the town hall," he said.
To further celebrate the band's induction onto the walk of fame, the band hosted a pop-up event at the Hallamshire Hotel.
Drummer Nick Banks and keyboardist Candida Doyle sat for a meet-and-greet with fans, some of whom had queued throughout the morning to catch a word with the musicians.
One fan, Eleanor, said she had travelled from Sweden for the event.
She said: "I've been a fan for many years. The music, I love the lyrics. It speaks to me in a sense. I try to see them as often as I can live."
When asked what she talked about with the band, she said: "I don't remember. I was just blacked out. I was like, hello!"
Molly, from Northumberland, said she had queued for two hours to get to speak to the band.
"I love them so much and I didn't know that I'd ever see them again," she said.
"When they reformed back in 2023, my lovely husband said I could go and see them as much as possible, so I've taken him at his word and I felt I needed to be here.
"I didn't know what to say to them, just apart from thank you for being in my life for the past 30 years and just to say how much joy they've brought."
Snaking down the pavement outside the pub were dozens of people waiting to meet Banks and Doyle.
The interior of the pub itself was decked-out with cardboard cut-outs and merchandise.
The pub also planned to host a Pulp-themed quiz, raffle, a fancy-dress competition and karaoke throughout the day.

title: Autism Essex teen was at risk before death, says report
text:
Failures in teen's care before death, says report
An autistic 14-year-old boy was at "significant risk" with a history of self-harm when he was found dead in his bedroom at home, a report said.
Scotty Henniker from Essex made several suicide attempts before he died on 24 September 2023.
In a new report, a coroner said his previous attempts were not "appropriately recorded" or shared among professionals.
Essex County Council and the NHS, which both had responsibility for his care, say they are making improvements since Scotty's death.
"The bulk of the responsibility for Scotty's complex needs was falling [to] one parent alone when it was known and understood that no single person could meet these needs," said Sonia Hayes, the area coroner for Essex.
Scotty, who also had ADHD, relied on an educational outreach team for extra support.
However, the support was not provided during the summer holidays - despite it being available - because his social care team failed to make a funding application, the report said.
In the final months of his life, the teenager also did not have any transport to take him to education support in term time, it added.
'Complex child'
An inquest concluded on 4 March and a prevention of future deaths report, written by Hayes, was published recently.
She said not being able to attend "a place that he felt safe" caused him a great level of distress.
She said Scotty was "the most complex child" the educational outreach team had worked with.
Hayes also noted that in May 2023, educational outreach raised concerns with social care at Essex County Council that Scotty had hurt animals and may "do something extreme to win back his family member's affection".
A request was made for a psychiatry review in June 2023 but was declined, and mental health services were reassured that Scotty was not depressed, the report added.
His family also raised concerns he was not being seen by the correct professionals and "wanted him to have a review".
"This did not happen," Hayes said.
The coroner gave a narrative conclusion to the inquest, which is a factual statement to explain the broader circumstances surrounding the person's death.
'Committed'
A spokesperson for Essex County Council said it had made a "number of improvements to strengthen our safeguarding practices".
"We offer our sincere condolences to the family of Scotty Henniker during this very difficult time for them," they said.
The North East London NHS Foundation Trust, which runs mental health services, said work was "ongoing" following Scotty's death.
"This was a devastating loss, and our thoughts remain with all those who loved and knew him," they said.
"We are committed to taking action and continuing to make improvements to our services to protect our service users."

title: Emmerdale actor remembers 'wonderful' mentor Sir Patrick Stewart
text:
'Kind and wonderful Sir Patrick was my mentor'
Former Emmerdale actor Gemma Oaten has paid tribute to her "mentor" Sir Patrick Stewart, describing him as a "kind and wonderful man".
Mirfield-born Sir Patrick died on Wednesday aged 86 at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
Hull-born Oaten, who appeared in the British soap as Rachel Breckle between 2011 and 2015, wrote to the Star Trek star while at drama school in 2008 and the pair met on numerous occasions over the years, including backstage chats during Sir Patrick's many theatre performances.
An emotional Oaten told BBC Radio Humberside she was "trying to process" his death.
"It's really hard because he was such a massive part of my life," she said.
She added that their friendship "really got me through so much".
"He became a mentor for me, he gave me advice.
"He was always there for me and he was always willing to give and I just know him as Patrick the kind and wonderful man."
Yorkshire-born Sir Patrick was a renowned classical theatre actor as well as finding international fame as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films.
He began his career in 1959 when he joined the repertory company at the Lincoln Theatre Royal, making his stage debut in Treasure Island.
The theatre's current stage manager, Ian Marston, said it would have provided a "thorough training".
"As well as performing he also worked backstage," he said.
"The repertory company at the time was really very well thought of.
"Lots of household names began here. We were quite important on the rep scene."
Meanwhile, Grimsby singer Michael Dore, who said he performed the music of British composer Nigel Hess with Sir Patrick a number of times, described him as a "lovely man".
"I was in awe," he said.
"I've been able to work with some great people, but he's a hero. It was very special."
In Hull, visitors to The Deep will be familiar with Sir Patrick's voice.
The aquarium has used him as its narrator since it opened in 2002.
Visitor Debbie Gillett-Ware said: "As you enter here, you feel really calm because you can actually feel his voice.
"He's such a big actor as well, but you can hear his voice right here in Hull."

title: Man from USA jailed for stalking UK victim for 10 years
text:
US man jailed after stalking victim for 10 years
A man who travelled from the USA to meet a UK man he had been stalking for 10 years has been jailed after being arrested at Gatwick Airport.
Robert Beckman, who lives in Ann Arbor, Michigan, has been jailed for a year and nine months after admitting causing his victim serious distress by sending him messages online and by post, as well as commenting on social media posts.
The 31-year-old, who was arrested at Gatwick Airport by Sussex Police on 25 August after flying from Boston with the intention of meeting the victim, pleaded guilty at a hearing last month.
At Lewes Crown Court on Thursday, Beckman was also handed a 10-year restraining order and ordered not to enter the UK.
According to Sussex Police, the 31-year-old had previously been given a police caution by the Metropolitan Police for harassing the same man in October 2021.
Despite returning to the USA and being told not to contact the victim, Beckman persisted with his communications, the force said.
Det Sgt James Gwynne said: "Over the course of 10 years, Beckman's conduct affected the victim's day-to day life, causing him to relocate and change his daily behaviours, impacting both his work and family life.
"This pattern of unwanted behaviour demonstrated a complete disregard for the victim, who we thank for coming forward and supporting this investigation."

title: 'One disaster after another' - Renfrew locals frustrated by bridge closure
text:
'One disaster after another' - Renfrew locals frustrated by bridge closure
People in Renfrew say they have been hit with "one disaster after another" after recent storms resulted in the closure of the bridge linking the town to Yoker and Clydebank.
Business owners told the BBC they fear the Renfrew Bridge closure - which is to last for months - will result in a big drop in trade, just days after shops and restaurants were flooded.
Other local residents said it will now take them much longer to visit sick family members in the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital.
Renfrewshire Council said earlier this week that the electrical systems that operate the bridge, which opened in May last year, had suffered serious water damage during the storms.
The bridge closed to road traffic from Wednesday night onwards.
The local authority was also criticised for not raising flood barriers last weekend. Businesses in the area were then flooded after the water levels from the River Clyde proved much higher than expected.
'I will lose customers'
Among those affected was Tarun Wadhwa, who runs the Green Gates Indian Restaurant.
His business was already damaged by the storms, and now he fears the bridge being closed will see a big drop in trade.
"This is one disaster after another for me," he said.
"Most of my customers are coming from the other side of the river and you're going from a five-minute drive to get here to a 20-minute drive. I will lose customers."
He added Renfrewshire Council had not yet spoken to him about the damage from last weekend.
"We feel abandoned. It would be good if someone wanted to know if we were doing alright," he said.
Near to the Green Gates is the Foundry Gym, which has been closed all week because of the storm damage.
While it is scheduled to open again on Monday, owner Sukhjinder Singh has already had gym-goers get in touch to say they will now have to go elsewhere due to the bridge closure.
He said: "We did not have a lot of members leave until Thursday, with the bridge being closed. The gym is no use to them now as it will take too long for them to get over the bridge to come here.
"It's just another blow, on top of the cost of getting everything back to normal - everything here was brand new."
He added that that the council have not visited his premises since the storms.
"We were under the assumption that we wouldn't get flooded, even near the Clyde. How has all of this happened?"
The bridge opened last year with the aim of linking Renfrew with Yoker and Clydebank on the north bank.
The leader of Renfrewshire Council, Iain Nicolson, said at the time that the bridge, part of an overall £117m regeneration project, would "bring the communities together."
Locals told BBC Scotland News the bridge had done that, and been helpful for reaching the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital.
However they now face the prospect of longer journeys for some time, with Renfrewshire Council saying the bridge will be closed for "a number of months."
Journey to hospital 'doubled'
John McGowan uses the bridge to travel into Renfrew and get to the QEUH, where his son is a patient.
"With the bridge, that was 15 or 20 minutes to get there," he said.
"This will now double the time - it would be up to 40 minutes or so every day. The bridge opening had made a great difference.
"You would think there would be things in place to make sure there is a contingency plan for something like this happening."
Renfrewshire Council's head of climate, public protection and roads, Gerard Hannah, said the operating room on the Renfrew side of the bridge - which manages the opening and closing of the bridge - had suffered significant damage last weekend.
The local authority said it was legally obligated to keep the Clyde open to river traffic, meaning the swing bridge must remain in an open position.
The 184m (604ft) bridge opened in May last year.
It is the first road crossing on the river capable of opening to allow large ships to pass and as well as a two-lane crossing for drivers, it offers access to cyclists and pedestrians.
The west of Scotland was struck hard last weekend by Storm Boleo.
Although an amber weather warning was issued for last Saturday, Renfrewshire Council said its data suggested the predicted tide levels would not meet the threshold needed to use the flood barriers - part of £10m worth of flood defences installed in 2016.
Singh and other local businesses have since contacted the council to formally complain about how the local authority handled the situation.
The letter, seen by BBC Scotland, says "adequate precautionary action" was not taken ahead of Storm Boleo.
The tidal surge on Saturday night saw the Clyde's water levels reach 6.7m at Renfrew.
The council previously said it was "very sorry for the inconvenience" caused by the bridge closure.

title: Court backs Scottish government appeal over Sturgeon inquiry evidence
text:
Court backs Scottish government appeal over Sturgeon inquiry evidence
A court has upheld a Scottish government appeal in a row over documents related to an inquiry into Nicola Sturgeon's handling of the Alex Salmond affair.
The Scottish Information Commissioner had ordered ministers to publish papers from the Hamilton Inquiry – the investigation into whether then first minister Sturgeon had misled MSPs over the probe into claims against her predecessor.
The Scottish government insisted that doing so would breach court orders guaranteeing the anonymity of women who lodged complaints against Salmond.
The Court of Session backed the ministers' appeal, ruling Information Commissioner David Hamilton had erred in law.
Salmond was initially investigated by the Scottish government in 2018, after complaints were made about his conduct.
But he successfully took ministers to court, arguing the process was "tainted by apparent bias" and unlawful.
Following a separate criminal investigation he was cleared of sexual assault charges at the High Court in 2020, four years before his death.
This was followed by a Holyrood inquiry into the botched government probe, and Sturgeon referred herself for investigation by James Hamilton KC - no relation to David - who ultimately cleared her of breaching the ministerial code.
A freedom of information (FOI) request was later made to the Scottish government for all evidence used in Hamilton's investigation, and there have been a series of legal disputes about whether this information can be published.
Following Salmond's acquittal of criminal charges, judge Lady Dorrian had put contempt of court orders in place which prohibited people from naming the women who had complained about him.
That ban also prevented anyone from disclosing single pieces of information that could be used together to work out the identities of the women, in so-called "jigsaw identification".
David Hamilton had ordered ministers to hand over documents, but saw this challenged in court by the Scottish government.
They asked judges Lord Pentland, Lord Malcolm and Lady Wise to overturn parts of the commissioner's decision on the grounds that disclosing the information would place the women at risk of identification.
In a written judgement, Lord Pentland upheld the government's case, ruling the release of documents could "permit assumptions to be made" about the identities of the complainers.
'Murray precedent'
Lord Pentland cited a case involving the political blogger Craig Murray, who was jailed for eight months after being found guilty of contempt of court relating to a series of articles he published online in the wake of Salmond's trial.
Prosecutors raised concerns the complainers could be identified by his writing.
Lord Pentland concluded that by applying the Murray precedent, the commissioner had no basis to order the disclosure.
Lord Pentland wrote: "The issue of jigsaw identification was clearly in play before the commissioner.
"It would be unrealistic and contrary to principle for this court not to apply the law as stated in that case."
He added: "It would be unconscionable for this court to ignore what was authoritatively stated in that case about the meaning and purpose of the various orders pronounced in the civil and criminal proceedings arising out of the investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct by Salmond."
Responding, the Information Commissioner's Office said it welcomed the clarity offered by the court ruling.
It said Hamilton would "reflect fully on the implications" of it before reassessing the original freedom of information cases.
A Scottish government spokesperson said: "The Scottish government welcomes the decision of the Court and will continue to uphold the court orders to protect the identities of women in cases of alleged sexual crimes."

title: Carmarthenshire Rugby Club at risk of closure after 52 years
text:
'Bleak' future for rugby club as player numbers fall
A rugby club is struggling to survive after 52 years due to a lack of players.
Llanybydder Rugby Club in Carmarthenshire has been struggling to find enough players to field a team each week, with player Wyn Davies, 30, saying it was "quite difficult to take in".
Club manager Nia Evans has urged the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) to give more support to grassroots clubs because "that's where all the rugby players come from".
"It's heartbreaking," she added.
The WRU said they "employ a network of club development officers who reach out to every club... offering help and support" including, recently, to Llanybydder.
Evans said people at the club were "devastated" to find itself with just one team remaining and an uncertain future, with Covid one of the issues impacting the club.
"We've seen lots of players not come back to play rugby, or move to clubs that are bigger [and] play in higher divisions," she said.
"On a weekly basis, it's probably about 12 that I'm able to get together - our faithful players."
Davies is in his 12th season with the club, and said training numbers have shrunk substantially since he joined.
Teammate Dan Jones, 33, described the situation as "heartbreaking".
"Unfortunately, we're at the brunt of it now, because we have hardly any players at all. Other clubs are struggling too.
"They're asking us for players, but we haven't got our own players," he said.
Cai Hamer, 24, another player, said the club was now on a "lifeline".
"It's very bleak. We have hardly played any games this season so far."
"You come across these bigger teams and they've got subs, and subs, and subs - and we're all knackered."
At the club's latest training session, 17 players were present, thanks to an appeal on social media.
Three new members turned up - but getting those players to be available on weekends for matches - was a bigger challenge.
Chairman Michael Wilson said diminished numbers can also lead to injury.
"We'll phone the opposition and they'll say 'come down, we'll give you two players,'" he said.
"On several occasions, we've gone and those two extra players aren't there - so we're starting a game with two less players than the opposition.
"We compete for an hour, and then our boys start getting tired. And then, lo and behold, two or three will get injured because they're trying to do too much.
"And then, the next week we've got a worse problem."
Evans has called on the WRU to do more for grassroots clubs, saying they represent the future of the national team.
"It's important because that's where all the rugby players come from," she said.
"Although they say that they support us, we're not their priority at all."
"I understand the WRU are not there to find us players - that is our responsibility as clubs. But to guide us and advise us and support us - that is what we're asking for."
Evans claims clubs are more likely to be penalised than supported, saying there had been "many walkovers" in cup games because the club could not field a team, leading to a £250 fine.
"I do understand the WRU are in financial difficulty themselves, but I don't think it's fair to put that back on grassroot clubs," she said.
"A season or so ago, we couldn't fulfil one fixture out of all the games, and we lost our grant of £4,000. That's quite a lot of money that could help further develop our team."
In a statement, the WRU said: "We employ a network of club development officers across Wales who reach out to every club during the course of a season offering help and support.
"This particular club has been offered this help on two recent occasions.
"Fines for clubs who do not complete fixtures are used as a last resort when attempts to rearrange fixtures have failed, as incentive for clubs to fulfill them. They are welcomed by the majority of clubs throughout the amateur game for this reason."
Llanybydder Rugby Club is now appealing for ideas and support from the public, in an effort to save their historic club.
"The response we've had from our social media [post] is overwhelming to be honest," said Evans. "We've had lots of enquiries from players.
"Hopefully this is us turning the corner and getting the momentum to build the rugby club back up again."

title: Galway: County Down man among those jailed for planned mosque attack
text:
County Down man among three jailed for planning mosque attack
A County Down man is among three men who have been jailed for attempting to engage in a terrorist activity, specifically damaging a mosque in Galway.
Garrett Pollock (36) of Kilhorne Greene in Annalong was sentenced to 10 and a half years with the last year suspended.
Darren Gorman (34) of O'Moore Place in Portlaoise was sentenced to eight years with the last year suspended and Karolis Peckauskas (39) of Newfoundwell Road in Drogheda was sentenced to eight years in prison with the last year suspended.
They had made advanced plans to blow up the Maryam Mosque on the Monivea Road between 4 and 5 November 2025 when they were arrested, the Special Criminal Court in Dublin heard.
Pollock also pleaded guilty to possessing an explosive substance which was found in four glass jars hidden in a drawer in his van on 4 November.
On Friday, Ms Justice Caroline Biggs said that modern Ireland is a multicultural and diverse country and that the actions of this group bring shame on the country.
It was, Biggs said, attempted arson with a terrorising message to be spread worldwide.
She added that it was clear that this was intended to be the first of many attacks.
The men were part of the self-styled Irish Defence Army, which Det Insp Alan McDevitt described as a violent right-wing extremist group.
He had previously told the court the group was a splinter of the online Irish Citizens Army which communicated on the messaging app Signal, RTÉ has reported.
McDevitt said gardaí (Irish police) didn't know when the attack was due to take place but the men had plans to use improvised incendiary devices such as pipe bombs and "Molotov cocktails".
Objects seized by Gardaí included cable ties, hatchets, knives, and masks.
Five litres of chemicals were also seized, and were found to be usable in pipe bombs.
They also found sunglasses, balaclavas, can of sealing putty and an Irish flag.
The video claiming responsibility
The men had filmed a video on Pollock's phone in Gorman's kitchen in Portlaoise claiming responsibility for the attack.
The footage showed four masked men in tactical gear standing in front of the Irish flag.
In the video, they said they would like "to take responsibility for destruction of first mosque introduced into our great country in Galway".
The court has also received a written letter from Pollock expressing his remorse and shame for his actions.
It heard that Pollock was "radicalised" online after he started misusing alcohol and cocaine.
Pollock, a gym instructor, consumed radicalised content about purported threats that immigrants posed to the community which was described as "emotive, ill-informed and AI-generated".
The court had heard that after making contact with a group and being invited into smaller groups, he found a sense of belonging and became radicalised very quickly and wanted to show them he was committed.
A doctor who assessed Pollock had said his actions were taken in the context of emotional dysfunction, low self-esteem and isolation.
Gorman's defence counsel had previously told the court that his psychological report highlights extremes of submissiveness and vulnerability, that he was a drug user and addict and also had certain mental health issues.
They had added that he had no history of violence, hatred or terrorism.

title: Building set to become Islamic centre in Wokingham broken into
text:
Building set to become Islamic centre broken into
Break-ins at a vacant cinema that is set to become an Islamic centre are being investigated by police.
The former Ritz Cinema in Easthampstead Road, Wokingham, has been unoccupied for several years but the Wokingham Islamic Centre bought it in the summer.
It was broken into on Monday and Tuesday and graffiti, including a spray painted "leave now", and other offensive messages were daubed onto walls there.
The Islamic centre recently acquired the building after its previous owner, Montreaux Homes, went into liquidation. It had previously secured planning permission to use the site for flats but that has since expired.
Anees Ahmad, one of the centre's trustees, said: "We are part of Wokingham; we are one community.
"One thing I can assure you of is that since we acquired the building, all the neighbours have been very supportive of us."
He said the group wants it to become a "centre for all".
Wokingham's MP Clive Jones said the offenders must not return to cause more damage to the building.
"We don't want that sort of thing here in Wokingham," he said. "That's not the town that Wokingham is. We are pleased to have this Islamic Centre here. The vast majority of people here in Wokingham welcome it.
"Whoever's doing it, they just need to stop. They will get caught if they come back and try to do it again. That won't be good for them."
Thames Valley Police said initially that it was investigating the break-ins as a hate crime but revised that on Thursday.
Sgt Kyle Seaton, from the Wokingham South Neighbourhood Policing Team, said "the offences appear more consistent with anti-social behaviour than motivated by racial or religious hostility."
Anyone who can assist the investigation is asked to contact Thames Valley Police quoting reference 43260561729.
