title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
text:
G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.
Two officials confirmed to BBC the cancellation of the "family photo" scheduled for Friday, which usually include representatives from all nations attending.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told his Russian counterpart at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Speaking with G20 foreign ministers on Friday, Miliband said that member countries must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine".
"Russia's war continues to cause colossal global harm - including the deaths of thousands of innocent civilians and disruption that hits energy and supplies and worsens food insecurity," he said.
"This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war."
Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.
One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.
In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

title: Treasury accepts role in staff member's death after inquest
text:
Treasury accepts role in staff member's death
The Treasury has accepted it contributed to the death of a personal assistant and said "immediate steps" have been taken to tackle outstanding risks.
Chloe Moffat, 26, took her own life in May 2025, the day after managers told her of allegations that she had shared sensitive confidential information, which she denied.
A coroner found a practice within HM Treasury of "informal fact-finding" meetings with employees accused of misconduct had no basis in the ministry's policy and posed a risk of future death.
Responding, the Treasury and the Cabinet Office wrote that they "accept the concerns identified" and "take them extremely seriously".
The Cabinet Office said it would also undertake a wider review of workplace conflict and resolution across Whitehall within a year.
At Moffat's inquest in August, the Treasury was found to have "materially contributed" to her death by not telling her that the likely penalty if allegations against her were proven would be a written warning and not dismissal.
In a response to the coroner's report, the Treasury "accepted the findings in the report in full" and said it had taken immediate action to mitigate the concerns raised.
- If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line
Strengthened "wellbeing safeguards" had been introduced and the use of informal fact-finding meetings had been stopped while a full policy review was conducted, the department said.
Employees facing misconduct allegations would be informed of the possible outcomes before being asked to respond and a suicide prevention framework was being developed, it added.
"HM Treasury has considered these concerns carefully and has taken immediate steps to mitigate the identified risks," according to the department's response.
"While this work introduces some enhancements, much of it is intended to strengthen, clarify and build on the procedures and support already in place."
A Treasury spokesperson added: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague.
"An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout."

title: Parents seek 'accountability' after baby's Leeds hospital death
text:
Parents seek 'accountability' after baby's death
The parents of a five-month-old girl whose death from meningitis was contributed to by hospital staff's neglect have said they want to see "real accountability".
Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary (LGI) in November 2023, days after she was taken into the emergency department with a high temperature and vomiting.
Following an inquest at Wakefield Coroner's Court, a jury concluded Esta "died of natural causes contributed to by neglect" and different care would probably have "saved or prolonged her life".
Her parents, Lynsey Carr and Leon High, have now called for changes to be made and for the General Medical Council to carry out a full investigation.
Esta's inquest heard she was a "happy, healthy, smiling girl" before she became ill on 31 October 2023.
Her parents took her to LGI as she was suffering from a high temperature and vomiting, and she later tested positive for Covid-19.
Her cause of death was given as Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis.
Jurors concluded that opportunities "to save or prolong her life" had been missed, as doctors continued to focus on a Covid diagnosis after Esta tested positive.
Her parents claimed doctors missed vital chances to test for a bacterial infection and start antibiotic treatment, with her mother saying their concerns were ignored until it was too late.
Carr said the couple had refused advice to take Esta home as her conditioned worsened with a fever and persistent vomiting.
By late afternoon on 2 November, Esta could not be roused and the inquest jury heard how scans and other tests showed evidence of meningoencephalitis and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Esta was taken to intensive care, where she died on 6 November.
The couple hopes by raising awareness of Esta's case, parents' concerns would be "taken more seriously".
"We want to give parents the confidence and autonomy to question doctors and nurses if they are not confident with what they're saying," said Carr.
"Nobody knows your child like you. We need to make sure this stops happening."
Carr urged hospital staff to take parents' concerns seriously and warned against dismissing their worries as anxiety.
"If we had been listened to, Esta would still be alive," said Carr.
High said there had been a "catalogue of errors" during Esta's time in hospital, and the couple now wanted to see "real accountability".
He is calling on the General Medical Council (GMC) to carry out an investigation into "the people who were supposed to be caring for Esta".
A spokesperson for the GMC told the BBC: "Esta's death is a tragedy, and our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Esta's parents, Ms Carr and Mr High, and their family.
"We carefully consider all complaints raised with us, and thoroughly examine all relevant information before making a decision."
'Truly sorry'
During the inquest, lawyers for Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust admitted that opportunities had been missed to diagnose the bacterial infection and administer antibiotics.
The trust's chief medical officer, Dr Elizabeth Garthwaite, said previously said the trust was "truly sorry we failed Esta".
"We recognise that serious failures occurred in the care provided to Esta and that these failures had devastating consequences," said Garthwaite.
"We are committed to responding openly and fully, and to taking any further action necessary to improve patient safety."
She said the trust had already taken steps to "strengthen" its services, including improving the recognition and management of deteriorating children, enhancing staff training in paediatric sepsis, strengthening escalation processes and implementing Martha's Rule to "help ensure concerns raised by patients and families are heard and acted upon".

title: How Maya Jama went from Bristol native to Celebrity Traitors star
text:
How Bristol shaped Maya Jama before her TV fame
Maya Jama has gone from Bristol schoolgirl to one of the UK's biggest television stars.
The 32-year-old Love Island host was watched by millions as she faced the last round table in the final of The Celebrity Traitors, which aired on BBC One and iPlayer.
But behind the glamorous television appearances and red carpet moments is a story that began in a council house with a young girl determined to make it on the small screen.
Maya was born and raised in Bristol, growing up in St Paul's with a family of Bristol Rovers supporters, putting on song and dance performances for them and charging 20p a time.
- Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode 10 of The Celebrity Traitors, series two
She was born in St Paul's in 1994 and grew up in Bristol with her Swedish mother, Sadie, younger brother Omar and extended family.
Although Bristol is where she spent much of her childhood, she also has strong connections to Sweden through her mum.
She spent time in Sweden as a young child, attended nursery there and regularly returned for family visits during Christmas, Easter and the summer holidays.
Her Swedish roots are something she has spoken about fondly, even recalling getting upset when Sweden lost to Brazil in a World Cup match as a child.
Back in Bristol, Maya grew up around Stokes Croft before moving to the Cotham and Redland area, where she attended Cotham School.
She has previously spoken about growing up in a council house and being surrounded by family and friends.
In a 2019 interview with the Evening Standard, she recalled being a "proper little show child", putting on performances in the front room and charging family members 20p to watch her dance and sing.
Her mum encouraged her ambitions, even when they seemed a long way from the world of television.
Maya's childhood was not without its difficulties. Her mother worked multiple jobs to support the family, and Maya has spoken openly about the financial pressures they faced.
In a 2021 interview with ITV News West Country, she explained how free school meals had been a "massive, massive help" while she was growing up.
She said: "We'd go to the cheaper food shops and my mum would make sure we'd ate everything on our plate because you didn't know when you were going to get your next healthy meal."
Despite the challenges, Maya had ambitions to work in entertainment from a young age.
At 16, she made the move from Bristol to London to pursue a career in the industry. It was a big step, but one she felt she needed to take if she wanted to make her television dreams a reality.
Her first opportunities came through music and online broadcasting. She began presenting a weekly music video countdown for production company JumpOff TV before joining MTV in 2014 as a presenter on The Wrap Up.
She also worked in radio, building her profile through stations including Rinse FM, before landing a presenting role on BBC Radio 1 in 2018.
Her career continued to gather pace, and in 2017 she became the youngest person to host the MOBO Awards, alongside Marvin Humes.
She went on to present a string of television programmes, including Channel 4's Stand Up To Cancer and ITV2's Don't Hate the Playaz, before taking over as host of BBC Three's Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star in 2021.
But perhaps her biggest presenting role came in 2023 when she became the new host of ITV's Love Island.
Taking over one of the UK's most talked-about reality shows made her a familiar face in households across the country.
She has since fronted further editions of the programme, including Love Island: All Stars.
This month she was back on our screens in a very different role, competing as a Traitor alongside King Kenny in the The Celebrity Traitors.
She made it to the final but was banished from the castle at the last round table.

title: Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
text:
Canada stops using 'avalanche dogs' for rescues in Rocky Mountains, stirring outrage
Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.
Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.
Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.
Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off.
The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world.
It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.
Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it.
William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety.
"How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.
The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer.
For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body.
After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow.
"It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.
In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites.
"We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said.
Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy.
The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August.
For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.
A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; £78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.
Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday.
In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".
Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO.
As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored.
He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."
description: A 55-year-old dog rescue programme that has found missing hikers and children in the Canadian wilderness was axed as part of government budget cuts.

title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
text:
'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.
SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".
Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.
Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".
"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.
"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid the political fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute.
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.
He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".
In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.
Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.
The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".
Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.
He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.
The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.
'Welcome start'
John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.
"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.
"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."
A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.
Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.
"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."
He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.
The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.
A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."
description: The meeting involved representatives from the UK's four nations to discuss devolving more powers to regions and cities.

title: Farmer killed father then himself after family row, inquest hears
text:
Man killed father then himself after row - inquest
A farmer killed his father before taking his own life after a "blazing row", an inquest has heard.
Brian Wright, 82, was reported missing on 20 November last year after missing an appointment to take his wife to hospital.
His 52-year-old son Charles Wright took his own life at the family farm near Newark, Nottinghamshire, two days later, and on 25 November Brian's body was found in a shallow grave by police.
An inquest at Nottingham Coroner's Court on Friday heard no third parties were involved, with Brian's death ruled as an unlawful killing and Charles found to have killed himself.
The court heard Nottinghamshire Police were asked to investigate a missing person report into Brian after a family member called at about 23:50 GMT on 20 November.
Brian had last been seen at about 15:10 that day, and had been set to take his wife to hospital, but neither he nor his vehicle could be found.
Det Ch Insp Ruby Burrow said Charles was among the people spoken to on the day, and he referred to a disagreement he had with his father about the farm, with others interviewed also mentioning "difficult family dynamics".
The court heard family disagreements were known to the police, which had resulted in a firearms licence being withdrawn for a period of time because of concerns firearms "could be used inappropriately because of tensions within the family".
'Truly tragic case'
At about 15:00 on 21 November Brian's car was found by a member of the public on a road, and CCTV established it had been driven there the previous afternoon.
Burrow told the court police were called on the morning of 22 November when a car was "apparently deliberately" driven at two people, which turned out to be Charles driving at his brother and a friend.
Later that day Charles left a voice note with a friend, in which he confirmed his father had called him "useless" and "an idiot" in the earlier row, and had suggested giving control of part of the farm to a different family member.
Mairin Casey, senior coroner, said in the voice note Charles said: "I just had a flash of red, and after 25 years and everything I've given him, he was just cutting me out like that."
Police found Charles's body in a working area of the farm that day, the court heard, with Brian's body found buried three days later.
A post-mortem examination found Brian died as a result of "pressure to the neck", with other injuries "consistent with some sort of altercation prior to the death".
Burrow confirmed police found Charles had taken his own life, adding there was no evidence of third-party involvement in either death.
"The evidence shows that Charles Wright murdered his father, and that there was no third-party involvement in the death," she told the court.
"The evidence showed [Charles] took his own life, and that there was no third-party involvement in that either."
Concluding the hearing, Casey described it as "a truly tragic case", and offered her condolences to the family.
"Whatever tensions there may have been leading to this tragedy, we have here the loss of two men, who were fathers to surviving children, and a grandfather," she said.
"The horror of this, I am clear in my mind, will have affected all of those who survive in a deep and painful way."

title: 'Murder accused Billy Allison hit another man with heavy blow'
text:
'Murder accused hit another man with heavy blow'
A man who was hurt in an unprovoked attack in a bar that left his friend with fatal injuries has described the punch feeling like being "hit with a sledgehammer", a murder trial has heard.
Giving evidence at Stafford Crown Court earlier, Adam Cooper, 62, who suffered fractures to his eye socket and nose, said there had been no warning of the events that unfolded at the Ricco and Loren bar in Lichfield, Staffordshire, on 24 May.
Billy Allison, 36, of Shirley, Solihull, denies murdering Matthew O'Gara, 44, but has pleaded guilty to manslaughter.
Allison has also admitted grievous bodily harm against Cooper, but denies the attack was carried out with intent.
Cooper told the court he was drinking at The Plough in Huddlesford, which O'Gara ran, on the afternoon of the incident before being invited to join O'Gara and a group of friends and colleagues in Lichfield.
Initially reluctant, Cooper decided to go along, leaving his car at home and meeting them at a pub in the city.
He told the court he had become friends with O'Gara and partner Rebecca Mullally through being a regular at The Plough.
"Matt was everyone's friend, one of the friendliest guys you'd ever meet," he said.
O'Gara knew the owner of Ricco and Loren, Cooper added, and said there was a happy mood among their group as they made their way to the venue and gathered on the dance floor inside.
He told jury he had noticed a "big guy" standing in the corner of the bar who he did not know.
"He was tall, well built, like, kind of strong," he told the jury, estimating he was about 6ft 5in (195cm) tall, adding: "I just noticed his Louis Vuitton bag, I bought my wife one, so I was looking."
He also noticed a woman who appeared to be with Allison, explaining: "I saw her dancing and thought she was enjoying herself."
Asked by prosecuting barrister Tim Hannam KC if he had paid any further attention to Allison, Cooper said: "Nothing really, I just looked around the room, just like anybody does."
Cooper then described feeling an "almighty blow" to his face that left him in shock.
"I didn't see it coming [...] I didn't see anything at all," he said, before describing being hit once to his right eye and again to his jaw.
"I [had] blood pouring out of my face," he said. "I put my hand to my head, I was just in total shock and walked straight out the back door."
Asked what it had felt like, Cooper said: "Like a sledgehammer, it was hard, very, very hard."
He told the court he did not realise until later that O'Gara had been punched in the same attack.
Asked by Hannam if he had done anything to "justify" being attacked, Cooper said: "Absolutely not."
He also told the jury he had since spent £6,000 on dental work to repair implants that had been damaged in the attack, and had already visited the dentist 11 times with further treatment planned.
Previously, the court heard how Allison had been visiting Lichfield with a group of friends including his girlfriend Charlotte Dean and friends Ryan Bridge and Ben Cullen, and had been drinking throughout the day before the attack on the two men, who he did not know.
Footage after the attack showed Cooper receiving help in a wooden shelter and Allison leaving through a gate.
The jury was told how after he left the scene, Allison swapped t-shirts with Cullen, and had tried to pull the top over his head to conceal his face from a camera.
The trial continues.

title: Teeth-whitening pair from Merseyside jailed over £8.5m tax fraud
text:
Teeth-whitening pair jailed over £8.5m tax fraud
Two men whose multi-million-pound teeth-whitening tax scam helped fund lavish lifestyles, including plans to build villas in Florida with matching teeth-shaped swimming pools, have been jailed.
Ian Barnes, 53, and Alastair Ramage, 44, both from Merseyside, admitted failing to pay over £8.5m in VAT and income tax from profits of importing and selling dangerous teeth-whitening products.
Their spending included £16,000 on a baseball cap, £100,000 on holidays and luxury cars. Other seized items included premium jewellery, cash and a solid gold bar.
They admitted fraud offences at an earlier hearing and were sentenced at Liverpool Crown Court today.
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) investigators proved the pair laundered more than £8.5m through 118 bank accounts, credit cards and cryptocurrency trading platforms.
The men imported and sold products containing dangerously high levels of hydrogen peroxide through UK Teeth Whitening Ltd and IBAR Trading Ltd, which operated from the Seychelles and Hong Kong.
More than £3.4m of the stolen money was funnelled through accounts held at Euro Pacific Bank in Puerto Rico.
The bank was shut down in 2022 following investigations by the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions of Puerto Rico.
WhatsApp messages recovered from the men's phones showed them boasting, including one from Barnes that said: "In a few hours, we'll be in 1st class" and "platinum luggage tags, that's how UK Teeth Whitening roll."
The messages also revealed they knew they were supplying dangerous products and could face prison if they were caught by HMRC.
In an exchange, Barnes wrote: "They said they used it for 30 minutes and it's taken the enamel off their teeth - dentist said they need new teeth."
Ramage added: "We're on the first plane out of here if they [HMRC] come knocking. We're talking millions and years in jail."
Barnes, from Formby, was sentenced to four years and four months, while Ramage, who had moved to Portugal, was jailed for four years and six months.
'Sophisticated operation'
Zoe Gascoyne, director of HMRC's Fraud Investigation Service, described it as a "sophisticated tax avoidance operation".
"Barnes and Ramage knew they were stealing from taxpayers and selling dangerous products at the same time," she said.
"Their messages show complete disregard for the hard-working majority who pay the taxes that fund our public services.
"Hiding stolen money in offshore accounts does not put anyone beyond reach and my team will now work with partners at the Crown Prosecution Service to recover the money they stole."

title: E-bike jousting captures spectacle of the medieval sport, says expert
text:
'Bike jousting revives the medieval spectacle'
Jousting while riding bikes is "absolutely a legitimate form" of the medieval sport, a professional jouster has said as details of a second planned duel circulate on social media.
Just a few weeks ago, hundreds of people congregated in London Fields, Hackney, east London, to watch actor Camtholomew the First and artist Jack Carden joust while riding Lime bikes.
Videos on social media showed them dressed as knights in armour, complete with chainmail and lances, attempting to knock each other off the rentable e-bikes. A "rematch" is due to take place on Saturday at a location yet to be disclosed.
Lime has been contacted for comment but previously said its bikes were "not for jousting".
In a statement released after the first duel, Lime discouraged others from "attempting similar events" due to safety concerns.
"While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first," a spokesperson for the company previously said.
But Andy Deane, captain of the Royal Armouries jousting team in Leeds, said it was a "joy" to see the bike jousting "capturing the spectacle" of the medieval sport.
"This is absolutely a legitimate form of jousting," he said.
"Historically, you had sort of piggyback jousting pictures in the 14th, 15th Century, you had jousting on water where you have people rowing boats towards each other with people at the bow with their lances and shields."
Deane has been jousting for 33 years and travelled across Europe, Asia, Canada and the US teaching and participating in the sport.
"You've got hundreds of people getting really enthusiastic, laughing their heads off and cheering on the knight they want to win," he added.
"That's what jousts are all about. They're loud, rambunctious, brilliant places to perform.
"If I was 20 years younger, I'd already be on the train down there with my bike."
The biggest danger, he said, was being flung from your horse or bike and "landing badly".
"There's definitely a risk involved, but that's why you're wearing the armour – to protect you and, for the most part, it does," he said.
"So bicycles – absolutely the way to go. Certainly if you can't afford a horse."
Despite their popularity, hospitals have reported an increase in injuries to both e-bike riders and pedestrians.

A section of railway will remain closed for longer than planned while repairs are carried out on a Victorian bridge.

title: 'Monster' who raped sleeping teenager on Isle of Man jailed
text:
'Monster' who raped sleeping teenager jailed
Warning: This article contains distressing content
A man who filmed himself raping a teenager and secretly recorded other girls with a hidden bathroom camera has been jailed for 20 years and eight months.
John Curtis, 41, recorded footage of the offences against a 16-year-old girl as she slept on 1 May 2026.
Douglas Courthouse was told devices seized when Curtis was arrested revealed the camera footage, as well as more than 15,000 indecent images of children.
Deemster Graeme Cook said it was a case of "extreme sexual depravity".
Curtis pleaded guilty to a total of 33 offences, including rape, attempted rape and the taking of and possession of indecent images.
The court heard the victim called police after waking to find him attacking her.
When he was arrested a short time later, he was carrying several devices, including a small camera, a hard drive and two mobile phones in a plastic box.
They were found to contain images of the rape, as well as footage of five other girls using a bathroom, including the shower.
The hard drive was also found to have folders containing images of children being abused, including one video showing the rape of a baby.
Jailing him, Deemster Cook said: "Some of your victims described you as a monster, and I totally agree."
The range of Curtis's offending was "beyond belief", he said, adding: "You have traumatised six young ladies."
The teenage victim who was raped "will perhaps never get over what you have done to her", he said.
The deemster also handed Curtis an extended licence period of 10 years after his release, telling him: "I believe the public are in need of protection from you."

title: Ex-Middlesbrough Mayor Dave Budd 'truly honoured' by town award
text:
Former mayor 'truly honoured' by town award
A former Middlesbrough Mayor has been awarded one of the town's most prestigious honours.
Dave Budd, who was the town's elected mayor from 2015 to 2019, received the Freedom of the Borough at a ceremony in the town hall on Thursday.
In his acceptance speech, Budd said he was "truly honoured" and thanked his wife and family for keeping him sane, adding: "And sometimes they've succeeded."
He was nominated for his more than 30 years in public office and his work to develop the Tees Heritage Trail, the MIMA art gallery and for being a "champion of culture in the town".
Budd praised the teamwork he experienced from people across town throughout the years, saying: "This is a remarkable place."
"This town is full of people who care."
The former Labour mayor was nominated by councillors Luke Henman and Lewis Young, who said the people in the area were fortunate to have Dave Budd "serving the town in public life for decades".
"It is even more fortunate that he continues to do so in his retirement," the Labour councillors said, adding he had been a "champion of culture in the town".
The award is given to those who have made an "outstanding contribution to the life of the town and its people", the council said.
Previous recipients included footballer Alan Peacock, artist Mackenzie Thorpe and Olympic swimmer Jack Hatfield.

title: Free youth classes aim to tackle anti-social behaviour in Garston
text:
New youth classes aim to tackle anti-social behaviour
Free boxing, dance and drama classes are being introduced in part of Liverpool in a bid to tackle anti-social behaviour.
The initiative comes as Garston is placed under a 72-hour dispersal zone, the longest ever imposed by Merseyside Police using new powers granted by the government.
In recent years, the south Liverpool district has been plagued by vandalism and criminal damage on so-called Mischief Night, the evening before Halloween.
"For the past few years, we've had an increase of criminality rather than antisocial behaviour," local councillor Sam Gorst said.
"The seriousness of what a lot of the young people and young adults have been causing has been horrendous for the community.
"I do feel like it's a hotspot that is easily accessible for people and young people to come into Garston. We're on a main bus route and a main train route as well.
"For some reason, Garston seems to get some of the most serious incidents and I blame that partly on the lack of youth provision, positive role models and opportunities for young people generally."
The free activities are funded through Community Renewal Funding in partnership with Liverpool City Council and are aimed at children living in the Garston area.
Free boxing sessions are being run by Strictly Boxing Gym on Mercer Street on 30 and 31 October, while dance and drama classes are being held at Topaz on Heald Street.
Funding has also been secured the dance and drama sessions to continue every Friday evening for the next year.
'Part of the solution'
Among those running sessions is Paul Coshott, who runs Strictly Boxing Gym.
He said boxing can help create focus for young people.
"It teaches the elements that, certainly now more than ever, kids need, which is discipline, structure, setting goals, respect towards each other and respect towards other people around them," he said.
"Rather than just talking about the problem, we want to be part of the solution."
The dispersal order runs until midday on Saturday and Insp Richard Smith of Merseyside Police said additional officers would also be on patrol.
"I want people to be assured that we are doing everything in our power to keep everyone safe," he said.
"I would appeal to parents and guardians and urge them to inform their children of the dangers of using fireworks and to know where their child is this weekend.
"No parent wants a knock on their door from a police officer informing them that their child has been arrested or been involved in a serious accident."
The Garston zone includes the area bounded by and including Garston Way, Whitehedge Road, Long Lane, Horrocks Avenue, Speke Road, Banks Road, Blackburne Street and King Street.
The order, authorised under Section 34 of the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, gives police officers, police community support officers and designated police staff the power to direct people they suspect are causing, or are likely to cause, crime, nuisance or anti-social behaviour to leave a designated area and not return for up to 48 hours

title: Men jailed after retrial over Sheffield 'Good Samaritan' killing
text:
Men jailed after 'Good Samaritan' killing retrial
Two men have been jailed for killing a "Good Samaritan" who stepped in to help a 17-year-old girl who had been assaulted.
Reece Radford, 26, was fatally stabbed when he intervened in the altercation in Arundel Gate, Sheffield, in 2022.
Louis James and Dereck Owusu were originally jailed for life in 2023 after being convicted of Radford's murder, but after appealing against their convictions a retrial was held and James was convicted of murder while Owusu was instead found guilty of manslaughter.
At Leeds Crown Court on Friday, James, 50, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 23 years, while Owusu, 43, was sentenced to 14 years.
During the original trial, the court heard Radford had confronted the pair after he witnessed Owusu punching the girl in the face in Arundel Gate in the early hours of 29 September 2022.
The jury was told that Radford, who had met the girl briefly earlier that night, saw Owusu striking the teenager "with such force that she fell to the ground", and he intervened by punching Owusu in the face.
"He did so in order to protect a young female who he had just seen being punched," prosecutor David Temkin KC said at the time.
Owusu, previously of Strathmore Grove, Rotherham, and James, previously of Manor Lane, Sheffield, then attacked Radford, with James stabbing him.
Radford died in hospital six days later as a result of a stab wound.
Following their retrial and sentencing, Det Insp Adam Watkinson, from South Yorkshire Police, said he was "glad" Radford's family "finally have closure and that the pair responsible for an innocent man's death have once more been returned to jail where they belong".
"Reece acted as a Good Samaritan, going out of his way to defend a young person who he did not know," Watkinson said.
"He should not have had to pay for this act of kindness with his life."

title: Melmerby man who stabbed victim in the neck jailed
text:
Man who stabbed pub landlord in neck jailed
A man has been jailed after he stabbed a pub landlord in the neck following an argument outside a village inn.
Builder Gary Holdsworth got into a row over payment at the George & Dragon in Melmerby, near Ripon, on 4 December 2025, before attacking 46-year-old Michael Ryan outside, Leeds Crown Court heard.
In August, the 52-year-old, of Melmerby, was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent and possessing a knife in a public space.
On Friday, the married father-of-five was jailed for six years and six months and handed a restraining order preventing him from contacting the victim and his partner.
The court was told that Holdsworth and his friend Radk Szatkowski, 41, of Wath near Ripon, had got into a drunken argument with Mr Ryan which spilled outside the pub where punches were thrown before Holdsworth took a knife out of his pocket.
As he slashed Mr Ryan "about three times" on the neck, Holdsworth told him: "You're gonna die; I'm going to kill you."
Following the incident, Mr Ryan was taken to hospital where he needed surgery to serious injuries.
Holdsworth fled the scene after the attack, but was arrested at his home address shortly afterwards.
Szatkowski was charged with affray, but was found not guilty.
In a victim personal statement, Mr Ryan's partner told the court: "My boyfriend is a kind, loving, and caring man.
"On that day, he was stabbed in the neck and nearly lost his life.
"This was not just an attack - it was something that could have taken him away from all of us forever."
She added her life had "completely changed" since the stabbing, leaving her with "constant worry" about what happened.
"This incident has deeply affected not just me, but our entire family. It has taken away our sense of safety, peace, and normal life."
Judge Neil Clark told Holdsworth: "You were hitherto of good character. You were a successful man.
"You had a successful business, and you have a loving and caring family.
"Very many people speak highly of you, yet despite all of that... you went for a night out with your friend... and you got monumentally drunk. In this state, you behaved in a way that was wholly out of character for you.
"This is exceptionally serious offending: had it been a few millimetres either side, it would have been murder [and] an automatic life sentence."

title: Tributes as Chinook crash 'champion of the truth' RAF test pilot dies
text:
Tributes as 'champion of the truth' test pilot dies
Family members, friends and campaigners have paid tribute to a "fearless" and "extraordinarily knowledgeable" former RAF test pilot.
Retired Sqn Ldr Robert Burke, from Hampshire, helped to clear the pilots who were wrongly blamed for the RAF Chinook ZD576 helicopter crash on the Mull of Kintyre in western Scotland on 2 June 1994, in which four crew and 25 passengers were killed.
The Chinook Justice Campaign said Burke had died on Monday at the age of 86, following a short illness.
Chris Cook, brother of one of the pilots killed in the disaster, said Burke had brought forward "clear evidence that proved, more than ever, how unjust the accusations of gross negligence were".
Campaigners called Burke "instrumental" in uncovering airworthiness failings on the Chinook Mark 2.
In evidence to the House of Lords in October 2001, he revealed he had been given "a direct order" by his superiors "not to discuss this crash with anyone".
Two RAF air marshals had accused Flt Lts Jonathan Tapper, from Norfolk, and Richard Cook, from Hampshire, for the accident.
But a fresh review found they should not have been blamed and the earlier ruling has now been set aside.
A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson previously said "the lack of certainty" about the crash had added to the distress for families.
Burke, who was based at RAF Odiham at the time of the crash, had exposed serious concerns about the aircraft's airworthiness and had challenged the MoD's account.
He also revealed to the BBC documentary Chinook: Zulu Delta 576, aired in 2024, that the fatal mission was a "show flight" by the RAF to prove to the army that the aircraft was safe.
He said the aircraft "had been cleared against the advice of Boscombe Down" where the most elite test pilots and test engineers had said the helicopter was "positively dangerous".
Susan Phoenix, from Dorset, who has campaigned for 32 years, said it was "heartbreaking" that Burke died "without seeing the MoD admit to the truth".
"But it makes us even more determined to get justice and a fresh inquiry independent of the MoD," she said, adding they hope the prime minister agrees to meet the families.
Former BBC correspondent Tim Reid, who is now spokesperson for the Chinook Justice Campaign, said Burke's death was a "huge and terrible loss to the families and to everyone who has fought for the truth about this disaster".
"His knowledge of the Chinook and the circumstances of the crash was second to none.
"He was an outstanding champion of the truth, an incredible character and a man of extraordinary courage and determination," Reid said.
Retired RAF Wing Commander Bill Southcombe, from Somerset, one of Burke's closest friends and a former colleague flying the Vulcan aircraft, called him "an exceptional man".
"He was fearless, extraordinarily knowledgeable and utterly committed to the truth. We have lost not just an expert, but a dear friend."

title: Two Lake District friend hikers separately rescued hours apart
text:
Two hiking friends separately rescued hours apart
Two friends who drove together into the countryside for separate hikes had to be rescued within hours of each other after both getting stranded.
Penrith Mountain Rescue said volunteers were called on the afternoon of 28 October to find a man who got lost in heavy fog on the High Street Ridge in the Lake District.
A rescue party found and escorted the walker back to his car, where it was revealed his friend had also gone missing, with the second man telling rescuers over the phone he did not know where he was.
With the help of 25 team members, as well as an additional eight from Keswick Mountain Rescue and a HM Coastguard helicopter, the man was found near the Kidsty Pike ridge.
Initially, six team members were sent to find the first hiker, who had managed to make it to the marker at the summit of the Mardale III Bell fell but was unsure of the route back down - with it being 16:00 GMT and getting dark.
However, more rescuers were recruited for the second, with concern he could be at risk of hypothermia due to the amount of time he had spent on the fell.
The helicopter was requested because it was difficult to narrow down where he was and it was anticipated a large area of ground would need to be searched.
However, discussions over the phone revealed he was to the west or southwest of Haweswater resevoir, around the Kidsty Pike fell.
After being winched off the cliffs by the helicopter, he was checked over by a team doctor and found to be safe and healthy.
The two friends were reunited and departed for their car journey home shortly before midnight.

title: Anticipation builds for The Celebrity Traitors finale
text:
Anticipation builds for Celebrity Traitors finale
- Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
Millions are expected to tune in to Friday's finale of The Celebrity Traitors, with a contestant from West Sussex still in contention to win.
Romesh Ranganathan, from Crawley, is one of the series' five remaining "faithfuls" who survived Thursday's bombshell roundtable banishment.
The former maths teacher-turned-comedian blamed his youngest son for his reluctant participation, saying he was "desperate for me to come on".
Amanda Collier, from Brighton, who appeared on the civilian series earlier this year, told BBC Radio Sussex: "Last night, I could not believe what happened."
The psychological reality game show, which saw a record of 15.7m viewers for the first episode of its second celebrity series, sees contestants face challenges and work together to unmask and banish hidden "traitors" from their midst at nightly roundtables.
The penultimate episode broadcast on Thursday saw vocal faithful Michael Sheen place heat on Maya Jama and James Acaster. Up until then, they had been unassuming traitors alongside King Kenny.
The pressure seemed to get too much for Acaster, who confessed he was a traitor at the roundtable - a series first.
Collier, a former Metropolitan Police senior detective, said the revelation had blown the game wide open: "There are so many permutations of what could happen."
"After episode eight, I said 'this is a traitors' win, it's going to be a slightly boring finale'," Collier added.
Now, she says she "cannot wait" for the finale: "It's going to be a fabulous final."
Ranganathan survived earlier elimination when his close friend and fellow comedian Rob Beckett was picked off by the traitors in a face-to-face murder.
After discovering his fate, Beckett said: "I know one thing - my boy Romesh will avenge my death and he will get them."
Joe Marler, a former England International rugby player from Heathfield, East Sussex, made it to the final of the first celebrity series before being pipped to the prize by traitor Alan Carr.
Marler previously told BBC South East the latest season was "carnage".
"Richard E Grant coming out like that, straight off the bat - I'm hooked."
Dr Gemma Graham, head of the psychology department at the University of Brighton, told BBC Radio Sussex the series is a "perfect game of deception".
"As the viewers, we know who the traitors are so we're screaming at the TV going what are you doing?", she added.
Collier agreed: "It's really easy from the sofa, so easy.
"Not so much when you're in there."

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
text:
Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

title: Palestine Action activists who targeted bank spared jail
text:
Activists who attacked bank spared jail
Four people from the Palestine Action group who attacked a bank in August 2024 have been spared immediate jail sentences.
The activists were convicted of criminal damage after covering a Barclays bank in Burnley, Lancashire, with red paint and breaking its windows, causing about £200,000 worth of damage.
The group said it had targeted Barclays over the bank's links to defence company Elbit Systems, which it claimed had supplied military components used by Israel in the conflict in Gaza.
Hmeera Atiqnisar was given a two-year prison sentence, suspended for 20 months. Mohammed Malik, Brendon O'Hagan and Amanda Kelly were each given 20-month suspended prison sentences. A fifth defendant, Alma Yaniv, will be sentenced in December.
'Distressed'
The group wore masks when they smashed windows and hurled red paint at the bank's Burnley branch in a 02:00 BST operation, while a security guard was "distressed" inside the building.
The damage cost £212,805 and the group filmed the attack and shared the footage online.
Judge Robert Altham, sitting at Preston Crown Court, said Atiqnisar, 31, was the principal organiser.
He jailed her for two years but suspended the sentence for 20 months and told her she must carry out 250 hours of unpaid work.
Brendon O'Hagon, 28, who filmed the late-night attack; Amanda Kelly, 32, who sprayed paint; and Mohammed Malik, 28, who smashed windows; were all handed 20-month jail terms, also suspended for 20 months, and ordered to carry out 240 hours of unpaid work.
A fifth member of the group, 70-year-old getaway driver Alma Yaniv, who failed to stop for police and went through two red lights in a Toyota Yaris, will be sentenced in December.
They were all convicted of criminal damage following a trial in June.
The judge previously ruled any terrorism element to their offending did not apply, meaning they would face lesser sentences.
The court heard the defendants, apart from Yaniv, were trained by Palestine Action, but this was before the Home Secretary proscribed the organisation.
Ahead of sentencing, the judge read references for the defendants, who were all of good character.
This included hearing how Atiqnisar had taught girls at a mosque and was the registered carer for her brother, Yaniv was a foster carer and volunteer with the Samaritans and Malik was a "compassionate" and caring member of his community.
Judge Altham said of the defendants: "They are otherwise perfectly law-abiding people."
But he took account of the planning the late-night attack took, the cost of the damage, and the distress caused to a security guard who was trapped inside the branch as multiple windows were smashed.
He said: "Whilst this was non-violent protest, it still involved the potentially shocking sight of masked people running through the streets of Burnley late at night armed with hammers and, without any regard at all for the security staff inside, taking those hammers to the windows of a building and causing significant damage."
The judge accepted the defendants were motivated by their "sincerely held beliefs" and they have now accepted that protests should remain within the law.
He said: "Nothing I say is intended to question the sincerity of those beliefs, still less to require any of you to abandon them.
"But in a democratic society there is a fundamental distinction between holding and expressing even the strongest political beliefs and deciding that the strength or morality of those beliefs entitles a person to break the criminal law in pursuit of them.
"The decisive factor which permits me to suspend these sentences is my conclusion that you four have now understood this distinction, that however sincerely a cause is held, that sincerity does not provide a licence to pursue it by unlawful means."

title: Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
text:
Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree
Andy Burnham's Number 10 North has gone on a multi-million pound hiring spree with dozens of new jobs being advertised.
The office in Manchester, set up by the prime minister in July, has launched 50 external job adverts, including a "rewiring the state deputy director".
It is the latest sign of how pivotal the government outpost - designed as a sister office to London's Downing Street - may prove to Burnham's aim to devolve power across the country.
Government sources say the roles will be paid for out of existing budgets.
The new recruits "will work with mayors and councils to identify barriers holding places back", but the Conservatives have described the office as a "gimmick".
There will be no redundancies elsewehere in the civil service as a result of the hiring spree, the BBC has been told, with some jobs expected to be relocated and other vacant roles closed.
The new roles, all based in Manchester, cover areas including strategy, communications, engagement, private office and policy.
BBC News has calculated they total up to £2.8m for basic salaries alone, excluding employer pension contributions in the civil service of 28.97%.
No10 North now has 120 members of staff, nearly half of the 280 staff who work in No10 London.
Among the highest paid of the roles are a "rewiring the state deputy director", with a salary band of £86,000 to £117,000, who will "lead the Rewiring the State Unit... shaping the government's approach to devolution across departments".
The government said it was launching a recruitment campaign for staff who would "bring fresh perspectives and knowledge of the places they serve, moving decisions closer to the people they affect".
No10 North "is driving the most significant transfer of power out of Westminster in a generation," the government added in a statement.
Some apprenticeships and secondments are also being advertised.
It comes as the government confirmed on Friday that No10 North would move from its current temporary home in Heron House, on Manchester's Albert Square, to a new government office on First Street in spring 2027.
No10 North will share the city centre building with other government departments spanning business, education, local government and the Cabinet Office.
Burnham made opening No10 North one of his first acts as prime minister, describing it as "the nerve-centre of a rewired Britain" that would help bring growth to more areas of Britain.
No10 North's deputy director Duncan Parish said in a speech last week that officials faced "institutional challenges" with delivering on these aims and called for a "mindset shift" across the UK's central government.
Conservative Party deputy leader Alex Burghart said: "He [Burnham] promised to streamline the civil service, but now he is hiring extra staff and, once again, won't say where the money is coming from.
"Manchesterism is just more bureaucracy at taxpayers' expense."
Meanwhile, Tory shadow cabinet minister Mike Wood has said there is "so little transparency" around No10 North after ministers told him they could not reveal figures on headcounts and office attendance.
According to the new job adverts, the Office for the Prime Minister - with exceptions for certain roles - expects No10 staff to be in the office a minimum of 60% of the time.
Since opening, No10 North has hosted summits of regional mayors, at least two of which have been partly held as video calls on Microsoft Teams. At one of these meetings, ministers unveiled controversial powers for mayors in England to charge new fees on visitors' overnight stays.
It has also hosted an education summit of school leaders and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin met Burnham for the first time as PM at No10 North in September.

title: Jaackmate dropped from Norwich Christmas event after review
text:
Podcaster dropped from Christmas lights event
A podcaster with over a million subscribers has been dropped from a Christmas lights switch-on event after a city council reviewed his past "published content".
Jack Dean, known as JaackMaate, was selected to appear at the event outside Norwich City Hall on Thursday, 19 November.
The 33-year-old, who is from the city, said the opportunity was a "bucket list dream", but a fortnight later the invitation has been withdrawn by the city council.
In a statement, the authority apologised and said it had "failed to identify issues from previous published content before announcing him".
He was due to turn the lights on with his Happy Hour co-hosts, Stevie White and Robbie Knox.
In a post on his Facebook, Dean claimed he was pulled from the event because "one person complained to the council about my old 'edgy' online videos from 2014".
In a subsequent video posted to social media, he said: "Even though it was over 12 years ago, I'm not proud of some of the language I used and some of the videos I made.
"The council has informed me that because the switch on is a family event and my old content is not family friendly I'm no longer suitable for the gig.
"I know it's just going up there and pressing a button but it was a real special moment for me. I'm gutted, I'm heartbroken and I'm disappointed."
Dean said he made "outlandish, brash and edgy" videos as a teenager and said some of it was "just stupid".
He added: "I don't know how many times I can apologise for the same thing.
"Ultimately I did say stupid stuff online when I was 19 but I promise you guys, I like to think I'm a decent bloke."
He has offered to meet with fans for a drink at the Murderers pub in Norwich, which he says is one of his favourites in the city.
The reversal follows Norwich's lord mayor, Karen Davis, appearing on Jaackmate's podcast to invite the presenters to turn the lights on two weeks ago.

title: 'Architect' of prostitution ring jailed after trafficking Romanian women into UK
text:
Men jailed for 'abhorrent' operation trafficking women from Europe into UK for sex work
The "architect and organiser" of a group that trafficked Romanian women into the UK to become sex workers has been sentenced to eight years and two months in prison.
George Filip, 45, led an organised crime group responsible for the "prostitution" of at least 16 victims, earning hundreds of thousands of pounds, Cardiff Crown Court heard.
He was assisted by his wife Ionela Filip, 35, to bring the women to work as sex workers in locations across Wales, England and Scotland. Alexandru Moco, 27 and Leonard Banica, 41, were also involved in the conspiracy.
Judge Francis said it was a "substantial and sophisticated criminal enterprise that operated over seven years".
The court heard that between June 2015 and October 2022, at least 16 identifiable victims had been brought to the UK from Romania and France to work in the sex industry.
Matthew Cobbe, prosecuting, said the operation was of a "significant scale" with women working in "Cwmbran, Hereford, a location near Alton Towers, Stoke-on-Trent, Aberdeen and Inverness".
Francis was told the women had not been brought under duress but George, of no fixed abode, had "plainly exploited the circumstances of these victims". Although there was "no suggestion of sexual violence" there were "very many customers", Cobbe said.
Francis said that some of the women, while coming to the UK to work in the sex industry had been "pressured to commit sexual acts they had not agreed to which had caused them considerable distress".
The court heard Ionela, of Waterloo Road, Smethwick, was second-in-command in the group but not involved in the trafficking of women.
Banica, from Romania, was involved in introducing sex workers to the enterprise, while Moco, of Friary Road, Birmingham, took sex workers to appointments and provided contraception.
Cobbe said Ionela took photographs of the women in "suitably provocative poses", which were often posted on websites within 24 hours of them entering the UK.
The business was controlled using a mobile phone that was examined by police after they raided a property in Newport in January 2020, which was being used for sex work following complaints from neighbours.
The contents of the phone enabled police to understand the scale of the operation, which was described as "a very busy operation on a national level".
George, Banica and Moco - Ionela's younger brother - fled the UK while Ionela continued to run the operation in Scotland for two years. The three were rearrested when they returned to the UK.
Francis said even though she accepted the women were not under duress to work as sex workers, "exploitation may exist even when there is an apparent degree of consent".
"It is necessary to stand back and consider the nature of this enterprise - a prostitution business, operating on a substantial commercial scale."
George was told "you are plainly the most responsible offender", while Ionela was told she was "a senior trusted manager rather than a person who exercised total control".
The judge described Banica and Moco as having lesser roles in the organisation.
'Actions were abhorrent'
George was told he would serve up to half his sentence in custody and would then be deported when released. Ionela was given a three-year suspended sentence.
Banica was sentenced to three years and nine months and was also told upon release he would be deported.
Moco was sentenced to one year and three months, and was told he was likely to be released immediately and deported.
A proceeds of crime hearing to recover finances associated with the offending is to take place in 2027.
Senior investigating officer Det Supt Robin Fuller said it was a "complex investigation that involved meticulous enquiries, evidence gathering and partnership working".
"During the investigation three of the offenders all fled the country to try and evade justice. However, we worked with our criminal justice partners internationally to bring them back to be held accountable for their crimes.
"The examination of bank accounts showed the group was making huge amounts of cash from the illegal business they'd been running since 2015.
"All initially denied being involved in any criminal activity but with the strength of evidence that we were able to present they pleaded guilty to various offences."
Louisa Robertson, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "This group ran a trafficking operation, exploiting women from other European countries.
"Their actions were abhorrent, treating human beings as commodities."
description: George Filip led a "substantial and sophisticated" crime group that trafficked at least 16 victims.

title: Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
text:
Russell Brand accusers 'haunted' for years by alleged crimes, court hears
Some of the women in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault case have been "haunted" for years by what they allege he did to them, jurors have been told.
In her closing speech at London's Southwark Crown Court on Friday, prosecutor Reil Karmy-Jones KC said the women had "nothing to gain" from coming forward apart from "some closure".
Speaking for the defence, Polly Dyer told jurors Brand had pleaded guilty and been fined over possession of cannabis in 1995, but had no other "convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings".
Brand, 51, is on trial facing seven charges; three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. He denies the charges.
Karmy-Jones KC told the court that this case brings together six different women, none of whom knows each other.
She said that while all the alleged victims have since moved on with their lives, due to this trial they have been forced to "relive what has happened to them".
None of the women involved has "sought the limelight" or "any kind of publicity", she said, adding there was "no benefit to them from perhaps some closure."
Referring to Brand's accusers' evidence the prosecutor said "how many said he was nice and then there was a like a personality change…
"His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty," Karmy-Jones KC said.
She added that the complainant's evidence had been that "he didn't listen when I said no, he didn't stop, he didn't care, pulling pushing… thrusting".
"In the rape cases, he kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim."
The prosecutor also dismissed the idea that a documentary had caused the women to "re-invent" what actually happened.
"There is no magic force in this documentary", she added.
"What in fact happened was these women have realised they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth."
She added: "Truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years."
She told the jury: "The experience of people raped may be something that looms a little bit larger in your mind rather than the intricacies of the outfit.
"The defendant couldn't really remember anything when he was interviewed, in stark contrast to now when he suddenly seems to remember all sorts of details about the week."
Addressing Brand's presented change in character, Karmy-Jones KC told the court "He may now be a completely different person to the man he was between 1999 and 2009."
She added: "He may well look back and not find some of his jokes funny".
"He may now treat women with kindness and consent".
Brand's wife Laura gave evidence yesterday, when she told the court her husband was a "kind and a wonderful father".
Karmy-Jones KC called her Russell Brand's "undoubtedly lovely wife", who "bravely" gave evidence.
However, she also noted that she was not with him at the time many of the alleged acts are said to have taken place.
"The reality is she wasn't there then, for the first five counts, she wasn't with him, nor was she with him for the final two counts."
"Any contact was, I believe, sparse."
In the final set of agreed facts in his trial, the court heard from Dyer about Brand's fine after he "pleaded guilty to one charge of possessing cannabis on 20 April 1995".
"He received a fine. He has no other convictions, cautions, reprimands or warnings", she said.
The trial continues.

title: Charity donations stolen from Halloween display
text:
Charity donations stolen from Halloween display
Thieves have stolen charity donations from a Halloween display which took months to prepare.
Philip Pattinson has been putting on displays at his home in Whitehaven for the past six years and this year is raising money for Hospice at Home West Cumbria.
But on Thursday morning, he discovered this year's wrestling-themed display had been damaged and a collection box with a week's worth of donations had been taken.
"I think if it had just been my stuff, I'd have just been angry, but I just started feeling sad, the money's for charity and somebody's stolen that money that people have donated," Pattinson told BBC Radio Cumbria.
"Part of the ticket booth was on the floor, when I had a look someone had broken in and taken the charity bucket out."
The bucket was left outside so people could visit the display when nobody was home and Pattinson said he did not know how much was in it.
"Sometimes there's loose change, sometimes when we open up the buckets, there's notes in, so we just don't know what's been put in," he said.
He said the actions had left locals shocked.
The theft is not the only setback Pattinson has suffered this year, with storms Austen and Boelo damaging the display last weekend.
He said he had to remove a fake dead body from a tree and lie it on his lawn and reapply "a lot of hair" to a spider which stands more than 2m (6.5ft) tall.
However, he and his wife plan to continue raising as much money as they can for the hospice.
They said visitors traveled from as far as Carlisle 38 miles (61km) away, just to see the displays.

Special powers to be used ahead of derby match

title: Eight building data centre planned near County Durham villages
text:
Huge data centre planned between villages
Early designs for a huge data centre complex will go on show to villagers who would be living near the development if it ever goes ahead.
Developer Tract wants to create the eight-building giant, which it calls Durham Technology Park, on land between the villages of South Hetton, Murton and Easington Lane in County Durham.
The project is still in the initial design stage and the company "does not know at this time" who might operate the facility.
Two public consultation events will take place in South Hetton next month with the developer hoping to submit an outline planning application in December.
Initial plans show seven main "data halls" alongside a logistics building, car parking and on-site electricity substation.
Tract said: "Development including power delivery takes six to eight years.
"Operators frequently plan ahead only for two or three years and we cover this gap by preparing the land and investing in land preparation, power development and supporting utility infrastructure."
Tract claimed the scheme would bring "up to" 1,500 construction jobs and, despite there being no company identified to run the centre, 310 full time roles at the finished data centre.
Documents offer no detail on how those figures have been compiled or how such variables as technological advances in the years until it is opened might affect staff requirements.
Tract listed the types of permanent roles as "network electrical engineers, technicians, operations management, customer services, security and welfare".
Two public events will take place at Robin Todd Community Centre on Front Street in South Hetton on 6 and 9 November.
"This is the first stage of consultation on the emerging proposals for Durham Technology Park," Tract said.
"We will reflect on your feedback before we submit an outline planning application."
