title: Lincolnshire family's vintage Christmas crackers sold at auction
text:
Vintage crackers have a new home after auction
A box of 12 unopened Christmas crackers believed to be about 100 years old has fetched £72 at auction.
It had been found in a wardrobe at John Goddard's house in Gainsborough, Lincolnshire.
His daughters, Nicky Goddard and Karen Grundy, think the crackers were given to their grandparents in the 1920s or 1930s by friends in Mablethorpe before being passed down to their parents as a wedding gift.
After the auction, Nicky said: "It was never [about] how much they were worth. The fact they were part of our wonderful family [meant that to us] they were priceless."
A sticker on the side of the box described them as "Joey Crackers" and said they were "filled with party hats and caps".
Auctioneer Paul Potter described them as a "little window into time".
He said: "We were pleased to sell them but would have liked a little bit more, perhaps.
"At the end of the day, it's an unusual item [and] there were quite a lot of bids.
"The story goes on. Someone else has got them now."
Nicky said: "It would be nice to know if the new owners were ever to open them. It would be lovely to know what was actually in them.
"But to us it was another legacy and memory of our wonderful parents."
The sale was held on Thursday at Potters Auction Saleroom in Messingham, North Lincolnshire.

title: Coventry teacher hopes poker will boost pension after retirement
text:
Deputy head hopes poker will boost pension
A deputy headteacher who took up poker as she approached her 50th birthday said she hoped to top up her pension by playing in tournaments around the world when she eventually retires.
Nicki Kelsall, from Nuneaton, only started playing the card game about three years ago, after being invited to attend a beginners' poker night run by her brother.
Despite being a bit nervous having never played it before, she said she "loved every minute" and went on to win her first tournament.
"I'd never played before, did not know what I was doing and I had beginner's luck because I actually won the whole tournament and ever since I've been hooked," she explained.
Kelsall, who works at a Coventry school, now runs her own league on a Monday night.
"I am a teacher, that is my day job," she said. "And working with lovely, wonderful children really helps me with my poker skills."
Kelsall also highlighted the social aspect of playing poker and described how it was a way to meet new people.
She added it was a great way for people she knew who had lost partners or who were a bit isolated, to find a new community.
"You can walk into a room full of strangers and by the end of it, they're all friends," she said.
"You can play from [age] 18 to 80 and you don't need to have a big, massive social network."
The teacher hopes to continue her love of poker after she retires by travelling to play at major poker tournaments.
"So I've decided when I get to retire... [in] whenever many years, I'm going to go around the world and play all the major poker tournaments and supplement my pension," she said.
"Currently there's a big tournament going on in Malta and I can't think of anywhere nicer to be."
Kelsall said poker was not as it was often portrayed on television, with spending limits in place.
"It's not, as you see on the TV, a smoky back room and it's all dark and people are losing their cars, it's not like that," she said.
"It's a £5 buy in and it's set at that so you can't be ridiculous. Some of them you might be able to enter twice but that is the maximum, so maximum you're going to be spending is £15."
She added: "Everybody's there just to have a great time and it's very friendly."

title: Fears over housing plans at Oasis leisure centre
text:
Fears over housing plans for Oasis leisure centre
Campaigners have called for greater support to reopen an "iconic" leisure venue amid "unsustainable" housing plans.
The Oasis in Swindon, Wiltshire, famous for its lagoon pool beneath a domed roof, closed in 2020. Last year, councillors approved plans for a developer to refurbish it, but refused permission for 700 flats to be built there.
During a drop-in event where people discussed the Swindon Local Plan, a blueprint that will shape future housing plans over the next 20 years, residents said they were disappointed about Oasis's uncertain future and called for more action.
Swindon Borough Council's local plan documents state a top priority is to support the delivery of new leisure facilities.
The Local Plan will guide the council's decisions on new homes, infrastructure, green spaces and community facilities over the next 20 years.
A public consultation on the proposals will close on 12 November.
In 2025, Seven Capital was granted permission to refurbish the Oasis, which included keeping the swimming pool and dome.
But the developer was told to go back to the drawing board when it came to building 700 homes on the site.
The developer is expected to submit a revised planning application and has already signed a deal with an operator to run the leisure site.
Neil Robinson, the lead campaigner of the Save Oasis Swindon campaign, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service the council needed to take action to ensure the town had enough leisure facilities to support new housing.
"I'm sad to see a lot of the leisure sites being allocated to housing, such as the Oasis.
"It's not sustainable. We are already creaking at the seams with our infrastructure.
"Like everyone, I want to see the Oasis back and reopened. However, there is a concern that there is going to be no sports hall.
"They only want it gone because they want to squeeze more houses onto the site," he added.
Speaking in April, Seven Capital chiefs said they remained committed to bringing the "iconic community venue" back into use.
Issues around houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) in Swindon were also discussed at the meeting.
Shelagh Gough, a resident of Old Town, said HMOs were "extremely useful" for young people who cannot afford deposits for houses, but said some had caused issues such as anti-social behaviour and fly-tipping.
Tim Thomas, lead planning policy officer at the council, added that the most positive part of the plan is the development of the town centre, which aims to "bring life back to the town" and improve facilities.
Under the proposals, the council wants to "strengthen its retail core" and "support the delivery of new leisure and cultural facilities".
Up to 3,800 new homes could also be built in central Swindon.
"Proposals for development in the central area will contribute positively towards its enhancement," the Local Plan's documents state.
"And [create] regeneration as a vibrant and regionally important mixed-use cultural, commercial and leisure hub, where people enjoy living, working, shopping, and relaxing."
Swindon Borough Council and Seven Capital have been approached for comment.

title: Orsett minor injuries unit moves to Grays
text:
Minor injuries unit moves to new location
A minor injuries unit (MIU) in Essex is to move to Thurrock Community Hospital on Monday.
The new site will be located at the John Tallack Centre in Long Lane, Grays, a mile and a half away from the former site in Orsett, and will open at 10:00.
Patients with a minor injury up until that point should contact NHS 111, visit their pharmacist or go to the Basildon Hospital emergency department, the Essex integrated care board said.
Dr Matt Sweeting from the board told BBC Essex that the move to the new unit, which cost £1m to upgrade, "would make services better".
He said the old unit did not have enough space to see the number of patients they would like.
"We think we can see double the amount of new patients in that facility, so I am excited it's being used," Sweeting added.
Plans for relocating health services at the hospital began in 2018, with critics fearing the move would amount to a "postcode lottery".
Gary Jones CBE, former head of the A&E department at the unit in Orsett, said he hoped patient services would remain the same after the move.
"One of the main concerns is that residents don't want to see any of the current facilities in Orsett moved away from the Thurrock area," he said.
The new site includes a purpose-built wound care room with integrated shower facilities and a dedicated plaster room.
NHS Essex has also reassured people that the 251 parking spaces at Thurrock Community Hospital would be able to accommodate visitors.
From April 2027, the unit is due to expand services to include minor illnesses as well as minor injuries, with longer opening hours.
The new Urgent Treatment Centre is expected to see almost 54,000 patients a year, compared with around 29,000 patients currently using the MIU service.

title: Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision
text:
Democratic senator blames Egypt press crackdown on US military aid decision
A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.
Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.
Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Mada Masr and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.
Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.
Washington sends Egypt £1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.
US law allows up to £320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.
In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.
Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.
Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".
Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.
"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.
US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.
The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Mada Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

title: Wildlife body loses lynx reintroduction High Court challenge
text:
Wildlife body loses lynx High Court challenge
An organisation trying to bring lynx back to northern England has lost a High Court challenge.
Lynx UK Trust applied for a three-year trial in 2022 which could have seen three of the animals from Sweden released into Kielder Forest, but it was refused by Natural England.
The trust challenged the environmental body over the refusal to proceed to a full assessment but Ms Justice Obi dismissed the claim, saying: "On Natural England's understanding of the law, the proposed release could not lawfully be implemented."
The big cats have been extinct in the wild in the UK for centuries, but those backing reintroduction have claimed it would benefit biodiversity and control deer populations.
In July, Northumberland County Council backed a motion stating it would not support any effort to release lynx into the wild, but a consultation last year found 72% of respondents in the North East supported the reintroduction of the big cats.
Non-aligned Rothbury councillor Steven Bridgett, who proposed the council's motion, called the High Court result excellent.
Lynx UK Trust originally applied in 2017 for six lynx to be released into the forest as part of a five-year trial, but this was refused by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) the following year.
The group then submitted a revised proposal in 2022 for a three-year trial involving the release of the three lynx from Sweden.
But that was also refused by Natural England the same year, with the body claiming such a release was prohibited by the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976 (DWAA), which makes it an offence to release certain animals into the wild.
Lynx UK Trust challenged the refusal in the High Court, with its lawyers claiming the animals could still be released under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 (WCA).
The WCA allows authorities to issue licences for the release of animals which are not "ordinarily resident" in the wild in the UK, despite the terms of DWAA.
The trust also argued at the hearing earlier this month the terms of the DWAA had been "impliedly repealed" by the terms of the WCA.
Natural England and Defra opposed the claim.
In a 16-page judgment, Obi said: "Properly construed, the DWAA continues to apply to lynx as a scheduled dangerous wild animal.
"I am unable to accept either the claimant's primary submission that the Act ceases to apply upon deliberate release pursuant to a licence under... the WCA, or its alternative submission that the relevant provisions have been impliedly repealed by the later enactment of the WCA."

title: How a passenger's confession helped convict her cousin of murder
text:
How a passenger's confession helped convict her cousin of murder
Warning: This article contains distressing content
One afternoon in April, a children's nursery worker approached her manager in what she described as an hysterical state.
Gabrielle Debotte said she had something serious to tell Nicola Goddard, adding: "You're going to hate me and I'm going to lose my job."
What the 27-year-old said next proved a turning point in the investigation into the death of popular head teacher Michael Mullins, who had been struck by a car the previous day and dragged under its wheels for more than a mile.
Debotte told the astonished Goddard she not only knew who was responsible for hitting the 56-year-old as he cycled home from work, but she witnessed what happened from the passenger seat.
That night, having initially been treated as a suspect, she sat in the interview suite at Stretford Police Station and named her cousin, 35-year-old former mechanic Simon Richardson, as the driver.
Thanks in part to the evidence provided by Debotte, Richardson was found guilty of murder after a two-week trial at Manchester's Minshull Street Crown Court.
The contrasts between the lives of the killer and his victim were stark.
Less than a month before he struck the head teacher, Richardson was freed from prison.
He had served 47 days on remand awaiting sentence for stalking, harassment, threats to damage property and assaulting an emergency worker, and was freed on 26 March after being sentenced to a non-custodial community order.
In the following weeks, he was "sofa-surfing" between various addresses - including the home Debotte shared with her father in Altrincham, Greater Manchester.
In contrast, the head teacher had spent the past 17 years leading Stretford Grammar School, where he was known as a man of "unshakeable principles and a compassionate leader".
To his family, he was a beloved husband, father and grandfather, who "truly excelled" in his "role as grandad".
He was a lover of sport and remained physically fit, regularly cycling the 19 miles between the school and his home in Northwich, Cheshire.
At 17:35 BST on 20 April, he changed into his cycling clothes, put on his helmet and set off as normal.
Detectives would later be able to plot his journey via his Apple watch, which monitored his speed, location and heart rate.
Not far from the cyclist's starting point, a black Volvo XC90 was already catching the attention of other drivers as it sped "erratically" along the semi-rural roads on the outskirts of Trafford and north-east Cheshire.
It was being driven by Richardson, who had agreed to give his cousin a lift from Altrincham to a beauty salon in Lymm to pick up some weight-loss jabs.
In court, Debotte told jurors Richardson had been driving very fast and when she told him to slow down, his only response was to "smirk" and claim he was "a professional driver".
At 18:07, the car reached a junction in Warburton, Trafford, which connected Dunham Road with Paddock Lane.
According to Debotte and other witnesses, the Volvo ignored stop signs and road markings on Dunham Road as it attempted to turn left.
Debotte told the court she shouted "bike" three times, but Richardson made no attempt to slow down or brake before the Volvo smashed into the left side of the cyclist.
Witnesses saw the head teacher being thrown into the air while his bike, phone, part of his helmet and a wireless earphone were scattered across the road.
Witness Leon Dalziel-Bush, who saw the crash from his own vehicle, said the Volvo was going at such speed that "by the time I processed what had happened, it had gone".
Dalziel-Bush and others got out to help, but after searching in ditches and grass verges, they realised the cyclist was nowhere to be seen.
Richardson, who according to Debotte, stopped for a "split-second" before accelerating away, was already guilty of very serious criminal offences.
What happened over the next four minutes or so, prosecutors argued in court, made him a murderer.
The prosecution case hinged on whether it could prove Richardson was aware the cyclist was trapped and suffering increasingly appalling injuries just inches from his feet.
Phil Barnes KC, prosecuting, told the jury that many of them would know what it feels like to drive "with a flat tyre, or with wheels that are slightly out of balance or misaligned".
"Now imagine driving your car, at north of 60mph, with a fully grown human being wedged in the suspension and steering assembly of one of your wheels," he said.
Barnes had suggested it "must have been obvious" to Richardson that the 56-year-old was there, but "he carried on regardless", knowing his actions "were in all likelihood killing the man beneath his feet".
But, thanks to Debotte's workplace revelation, the case was built on much more than that simple premise.
When she gave her statement to police, she described a scene of absolute shock and panic in the car, complete with "screaming and crying".
"I had never seen anything like that in my life," she said, adding: "I still have visions of it."
She also recalled how "moaning" could clearly be heard from beneath the Volvo as it sped away and that Richardson blurted out: "He's under the car."
Detectives would be able to prove, via watch and phone data, that his car had stopped on Wet Gate Lane in Lymm a short time after the collision.
The data showed the car had remained stationary on the rural country lane for about 90 seconds, as the cyclist was still clinging to life.
Debotte's account of those moments was absolutely crucial to proving Richardson was guilty of more than causing death by dangerous driving and failing to stop.
She said as she sat "frozen" in the passenger seat, he got out, walked around the front of the vehicle and tried to pull the head teacher free.
When the first attempt failed, he returned to the driver's seat and moved the steering wheel to try and free the wheels.
Debotte said Richardson got out again and crouched down to make another attempt to pull his victim free.
After failing again, he started the engine and drove further along Wet Gate Lane.
CCTV from a nearby farm showed the car swerving from side-to-side before the cyclist was finally thrown clear on to a grass verge.
From the position he was found, prosecutors were also able to say that the car must have driven over his body when it reversed and turned back towards the main road, all but ensuring his injuries were fatal.
The court was shown distressing evidence in support of Debotte's account, including images of a sharp-angled tyre mark left in a pool of blood where the car had stopped.
The jury heard the mark could only have been made by the wheels being turned while the car was stationary.
Nobody was around when the 56-year-old was thrown from the vehicle and left to his fate, but a few minutes later, motorcylist Andrew Beasant-Roberts found him after following a trail of blood from close to the crash site just over a mile away.
Beasant-Roberts made a 999 call and tried to perform CPR, but it was too late.
Detectives later found CCTV footage which showed Richardson and Debotte at Lymm Service Station minutes later, filling the car with petrol.
The pair then finished the errand they initially set out to do and picked up Debotte's jabs from the salon in Lymm.
She was dropped off at her Altrincham home at 18:45, where she stayed until she left for work again the following morning.
After dropping her off, Richardson quickly arranged to swap the Volvo for a silver Ford Transit work van with an associate.
He returned to Debotte's house in the van with a friend and the pair came and went from the house throughout the night.
Debotte said the men had been "laughing and joking" while listening to music and drinking her father's alcohol, but Richardson also lost his temper when she asked them to leave, punching a hole in plasterwork and kicking a chair.
She said there were no direct threats, but Richards outlined an account for her to give to police if they came knocking, which she wrote down in a note-taking app on her phone.
It included instructions to say she had lent Richardson her bank card on the day before and had not seen him again until late on the day of the crash.
However, Debotte said she already "knew she was going to talk to the police" and would be telling the truth.
In court, Debotte accepted she "absolutely" could have done more to alert the police to what had happened earlier, but her decision to seek them out before anyone else knew she had been in the vehicle allowed them to treat her as a witness.
Based on her description of the van, Greater Manchester Police officers found it the following day in Failsworth.
Despite knowing he was being tailed by a trained pursuit driver, Richardson tried to flee, first speeding through narrow residential streets and then making a final futile attempt to escape on foot.
He has never given a public account of his actions on 20 April.
The court heard he declined to answer police questions and on 22 October, at the conclusion of the prosecution case, the jury were told he would not be giving evidence in his own defence.
Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, explained while questioning witnesses that Richardson denied he knew the cyclist was under the car and denied he had got out of the vehicle on Wet Gate Lane.
However, the evidence and the testimony of Debotte meant the jury were sure he was guilty of more than a serious driving offence and fully convinced he had made the conscious decision to drag a helpless and well-respected family man to a most horrific death.
Richardson is due to be sentenced on Monday.

title: Fears for mature Scots Pines burned by huge Cairngroms wildfire
text:
Fears for mature Scots Pines burned by huge Highland wildfire
Mature Scots Pine trees may be lost from a Highland landscape hit by a huge summer wildfire, experts fear.
Forestry and Land Scotland say the blaze around Glenmore in the Cairngorms may have led to the loss of many so-called "granny pines" which have matured over centuries.
They say their loss removes important seed sources and makes it more difficult for the species to regenerate.
However, the Scottish government agency said there were many encouraging signs of natural recovery among other species following the fire.
It burned through about 10 sq miles of forest and moorland near Aviemore in July and August.
Forestry and Land Scotland staff who have been monitoring the site have recorded birch, rowan and willow regenerating from surviving stems and root systems.
Large areas of hillside have also been observed turning green again as grasses, bracken and blaeberry begin to make a comeback.
The agency said this was particularly apparent where moisture had remained in the soil or where fire intensity was lower.
Deer and capercaillie are now being regularly spotted in the fire damaged area, attracted by the new grass growth.
FLS forestry management and stewardship forester Eelco de Jong said the recovery of broadleaf vegetation was promising with lots of birch, rowan and willow expected to grow back quickly.
However, he warned that there were "significant challenges" ahead because of organic soil layers being badly affected and due to damage to the area's renowned Scots pine.
He said: "The concern is many of the oldest 'granny pines' could be lost, removing important seed sources and habitat for species such as capercaillie."
"Some of these veteran trees were more than 100 or 200 years old and, where losses occur, it could take centuries for trees of a similar stature to return to the landscape."
description: Experts say some older Scot pine damaged by fire could die removing an important source of seeds

title: Senior Staffordshire Police officer charged with sex offence
text:
Senior police officer charged with sex offence
A serving senior police officer has appeared in court charged with a sex offence.
Darren McGrath, who worked as a chief inspector for Staffordshire Police, has been charged with sexual assault by penetration against a woman aged 16 or over, alleged to have taken place between 1 July 2015 and 31 July 2016.
At Cannock Magistrates Court on Friday, the 44-year-old, of Stoke-on-Trent, spoke only to confirm his name.
McGrath has been released on bail and is due to appear at Stoke-on-Trent Crown Court on 30 November.
He was appointed commander of the Staffordshire Moorlands policing team in 2025.
In a statement, Staffordshire Police said the incident had happened in 2015, and that McGrath was suspended from duty at the start of the investigation.

title: Swansea Council cancels 'too raunchy' Magic Mike-style strip show
text:
Magic Mike-style strip show cancelled for being 'too raunchy'
The frontman of a male strip show says he was "disappointed" after indirectly finding out one of its performances had been cancelled for being "too raunchy".
The Magic Men Australia World Tour, featuring choreographed routines, shirtless dancers and audience interaction, was set to perform at Brangwyn Hall, Swansea, on Friday.
Headliner William Parfitt said he found out about the cancellation "one week" before the show was set to take place, although he was not officially informed of the decision by either the venue or the council at the time.
Swansea Council apologised, and said it had taken the decision not to let the Magic Men show go ahead following "concerns raised with us".
In a statement, a spokesperson for the council added: "We're sorry for the disappointment this will cause."
Parfitt said he had only received a response regarding the nature of the cancellation after he had contacted the organisers.
He said the explanation was "extremely vague" with references made to concerns that the show was considered "too raunchy".
In an Instagram post, TikTok star Parfitt said "I never thought that we would get cancelled in Wales for being too raunchy", adding that it was "a first for Magic Men Australia".
Parfitt described the decision as "incredibly disappointing" - not only for the team who had spent "considerable time and money preparing" - but also for "the hundreds of women who were looking forward to attending".
Reacting to the cancellation, 20-year-old Grace Rogerson said people should be "able to go and see what they want".
"If it's a show being put on and people have bought tickets for it, I think you're well within your rights to go and see it," she said.
"And I think the arts is something that should not be censored," the student added.
Tracey Garey, 61, from Swansea, was shocked to hear it had been cancelled.
"Those ladies wanted a good night, going out to enjoy and going out for a laugh," she said.
"I went to see the Chippendales from a distance... each to their own."
But others were not convinced the venue was the right location for the show, as Audrey Chapman, 86, and her friend, Vera, 84, asked why Swansea council had agreed to it the first place.
"The Brangwyn Hall is not for something like that, for starters. They could find a club to do that in," said Audrey.
Considered one of Swansea's "landmarks" Brangwyn Hall is a Grade II listed building, which has previously hosted a number of acts, ranging from Queen, to the London Philharmonic Orchestra, and the Manic Street Preachers.
Lian Cruz, 19, agreed it was not a fitting location and claimed the show sounded "a bit weird".
"I wouldn't have thought that Swansea would do that, in Brangwyn Hall," he said.
"I mean, if it was too raunchy, it was too raunchy.
"I wouldn't want that here," he added.
Ticket holders have been contacted and informed they will receive a full refund.
Parfitt told his TikTok followers that any Swansea ticket-holders booking an alternative show elsewhere in the UK would be upgraded to VIPs, promising "a meet-and-greet with the boys" so fans could decide for themselves whether the show is too raunchy.
He said the team "sincerely hope to return to Swansea in the near future with a venue that welcomes the show" and give "Welsh fans the experience they were looking forward to".
description: Magic Men frontman says he was "disappointed" by Swansea Council's decision to cancel amid "concerns".

title: US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
text:
US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon and Reddit down
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
'Investors have turned ruthless'
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.
description: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.

title: Children's safety tops online worries, Guernsey survey says
text:
Children's safety tops online worries, survey says
Harm to children poses the greatest risk online, a survey by Guernsey's data protection commissioner has suggested.
Of those surveyed, 73% of people highlighted concerns about online harm to children.
The Office of the Data Protection Authority survey also suggested "the adoption, potential and risks of artificial intelligence is at the forefront of people's minds".
Commissioner Brent Homan said the results highlighted gaps in people's understanding about their rights and his office planned to launch more support.
The commissioner said he was not surprised by the results on the protection of children and his office had an education programme to promote and protect children's rights.
Homan said it was also "clear that people care about information and the protection of information".
The survey suggested 73% of respondents had used it for personal work but 60% of businesses said they were not using it.
"There is a demand and desire to do it right," said Homan.
The survey suggested "very few" people were confident they could recognise when AI was used and "a clear majority" were concerned about how it was used.

title: Pope Leo XIV casts historic vote in US midterm election
text:
Pope Leo XIV becomes first pontiff to vote in a US election
Pope Leo XIV has submitted his mail-in ballot in Illinois, for the midterm elections, becoming the first-ever pope to vote in a US election.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement.
The Chicago-born pontiff is the first US citizen to hold the Vatican's highest seat, after his selection in May 2025.
Since then, he has clashed with the Trump administration over various issues, including immigration enforcement and the US-Israel war with Iran.
"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office said, including during his years in Peru.
The US midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress and have a significant impact on the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Elections will be held nationwide on 3 November, but early voting has begun in most states.
According to NBC News, the Pope requested his mail-in ballot from the Will County Clerk's Office on 3 October.
Less than two weeks later, the Vatican announced he had surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung after he was diagnosed with lung cancer.
The Vatican confirmed last week that the Pope, aged 71, will travel as planned to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in early November.
Tensions escalated between the Pope and the US president in April, after the Pope called for peace in the wake of US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
"I don't think he's doing a very good job," Trump said about the Pope afterwards.
"We don't like a Pope that's going to say that it's OK to have a nuclear weapon," he continued. "I'm not a big fan of Pope Leo."
Pope Leo followed with his own remarks later, saying: "The mission of the Church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace," according to Reuters.
"If someone wants to criticise me for preaching the Gospel... I hope simply to be listened to because of the value of God's words."
In the final few days before the midterms, Republican and Democratic officials alike are sprinting across the country to boost their party's chances of success.
Polls suggest Democrats are the favourite to gain control of the lower chamber of Congress, called the House of Representatives, and are poised to win seats in Republican-leaning areas that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
Democrats also appear to have a chance to win additional seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress.
The gloomy outlook for Trump's Republican party has seen the president hold several rallies in states where Republican victories are typically all but guaranteed.
description: The Chicago-born pontiff, who has a tense relationship with Trump, mailed in a ballot for the midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress.

title: Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
text:
Police watchdog to investigate Met over letter about Meghan's father
The UK police watchdog is to investigate the Metropolitan Police's handling of a letter containing allegations against Thomas Markle that was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had decided an investigation was required into the force's "failure to pass on allegations of serious offending... to relevant overseas authorities at the time".
The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.
He has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".
On Thursday the Met said it had voluntarily referred itself to the IOPC.
The letter at the heart of the IOPC investigation was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.
The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".
Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.
Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".
The IOPC will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas.
The policing watchdog also said it had decided a further matter, relating to an alleged data breach in which information was passed on to a third party, "should be returned to the force to be appropriately dealt with". No details were provided about the circumstances of the alleged breach.
The Met said on Thursday that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".
The letter was forwarded by officers to the Sussexes' royal office rather than to Meghan personally, while there have been reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to ask for one from the Sussexes.
The watchdog will have to consider how the contents of the letter were treated by the force at the time.
Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, previously told the BBC she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".
"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken [and] why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies."
Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told the police in the Philippines about material which was alleged to contain sexual images of children, which he had claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.
Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.
Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims. Police there have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.
However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they can examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".
description: The police force faces probe over its handling of a letter containing allegations about Meghan's father.

text:
Woman on train slapped six-year-old boy she didn't know across the face
Police are searching for a woman who slapped a six-year-old boy across the face on board a train in Edinburgh.
The incident happened at about 15:00 on Saturday on a rail service that had travelled from Morpeth, Northumberland, and had just arrived at Edinburgh Waverley - its final stop.

title: Scientists looking for Barrow locals to help with accent study
text:
Tongues a talking point in accent study
Linguists are looking for volunteers - and their tongues - to help them better understand variations in north-west England accents.
Professor of phonetics at Lancaster University Claire Nance said her team was looking for 40 people in Barrow, Cumbria, to help with their study.
The scientists are seeking to better understand how tongue position can affect accents.
"Barrow is particularly interesting for accents due to its rich industrial history and rapid growth in the 19th Century," Nance said.
The team will be taking recordings from individuals at Barrow Library on 7 November between 11:00 and 15:30 GMT.
Nance said the study would involve individuals reading a few words out loud while a ultrasound probe held beneath their chin records the position of their tongues.
It is part of a wider project looking into how the long-term positions of the tongue, mouth and jaw can lead to regional accents and different ways of speaking.

title: Investigation after contractor dies on Blenheim Palace estate
text:
Investigation after contractor dies at Blenheim Palace
An investigation has been launched after a man was killed by a tipper truck on the grounds of Blenheim Palace.
Thames Valley Police said it was called to the Unesco World Heritage site at about 13:00 BST on 14 October following an incident on the palace grounds.
It said a 50-year-old man had died in the "industrial incident", and that it was investigating the fatality alongside the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).
Blenheim Palace, in Woodstock, Oxfordshire, is one of the country's most complete country estates, and the ancestral home of wartime Prime Minister Sir Winston Churchill.
Dominic Hare, the palace's chief executive, said he was "deeply saddened" by the death - which he said had taken place on a construction site on the wider estate.
He said the man had been working as a contractor at the site, and that "heartfelt condolences" were with his family, friends and colleagues at this "extremely difficult time".
"We are supporting Thames Valley Police and the Health and Safety Executive with their investigation, and it would not be appropriate to comment further while that continues," he added.
The HSE confirmed to the BBC that it was investigating the incident.
The 12,000-acre Blenheim estate is the current ancestral seat of James Spencer-Churchill, 12th Duke of Marlborough.
It was built as a gift to the 1st Duke of Marlborough from Queen Anne after his victory at the Battle of Blenheim in 1704.
In recent years, it has become one of Oxfordshire's top tourist attractions, and has hosted European leaders as well as US President Donald Trump, who attended a dinner as part of a state visit to the UK in 2018.

title: Barrier plan for Shipley Country Park delayed
text:
Barrier plan for country park delayed
The brakes have been put on plans to block off a car park at a country park overnight to tackle nuisance driving.
Derbyshire County Council said a barrier would be installed at Coppiceside Car Park in Slack Lane, Heanor, from 1 November after complaints about vehicle-related disturbances, illegal off-road driving and vandalism, including damage to parking machines after dark.
But the barriers to the car park, which is used to access Shipley Country Park, will now not come into force until 16 November.
The council said this will allow time to work with partners including Parkrun to organise earlier access on certain days.
The barrier will be locked overnight throughout the year, with different closing times depending on the season.
Between 1 April and 31 October, the car park will close from 20:00 until 09:00. From 1 November to 31 March, it will close from 17:00 until 09:00.
Drivers have been warned to remove their vehicles before the gates close. An out-of-hours service will be available to release vehicles, although a charge will apply.
The council said the measures followed reports of "vehicle-related anti-social behaviour, nuisance driving and illegal off-road vehicle use" in and around the park.
Additional parking will remain available at the nearby Mapperley Car Park.
Visitors have also been asked to continue reporting criminal damage, anti-social behaviour and nuisance vehicles to Derbyshire Police.
Heanor resident Steve Beer, 62, visits the park twice a day with his dog Sulley and said the new arrangements had been met with opposition.
He said: "The gate's not a problem, it's just the times.
"They're not prepared to move on 9 o'clock in the morning, and when I walk my dog, there's loads of dogs there from six onwards.
"It's fine for me but a lot of the older people that's disabled they just can't walk down there."
The county council has been approached for comment.

title: Man on trial thought he had drugged wife's consent, court told
text:
Man thought he had drugged wife's consent, court told
One of four men on trial for sexually abusing a woman who had been drugged by her husband thought he had her consent and stopped when she became uncomfortable, a court has heard.
Philip Young, a former Tory councillor for Swindon, has admitted to drugging and raping his now ex-wife Joanne over a 13-year period.
Four men who Young is alleged to have recruited to abuse his wife at their home are now on trial at Winchester Crown Court.
The jury heard that Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, told police he thought he was helping a married couple to "live out their kink" but left after getting the "vibe [Joanne] wasn't enjoying it".
Warning: This story contains distressing details
The jury was told that Wiltshire Police's investigation into Young was sparked when he put extreme pornographic images online.
Officers went to speak to Young on 4 July 2023 about three extreme image of bestiality they had been alerted to.
Police then found "intimate" videos on his devices of Joanne restrained and blindfolded while other men engaged in sexual activity with her, the court was told.
Joanne - who has waived her legal right to anonymity - told police this was being done without her consent or knowledge, the jury heard.
Sanderson-Doyle, Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, are on trial accused of sexual offences against Joanne - which they deny.
The court was cleared earlier so only the jury, defendants, barristers and Joanne could watch videos of alleged sexual abuse by three of the defendants.
'Just a young guy trying things'
Sanderson-Doyle, of Swindon, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in 2016, told police he answered Young's advert on Craigslist, which said something like "you'll come in, have sex with her and leave".
In the transcript of his police interview read to the jury, the defendant said he thought it was "just a married couple trying to live out whatever their kink is," and he was "just a young guy trying out new things".
Sanderson-Doyle said when he arrived at the house, Young took him to their bedroom where he found Joanne "tied up and blindfolded" as she had been pictured in the online ad.
The defendant said he started to perform a sex act on Joanne but there was "a clear line where I could tell she wasn't comfortable", which prompted Young to say "I don't think she's feeling it".
"I thought I had her consent, I didn't know she was drugged," he told police.
Sanderson-Doyle said that he had believed Joanne was consenting because she seemed "relaxed", was moving and "didn't seem distressed at all".
When asked by the detective if he had done his due diligence to get her consent, he said: "Yeah I think so, from the conversations I had with him and what I walked into, I thought I had consent from them."
In the police interview with Norman Macksoni, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, who denies one count of rape in 2017, he said Young contacted him on a website called Fab Swingers.
In the transcript read out in court, he said he thought he was taking part in a couple's "fantasy".
The defendant said when he entered the bedroom, Young sat next to Joanne on the bed and had a conversation with her.
Macksoni told police he had sex with Joanne, then got up and left, without interacting with her.
"But there was no way that she was drunk or wasn't coherent," he said in his interview.
"I wouldn't be sleeping with someone who wasn't coherent, I wouldn't do that, that's not what Fab Swingers is about."
He said he had arranged to have sex with couples before and "it's normally the husband that does the talking".
The jury also watched video footage of the arrest of Richard Wilkins, of Toothill, Swindon, who denies one count of rape and one of assault by penetration in 2016.
The fourth defendant is Mohammed Hassan, of Swindon, who denies one count of sexual touching in 2023.
Young, a former Conservative Swindon councillor, previously admitted to 48 offences against his ex-wife, including voyeurism, rape, administering a substance with intent, assault by penetration and sexual assault.
He has also pleaded guilty to three charges of making indecent images of children, one of possessing prohibited images of children, and four of possessing an extreme pornographic image.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
Young and Hamilton will be sentenced at the end of the trial, which is expected to last up to four weeks.

title: Hampshire parents fined for employing teen son in family food trailer
text:
Parents fined for employing teen son in food trailer
The parents of a 14-year-old boy have been fined for allowing him to work on the family's mobile food trailer.
Karen and Greg Olejarka pleaded guilty at Southampton Magistrates' Court to breaching Hampshire County Council's byelaws prohibiting under-16s from working in commercial kitchens.
The Hampshire couple have been fined £600 each and ordered to pay a further £6,000 in costs.
The family had argued they were supporting their son Dexter's passion for cooking by allowing him to prepare food in the trailer from the age of 12.
District Judge Anthony Callaway said it was significant that Dexter was seen using deep fat fryers, knives and working in a commercial kitchen run for profit.
The family had argued the food trailer should not be regarded as a commercial kitchen, and insisted that Dexter's education was not affected.
Greg Olejarka said: "No one considered Dexter in all of this. They prosecute us as parents for supporting our child to become someone with skills."
Hampshire County Council became aware of Dexter after a YouTube video praising the teenager's cooking skills showed him using a grill and a deep fat fryer.
The family said they were tackling the dispute with the council while supporting another son, while he received treatment for blood cancer.
Karen Olejarka said they pleaded guilty as fighting the case would have been too expensive.
"We've gone from fighting for our second son to be able to live his life, to fighting for our oldest son to live," she said.
At an earlier hearing, Hampshire County Council said it had attempted to resolve the issue before prosecution, but prosecutor Ian Jenkins said Dexter's father had "gone nuclear" and made it a national issue.
What is the law?
Child employment in England is covered by the Children and Young Person Act 1933, and also by local byelaws drawn up by each local authority.
While Hampshire's byelaws state that "children may do light work from the age of 13 years until they are no longer of compulsory school age", employment in commercial kitchens is prohibited until the age of 16.
The council said: "We will only consider legal action in the most exceptional circumstances, where there are safeguarding concerns that cannot be addressed in other ways.
"The defendants in this case pleaded guilty and they appear to have recognised that the employment of Dexter in a commercial kitchen was unlawful."
Dexter's parents said he was no longer helping out on the food trailer.

title: Speeding Sunderland teen with no brakes killed loved grandad
text:
Speeding teen with no brakes killed loved grandad
A speeding teenager with broken brakes who killed a beloved grandfather in a crash has been jailed for seven and a half years.
James Waddell was travelling at 72mph in a 30mph zone when he smashed into Paul Andrew Fulcher's car in Sunderland in April 2025, Newcastle Crown Court heard.
The 53-year-old's family said he was a "real man" who had been stolen from them, while Waddell was an "arrogant boy" and "killer".
Waddell, who was 19 at the time and is now 21, admitted causing death by dangerous driving. Judge Tim Gittins said he had been driving "like a maniac" and the teenager's "selfish, arrogant and thoughtless actions" had killed a much-loved family man.
Waddell had bought the red Subaru Forester XT on Facebook three days before the crash, prosecutor Emma Dowling said.
Shortly before 11:00 BST 14 April 2025, Fulcher was turning on to the A690 out of Ettrick Grove when Waddell, who was speeding along the main road, struck his VW Tiguan "with force", the court heard.
He suffered multiple injuries including broken ribs and a collapsed lung and died 11 days later in hospital from blunt force chest injuries, the court heard.
An investigation concluded three of the Subaru's four brakes were "metal on metal" with "no braking capacity left", Dowling said, with their defectiveness immediately obvious to anyone driving it.
Waddell was travelling at "no less than" 72mph in the 30mph zone when he hit Fulcher, the court heard, and had already alarmed other drivers with his impatience and speeding in the moments before the crash.
The grandfather would have had plenty of time to complete his manoeuvre safely if it were not for Waddell "tearing" along at excessive speed, Dowling said.
Five members of his family, including his mother, wife and daughters, attended court to tell Waddell of the utter devastation he had caused.
"The day you stole him you also stole our future plans," his wife told Waddell, adding the teenager had been driving like he was on a "racecourse" and her husband stood no chance.
"As you stand here, probably crying for your self pity, just remember, our family has been given a life sentence of pain and sorrow," she said.
One of the victim's daughters said she would be "forever haunted" seeing him "petrified" and "in so much pain" in hospital before he died.
"You are an arrogant 21-year-old boy who thinks you are above the law," she told Waddell, adding her father was a "real man" whose shoes the teenager would never be able to fill.
"You are not a human, you are a killer," she said.
Fulcher's family said he was the "best" man, hilarious and kind with hundreds of friends.
"This is the man you killed on the day you chose to drive like an idiot," one of them told Waddell.
The teenager had "ruined" so many lives, they said.
'Left painful void'
The court heard Waddell had a clean licence and no previous convictions, but had accrued eight points for driving without insurance five months after the crash.
He had also initially denied offending and sought to blame his victim, the court heard.
In mitigation, Harriett Snookes said Waddell was sorry and had been "demonstrably traumatised" by the crash.
Judge Tim Gittins said Waddell's car was in a "deplorable state" and the disrepair of its brakes "would have been readily apparent as a serious and dangerous problem" to the driver.
He said it was obvious Fulcher was the "embodiment of the heart and soul of a close family", who was "clearly much loved and loving" and "well respected" by many.
"Your selfish, arrogant and thoughtless actions in driving like a maniac that day have cost a man his life when he had years left to enjoy it with his family," the judge told Waddell.
"Just as importantly, you have left a painful void in the family's lives that clearly cannot be filled," Gittins said, adding their words should "echo in your conscience for the remainder of your days".
Waddell, of King Edward Street in Sunderland, was also banned from driving for 11 years and will have to pass an extended test.
description: The family of Paul Andrew Fulcher say his killer is an "arrogant boy" who "ruined" many lives.

title: Five men jailed over multi-million pound drug money ring
text:
Five gang members jailed over multi-million pound drug money ring
Five gang members have been jailed for their multi-million pound dirty cash operation.
They were accused of collecting, storing and moving criminal cash - most of which related to payments for cocaine, heroin and cannabis - between January 2020 and June 2020. However none of the men were involved in the supply or storage of drugs.
Anthony Carroll Sr, 57, his son Anthony Carroll Jr, 37, Ryan Carberry, 46, Marc Cooper, 34, and Michael Monaghan, 37, were caught after police broke into the EncroChat phone network in 2020.
They all pleaded guilty to an organised crime charge at the High Court in Glasgow.
Carroll Sr, of Glasgow's Milton, was jailed for four-and-a-half-years and Carroll Jr, from Glasgow's Maryhill, received three years.
Carberry, of Kirkintilloch, East Dunbartonshire, got three years and three months, Cooper, of Maryhill, was sentenced to two years and nine months and Monaghan, from Glasgow's Drumchapel area, will be locked up for three years.
Judge Lord Scott told them at the sentencing: "You each took part knowingly for months in a significant organised crime operation.
"Based on the snapshots and the scale of the money involved shows that it was a multi-million pound operation."
He said Carroll Sr's role was "significant" as he was "trusted with important parts of the working" of the gang.
The judge added: "The other four, your roles might be lesser roles but serious organised crime groups would not operate as they do without people like you prepared to carry out lesser but crucial roles."
All five men were given serious crime prevention orders, lasting five years for Carroll Sr and four years for each of the other men.
'Vast sums of cash'
The court heard Carroll Sr was in charge of counting, storing and distributing the large hauls of dirty cash from illegal activities - with almost £20m amassed in over just five months.
Prosecutor Leanne Cross said: "He also directed the other four to carry out this work on his behalf.
"He, in turn, answered to those at the top of the organised crime group, who were, by and large, based overseas."
Carroll Sr kept a record of the money controlled by by him and sent "lists" to high-ranking members of the gang via EncroChat.
Cross said Carroll Sr recorded £4m as income for the gang in January 2020, £3m the following month, another £2.6m in March, around £4m in April and £4.8m in the first half of May that year.
These were noted as payments for cocaine. The other list revealed around £1m was brought in from cannabis trafficking in the early part of 2020.
Cross said: "It is clear Carroll Sr was trusted by the organised crime gang to control vast sums of their cash over a significant period of time."
Carroll Jr was often in touch with his father about "stashes" to hide the illegal funds. It was also apparent he had ferried money to other gang members.
The gang had been kept under watch during the Operation Delfin police probe.
Police went on to discover £780,000 under floorboards in the son's home in May 2020.
This was shortly after Carroll Sr ordered him to remove the money from his own home after police swooped on two other gang members.
Carroll Sr's property was searched days later and officers seized mobile phones, £5,000 and just over 1,000 euros inside a cooker hood.
Meanwhile Carberry was described as a "cash collector" who helped organise a total of 75 pick-ups totalling over £6m.
He was directed by Carroll Sr, but also got orders from senior gang bosses.
Carberry's partner's home was raided in June 2020 and a total of £195,000 was discovered inside rucksacks.
As for Cooper, it was his job was to look after one of the mob's "cash counting houses" which involved reporting back to Carroll Sr.
One of his last messages said he had counted £1.8m in just a matter of weeks in May and June 2020.
Monaghan had a similar role to Cooper. Police seized two cash counting machines in a bedroom cupboard at his home in June 2020.
The prosecutor said: "Overall the messages show that this operation was well-organised from the top with everyone having clear roles and responsibilities.
"Cash collectors passed to the counters before everything was 'funnelled' to Carroll Sr.
"He then passed on to the safehouse holders for onward transportation."
The five were paid between £500-£1200 per week in "wages" for their involvement.
Prison sentence 'inevitable'
Simon Gilbride, defending Carroll Sr, told the sentencing: "His reward was small but significant and he acknowledges that he was involved in a role which facilitated the operation.
"It is something he profoundly regrets and wishes he never got involved in it at all."
Calum Weir, defending Carroll Jr, told the court that his client's relationship with his father had ended.
The lawyer added: "He is not stepping back from culpability - he realises what he became involved in and is paying the price for that."
Ross Yuill, defending Carberry, said: "He accepts the consequences. His financial reward was low here. He accepts his role in the overall process."
Tony Lenehan KC, defending Cooper, stated that his client took on the role due to his and his partner's financial circumstances at the time.
Kevin Jarvis, defending Monaghan, acknowledged that custody was "inevitable" due to the nature of the offence.
Two other men linked to the dirty cash gang were jailed earlier this year.
Alistair MacKenzie, 60, and Daniel Kerrigan, 56, were caught after a raid at a warehouse in Clydebank, West Dunbartonshire in May 2020.
description: The men amassed almost £20m over five months, mostly relating to payments for cocaine, heroin and cannabis.

title: Two arrested as 'small explosive devices' made safe in Brentwood
text:
Two arrested as 'small explosive devices' made safe
A man and a woman have been arrested after three "small homemade explosive devices" were discovered and "safely dealt with" at a property in Essex.
Police forced entry to a home on Sawyers Grove, Brentwood, at about 07:20 GMT, following reports of a disturbance.
The discovery of the suspicious items led to bomb disposal experts being called and a 100m (328ft) cordon being put in place, with 40 properties evacuated.
Essex Police said the arrested pair, in their 40s and from Brentwood, remained in custody for questioning on suspicion of offences under the Explosive Substances Act.
A number of wraps of suspected crack cocaine were also recovered during a search of the property, police added.
The cordon has since been lifted, and an investigation into the circumstances remains ongoing.
Police and Brentwood Borough Council established a rendezvous point for affected residents at the King George playing fields pavilion, while officers carried out their work.
Resident Michael Page, 84, said he was told to leave his home at about 11:30.
He said: "I got a rap on the door to say you've got to get out. They wouldn't tell me anything."
Vaughn Waites, 57, told the BBC he was out shopping with his wife and dog, but "came back and they wouldn't let us on to the estate".
Ch Insp Terry Fisher thanked people for their patience and understanding.
"We fully appreciate the disruption this incident has caused to residents, particularly those who had to leave their homes at short notice," he said.
"The cordon and evacuations were necessary precautions to ensure people's safety while specialist colleagues assessed the items and a thorough search of the address was carried out."

title: River Mersey tidal power project preferred location revealed
text:
River Mersey tidal power project location revealed
The preferred location for a "potentially transformational" tidal power scheme on the River Mersey has been revealed.
The proposed barrage has been a long-time ambition of Liverpool City Region Mayor Steve Rotheram who said he wants to harness the power of the river.
A 1.5 mile (2.4km) stretch of the River Mersey between Bromborough in Wirral and Otterspool in Liverpool has now been identified as the preferred area for the project.
The Liverpool City Region Combined Authority will be asked to approve the location at a meeting on 6 November. No construction work can take place until a Development Consent Order is granted and investment is in place.
A tidal power scheme has been mooted for the River Mersey since 2005 but was put on hold in 2011 when it was deemed not profitable enough in the medium term to attract investment.
A long ambition of Steve Rotheram, the plan was revived by Liverpool City Region Mayor in 2017 and in 2020 £2.5m of funding was approved for the project.
"For as long as I can remember, people have talked about harnessing the power of the River Mersey," Rotheram said.
"Identifying where the barrage could be built is a major step forward for a project that has the potential to be genuinely transformational – not just for our region, but for the country."
"At a time when events around the world can send energy prices soaring, we need to make better use of the resources we have on our own doorstep.
"We should be generating more of our own energy, strengthening our energy security and creating good jobs here at home."

title: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put 2 Dan Sullivans on ballot
text:
Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.
The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, including a request for election officials to separate ballots that rank retired teacher Dan J Sullivan.
Senator Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.
"I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."
Alaska's Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an official inquiry earlier this week into the alleged scheme.
Heyman did not immediately provide details of specific crimes his office would investigate.
Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.
The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to her campaign.
But those denials have not stopped the justice department (DOJ) and Republicans from attacking Peltola.
The DOJ has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the recruitment effort, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
No charges had been filed as of Friday evening.
"There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that are ongoing," Michael Heyman, the US attorney for the district of Alaska, said at a Friday afternoon press conference.
Later that day, lawyers for the Trump administration asked a federal judge to issue an order before Monday that would direct state election officials "to preserve and segregate" all ballots that rank Dan J Sullivan.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward argued in court documents that the move would be to investigate whether such ranking "was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary".
"These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration," he said.
But the state's Republican attorney general - the top prosecutor in the state - asked the court to toss the lawsuit and said the request from the Trump administration was "inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters' vital right to ballot secrecy".
The filing said there was "no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer".
What legal experts say about 'spoiler candidates'
Scott Kendall, an attorney who worked with Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in her 2010 and 2016 campaigns, told the BBC he was sceptical the actions described in the New York Times story broke the law.
Alaska law does not have specific good-faith requirements for candidates, Kendall explained - noting that spoiler candidates sometimes emerged in their contests.
"I freely admit there could be more facts, but I'm not going to speculate they exist," he said.
The spectre of a federal crimes could come into play if there was potential evidence of campaign finance violations, Kendall, as well as other legal experts, told the BBC. But such evidence has not yet emerged.
Kendall believed the primary risk to Peltola from the allegations is "absolute reputational harm".
The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.
On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.
A federal judge has expedited consideration and will weigh motions to dismiss brought by Alaska election officials and backed by the Peltola campaign and voting rights groups.
The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate.
The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up.
As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.
The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.
description: The incumbent Republican running for re-election and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters by recruiting a second Dan Sullivan to also stand in the race.
