title: Mayor defects from Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion
text:
Mayor defects from Greens after Zionism motion
The leader of the Green Party on Cornwall Council has defected following the party's recent "Zionism is racism" motion.
Drew Creek joined the Labour and Co-operatives on Thursday after the policy motion was passed at the Green Party's conference earlier this month.
Creek, who is Mayor of Newquay and serves as a councillor for Trenance ward, said he had "huge respect" for Greens across Cornwall but the motion "crossed a line".
The Cornwall Green Party said it was "deeply saddened" by Creek's decision to join Labour and said it does not "try to impose uniformity of belief" among its members and elected representatives.
The motion backed by Green members at its party conference said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
It has been criticised by Jewish groups, as well as some Green MPs and opposition political parties.
Creek said he hoped the Green Party would step back from the stance – but said instead, "Zack Polanski and the leadership has doubled down".
"I can't stand behind that, and I won't pretend otherwise," the councillor said.
He added: "People in Newquay don't want politicians driving division. They want someone who'll fix the roads, protect our coast, fight for local services and bring people together.
"That's the kind of politics I believe in and the kind of politics Andy Burnham has shown.
"Newquay is my home and where I am raising my family. I came into politics for one reason, to stand up for this town and the people in it. Labour is where I believe I can do that best, and I'm looking forward to getting on with the job."
Councillor Kate Ewert, Labour and Co-operative Group Leader on Cornwall Council said Creek's decision "highlights the serious questions about Zack Polanski's leadership".
Noah Law, MP for St Austell and Newquay, added: "In this period of polarised politics, it takes great courage to stand up for what you believe in.
"Having worked with Drew since my election, I have always found him to be steadfast in his beliefs, easy to work with, and a good advocate for Newquay."
'Disagreements'
A spokesperson for the Cornwall Green Party said Creek had "done excellent work as a Green councillor" and they understood there were "different views within the Green Party on the 'Zionism is Racism' motion".
They said: "Disagreements over the wording of this one motion should not distract from the fact that the Green Party is united in its condemnation of the racist genocide and ethnic cleansing that Israel is perpetrating in Gaza and the occupied territories, and united in its demand for much tougher sanctions on Israel.
"Labour, by contrast, refuses even to recognise that what we are seeing is genocide, and continues to allow arms exports to and intelligence-sharing with the government that is committing it.
"It's hard to see how anyone who is serious about action on climate, action to end extreme inequality, and action to prevent an ongoing genocide could switch their support to a party that is not serious about any of these."

title: Campaigners welcome Historic Railways Estate pledge
text:
Campaigners welcome rail bridge maintenance switch
Campaigners have welcomed plans to take the management of 3,000 railway bridges, tunnels and viaducts away from a government department accused of "cultural vandalism".
National Highways and its forerunner the Highways Agency have had oversight of what is known as the Historic Railways Estate since 2013, but control is to be given to new state body Great British Railways (GBR).
An alliance of campaigners called the HRE Group has been critical of National Highways' efforts, which included an arch near Brough, in Cumbria, being filled with tonnes of concrete in 2021.
This week, Rail Minister Lord Hendy said GBR would have "the capability, knowledge and experience to maintain the estate".
National Highways claimed the arch at Great Musgrave was unstable, but the work was refused retrospective planning permission and the local council ordered it to be removed.
At the time, Upper Eden Railway Heritage Partnership chair Phil Dew said National Highways had ignored objectors and acted with "total impunity", calling it "a case of cultural vandalism and desecration of a highly valued structure".
It was later revealed it cost about £352,000 to remove the infill - about three times the £124,000 it cost to do the work.
Great British Railways is set to take over the operation of many of Britain's rail infrastructure and passenger services a year after a railways bill currently going through the House of Lords is given Royal Ascent.
Speaking during a debate earlier this week, Lord Hendy added the government had "already been clear that the Historical Railways Estate will transfer to GBR" and the bill "contains the appropriate mechanisms to enable this".
The Department for Transport said timelines for the transfer of the estate were still to be decided.
HRE Group spokesman Graeme Bickerdike said the switch would be a positive step whenever it happened.
He said: "The broader and deeper expertise that's embedded within Great British Railways - and a more enlightened culture - should result in better outcomes, both for communities and the taxpayer."
He also called on the government to "expedite the transfer" and "intervene to ensure all proposed infilling and demolition schemes are paused pending its completion, unless there is an absolute imperative to act due to demonstrable safety concerns".
description: They say new state body Great British Railways will have more expertise than National Highways.

title: Plans which could see more Guernsey care costs due before 2028
text:
Fundamental health plans due before end of 2027
Proposals which could see people in Guernsey pay more for healthcare are due to be published before the end of next year.
Health and Social Care (HSC) started work on the creation of a new model for healthcare locally last year, and warned it could see people pay more for things like meals at hospital and treatments.
The committee has made it the top priority in its workplan for the political term and HSC President George Oswald said he believed a policy letter on the plans would be published before the end of 2027.
Oswald said: "This will probably require some fairly difficult decisions for both the island to make as a whole and for the States of Guernsey in particular to make."
Oswald said there was nowhere in the developed world that had managed to reduce its healthcare budget, without big cuts to the service it provides.
Under option A in Policy and Resources' budget for 2027 HSC's budget would be £267.5m, whilst under option B it would be £270.6m.
When it came to charging more for healthcare, Oswald said: "We have to look and see what we're subsidising and whether actually there's room for gaining extra income from these areas.
"We've got an inexorable rise in demand, pressure of about five to six million quid a year, which is considered to be unsustainable."
'Too late'
Despite HSC working to produce its proposals before the end of 2027, meaning they'll be debated this political term, Oswald warned any changes agreed by the States were unlikely to be introduced before the end of this term in 2029.
"If we don't do anything it will be too late and we will end up with the needs of healthcare delivery on the island consuming an increasing amount of the States of Guernsey budget as a whole."
Oswald suggested Guernsey may need to rely more on the NHS and off-island partnerships with Jersey in future as growing specialisation made it harder for a small island to provide all healthcare services itself.
Part of the review will see a renegotiation of the multi-million pound contract with Guernsey's Medical Specialist Group (MSG), which provides secondary healthcare services locally.
Oswald was one of the founders of the group and said he would take part in these negotiations and there was no conflict of interest.
In 2025 it was revealed issues with fire safety had led to delays with the opening of a new critical care unit at Guernsey's Princess Elizabeth Hospital.
Those problems mean the facility is now slated to open next year, and is set to come in millions of pounds above its original budget.
Oswald would not say who he felt was responsible for the problems.
He said: "What has put it about £4m over is extra work which has resulted principally because of change of fire regulations and fire issues in the UK, subsequent to the Grenfell Tower issue.
"There were issues which related to remedial work which the contractor has acknowledged and has taken responsibility for repairing.
"We have to deliver a building which is safe for the public to use."

title: Stabbed boy felt Huntingdon train attacker 'was not sane'
text:
Stabbed boy felt train attacker 'was not sane'
A 14-year-old boy stabbed by a man who went on to attack people on a train said he did not feel the knifeman was "mentally sane", a court heard.
The teenager was attacked in Peterborough the day before Anthony Williams is accused of trying to kill 10 people on a train that had to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon in November 2025.
In a video recorded interview played to jurors at Cambridge Crown Court, the boy said: "This random guy… he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."
Williams, 33, of Langford Road in Peterborough, denies 14 counts of attempted murder - four of which concern attacks prior to the mass train stabbing.
At the time of the attack, the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was waiting with a friend on a footbridge over the River Nene, before going trick or treating.
Williams drew a knife from his waistband, he said, and "because I was closest to him, he's just stabbed me".
"I didn't feel like he was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something," he said.
"My friend said he was shouting something like 'are you involved?'.
"When he stabbed me, it's like he was there for a knife fight. Like he was waiting for me to pull out something."
The teenager said he had "so much adrenaline" that it felt "like a poke in the chest".
The jury heard the pair ran away and hid in some bushes, where they called the police.
Jurors later watched video of a recorded interview with Dawid Taborski, who Williams is also accused of attempting to murder, also near the River Nene in Peterborough.
Taborski said he was going to a rave with a friend when he heard a man with a "very, very deep voice" asking "are you involved, are you involved?".
He said the man pulled a knife out of a backpack and lunged at him.
Taborski said he told the armed man, "mate, just step back" before he "literally... ran for my life".
Jurors also saw a video interview with William Ogelby, who was on his way to a cashpoint when he was attacked.
A man walking towards him said "wagwan" to him, which he understood to be a greeting, and he said it back.
Ogelby said the man then pulled a kitchen knife out from a rucksack "and he's tried to stab me three times in the stomach and once in the chest".
Ogelby said he jumped back as soon as the man lunged and "in that moment I've just ran off".
"I thought he was going to kill me," Ogelby said.
During the prosecution opening, jurors were told Williams "has some mental health issues which may or may not become relevant during this trial".
The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.
Williams is accused of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Sachin Balakrishnan, Scott Bletcher, Stephen Crean, Kevin Deely, Jonathan Gjoshe, Scott Green, Michael Paffett, David Presland and Samir Zitouni on the London-bound train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on the Saturday evening.
As well as the attacks in Peterborough, he is accused of attempting to murder a teenager on a Docklands Light Railway train in east London in the early hours of 1 November.
The trial continues, with jurors asked to return to court on Monday.

title: The Garden Army care farm in West Hoathly needs new home
text:
Therapy farm facing closure unless new home found
A project which helps people manage their mental health through farming and horticulture says it faces closure unless it can find a new home in under a year.
The Garden Army in West Hoathly, near East Grinstead, is coming into its seventh year after being founded by Tom Morphew, who was inspired by a conversation with a late friend who had post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Morphew said his friend Dave, who died from a brain tumour as the idea was coming to fruition, told him to "never give up, never give in and keep going forward".
But the founder says the team now has "11 months to take down everything, pack it up, and move it to a new site".
With a sense that the farm's current location would not its forever home, and now the landlord planning to change its use, Morphew said he had been on the lookout for a while.
While the Garden Army was initially conceived for those from a military background, as Dave was, Morphew said it soon became apparent that the farm needed to be for everyone.
He said: "I really saw that there was this divide in society, where if you have additional needs you go 'here', if you've got PTSD, you go 'here'.
"In the real world, we're all together, all meeting these people all the time, and so understanding how each other work, and how we can help each other, is hugely important."
Now, about 60 adults with mental health concerns or additional needs attend the farm each week, as do about 16 children.
"The new site needs to be as big as what we've got now, a minimum of 10 acres (4.04 hectares), preferably with outbuildings that we can convert into the canteen and kitchen, and tool room," Morphew said.
"That's not essential, we can get some funding, hopefully, and get some shipping containers."
Mains electric and water would also be "ideal", he said, adding that the aim was to secure a long-term tenancy of 10-15 years.

title: Bus driver toilets provided for six routes with no facilities
text:
Bus drivers on six routes get temporary toilets
New temporary toilets have been installed for drivers of six London bus routes without facilities at either terminus.
Drivers on the affected routes will have "improved access to facilities at their termini, rather than needing to rely on facilities mid-route or a short walk away", Transport for London (TfL) said.
The authority said it was planning to build an additional 53 new toilet buildings for bus drivers across the capital over the next three years.
The Unite union said the measure was welcomed, but TfL needed to be quicker in providing facilities as "some drivers are still taking toilet breaks by the side of the road".
Mayor of London, Lord Sadiq Khan, said bus drivers "play an essential role in keeping London moving" and every bus driver "should have the facilities they need to do their work safely and comfortably".
Carl Eddleston, TfL's Director of Streets and Network Operations, said: "We're pleased to be making further progress by providing facilities for these six routes, while continuing our wider programme of investment in bus driver welfare across London.
"We know there is more to do and this builds on the significant improvements already made and our commitment to provide even better facilities for drivers in the years ahead."
Last month, the mayor of London, TfL and Unite, as part of a taskforce to improve working conditions for drivers during periods of extreme weather, reached an agreement to install air conditioning in all bus driver cabs by the end of May 2027.
'Health problems and fatigue'
Unite regional officer Nadine Edwards said the union's polling found more than half its drivers still have poor facilities at work and some drivers are still taking toilet breaks by the side of the road.
"We welcome today's plans by TfL to introduce these six new toilet facilities, however we must move faster.
"Many London bus drivers still do not have access to the toilets and break facilities they need, which is leading them to experience health problems and fatigue.
"Through our Fight Fatigue Now campaign, Unite will continue to lobby TfL, the mayor and bus operators on ensuring every London driver has access to clean and safe rest, toilet and welfare facilities".

title: Fancott nature reserve fly-tipping costs charity £13k to clear
text:
Nature reserve fly-tip costs charity £13k to clear
Several tonnes of fly-tipped waste took more than a week to clear, costing a charity more than £13,000.
The Wildlife Trust for Beds, Cambs and Northants said the rubbish was dumped at the Fancott Wood and Meadows nature reserve, close to Toddington, Bedfordshire, in August.
It appeared overnight in its wildlife meadow and included flooring, mattresses, rubble, plastic, broken glass, insulating foam, gas canisters, appliances and plasterboard.
Aidan Matthews, its senior reserves manager, said: "It is unbelievable that someone thinks a nature reserve is an acceptable place to dump waste like this."
The trust said: "Staff time plus skip hire and removal has been a significant cost to the charity and taken the reserve team away from their work protecting nature sites in the area."
It confirmed that information that could potentially identify items was passed to Bedfordshire Police.
Matthews said: "It was a shocking sight when our team arrived for a routine check of the nature reserve.
"There were piles and piles of rubbish everywhere, which must have taken someone quite a while to offload.
"This is the latest incident in the growing problem of fly-tipping on our nature reserves, and it is certainly the largest we've seen."
Specialist contractors had to be called, and it was money and time "that should have been spent on protecting wildlife".
He said staff from across the trust were called in to help, along with land management partners Natural England, the grazier, and a dedicated team of volunteers "to literally pick up tens of tonnes of fly-tipped material from the wildflower meadow".
The site is cut for hay in late June, and then cattle graze on the land from September.
Matthews added that grazing had to be delayed by four weeks "due to the site needing to be cleared before the animals could enter the field".
The reserve is home to cowslips, adder's tongue fern, ragged-robin, great burnet and saw-wort, the trust said.
Its wildlife seeds are also collected and donated to other meadows.

title: 'He's sparko', said one-punch killer after Bury St Edmunds attack
text:
'He's sparko', said one-punch killer after attack
A one-punch killer who said his victim was "sparko" after unleashing a violent attack outside a row of shops has been jailed for manslaughter.
Andrew Allen, 55, assaulted Scott Lisney, 56, at St Olaves Road shopping precinct in Bury St Edmunds on 26 July 2025.
Lisney was taken to the town's West Suffolk Hospital and placed in an induced coma after suffering a bleed on the brain, but he died two days later.
Following a six-day trial at Peterborough Crown Court, a jury returned a unanimous guilty verdict and Allen, of Severn Road in Bury, was sentenced to four years in prison.
Det Supt Matt Adams, senior investigating officer, said Lisney had lost his life through a "single act of violence" and "no sentence" would ever undo that.
"This case is a stark reminder of the consequences that can follow a single act of violence," he said.
"A moment's loss of control can change lives forever, affecting not only those directly involved but the families left behind.
"The message remains a simple one: if you find yourself in a confrontation, walk away. One punch can have irreversible consequences."
Suffolk Police said the pair were known to each other as the victim was the ex-partner of Allen's current partner.
Throughout the confrontation, which happened between 19:55 and 20:05 BST, the force said Lisney appeared calm with his fingers interlaced or arms folded and showed no signs of aggression.
After walking away, he was followed by Allen who grabbed his arm and then punched him, causing Lisney to fall backwards and hit his head on the ground.
Police said the defendant declared "he's sparko" and made his way home, where he was arrested in the early hours of the following morning.
When he arrived at Bury St Edmunds Police Investigation Centre, police said Allen made further admissions saying: "It's quite simple - I knocked him out."
The force said that during the trial, Allen, who denied manslaughter, accepted he had struck Lisney, but claimed he had been acting in self-defence. However, the jury convicted him on Wednesday.
"Scott's family have shown considerable strength and dignity throughout the investigation and court proceedings," added Det Supt Adams.
"I hope they are able to grieve away from the criminal justice process and continue remembering Scott for the person he was."

title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
text:
US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in the statement.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.
She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Pike is thought to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said in her statement on Friday. "But healing is not the same as being okay."
Her lawyers previously said she had suffered from pneumonia following the attempted execution, had significant swelling on her arms and was also unable to swallow.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike's botched execution captivated and shocked the world last month and shocked Pike, too.
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said in her statement.
Bethany Mann, a friend of Pike's and a founder of Child Arise Tennessee, which supports children and families affected by parental incarceration, told the BBC on Friday that she had been in direct contact with Pike since the botched execution attempt.
When asked about her reaction to Pike's statement, Mann said: "Truthfully, I don't know that I have anything to add to what Christa has already expressed so powerfully herself, and I want to be respectful of her privacy."
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".
Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.
Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."
She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess".
She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology.
"All I wanted was justice," Martinez said.
Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.

title: Murder arrest after man attacked by armed group in Leeds
text:
Murder arrest after man killed in group attack
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following the death of a man attacked by four people in Leeds.
Rahiem Jackson, 38, was attacked outside a property in Hedley Chase, in New Wortley, Leeds, on Saturday, by a group armed with weapons, West Yorkshire Police said. He died shortly afterwards.
Paying tribute, his family said he had a "beautiful heart and soul", adding: "His smile was so infectious, and he lit up the room with his presence."
The force said a 26-year-old man had been arrested overnight in London by the Met Police. He remains in custody.
Det Ch Insp Dan Bates said: "This arrest is significant development in the murder investigation of Rahiem Jackson.
"Officers are continuing to support the family.
"Extensive inquiries remain ongoing and we continue to appeal for information around the attack.
"We continue to ask anyone who may have seen people arrive or leave the scene on Hedley Chase on Saturday night to come forward."
The family said Rahiem - known as Reema - "would have gone above and beyond for anybody he cared for" and that "a very cowardly, cruel and senseless act of vicious violence" had resulted in his death.
"He wasn't just a brother he was a son, an uncle, a father, a partner, a nephew, a cousin, a grandson, brother-in-law and friend, and he did not deserve to die the way he did," they added.
"We are heartbroken and in so much pain and have been left inconsolable as a family."

title: Royal Shakespeare Company recalls Sir Patrick Stewart's legacy
text:
'RSC was where Sir Patrick Stewart felt at home'
Sir Patrick Stewart felt "most at home" at the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC), its former artistic director has said.
Tributes have been paid to the renowned British actor, who died at the age of 86 on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles, following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
Sir Patrick began his career on stage in Warwickshire, where he honed his craft by performing Shakespeare, before finding international success on screen and in Hollywood.
Gregory Doran, the RSC's former artistic director, said Stratford-upon-Avon and the theatre company remained at the heart of the actor's life, describing it as the place where he "felt most at home".
"Patrick felt that Stratford was home to him," he told BBC CWR. "Shakespeare was what he loved.
The actor, who trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School from the age of 17, joined the RSC in 1966 and performed roles including King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.
Remembering Sir Patrick's time at the company, Doran described him as "magnificent", recalling a moment when he portrayed Hamlet's uncle King Claudius in the famous Shakespearean tragedy.
"He just was a great company man, very democratic, never forgot his Yorkshire roots, always just really loved working with young actors and passing on what he knew," Doran explained.
"That was, I think, one of the great genuine things about his generosity as a human being."
In a tribute, the RSC described Sir Patrick as a "colossus of both stage and screen" and "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation".
Well-known for his iconic role playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, the award-winning actor also went onto to portray Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise.
Doran, who stepped down as the company's artistic director in 2022, said Sir Patrick was a "lovely person to have in a rehearsal room".
"He was at heart, a craftsman... whether that was in Shakespeare or, in a sci fi franchise, that was really at the heart of who he was and Shakespeare had been a passport through his life.
"I feel very privileged to have been able to work with him and count him as a friend."
Despite going onto to have an extensive career in Hollywood, the actor returned to the RSC on occasion for productions or campaigns, and was also involved in fundraising efforts.
He visited the theatre last year following the release of his autobiography, Doran explained.
"He was very funny, telling wonderful anecdotes about growing up in the field and about his early days at Stratford and it was a joy to have him and the audience just lapped up the fact that this Hollywood star had arrived back on home turf."

title: Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, Neil Kinnock says
text:
Winter fuel cuts turned the Welsh against Labour, former leader Neil Kinnock says
Former Labour leader Neil Kinnock says the party's welfare policies turned disillusionment with Labour in Wales into "active dislike".
He said that UK government decisions on benefits and winter fuel payments had driven voters in Wales away from the Welsh arm of the party before the country's Senedd election in May.
Lord Kinnock made the comments as part of a Newyddion S4C YouTube special on Andy Burnham's first 100 days as prime minister.
Governing "at both ends of the M4" before Wales' parliamentary elections had presented an extra challenge for his party, he said.
He said: "If there is any opposition or resentment to the government on either end of the M4, the other lot are going to pay as well.
"There is no doubt in my mind," he said, that "alienation... had been creeping up".
"It could be a mixture of boredom. It could be a mixture of dislike," Kinnock said.
He said "what turned that into active dislike" had been things "like the withdrawal of the winter fuel allowance, the threats to the welfare system" and not scrapping a cap on two child benefits quick enough.
In June last year, the Labour UK government U-turned on its controversial decision to means-test winter fuel payments for pensioners in England and Wales.
Almost one year later, Labour lost power in Wales in a seismic election in May, returning just nine Senedd members after running the Welsh government for 27 years.
Lord Kinnock, who is the father of Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock, also said he had reservations about devolving justice to Wales - a key demand of the Plaid Cymru Welsh government.
Plaid ministers say it would allow for a more effective system tailored to Welsh communities and better integrated with health, housing and education.
Kinnock said there would no be "much of an argument" against the idea if it meant that "Wales was better protected, that the streets were safer" and "that the justice system was more efficient".
"But those guarantees are absent at the moment," he said.
"Until they exist, until they're in place, the upheaval of creating what would have to be effectively a new system with new management... with an introverted view of the justice system - there would be more downsides than upsides.
"Now that picture might change, but as I can see it now in October 2026, that's where we are, there are more disadvantages than advantages."

title: Beavers to return to River Ness area after 500 years
text:
Beavers to return to River Ness area after 500 years
Beavers are set to be released into the waters around Loch Ness, 500 years after they were last recorded there.
NatureScot has approved the release of up to 15 beavers over three years at agreed sites in the River Ness catchment.
Their assessment concluded that beavers could "significantly boost biodiversity" in the catchment, with the landscape at "low risk of negative impacts from beaver activity."
Beavers were first reintroduced to Scotland in 2009 after being hunted to extinction about 400 years ago.
The licence has been granted to Trees for Life and the Beaver Trust.
They said the last widely-cited historical record of Scotland's beavers, dating from 1526 to 1527, placed them around Loch Ness.
The River Ness catchment was identified by NatureScot in 2022 as one of the most suitable locations in Scotland for the rodents.
NatureScot said responses to the applicants' consultation process were positive, with more than 73% of respondents supportive.
NatureScot's Robbie Kernahan said: "Beavers can bring many benefits for nature and people, creating habitats such as ponds and wetlands where other species thrive, as well as moderating water flows in times of flood and water scarcity."
He said concerns had been raised by land managers and residents through the consultation process, and these would be taken seriously.
Kernahan added: "We have assessed the monitoring and mitigation plans set out by the applicants and believe that, along with our existing beaver mitigation scheme, any potential conflicts that may arise can be resolved."
NatureScot said any beavers released would be trapped and taken from areas where they were having a negative impact on prime agricultural land and where mitigation measures had not been successful or possible.
The beavers will undergo appropriate health screening before being released.
Alan McDonnell, from Trees for Life, said: "Beavers are key allies in tackling the interconnected climate and biodiversity crises facing us all, so this successful result brings real hope for the future.
"There has been huge interest from communities and local businesses.
"Our engagement has been locally focused, with the team meeting people on the ground to listen to their views first hand."

title: Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
text:
Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

title: Plans for vulnerable care unit in Jersey with additional cells
text:
Plans for extra cells at vulnerable care unit
Additional cells for a new vulnerable care unit have been proposed at Jersey's prison, ahead of new laws to protect women and girls.
Politicians approved a series of laws offering more protection for women and girls from violence and domestic abuse. The changes include stand-alone offences for stalking and non-fatal strangulation.
Home affairs minister, Senator Helen Miles, said a new care and separation building had been proposed with more flexible accommodation for prisoners with varying health and other needs.
Miles said it would provide extra capacity to match the "anticipated growth in demand" from the new legislation and other prison population pressures.
"The proposal is currently at an early feasibility and design stage, with the high-level principles scoped as part of a business case which will now be subject to internal appraisal and refinement," Miles said.
"Capacity, costs, funding and timescales have therefore not yet been determined.
"Any development would need to be considered as part of the government's long-term capital planning process."
Pressure set to increase
The first of five new laws to protect women and girls is due to come into force on 1 December.
It follows a letter by the children, education and home affairs scrutiny panel regarding the proposed budget 2027-2030 review.
In a response letter, Miles said planning permission had been granted for a new sexual assault referral centre, with work set to start at the end of November and be completed in 2028.
The justice and home affairs minister said she was satisfied the proposed budget provided an appropriate level of funding to meet the policing and emergency service demand.
In terms of policing, Miles said crimes related to violence against women and girls had increased by about 30% across four years.
The minister said 844 offences were recorded in 2025, while rape and serious sexual offences increased by 58%.
"Policing demand has increased significantly over recent years, particularly in violence against women and girls, public protection and complex investigations," Miles said.
"This existing pressure is expected to increase further over the budget period following implementation of the five new VAWG laws approved by the States Assembly.
"Depending on where demand falls within that range, the modelling identified a potential requirement for an additional 11 to 23 police officers, 5 to 13 police staff and further capacity across victim services."
The minister said the proposed resource allocation addressed both current demand which has built up over recent years and readiness for the new legislation.

title: RSPCA's longest-staying dog 'settling in lovely' in new home
text:
RSPCA's longest-staying dog finds new home
A dog named Delboy - who spent nearly two years in the RSPCA's care - has finally been rehomed.
The French bulldog cross arrived at Longview Animal Centre in Stalmine, Lancashire in October 2024 and became the centre's longest-staying resident.
His new owners, Mike and Corrine Neale, from the Fylde coast, visited the rehoming centre 10 times to build up a rapport with him.
"He is settling in lovely, enjoying walks, sofas, beds, treats and being loved, which is his favourite pastime," Mike said.
Signed over into RSPCA care because of welfare concerns, Delboy - named after the Only Fools and Horses character - was affectionate with people he knew, but needed time and patience to learn to trust unfamiliar faces, especially men.
Mike and Corrine saw one of the animal centre's appeals and felt Delboy could be the dog for them as they had lots of experience caring for rescue dogs with behavioural challenges.
Mike said: "We chose Delboy because he desperately needed a forever home.
"The staff at Longview were really helpful, patient and kind throughout his adoption process and explained his needs and quirks.
"He's been with us for little over a month and he's already been on his first holiday with us to Northumberland and we have lots more adventures planned.
"We're so happy to have been able to give Delboy a new life with us."
Hannah Mainds, from the RSPCA's Blackpool and North Lancashire Branch, said the couple "took him out for days out, they took him home for sleepovers to really spend the time and develop that trust with him".
"They really worked with us to make sure it was the right fit and the right match and we're very grateful to them," she said.
"Sometimes people think 'oh I'll just go to the animal centre, we'll pick up a rescue dog and we'll take it home' but some of them need a lot more care, a lot more time and a lot more patience and they really did put that effort in.
"I'm so glad Delboy finally got his happy ending."
Longview Animal Centre is run by the RSPCA's Blackpool & North Lancashire Branch which is an independent, self-funding charity.
At its busiest, the centre can have over 100 animals in its care and currently has 28 dogs as well as cats and rabbits.

title: McDonald's staff in shock as Feckenham man turns up on pony
text:
'I took my pony to McDonald's and he was lovin' it'
Fast food staff were left shocked and confused when a man on a pony turned up at a McDonald's drive-thru.
Eventing horse rider, Nick Holden, posted a reel on his Instagram feed documenting his journey to the branch in Wychbold, Worcestershire, atop his black and white steed, Sparky.
It has since been viewed more than 590,000 times and received hundreds of comments, with many describing the pair's adventure as "awesome".
Holden, from Feckenham, revealed he did the same journey on horseback about 10 years ago, when he could not drive.
"It was my only way of getting there," he told BBC Hereford and Worcester. "So I figured I'd give it a go and see if we could still do it."
Sparky measures about 14.2 hands, which Holden described as being on the cusp between a large pony and small horse.
"I figured he was more acceptable," he added. "I've got some bigger horses that are like 18 hands, but I don't think I'll be getting them under the height barriers."
When the pony and rider arrived at McDonald's, they waited by the speaker at the beginning of the drive-thru lane but nobody responded.
So Holden took Sparky to the first window and waited until a staff member saw them.
"The woman came to the window and got a bit of a shock," said Holden.
But he said they were "really lovely" and more than happy to serve Holden his chicken nuggets and fries, while Sparky got a free bag of apple slices, as bemused diners looked on.
The pair then left the drive-thru and, on the way back to Feckenham, they stopped in Hanbury Woods and had a picnic.
Asked how Sparky reacted, Holden said: "I think he loved it, he loves attention. He's technically retired now from competition so he doesn't get out massive amounts at the moment.
"Any opportunity he has for going out and exploring the world, I think he's grateful for."
According to McDonald's guidelines, drive-thrus should only be used by motor vehicles and road-worth mobility scooters, not by pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders.
When asked about this, Holden said: "Well, I'd argue horses were the original mode of transport so they should be exempt."

title: Young Gun,14, out to beat Littler in darts showdown for £501k prize
text:
Young Gun out to beat Littler for £501k darts prize
A 14-year old darts player is set to take on Luke Littler in a live darts showdown for a shot at £501,000.
Jayden Walker, from Christchurch, Dorset, is one of 24 players picked for Beat Luke Littler, a live Netflix show in which contestants take on the world champion in a single leg of 501 unless someone beats him ending the challenge.
Jayden, whose playing nickname is The Young Gun, has played Littler twice, he said: "He beat me 3-0 the first time... he was on fire, then the second time I lost 2-1 but I won the first leg so I got the leg I need tonight to win the money."
Ahead of the live show in Manchester at 19:00 GMT on Friday he said he was "excited... but then also a little bit nervous".
Jayden, who started playing darts in local leagues aged about 10 years old, said his family was "so proud" and planned to hold a watch party because his two brothers were too young to go to the show.
The first contestant to beat the 19-year-old two-time world champion will land the big-money prize and bring the competition to an end.
Jayden got on the show through an audition with thousands of hopefuls who had to complete a leg of 501 in 24 darts or fewer.
Successful players then progressed to an interview with the show's producers before a final stage assessment with a judging panel, which included 16-time world darts champion Phil Taylor.
Jayden said the interview with Phil "The Power" Taylor was quite "nerve-wracking" as he is the "GOAT (greatest of all time) of darts" and added he said "I was a nice kid".
He added if he lands the top prize, the money will be put into a trust fund until he turns 18.

title: Arrest after woman killed in crash during Leeds police pursuit
text:
Arrest after woman killed in police pursuit crash
A man has been arrested following the death of a pedestrian who was hit by a car during a police pursuit in Leeds.
The 36-year-old woman died in hospital after being struck by a Vauxhall Corsa in Beckett Street at about 09:52 GMT, just minutes after it failed to stop for officers in Harehills Road.
The car was later found abandoned in Nippet Lane, with the occupants having fled the scene, West Yorkshire Police said.
A 19-year-old man has since been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and remains in custody, the force said.
A police spokesperson said on Thursday an investigation had been started by its Homicide and Major Enquiry Team, and appealed for witnesses or anyone with dashcam to come forward.
They added that a mandatory referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct in relation to the incident, due to prior police involvement.

title: Spain train crash: Transport minister says he won't resign over disaster
text:
Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Óscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto Ibáñez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of Wednesday's disaster, but many families are still waiting for information from authorities about their loved ones.
Esther San Emeterio, whose 54-year-old brother Pepe is still missing, told reporters in Toledo, near Urda, that officials were forcing families to wait in "uncertainty".
"We went to bed crying, outraged and full of shame," she said. "We are desperate and I want all of Spain to know. How can they keep us like this?"
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

title: Banstead roofer transforms home into Halloween house of horrors
text:
Halloween home transformation with props and skip waste
A roofer from Surrey has transformed his home into a spooky haunted house for Halloween, hoping to raise thousands of pounds in the process.
David Donovan's home in Hillside, Banstead, usually looks like any other but this week has a 10ft (3m) skeleton, a gory scarecrow and a gruesome graveyard outside.
He has been collecting the giant props for years and builds the scene for the annual event largely from building waste materials and what he finds in skips.
Donovan says hundreds of families turn up to see his house and play the games he lays on each year, adding: "It can get a little bit overwhelming when there's people queueing to get on to your drive."
He said the decorating started "as a family thing" but as it grew, they started to do it for charity.
Donovan raised £3,000 for the Royal Marsden cancer charity at last year's event.
It takes him about four weeks to build, but he said it was touch and go this time around due to recent storms.
"It's just been too wet to do any of the building and then with the wind, with the larger items that are over 7ft (2m), there's a fear of them snapping, we've had to leave quite a lot of it to the last minute," he said.
"It gets busy. Then there's trying to run the stalls, make sure everything's working OK. And having enough sweets! That's a big factor."
But what do the neighbours have to say about all this?
"They frowned upon it at the start. I think they're used to it now," he said.

title: Council apology after two women's rights campaigners banned
text:
Apology after two women's rights campaigners banned
Bristol City Council has apologised "unreservedly" and agreed to pay some legal costs after two gender critical campaigners were banned from the chamber.
Phoebe Beedell and Wendy Stephenson were excluded from public meetings for six months, after the authority said their conduct led to some councillors feeling "intimidated".
The women launched a legal challenge, and now the council has agreed to settle the dispute out of court.
In a public statement, the council withdrew its allegations against the women and admitted there should have been an investigation before they were banned.
During a full council meeting in November 2025 Beedell and Stephenson were accused of "confronting two councillors in the reception area in a way that they found intimidating".
The women are part of the "Women of Wessex" group, who advocate gender critical views and have repeatedly raised questions about the council's policies in relation to trans rights.
On one occasion Green Party councillors walked out of the chamber while the women were speaking, on another they held up placards.
Following the meeting, Beedell said she approached one of the councillors who had walked out and asked a question about the Supreme Court ruling that the "concept of sex is binary".
"I would say that that conversation lasted less than one minute... and then they turned away," she said at the time.
Beedell claims that Stephenson, who was also dismissed from her position as chair of the council's independent remuneration panel, "was not there for that conversation".
The pair said they had not been given the opportunity to respond to the allegations, and had lawyers preparing for a judicial review of the decision in court.
In a public statement, the council said it accepted that the process it had followed before it took action against Beedell and Stephenson was "inadequate".
"Before those decisions were taken, a proportionate investigation should have been conducted," the statement said.
It went on to say that the two women should have been informed of the substance of the allegations, provided with a summary of the evidence, and given a meaningful opportunity to respond.
"The council does not maintain, and will not repeat or rely upon, allegations that Dr Beedell or Ms Stephenson acted in a threatening, abusive, disorderly or intimidating manner towards councillors on 4 November 2025."
The six-month exclusions have been rescinded and the council says they will not be relied upon in future as findings of misconduct.
The statement goes on: "Ms Stephenson's removal from the Independent Remuneration Panel did not constitute or follow from an adverse finding about her integrity, objectivity, ability to comply with public standards or suitability for future civic roles."
Personal apology letters issued to the two women acknowledge "the delay in resolving the inadequacies."
'A tragic waste of money'
Speaking after the statement was issued, Beedell said the whole situation had been "a tragic waste of money".
"I was disgusted by their behaviour," she said. "It has cost the council tens of thousands pounds.
"We're not intimidating or harassing anyone," she added. "We're just standing to defend women's rights."
Stephenson described it as "long and difficult dispute".
She said she was "relieved" by the outcome, but "furious" that it had happened in the first place.
"It's been a cloud hanging over us for the past year," she said.
"We will continue to campaign on behalf of women's rights and to ask questions of the local authority."
The council's Trans Inclusion and Gender Identity Policy, which was at the heart of the dispute, was updated in August 2026 to bring it into line with the Supreme Court ruling when judges unanimously concluded that a woman is defined by biological sex.
Bristol City Council chiefs said an outline procedure will be introduced, to be applied to any future cases where complaints are made.

Thief took police on 'Great Windsor Triathlon'
A thief who tried to evade police by hiding in a wardrobe had earlier tried to shake them off by running, swimming and cycling off in what officers dubbed the Great Windsor Triathlon.
Alan Styles, 51, admitted one count of theft after he was caught on CCTV stealing food from the Windsor Farm Shop in Old Windsor on 24 September and then riding his getaway bike into a metal gate.
He also admitted stealing a bike in Eton Court in Eton two days later, and to outraging public decency in Meadow Lane, Eton, on 30 September.
Styles was given an 18-month community order at Reading Magistrates' Court on 19 October.
He also admitted stealing from Marks & Spencer in Windsor on 8 September and an assault in The Brocas, also in the same town, on 13 August.

title: The Wrekin bridleways to reopen but landowners raise concern
text:
Bridleways to reopen but landowner is concerned
A decision to give horse riders the right to use established routes has been met with caution by landowners who own a large part of the area.
Raby Estates said it would add to "visitor pressures" around The Wrekin and the permission would need to be "managed carefully and sensitively".
The decision to open up the bridleways came after a public inquiry in September and Sally-Anne Robinson, of Telford Bridleways Association, said it was "the biggest bridleway gain ever in Shropshire".
Horse riders argued they needed safe places to ride after being squeezed out of Telford due to housing developments.
Raby Estates had told the inquiry that use of their land at The Wrekin had been formally contested legally in 1996.
But 80 people gave evidence that they had used a network of routes for 20 years before then, between 1976 and 1996.
The planning inspector concluded there was insufficient proof the rights had been ended and granted permission for the two bridleways to be used.
Robinson said: "Horse riders need safe places to ride and are being squeezed out of Telford due to the housing developments.
"We don't want to go up the Wrekin, it's far too busy, just gently hack around the base with access routes off the surrounding lanes."
The two bridleways will pass through Little Wenlock, Uppington, Wroxeter, and Wrockwardine and there will also be six footpaths upgraded.
Robinson said they would be "a huge gain for horse riders for generations to come" and added: "I can't believe it after all this blood, sweat and tears."
Landowner concerns
Raby Estates said it respected the decision of the planning inspector, but also said leisure activities needed to be managed to "protect the site's heritage and special interest".
Duncan Peake, chief executive at Raby Estates said company remained "concerned about the consequences of this decision for visitors and the site itself".
He described The Wrekin as "an iconic and highly designated landscape attracting hundreds of thousands of visitors each year".
But he said it had seen "an increasing number of mountain bikers using the area, in addition to horse riders and walkers adding to visitor pressures".
Because of this, he said: "These activities need to be managed carefully and sensitively to protect the site's heritage and special interest as well as the health and safety of all visitors."

title: Police to destroy electric bikes and scooters seized in crackdown
text:
Police to destroy electric bikes and scooters seized in crackdown
More than 140 electric bikes and scooters will be destroyed after they were seized by Police Scotland during a nationwide crackdown.
Officers confiscated 99 e-bikes and 43 e-scooters during Operation Overlap, which ran between 19 and 25 October.
The largest number were confiscated in Glasgow bringing the total for the year - up to 16 October - to 1,000.
Supt Andy Barclay said illegally modified e-bikes were dangerous and not suitable for public roads.
He added: "They pose a risk to their own riders, the emergency services and other road users, particularly pedestrians.
"We also want to make sure that people are aware of the legislation and their personal responsibilities if using an e-bike or e-scooter.
"Please be mindful of where you can and can't use vehicles of this type and take responsibility for your own actions and the safety of other road users."
Police said that e-bikes and e-scooters were becoming increasingly common in towns and cities across Scotland.
Most are used appropriately and in line with legal guidelines.
However, some are modified to exceed speed and power limits, which can reclassify them under motorcycle legislation.
E-bikes can legally be used on public roads if they meet specific requirements, including that the motor should not be able to propel the bike when it is travelling more than 15.5mph.
It must also have a maximum power output of 250 watts.
Vehicles that exceed these limits are motor vehicles and are subject to the Road Traffic Act, meaning the rider must hold a full UK driving license, have insurance, and wear an approved helmet.
Failure to comply with these legal requirements could face enforcement action.
E-scooters are not permitted on public roads, pavements or other public spaces, as they do not meet the necessary legal standards.
Their use is only legal on private land with the landowner's consent.

title: West Belfast: Homes evacuated following secuirty alert
text:
Homes evacuated as 'suspicious devices' found
A number of homes have been evacuated after police found "a number of suspicious devices" during a search operation in west Belfast on Friday morning.
A 35-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of offences under the Terrorism Act, remains in police custody.
Officers are at a house in Edwina Street, off the Shankill Road, accompanied by Army Ammunition Technical Officers (ATO).
Meanwhile, residents in Dervock in Ballymoney have returned to their homes following a separate security alert.
Earlier on Friday, police said they were searching two properties in the Shankill Road area as part of an investigation into suspected terrorism offences.
Police said on Friday evening that a safety cordon is in place and they have asked the public to avoid the area.
DUP councillor Ian McLaughlin said he was "shocked and saddened" by events in the area.
He said he understood what began as a "low level house search" had quickly escalated.
McLaughlin described it as an "unwanted and completely unwarranted incident" in what he said was a normally quiet community.
TUV councillor Ron McDowell said police should be "given the time and space to conclude their investigation".
The PSNI also confirmed a suspicious object was found in the Greystone Crescent area of Ballymoney in County Antrim.

title: Bedford council 'recognises seriousness' of inspectors' bullying report
text:
Council 'recognises seriousness' of bullying claims
Bedford Borough Council has said it "recognises the seriousness of the findings" of a government inspection that found evidence of bullying and a misogynistic culture across political groups.
Inspectors also accused Conservative Mayor Tom Wootton of "avoiding difficult decisions and conflict" and this meant commissioners could be overseeing work at the council for the next three years.
The local authority's chief executive Laura Church said: "The council has carefully considered the report's recommendations and recognises the need to accelerate our transformation and improvement journey."
The authority said it would continue its daily operations and address the issues raised in the full report.
The inspection team was appointed by the secretary of state for housing, communities and local government in February at a cost of up to £3,400 per day, with three inspectors spending three months at Borough Hall.
At about the same time, the authority was offered up to £80m of exceptional financial support from the government to tackle a multi-million pound shortfall.
A Best Value Inspection is a formal, statutory investigation ordered by the UK government to assess whether a local authority or public body is meeting its legal Best Value Duty under the Local Government Act 1999.
Wootton faced a no-confidence vote in July and Inspectors said he "lacks the leadership skills to create a positive leadership environment".
It added that this "contributed to poor decision-making and lack of prioritisation" while a background of "very competitive electoral politics" had created conditions for "low trust and highly combative politics in the council" across all political groups.
At the time Wootton said: "I understand the findings will concern residents and I take them extremely seriously. I am determined to see this work through and build a council residents can have confidence in, and be proud of."
Evidence was found of poor behaviours which had led to "low trust between members and officers, with capacity and capability challenges at officer level further damaging relationships".
The report added "the council faces challenges largely of its own creation and it could do a much better job of resolving them than it currently does".
The authority had 10 working days to formally respond to the government and said it recognised the importance of demonstrating sustained and measurable improvement. It said it was committed to addressing the issues and ensuring that it secured continuous improvement, financial sustainability, effective governance, and the organisational capacity required to deliver good outcomes.
Church added: "As we wait for the government's feedback to our response, we continue to work closely with staff, members and partners to provide vital services and support to residents in the borough."
Lib Dem opposition leader Henry Vann said: "We have put aside political differences to support the council's response collectively.
"But we must be realistic — there are sections of the inspection that are not fully addressed and need to be tackled, including waste and the ongoing financial and leadership crisis at the council.
"This year's budget alone is predicated on borrowing an extra £25m from government. We will continue to encourage the Conservative mayor to take these issues seriously."
The Labour party's group leader at the council, Abu Sultan, added: "The Labour group has strongly endorsed the inspection's findings and supports the intervention needed to put the council back on track.
"We will work constructively with the government, commissioners, council officers and colleagues across the political divide."

title: Sea Palling villagers left 'stranded' as roadworks block buses
text:
Villagers left 'stranded' as roadworks block buses
Villagers said they would be left stranded without a bus service for nearly two weeks due to roadworks.
CityFibre is planning to dig up a section of Stalham Road in Sea Palling, Norfolk to install new cables between 2 November and 13 November.
Bus firm Sanders Coaches said it would be "unachievable" to serve the remote coastal village during this time as a diversion would add nearly 32 miles (51km) and 85 minutes to the journey time.
Resident Wendy Dickson, 59, said it had caused a great deal of stress and would make it hard for her disabled daughter Keila to attend hospital appointments.
The 34 Sanders Coaches bus service normally travels up from Stalham, towards the coast to Sea Palling and other villages like Walcott and Mundesley, before reaching North Walsham and returning.
The route makes its way through the Norfolk Broads, and reaching Sea Palling would require buses to circumnavigate Hickling Broad - one of the largest expanses of open water in the region.
Bus operations manager Kieran Smith said: "With a network now spanning Norfolk, we face hundreds of planned road closures and usually take whatever steps necessary to still maintain a reasonable service around whatever is closed.
"Unfortunately, on this occasion, the only available diversion is unachievable. In effect, the village is cut off from the west, which sadly is the direction the bus route approaches from."
Dickson said the disruption had caught villagers by surprise.
She said: "We feel residents need to be better informed by Norfolk County Council.
"We have a community of elderly people who have health conditions as well, who absolutely rely on that service to go and fetch medication.
"It's a bit of a lifeline to them, really. It means we will be stranded for a fortnight."
Dickson added she did not yet know how she would manage to collect prescriptions for her daughter.
However, Sanders Coaches has come to an agreement with CityFibre to allow a bus to stop at Sea Palling at 07:00 GMT and then another in the late afternoon to provide transport to schoolchildren.
CityFibre roadworks have also caused concern elsewhere. A closure was planned for Stalham High Street but this has been delayed to January to avoid disruption to businesses in the run up to Christmas.
CityFibre said it was installing full-fibre broadband connection to the area.
A spokesperson said: "We've engaged with Norfolk County Council and other local groups to ensure ongoing access for school services alongside an alternative route for other traffic, but we appreciate any road closure causes disruption and our team will work hard to complete the work as quickly as possible."
Norfolk County Council said: "Unfortunately there is no suitable local diversion route for buses available whilst this work takes place.
"We have worked with the utility provider to enable school buses to pass through the closure but public services cannot be safely accommodated."

title: Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
text:
Academic says he has been barred from UK over event with Palestine Action founder
A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.
Andreas Malm told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had received a letter from the Home Office notifying him that his presence was "not conducive to the public good", with no further details given.
He said he could not "see any other explanation" for being denied entry than his scheduled appearance with Huda Ammori, a founder of the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.
The Home Office said it did not comment on individual cases.
Malm is a senior lecturer in human ecology at Sweden's Lund University, whose work includes the 2021 book How to Blow up a Pipeline and 2025's The Destruction of Palestine is the Destruction of the Earth.
He said he had asked the Home Office to explain its decision, but could not see a reason beyond the upcoming talk in London with Ammori organised by the left-wing magazine Tribune - calling the move a "severe restriction on the free exchange of ideas".
Malm said he was not a member of Palestine Action, had never publicly endorsed it, nor had he given it any financial support.
"The only link to Palestine Action is her as a person," he said, criticising the UK government for ascribing "guilt by association".
The academic acknowledged that he had previously described the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel - in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage - as "fundamentally an act of liberation".
Malm said it was possible that these remarks, during a December 2023 talk in which he also condemned the "deplorable" killing of civilians in the cross-border attack, had been the reason for the Home Office's decision.
But he argued that these views had been in the public realm for a long time, including when he was last allowed into the UK to deliver a talk in May.
"I don't expect the British state to agree with me on Palestine or climate or anything. What I expect the British state to do is to continue to let me enter the country and to discuss with colleagues, with people who disagree with me - as I have done for years."
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's controversial ban under terrorism legislation. The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of the group. About 2,500 have been charged, though none have gone to trial as the legal challenge to the proscription continues.
The government has broad discretion to bar foreign nationals from entering the UK if their presence is deemed to pose a risk to society.
In April, 11 people described by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer as "far-right agitators" were banned from entering the UK ahead of a rally led by Tommy Robinson.
Kanye West was also denied entry that same month after backlash to his planned set at London's Wireless Festival, following a string of antisemitic, racist and pro-Nazi comments. He had previously apologised for the remarks and said his bipolar disorder had caused him to lose "touch with reality".
Left-wing political commentators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur claimed in June that their visas had been revoked ahead of planned appearances in London and Oxford, allegedly "for criticising Israel".

title: East Surrey Council approves Reigate Priory Junior School move
text:
Shadow council signs off on junior school move
Plans to move a Surrey school away from its current premises have been given the green light by councillors.
A planned relocation of Reigate Priory Junior School to new purpose-built facilities at Woodhatch Place, Cockshot Hill was brought before East Surrey's shadow cabinet this week.
The shadow council, which will be responsible for East Surrey's schools from April, was asked to authorise the move following the same decision previously by Surrey County Council.
Council leader Steve Wotton said there was "broad agreement" that the current site was not fit for purpose, but added: "The question is how best to provide a suitable teaching environment and accommodation for children."
Concerns have previously been raised over the location of the new school site – including the potential for increased traffic on the road, and its location further from the centre of Reigate.
A consultation in 2024 deemed the current school site "not fit for providing a 21st Century education to its pupils", according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Children and youth services lead member Ashley Tilling spoke against the decision, adding that if the school was moved "we will leave a legacy of a boarded up, looking rather ugly Grade I building – which is actually at the heart of Reigate and is one of the features that makes Reigate such an attractive place to live in".
The cabinet voted through the plans, with seven members in favour and two against.
