title: Asda: Petrol station investigation launched after car issues reported
text:
Motorists angry as car problems shut Asda petrol station pumps
Some motorists are angry after they said their cars developed problems after refuelling at an Asda petrol station.
Sandra Reid is among the people who have reported issues with their vehicles after buying fuel from the same Asda-owned forecourt.
She said her car started to "chug along and struggle to accelerate" and eventually broke down, after leaving the filling station.
Asda has apologised for any inconvenience and removed some pumps from service at the site in question while an investigation is carried out.
Reid said she noticed issues with the car shortly after topping up at the garage in Coleraine, County Londonderry, in Northern Ireland.
"I eventually managed to get the car started again and it again was struggling, but I nursed it to a car park in Long Commons area of Coleraine and there it has stayed ever since," she told BBC News NI.
"It's a paid car park so I have had to top up the parking app for four days now just to keep my car there until I can get someone out to look at it.
"I think I am down about £20 already on parking as I can't move the car."
Reid said not being able to use her car has been a "disaster", especially as she usually uses it to get to and from work, which is a 45-minute walk away.
Reid added that to get the fuel removed from the vehicle, it could cost more than £500.
It is not yet known what may have caused the reported vehicle problems or just how many cars are affected.
Asda said the "isolated incident" affected some - but not all - fuel purchases made at the Coleraine site between 25 and 29 October.
"We're working with customers who may have been affected and asking anyone experiencing issues with their vehicle following a purchase during this timeframe to contact us so we can put things right," a spokesperson said.
"We've safely reopened the majority of pumps following a full investigation, while some remain out of use as we work to resolve the issue."
'Sister and girlfriend's car both broke down'
Dean Law said two cars belonging to his girlfriend Courteney and sister Emma broke down after they had filled up at the petrol station.
He said he and his girlfriend had now spent about £1,000 on mechanic bills after her car broke down on Monday when she was driving to work.
"She told me the car felt different and started to vibrate when she was driving, but she managed to get it to work.
"After work, she then went out and tried to start the car and it wouldn't move."
"It was only after we spoke to my sister, who had also filled up her car at the same petrol station on Sunday and whose car had also broken down, that we eventually realised the issue could be linked to the fuel," he said.
"I actually put up a Facebook post asking if anyone else had experienced the issues that we had and I couldn't believe the response.
"So many people started commenting and messaging me about it, so it seems to have impacted a number of people."
Law said the car was bought a year ago and that it was really frustrating to have to spend so much money on it.
David Jardine, from Belfast, said he was on a family holiday on the north coast at the weekend and filled up his car at the petrol station on Sunday night and broke down shortly afterwards in Portstewart.
"We were just heading up for a few days and filled up at Asda and I remember turning to my son in the car and saying the car doesn't feel right," he said.
"It was like jumping a bit and sounded strange.
"We got to Portstewart where we were staying and the car just completely died on us."
Jardine said his partner and two sons were fortunate that they had another vehicle to rely on during their stay.
"Thankfully my other son was driving his car up as he wanted to go off and meet up with his friends and we had two cars, but a lot of the plans we had were obviously impacted because we were down to the one car."
He said his car had to get towed back to Belfast and cost about £225 to fix.
East Londonderry assembly member Claire Sugden said she had received a number of messages from constituents at the beginning of the week who had raised concerns after filling up their cars at the petrol station.
"One constituent had fuelled up and then, the following day, his car wouldn't start and he then took it to a mechanic, and it is still there. He is now without a car so it is concerning," Sugden said.
"He had seen on social media that others had experienced similar issues after filing up at this station so it seems to be a pattern which has seen Asda conduct an investigation."
Sugden said anyone who may have filled up their cars at the petrol station should be made aware of any potential issue.
"It is pleasing that Asda have responded quickly in relation to this, but it is important that other people who have fuelled up at this station are made aware that this issue could potentially affect them too."

title: Thousands raised for Wolverhampton Lidl crash victim's family
text:
Thousands raised for Lidl crash victim's family
Thousands of pounds have poured in for the family of a "much-loved" man who was killed after a car crashed through the entrance of a Lidl supermarket.
Father-of-two James Singh Jagpal, 39, was pronounced dead at the scene of the crash in Wolverhampton, which emergency services were called to just before 18:00BST on 23 October.
An online fundraiser has been set up to help towards his funeral costs and, within just two days, more than £8,100 has been raised.
"No family should ever have to experience such heartbreaking loss, and no words can truly express the pain and emptiness left behind," said Sophie Jagpal, a family member who set up the page.
She added: "In a moment, this family's world has been turned upside down as they try to come to terms with a loss they could never have prepared for.
"We want to bring our family, friends and wider community together to show them that they are not alone and that they have people around them who care deeply and want to help in any way they can."
In a statement issued by police, James, from Wolverhampton, was described by his family as "a much-loved son and brother, devoted partner of over 20 years and loving father to two wonderful daughters".
They paid tribute to his "kindness, generosity and wonderful sense of humour".
Two people who suffered serious injuries inside the building have since been discharged from hospital, West Midlands Police said.
The driver, a woman in her 70s, has also been released from hospital and will be "spoken to in due course", the force added.
Four other people were treated by paramedics and discharged at the scene.
Floral tributes have been left at the site, and the store remains closed while repair work is carried out.
In a statement, Lidl said it was saddened by the incident and that the store would remain closed until further notice.
Police have asked anyone who was in the Finchfield Hill area on the evening of the crash and saw a blue Renault Zoe to contact the force. The death is not being treated as suspicious.

title: Gateshead flyover demolition costs almost double to £33m
text:
Flyover demolition costs almost double to £33m
The expected cost of the Gateshead Flyover demolition has passed £32m, almost double initial estimates.
The concrete structure was closed in December 2024 due to fears it could collapse, with a six-month demolition completed on 1 October.
Gateshead Council initially set aside £18m for the works, but figures due to be presented next week estimate a total of £32.6m with the possibility of further change, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.
A council spokesperson said the final overall cost of the project was expected to be confirmed in Spring 2027 once all remaining works had been completed.
A council report stated contractors BAM had provided an initial estimate of £17.3m in March 2025 to demolish the flyover in a "timely manner".
However, the price was subject to change as the scheme developed and became more detailed, the cost having risen to £31m by July.
The initial estimate has been branded as "not comparable" to the current forecast due to a series of factors.
These included the procurement of 10-tonne steel props used to prevent the structure from collapsing, paying for 24-hour work periods during certain phases of the scheme, protection measures for the East Street flats and monitoring of the underground Tyne and Wear Metro tunnels.
The local authority also cited relocation of some East Street residents, fuel price increases, the running of shuttle buses during the Five Bridges roundabout closure, structural monitoring and surveys as further costs.
The final works are expected to be completed in December 2026.
The flyover's removal is viewed by local leaders as a major opportunity to reshape Gateshead town centre and attract investment.
The government has repeatedly been urged to commit funds towards its removal and the town's subsequent regeneration, but is yet to do so.

title: Original Hertfordshire Traitors star became film actor after show
text:
Original Traitors star became film actor after show
A contestant from the first UK series of The Traitors has said the show transformed his life and helped launch his acting career.
Kieran Tompsett, 46, from Stevenage, Hertfordshire, was recruited as a traitor towards the end of the 2022 series, he was banished during the final episode, but memorably hinted at the identity of the last remaining traitor as he left.
Tompsett said the experience prompted him to ask: "What else do I want to do now?" He then decided to attend Ashley Walters' Kingdom Drama School.
He said: "I've trained for a year and a half and I've done three or four films now, I've done some supporting artist work to get some experience on set."
Earlier this year he appeared in the He-Man film Masters of the Universe, and will appear in an upcoming dark comedy called Damaged Goods.
Tompsett was working as a solutions consultant when he appeared on the hit BBC show in 2022 and now runs an AI workflow automation company.
He said: "I've just secured lead cast in a horror film for next year as well, so yeah, I'm going down a completely different path."
However, the former traitor admitted he initially found being in the public eye difficult.
He said: "I think in the first two years it was overwhelming. Anyone who has been on it will know you can't even go to Tesco and buy a meal deal at lunchtime without everyone staring at you.
"It's not a negative thing, but your privacy goes... I've always stopped and talked to everyone, still, it's quite hard to experience that loss of privacy, really."

title: China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
text:
China denies allegations of spy operation targeting Nvidia CEO
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times.
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia said their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed and the White House for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed told the paper its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.
description: US intelligence officials believe a Chinese businesswoman was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, The New York Times reports.

title: Isle of Man Yacht Club concerned over RNLI lifeboat changes
text:
Yacht club expresses concerns over lifeboat changes
The directors of a sailing club in the south of the Isle of Man have expressed concerns about plans for a nearby rescue boat to retire and not be replaced.
The Isle of Man Yacht Club (IOMYC) said decisions that may affect the safety of people using the island's waters deserved "open discussion, public understanding and appropriate scrutiny".
It comes after the Royal National Lifeboat Institute (RNLI) confirmed earlier this month the Trent-class vessel based at the Port St Mary station would retire in 2028 and would not be replaced.
The IOMYC said the issue was not whether rescue cover will continue to exist, but whether the same level of response capability, resilience and speed of attendance could be maintained for incidents occurring in southern waters.
The RNLI has been invited to comment.
In a previous statement, the organisation said it was confident neighbouring stations on the island could provide overlapping cover and respond to incidents in the south.
"The removal of the boat would not leave it without rescue coverage," the RNLI added.
'Clear and accessible evidence'
The yacht club is not the first to voice concerns about the news. A former Port St Mary crew member and an experienced skipper from North Wales who was rescued by the station in May also expressed sadness and nervousness at the loss of its all-weather lifeboat.
The club's directors said that while the station would retain its D-class inshore lifeboat, "there will be incidents where an all-weather lifeboat is the more appropriate asset to meet the rescue requirement".
They also described the waters around Langness, the Calf of Man, Chicken Rock and the southern approaches as "some of the most challenging around our coastline".
"There are strong tidal streams, overfalls, exposed sea conditions and fog," they said.
The directors added that commercial fishing activity mixed with recreational sailing combined to create an environment where conditions could deteriorate quickly and unexpectedly.
While welcoming the RNLI's commitment to safeguarding those at sea, the IOMYC said the scale of the change warranted greater transparency about the operational modelling, response-time analysis and risk assessments behind the decision.
"Such a significant alteration to lifesaving provision around our island should be accompanied by clear and accessible evidence, demonstrating how equivalent levels of protection will be maintained for those who operate in southern waters," the directors said.

title: Reform wins Labour MP's old Bassetlaw council seat in by-election
text:
Reform wins Labour MP's council seat in by-election
Reform UK has won a by-election to take a district council seat previously held by a Labour MP.
Nancy Wright was elected as councillor for Worksop East on Thursday with 600 votes, beating Labour's Cameron Holt, who received 485 votes.
The by-election was held after Bassetlaw MP Jo White resigned following 14 years as a councillor in September.
White, who campaigned for Holt alongside mayor of the East Midlands Claire Ward, said the decision to step down was due to a "risk of a conflict of interest" with her role as MP.
In a social media post after her victory, Wright said: "The days of Labour running Bassetlaw are numbered, and only Reform is able to provide the change we need.
"This election is a clear wake-up message to the Labour establishment in Bassetlaw and across the country that residents will no longer be taken for granted.
"I will get straight to work fixing Worksop and putting residents first rather than Westminster."
Results in full
- Nancy Wright, Reform UK: 600
- Cameron Holt, Labour: 485
- Anne Froggatt, Restore Britain: 91
- Ben Storey, Conservative: 89
- Anne Kean, Green Party: 42
The Conservatives also won by-elections for Nottinghamshire County Council and Newark and Sherwood District Council.
Penny Rainbow was elected as Southwell's county councillor, while former county councillor Scott Carlton won the Dover Beck seat on Newark and Sherwood District Council on Thursday.
Both seats were previously held by Conservative councillor Roger Jackson, who died from cancer in July.
Carlton received 409 votes to Reform candidate John Hart's 328, while Rainbow had 2,019 crosses on the ballot paper, while Reform's Edward Stubbs received 1,159 votes.

title: Wanted Leicester pub toilet rapist caught after running red light
text:
Wanted pub rapist caught after running red light
A man who raped a 17-year-old girl in a pub toilet in Leicester before going on the run for two months was arrested after driving through a red traffic light, police have said.
Police said Pandeli Dervishi, 24, forced the girl to perform oral sex on him inside the toilets of a pub in The Newarke on 1 October 2025.
Officers were called after the victim was heard in distress by a member of the public, and Dervishi was arrested before being charged with rape in February.
After failing to answer bail, Dervishi was eventually arrested when a police officer spotted him running a red light in Surrey on 16 April. Following a trial, Dervishi was jailed for seven years and six months on Thursday.
Following initial inquiries, Leicestershire Police said detectives investigating the case bailed Dervishi while they "continued to obtain and review key evidence, including CCTV, forensic evidence and digital material".
When he failed to answer police bail at a designated police station, the force said he was added to the Police National Computer as a wanted person, while officers carried out inquiries to find him.
'Held accountable'
In the early hours of 16 April, police said Dervishi's whereabouts were discovered when an officer spotted him driving a white Mazda through a red traffic light in Guildford.
After initially attempting to drive away, Dervishi was eventually stopped.
Subsequent inquiries confirmed he was wanted by Leicestershire Police.
At Leicester Crown Court, Dervishi - of no fixed abode - was convicted of one count of rape and jailed.
Det Con Jon Williams said: "During the time Dervishi remained on the run, the victim was left facing considerable uncertainty.
"While I continued to reassure her that we would find him, it is entirely understandable that she was anxious and concerned that she might never receive the justice she deserved.
"I hope the outcome provides the victim with some measure of comfort and allows her to move forward knowing that Dervishi has been held accountable for his actions."

title: Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
text:
Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
English regional mayors due to be handed a share of tax revenues by central government will be free to use it to give cash grants to individual residents and businesses, it has emerged.
In his Budget, Chancellor John Healey unveiled plans to allow mayors to keep some cash from income tax and business rates collected locally, describing it as "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants local leaders to be given more control over how money is spent in their areas to boost economic growth and services.
But Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he has been given assurances that he will be able to give grants to local residents instead.
Lord Houchen told the BBC he is working on a voluntary scheme that would give local residents the opportunity to apply for a share of the tax distributed to his region.
He said Treasury officials had told him this would be acceptable within the government's rules around the devolution of funding.
"It's a technical point around spending decisions," Lord Houchen told the BBC.
He said devolution of funding was a "good thing" and "means mayors are able to decide spending commitments, which includes rebates".
The BBC has been told mayors could choose to use the tax revenues they received from the government to offer grants to individual residents or businesses.
But any mayor who decided to use the money in this way would have less for other local priorities, such as housing and transport.
Lord Houchen has described his proposal as a "tax rebate scheme".
The Treasury would regard these payments as grants, because His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is the only government authority in the UK that can issue income tax rebates.
Most of England's 14 strategic authorities are led by Labour mayors who have welcomed the move to give them a portion of income tax receipts.
Sources close to Reform UK's Greater Lincolnshire Mayor Andrea Jenkyns, and her counterpart in Hull and East Yorkshire, Luke Campbell, say they are waiting for more details to fully understand how they could use these tax revenues to benefit their regions.
The government published its broad approach to reforming funding for local and regional government in England after Wednesday's Budget.
As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding from ring-fenced grants, allocated by central government to be spent on specific policy areas.
From April 2028, all mayors of strategic authorities in England will be assigned a share of basic-rate income tax generated in their areas.
Each mayor will receive a bespoke funding allocation that takes into account regional inequalities in tax bases, with the exact amounts to be set at the government's spending review next year.
"The government is not devolving the power to set income tax rates or thresholds to mayors but will be granting significantly more flexibility as to how assigned revenues are spent locally," the government's plan says.
"Mayors will be able to choose where to target funding, for example whether to maintain funding for local transport or prioritise other interventions."
From next year, mayors will also receive a 20% share of locally retained business rates.
This will be the first step towards allowing local and mayoral authorities to retain 100% of their business rates income before the end of the decade.
From 2028, strategic authorities led by mayors will also be given the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, often dubbed a "tourist tax".
This charge will be an uncapped levy as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.
Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge to 5%, but others - such as Lord Houchen - said they would not introduce the levy.
Burnham - who used to be a mayor himself in Greater Manchester - argues that funding and decision-making powers are too centralised in the UK.
The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, a global policy forum.
That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).
But critics of fiscal devolution raise concerns about local capability, and inequalities between areas.
The Centre for Cities think tank says some areas may not have the expertise to manage developed powers effectively, risking deeper economic inequalities between areas.
The think tank supports fiscal devolution and believes it can offer significant benefits, if the challenges are managed effectively.
The Tees Valley Combined Authority (TVCA) led by Lord Houchen is facing a government inspection into its finances, after Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said he had concerns about its "long-term financial sustainability".
The authority said it welcomed the scrutiny and would continue to make improvements where needed.
description: The Tory Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he's working on what he's calling a "tax rebate scheme".

title: Binance hack - who is behind it, is my money safe and what we know so far
text:
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).
Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.
Binance said the hackers raided its digital assets in part by conning a company engineer through a fake job interview.
North Korea is being widely blamed - but it insists it had nothing to do with it.
What is Binance?
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.
It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.
The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.
Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.
In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.
How did the hack happen?
Binance has described the attack in its initial findings as a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that took place over several months.
It said hackers deployed a range of techniques, including social engineering - which seeks to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details that can be used to gain access to their accounts.
According to Binance, hackers contacted one of its engineers through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited them to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
During a second interview, the engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" which deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.
Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
Experts say it underlines the threat posed by so-called social engineering attacks, where individuals are tricked into helping hackers.
"You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.
Who is behind the hack?
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack.
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.
These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor.
North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".
Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.
North Korea has denied the claims.
Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
What does it mean for Binance users?
The company has said from the outset that it will cover the losses and that customer funds are safe.
Binance chief executive Richard Teng stressed on Friday that the incident had affected its own wallets, not those belonging to its customers.
But users globally were could not withdraw their balance from the exchange until the service was restored on Sunday.
According to a Binance representative, a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC.
Users of other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.
Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet".
"Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase," he said.
What does this mean for cryptocurrency and the wider financial system?
Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance".
"More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said.
"If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."
She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers.
Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.
The Bank of England has warned this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.
How many people use cryptocurrency?
Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.
This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.
But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.
According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.
description: Binance has been hit by be the biggest crypto hack ever - here's what we know so far.

title: Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell Balmoral visits
text:
Police Scotland carrying out 'active inquiries' into Andrew and Epstein Balmoral visits
Police Scotland is making inquiries into the activities of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislane Maxwell during their time at Balmoral Castle.
The Daily Express reported that the inquiry relates to allegations that women were trafficked to the royal residence in Aberdeenshire.
Sex offender Epstein - who died in 2019 - and Maxwell, who was jailed in 2022 for sex trafficking, are understood to have visited the castle with Mountbatten-Windsor, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Police Scotland said inquiries were at "a very early stage" and that it would be inappropriate to comment further.
Representatives of Mountbatten-Windsor have been contacted for comment.
The Royal family traditionally spend summer at Balmoral, where Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022.
Asked about the Express report, a Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have received information and active inquiries are ongoing but these are at a very early stage.
"All inquiries are evidence led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries.
"We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
In February, the force said it wanted to "speak to anyone with information" about Epstein's private jet using Edinburgh Airport.
At the time officers said they had not received any reports or complaints in relating to the trip.
Flight logs show Mountbatten-Windsor and Maxwell flew from Luton to Edinburgh on Epstein's private jet with two other passengers on 1 September 2006.
An image believed to show disgraced financier Epstein and former socialite Maxwell at Balmoral was also released by US prosecutors during her sex trafficking trial.
It is thought to have been taken in 1999, when Mountbatten-Windsor reportedly invited the couple to stay at the castle.
Epstein and Maxwell were reportedly regular guests at royal residences in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
Last year, the so-called Epstein Files were released by the US Department of Justice.
Among them was an email from someone named 'A' to Maxwell which said they were at Balmoral and asked for "new inappropriate friends".
The message, sent to Maxwell on 16 August 2001, begins: "I am up here at Balmoral Summer Camp for the Royal Family."
Later in the email, the sender asks: "How's LA? Have you found me some new inappropriate friends?" before signing off "see ya A xxx".
Jeffrey Epstein was 66 when he died by suicide in 2019 in a US prison while awaiting trial for sex trafficking charges.
Maxwell, 60, was jailed for 20 years in 2022 for her role in procuring girls for Epstein.
Last October it was confirmed Andrew had been stripped of his "prince" title and would be leaving his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge.
In February he was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US, and later released.
Earlier this month it emerged he was taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over search warrants issued before his arrest.
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.
Asked about the latest reports, Scottish First Minister John Swinney said: "I understand the seriousness of the points that have been made and the concern that has been expressed.
"This is an operational matter for Police Scotland to fully and comprehensively investigate and I'm very confident that's exactly what Police Scotland will do."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he did not want to comment on the police inquiries, which "should properly be independent".
description: The force said it had received information and stressed its inquiries were at "an early stage".

title: Car driver who dragged head teacher to his death guilty of murder
text:
Driver guilty of dragging head teacher to his death
Warning: This article contains distressing content
A man has been found guilty of murdering a head teacher who was dragged to his death for more than a mile while trapped under the wheels of a car.
Simon Richardson crashed into 56-year-old Michael Mullins, who was cycling home from his job at Stretford Grammar School on the evening of 20 April in the village of Warburton in Trafford, Greater Manchester.
Prosecutors claimed Richardson, 35, fled the scene of the crash before stopping to try to dislodge the injured but still-living cyclist and then driving on with Mr Mullins still lodged underneath the vehicle.
Richardson was also convicted of dangerous driving and will return to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to be sentenced on Monday.
There were shouts of "Yes!" from the court's public gallery as the guilty murder verdict was announced.
Others could also be heard crying.
The judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, told Richardson that there was only one sentence for murder, namely life imprisonment.
In a statement released after the verdicts had been returned, Mr Mullins' family described him as "an anchor", "the perfect dad" and "our everything".
"My past, present and future have been brutally and callously torn apart," said his widow.
"My memories of being with Michael through the rough and the smooth are now permanently tainted with sadness."
Mr Mullins' son described his late father as "the type of Dad that would show up to everything".
He said: "Our last exchange of words together before he dropped me at the station was him reminding me of how proud he was of me."
Mr Mullins' daughter added: "I made a promise in those first days that I would live the rest of my life for my Dad and give myself the life he had started to see me grow into and wanted for me.
"I am here telling you all that my Dad was and always will be our everything."
The court heard Richardson, of no fixed address, had driven through "give way" markings at a junction in Warburton before colliding with the father-of-two, who went under the Volvo XC90.
Richardson then drove off before stopping in a country lane and twice getting out of the vehicle in attempts to pull Mr Mullins free, the jury was told.
He then mounted the grass verge in his Volvo and finally dislodged him before reversing over Mr Mullins, causing "crushing" chest injuries.
Richardson's cousin Gabrielle Debotte, who was a passenger in the front seat of the car, previously told the court that both of them had heard "moaning" shortly after the collision in Paddock Lane and that he had gone on to say: "He is under the car."
The prosecution claimed Mr Mullins' injuries were caused by "dragging and crushing" rather than the impact of the crash itself.
Prosecutor Phil Barnes KC told jurors: "Simon Richardson knew he was there and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway.
"For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down.
"But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away.
"The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done."
A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood and discovered Mr Mullins alone and barely breathing as he lay on a grass verge in a secluded country lane in Lymm, Cheshire.
The head teacher was pronounced dead at the scene shortly afterwards by emergency services.
Richardson was arrested the next day following a police chase.
He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mr Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle in a bid to free him.
But jurors did not believe him and found him guilty of murder.
Mrs Justice Brunner KC thanked members of the jury and acknowledged their job "cannot have been easy".
She discharged the jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: "This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing."

title: Road in Banbury partly reopens following building collapse
text:
Road partly reopens following building collapse
A road which had remained closed for more than a week after a building site partially collapsed has partly reopened.
Two people were taken to hospital after an apartment block under construction partly collapsed alongside scaffolding on the A4260 Cherwell Street in Banbury, Oxfordshire, on 21 October.
The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) previously said it was investigating the incident, and its inspectors had visited the site as part of its inquiries.
The key route had remained totally closed since the incident, but Oxfordshire County Council said that the route had reopened on Friday afternoon.
Following safety advice, the county council said it had created two lanes in the road space furthest from the collapse between the George Street and Bridge Street junctions.
The two temporary lanes run in opposite directions - allowing traffic to flow through from either side of the collapse.
It said some right turns into Lower Cherwell Street and Morrisons petrol station are restricted as part of the reopening.
The road, which sits on one of the market town's busiest junctions, had remained closed since the incident, causing traffic to divert and build up elsewhere.
A proposal by the site's owner to make the site safe and for materials to be removed is currently being considered by the HSE.
Councillor Gareth Epps, who is in charge of Oxfordshire's roads, previously said: "We can't afford to take any chances with people's safety."
Announcing the partial reopening, the county council said the road would likely need to be closed again in its entirety to allow crane operations to make the building site safe.
The authority added that it would wait for further information from Cherwell District Council and the HSE before fully reopening the road.
Since the road closure, locals had taken to social media to report widespread congestion and long delays around other town centre routes, including at Banbury Cross.
Thames Valley Police said nine workers had been at the site when the scaffolding and building both partially collapsed - with two injured and taken to hospital.
description: Cherwell Street in Banbury had been shut more than a week after a building and scaffolding collapsed.

title: Major Soho development gets green light from Westminster council
text:
Major Soho development gets green light
Plans for a major development of four linked buildings on Soho Square have been approved by Westminster City Council.
The project, which includes the former home of 20th Century Fox Film Corporation, will form part of an almost 9,000 square-metre complex featuring new office space, an archway onto Soho Square and retail units.
The scheme, brought by the Royal London UK Real Estate Fund, was approved at a committee meeting on Tuesday, said the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).
Alistair Martin, from Simten Developments said the project was "about giving a long, underused part of Soho a sustainable future, one that represents the very best of Soho".
An eight-storey tall building will comprise what is now 31-32 Soho Square and 65-66 Frith Street, while two further buildings, 22-25 Dean Street and 10 Chapone Place, will be refurbished.
The area will be expanded by 2,477 m sq, and a new landscaped public court yard will be fitted by Chapone Place.
Residential flats that are clustered in Townsend House, one of the existing buildings, will be incorporated in the new development.
Residents have asked developers for noise reduction glazing to be applied to their rear windows, and for heat pumps to be installed.
The scheme will also provide 150 long-stay cycle spaces, seven of which will be for residents, and an affordable workspace for the community at the Dean Street building.
A new archway entrance on Soho Square has been proposed to form a pedestrian route to Dean Street.
However, local community group and charity Soho Society opposes the archway and has said that it should be protected as a space for "rest and recreation".
Its chairperson Tim Lord said: "The purpose and role of Soho Square is respite.
"Soho Square is a protected square under the London Squares Preservation Act 1931, limited to garden, rest and recreation use."
He also said that the archway would disrupt the symmetry of the green space.

title: Exhibition highlights Bristol memorial to those lost in WW1
text:
Exhibition highlights memorial to those lost in WW1
The names of men who never returned from World War One are at the centre of efforts to bring a little-known memorial back into public view.
The memorial, which commemorates 114 men from Eastville, is housed inside the New Testament Church of God on Fishponds Road and is the focus of a new exhibition aimed at preserving their memory.
The names include several brothers, a former Bristol Rovers footballer and a merchant seaman who was lost when a troop ship was sunk by a German submarine.
"I almost feel as if it's actually forgotten," said parishioner Sharon Francis, who wants people to use the exhibition to discover the stories behind the names.
Made up of two elaborate panels, it was erected in 1921 at a cost of more than £300, a considerable sum at the time.
Francis, who has long admired the memorial, said: "It's hand painted, it's quite lavish and it's huge. The craftsmanship is really nice."
The panels feature St Alban and St George, alongside the names of the men who lost their lives.
Local war historian Jeremy Banning has helped research the stories behind those commemorated.
He added: "Most memorials at that time were sort of wooden panels or pretty simple memorials, and this is really something I haven't seen before, certainly in Bristol.
"It's really elaborate, golds and blues and reds really jumping out, and very ornate stonework. I mean, it's stunning."
The men served in a range of forces, including the Gloucestershire Regiment and Canadian forces. One Bristolian even travelled to Australia to serve.
Banning said: "They are all literally from the streets around here.
"Some would have been neighbours. So the loss that they would have felt within Eastville and all across Bristol is unbelievable."
He thinks the memorial could help reconnect local families with their history.
"There undoubtedly will be families around here who are still in the area, who don't know about this," he said.
Francis said: "We need to remember the names of these brave men."
The exhibition will run on Friday 6th and Saturday 7th November from 11:00 to 15:00 and aims to open up the church to the wider community and encourage descendants and local residents to discover the memorial.

title: Section of A417 to close to traffic for roadworks
text:
Key route to close for weekend roadworks
Drivers face a weekend closure of a major route as roadworks continue.
The A417 will be closed in both directions between Shab Hill junction and the A429 Burford Road from 23:00 GMT until 06:00 on Monday.
National Highways said the closure was needed to complete work on the Missing Link project at Cowley junction and to open a northbound slip road. The work will allow drivers travelling north from Cirencester to leave the A417 at Cowley junction and continue towards Birdlip via the old A417.
A diversion route will be in place throughout the weekend, with motorists advised to follow road signs.
The disruption comes weeks after the new A417 route opened, allowing motorists to bypass the Air Balloon roundabout when travelling between Gloucester and Cirencester.
The old A417 route will remain in place until the new B4070 opens later this year, National Highways said.
The Missing Link scheme has been under construction since 2023 and is expected to be completed in 2027.
Senior project manager at National Highways Céline Acard said road closures were necessary to allow work to be carried out safely on and around the junction.
"We plan very well in advance to make sure that we impact as few people as possible", she said.
"We do appreciate that it's frustrating and we can only thank everybody for their patience while we carry out this essential work".

title: Paul Heaton to headline at Ludlow Castle in July
text:
Paul Heaton set for beautiful south Shropshire
Former Housemartins frontman Paul Heaton is set to perform in beautiful south Shropshire next year.
Heaton will be joined by Scottish singer-songwriter Rianne Downey on 17 July, when he plays as part of the annual summer concert series in Ludlow.
The Live at Ludlow Castle shows will also feature McFly, Becky Hill and UB40 ft Ali Campbell, with more acts due to be announced.
The concerts began in 2023, with 50,000 people visiting this year over two weekends, to see the likes of Snow Patrol, Paul Weller, The Human League, Tom Grennan, The Streets, Rick Astley, Richard Ashcroft and Scissor Sisters.
Heaton founded The Housemartins in 1983 and found success with Happy Hour, Caravan of Love and Build.
Later, he created The Beautiful South, who released 10 albums and had chart success with songs including A Little Time, Don't Marry Her and others.
The band sold 15 million albums and their 1994 singles compilation, Carry On Up The Charts, has been one of the best-selling albums in British history.
Since The Beautiful South broke up Heaton has continued as a solo artist and during the coronavirus pandemic he discovered Downey after she posted a video of herself singing The Beautiful South's single, Rotterdam (Or Anywhere).
The pair now tour together and have appeared at festivals including Radio 2 in the Park and Glastonbury.
Support acts for Heaton are yet to be announced.
Boost for Ludlow economy
The Live at Ludlow organisers, Futuresound, said the concerts sell out every year and had become "a vital and highly anticipated event in the town's cultural calendar".
Futuresound said they brought more than £1m into the town in 2025 and an agreement was signed this summer to continue them until at least 2033.
Tickets for the Paul Heaton concert are due to go on sale to people in the Ludlow area on 4 November with general sale starting on 6 November.

title: Tributes pour in for Bristol-trained actor Sir Patrick Stewart
text:
Sir Patrick Stewart 'used his stage on behalf of others'
Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, has been described as a "treasured" actor and a "true champion" of the Bristol theatre school he trained at.
Tributes have poured in since Sir Patrick's death at his Los Angeles home on Wednesday after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement shared on his social media.
The acclaimed actor, who found global fame in Shakespeare productions, Star Trek and X-Men, had trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School from the age of 17.
He was also a patron of local theatre company Unique Voice which tours schools, running drama workshops to educate children about domestic violence.
A spokesperson for the charity said: "He knew he stood upon a stage and he used that stage on behalf of others countless times."
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.
His most notable roles included Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films.
He also had a distinguished stage career with the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) that established him as one of the country's leading Shakespearean actors.
Bristol Old Vic Theatre School (BOVTS) principal Stuart Harvey said his "exceptional" career stood as a testament to "the power of rigorous classical training".
He said: "Before becoming an international icon on stage and screen, Patrick honed his craft right here at the school as a member of the class of 1959.
"In recent years, we were deeply privileged to receive Sir Patrick's support. He remained forever proud of his BOVTS heritage.
"His legacy as a master of his craft and a true champion of our school will endure always."
Fellow alumnus and theatre director Sir Gregory Doran worked alongside Sir Stewart on a production of Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra in 2006.
He recalled how the acclaimed actor "restored the magnificence" of the role.
"I'm realising that was why he was so great - he had this very solid, firm foundation [of training]," he said.
"That allowed him, in a way, to take the helm of the Starship Enterprise and fly around the galaxies. I shall miss him greatly."
Sir Doran said a performance of Romeo and Juliet at the Tobacco Factory in Bristol later would be dedicated to his memory.
Outside of work, Sir Patrick was a prominent campaigner against domestic abuse after witnessing his father beating his mother as a child.
He became a voluntary patron for Unique Voice in 2011, with co-director Krystal Keeley describing him as a "perfect fit" and an "amazing inspiration".
She said: "When we met him we were still like 'we can't believe you've chosen us', but he said it was a no-brainer.
"He cared deeply about giving a voice to people who were underserved. We will be forever grateful to him and incredibly proud that he chose to stand alongside us.
"He did it all with such warmth, such genuine care and kindness. It's a very sad day that the world has lost such a treasured artist."

title: Retrial for Jersey gas worker over fatal explosion
text:
Retrial for gas worker over fatal explosion
A retrial has been ordered for a man accused of gross negligence manslaughter after a fatal gas explosion.
Ten people died following an explosion at Haut du Mont flats in Jersey in the early hours of 10 December 2022. Lee Ward denied 10 counts of the charge and jurors were previously unable to reach a verdict and were discharged.
Gas workers Neil Armstrong and John Wright were found guilty of the same charges and Island Energy was found guilty of health and safety breaches.
They will be sentenced over four days between 26 and 29 January. Jersey's Attorney General ordered the retrial for Ward at Jersey's Royal Court on Friday.
Crown Advocate Simon Thomas told the court he anticipated the retrial could last about two weeks, but "it was difficult to say with any certainty".
The States Employment Board (SEB) had already pleaded guilty to two charges under the island's health and safety at work law.
The board, which employs the island's public servants, faced charges concerning the actions of Jersey Fire and Rescue Service and its emergency control room on 9 December 2022 - the day before the explosion.
It will also be sentenced over the same dates in January.

title: Lancashire political leaders frustrated by council reform delays
text:
Leaders frustrated by council shake-up delays
Political leaders have expressed frustration after a planned major shake-up of local government was pushed back.
Lancashire had been set to undergo local government reorganisation, which would have seen the county council and 14 district councils and unitary authorities replaced with four new unitaries.
But the planned reforms - which would have impacted 14 areas across England - were put on hold by the government in September.
Local Government Minister Jim McMahon confirmed that only five of the original proposals would go ahead as planned - Lancashire not being one of them.
'Absolute mess'
In a letter to leaders in the nine areas where the plans have been withdrawn, McMahon said the decision was "not a reflection of the quality of the proposals submitted by councils in your area, but rather the need to give each decision of such significance the careful consideration it deserves".
He added: "All options and proposals in your area will remain under consideration as part of the review."
It is expected that more details will be made public before Christmas and a new decision about what to do next will be made in 2027.
Existing councils in Lancashire had been expecting to be scrapped next year but will now hold elections in May.
The leader of South Ribble Council, Labour's Matthew Tomlinson, said: "The uncertainty that this is causing - for our staff, for councillors and elected officials and for our residents too - is not helpful and it doesn't look great on the government."
The Independent leader of Burnley Council, Afrasiab Anwar, said the government had "made an absolute mess of this".
He added: "What that means is all options are now back on the table, there is an option here to look at the decision again and I think it's best to get two authorities for the Pennines."
Leader of Wyre Council, Conservative Michael Vincent said: "They have done everything they can to undermine local government, they've backtracked and changed their minds that it's difficult to take it seriously."
"It's a shambles," Caroline Jackson, Green leader of Lancaster City Council, said: "And we're beginning to think we're being treated with contempt in local government, what are we going to do next, yet more delays?"
Reform UK deputy leader of Lancashire County Council, Simon Evans, said: "It's a never-ending can that's being kicked down the line, we're no clearer, we still haven't got the detail, we're being asked to sign up to something that we don't actually know how or when it's going to work."
"It feels like we're still in that period of the unknown," Chorley Council's deputy leader, Labour's Peter Wilson, said.
"We were hoping for some real clarity and sense of direction but it appears that we have to continue to wait."

title: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
text:
They strangled us, says founder of Russian newspaper shut under pressure from authorities
At the editorial offices of Novaya Gazeta, they are packing up and shutting down.
Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.
For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.
Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.
It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.
"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."
"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.
"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."
In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.
Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.
As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.
In a statement on its website announcing the closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities.
"They've killed us," it starts. "The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
The publication claims it is the victim of "a coordinated act" and blames "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime… The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the 'special military operation', new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Earlier this year there was a police search of Novaya Gazeta's editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case the newspaper's current editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form. Loyal readers used VPNs, virtual private networks, to circumvent official blocking of the website. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions were a major blow to the publication.
How does Dmitry Muratov view the future?
"We are in the middle of a terrible catastrophe," Mr Muratov tells me. "Different dictatorships in the world seek chaos. They use chaos to rule their countries and peoples and to strengthen their personal power.
"I don't know what will happen next. I do know that we will do everything to stay true to our values: the human right to life. Human rights override the rights of states."
Novaya Gazeta's demise is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

title: Lead and mercury in fake make-up seized by GMP
text:
Mercury, lead and methanol in fake beauty products
Mercury, lead and methanol have been found in counterfeit beauty products seized by trading standards officers.
Police found 1,660 fake hair extensions, shampoo and conditioners during a raid at a warehouse in Manchester in July.
Trading standard officers also seized fake perfume, cosmetics, clothing and vapes worth £2m at a warehouse production base in Bolton.
Cosmetics, skincare and perfumes are now among trading standards' 10 most commonly investigated fakes, with four in 10 seized cosmetics containing potentially harmful substances.
The raids were carried out by the Police Intellectual Property Crime Unit and Greater Manchester Police (GMP).
Tests found 13,200 parts per million of mercury in one skincare product, high levels of lead in lipstick, eyeshadow and contour products, nicotine in perfume and a counterfeit fragrance made up of around 80% methanol.
A fifth of 18 to 24-year-olds who bought beauty products last year knowingly purchased fakes, up from 6% in 2023, according to the latest Intellectual Property Office (IPO) counterfeit goods tracker.
The IPO's Face the Fakes campaign is working with influencers and the beauty industry to raise awareness of the potential harms of counterfeit beauty products.
Independent toxicologist Rani Ghosh said: "When you hear that mercury has been found in face cream, lead in make-up or nicotine in perfume, it raises serious questions about what is going into these products and how they are being made.
"Some reactions to unsafe cosmetics may be visible, such as irritation, swelling or changes to the skin.
"But what concerns me as a toxicologist is what you might not see.
"Substances such as mercury and lead can affect the body internally, and those effects may not be immediately obvious."
'Appalling conditions'
Helen Barnham, head of enforcement engagement at the IPO, said: "Products can look remarkably convincing, but behind the packaging they can contain dangerous substances that have no place in the cosmetics people use every day, and can be made in appalling, unhygienic conditions.
"Counterfeiters exploit the names and reputations of brands that consumers know and trust, while bypassing the rigorous safety standards that legitimate businesses work hard to meet."

title: Men jailed over plot to distribute cocaine smuggled in cheese
text:
Men jailed over plot to smuggle cocaine in cheese
Fifteen men who were part of a gang which distributed up to £1.4bn of cocaine smuggled into the UK hidden in cheese, chocolate spread and cod mince have been jailed.
The criminal network, described by West Yorkshire Police as the "largest criminal enterprise" the force had dismantled, was estimated to have moved more than 4.5 tonnes of drugs across the north of England in just 18 months.
Sentencing the men at Leeds Crown Court, His Honour Judge Christopher Batty said those involved were responsible for distributing "astronomical sums" of cocaine.
Det Insp Kevin Daly described organised crime groups as "very ingenious in coming up with different ways to be able to hide the drugs".
The exact amount of drugs the gang distributed - and their value - is unknown, but a Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) spokesperson said available intelligence and evidential assessments estimated it to be between four and 14 tonnes, which equated to a street value of between £400m and £1.4bn.
'Sophisticated conspiracy'
The police investigation into the gang was sparked when cocaine and ecstasy worth £2m were seized from a car whose driver was stopped in the East End Park area of Leeds in January 2023.
The discovery led officers to uncover what Batty described as a "sophisticated conspiracy to distribute what were huge quantities of cocaine that had been imported from South America via Europe".
More than 100,000kg of gouda cheese was transported as commercial freight into Dover and then on to a legitimate distribution hub in Derby between December 2022 and April 2023, police said.
Refrigerated trucks then collected shrink-wrapped pallets of cheese and delivered them to industrial units in Huddersfield, Cleckheaton and Halifax in West Yorkshire and Blackburn in Lancashire.
At those locations, blocks of cocaine hidden within large wheels of the dairy product were unpacked and then re-packaged in cardboard boxes and black bin liners.
A network of couriers from the Midlands, Lancashire and the North East would then collect the drugs for onward distribution.
After two members of the distribution network were arrested in May and July of 2023, officers said they "observed a change in tactics", with pick-ups instead taking place at motorway service stations and consignments of chocolate spread and frozen fish mince used to hide the drugs.
One defendant, Craig Goulding, who was jailed for 25 years in May, was paid "thousands" to dispose of the waste food from the operation, police said.
Many of those sentenced in May and this week were arrested in December 2023 and have been convicted in a series of linked trials.
Reporting restrictions had been put in place by the judge to avoid prejudicing the trials, but have since been lifted.
Daly said tackling "sophisticated" gangs such as this was a constant challenge.
"To a certain extent we take out one and another will try and repopulate," he explained.
"It's something we are continually looking at. We are continually looking to try and tackle serious and organised crime."
To date, all those sentenced for their involvement in the conspiracy have been jailed for a total of 196 years.
Two of those convicted - Sammy Stapleton, 42, of Peel Hall Road, Manchester, and Nathan Reilly, of Oxton Avenue, Manchester - are due to be sentenced next month.
Meanwhile, Mark Briggs, 30, of Norham Avenue South, South Tyneside, will also be sentenced at a later date.
The others received the following sentences:
- Craig Asquith, 44, of Gill Sike Grove, Wakefield, 10 years imprisonment
- Craig Goulding, 39, of Church Lane Avenue, Wakefield, 25 years imprisonment
- Aiden McCullagh, 58, of Mill Grove, Brighouse, 25 years imprisonment
- Ikram Sadfar, 44, of Willowfield Road, Halifax, eight years and nine months imprisonment
- John Whittell, 43, of Spa Grove, Wakefield, 12 years and nine months imprisonment
- Harry Johnson, 26, of Caledine Road, Leicester, 16 years imprisonment
- Darren Johnson, 31, of Caledine Road, Leicester, 15 years imprisonment
- Jordan Miles, 33, of Winchat Close, Coventry, 12 years and eight months imprisonment
- Aaron Gowans, 28, of Chivers Court, Stockton-on-Tees, five years and 11 months imprisonment
- David Jackson, 48, of Broadoak Avenue in Manchester, 14 years and four months imprisonment
- Umaar Farooq, 37, of Gladstone Road, Halifax, 15 years imprisonment
- Lewis Ockenden, 36, of Esther Avenue, Wakefield, 13 years and four months imprisonment
- Brandon Eley, 31, of West Street, Tamworth, 10 years imprisonment
- Anthony Etheridge, 70, of HMP Fosse Way, 18 months imprisonment
- Aaron McNally, 38, of of Ada Street, Manchester, 10 years and nine months imprisonment
A CPS spokesperson said other defendants had also been sentenced over their roles in the wider operation.

title: Number plate camera plan to tackle Ninewells Hospital parking issues
text:
Number plate camera plan to tackle Ninewells Hospital parking problems
Number plate cameras could be used to tackle parking problems at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, according to an NHS Tayside report.
The health board launched a review following complaints that patients, staff and visitors regularly faced long queues to get a parking space.
A traffic survey showed about 7,000 vehicles normally enter the site between 07:00 and 15:00 on weekdays, despite there only being 2,500 available spaces.
Parking fees at the hospital were scrapped by the Scottish government in 2021, but there are claims that some drivers use it as a park-and-ride to travel into the city centre.
Health chiefs said some patients can face waits of up to an hour, making them late or forcing them to miss appointments altogether.
At present, Ninewells visitors using short-stay car parks must display a free ticket on their vehicles, but can be fined if they stay beyond the four-hour time limit.
During 2025, more than 14,500 fines were handed out at Ninewells car parks – a rise of more than 3,500 on 2024.
The health board said this "indicates that the existing arrangement and approach is not sufficient to prevent or deter parking violations".
A report presented to the NHS Tayside board set out measures proposed for both Ninewells and Perth Royal Infirmary.
During the first phase, NHS Tayside will renew its car park management and enforcement contract at both hospitals.
It will also cost the introduction of automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras in three car parks at Ninewells to enforce the four-hour limit.
NHS Tayside hopes these cameras will "improve turnover" in high-demand public parking areas closest to the main entrance, and provide more reliable real-time information on parking use which can "support future decisions about parking allocation and traffic management".
The second phase of the plan involves "operational changes to improve traffic flow and better align parking provision with the needs of patients, visitors and staff".
These include changing drop-off areas and additional provision for blue badge holders.
The health board says it will also introduce "transparent, evidence-based permit criteria" for staff and the "redefinition of staff and public car parking areas".
Speaking at an NHS Tayside board meeting, director of infrastructure Rose Jenkins said that "everybody recognises there's a long-term issue" around parking at the hospital.
"There is no intent to put charges back in," she said.
"If you don't follow the rules, you'll get a ticket, and therefore you'll be expected to pay a fine for that.
"Overall, we are hoping this will make improvements."
There is no current timescale for the introduction of the new measures.
Story by local democracy reporter Liam Rutherford.

title: Hull escapology event marks 100th anniversary of Houdini death
text:
Remembering Harry Houdini and his great escape
Magicians in Hull have held a series of events to mark the 100th anniversary of the death of legendary escapologist Harry Houdini.
The illusionist performed in the city a number of times, including escaping after jumping into the Humber from Victoria Pier while in handcuffs and chains in 1914.
Jon Marshall, from Hull Magicians' Circle, said 8,000 people turned up to witness the stunt, which was to publicise his performance at a local theatre.
Marshall said despite dying a century ago, Houdini was "still a household name".
"Houdini, of course, was such an incredible publicist that created this legend and he is world famous still," he told BBC Radio Humberside's Kofi Smiles.
"In 1914, he jumped into the river Humber, chained and manacled. He escaped, of course, to advertise his performances at the Palace Theatre.
"He appeared at the Palace Theatre six times, from 1903 right through to 1920."
To mark his death on Halloween in 1926, the circle held a family magic show in Hull Trinity Market, including an escapology demonstration by Victoria Pier, close to where Houdini performed in 1914.
Will Frow managed to escape from a 100ft rope quicker than the time it took two members of the public to bind him.
"They tied me up in a minute and 47 and I managed to scrape through a minute and 35, which was brilliant to hear that I managed to make a successful attempt within time", he said.
"The hardest bit of it was probably getting back up off the floor after I fell over."
Hull Magicians' Circle, which was founded in 1933, is also holding a talk for its members on Houdini's life and legacy.

title: Seoul crush scene to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
text:
Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty game after an angry reaction from victims' families.
Real life news coverage of the 2022 disaster which killed almost 160 people was included in an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4 to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.
Bereaved families said they were "appalled" to see the footage - which included people being removed on stretchers, body bags on the street and resuscitation efforts - repurposed for the game.
Activision, which makes Call of Duty, has since apologised and confirmed it would be removed in the game's next update on 12 November.
The crush happened in the narrow alleys of Seoul's Itaewon district when more than 100,000 people went to the area to celebrate Halloween four years ago.
The streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.
In a statement on Thursday, the families of those who died said the disaster "was a tragedy that caused hundreds of casualties, and citizens who took part in the rescue or witnessed it have suffered from trauma until now".
"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used to create a scene in a game.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless."
'Not intended to trivialise'
Activision confirmed it had used real news coverage of the disaster "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insisted it had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
Confirming on Friday that the footage would be removed in a statement, the company offered its condolences and apologised to the bereaved families and victims who have been hurt by this incident.
The decision was welcomed by the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association, however the group told the BBC they had not received a direct apology from Activision.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told BBC Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".
Additional reporting by Sophie Jeong

title: Date confirmed for start of Lincolnshire's tips booking system
text:
Date confirmed for start of tips booking system
A date has been confirmed for when bookings can start being made for visits to Lincolnshire's tips.
The county council said people would be able to book slots from 30 November, with the system getting under way on 7 December.
The scheme is being introduced at the county's 11 tips in a bid to reduce queues.
There has been some criticism of the move, but Danny Brookes, a member of the council's executive, said: "People don't like change. This is one of the biggest reasons why people don't like it. You've got to give it a chance, we've got to do something."
Speaking on BBC Radio Lincolnshire, Brookes said: "The problem is a lot of people are turning up at once, all at the same time with the same amount of waste, and the waste streams are full.
"If you've been sitting in a queue for nearly an hour and you can't dispose of your waste, people get pretty angry.
"It's why the staff are getting verbally abused, and you can't have that when they're just trying to help people and do their job."
Brookes said that the council was planning to have the tips open six days a week, but was also looking at staggering the opening hours so they are not all closed on the same day.
How will the booking system work?
Visitors will be able to book up to two weeks in advance, but Brookes said at least 10% of the bookings can be made on the day.
- Bookings will be able to be made online and over the phone.
- People will be given 15-minute time slots when they can arrive at their chosen recycling centre
- They will confirm their vehicle and the types of waste they want to take
- Confirmation will be received by email or text message, and amendments or cancellations can be made
