title: Enoch Burke: Police investigating reported assault Church of Ireland leader
text:
Police investigate alleged assault after Enoch Burke confronts church leader
Police are investigating a report of an assault following an incident involving Enoch Burke and the head of the Church of Ireland.
A video posted on social media by former teacher Burke shows him confronting and grabbing the arm of Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland John McDowell.
A spokesperson for the church said Burke and members of his family approached the archbishop following a funeral service at St Patrick's Church of Ireland Cathedral on Thursday.
Burke has been in a long-running legal battle for defying court orders to stay away from a school that dismissed him for gross misconduct.
The dismissal arose out of his refusal to obey a direction of the school that a transgender pupil be addressed as 'they' and "because of his gross misconduct at a school religious service (and other events) and the manner in which he conducted his objection to transgenderism", according to the legal judgement.
The school also obtained an injunction restraining Mr Burke from trespassing on the school premises, which he has defied a number of times.
The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed it was investigating a report of an assault on a member of the clergy.
"Police enquiries are ongoing," a spokesperson added.
In the video, Burke, along with another man, confronts McDowell and grabs his arm before the Archbishop says "you are assaulting me".
He accuses McDowell of staying "silent" after Burke said he was in a "prison cell for 700 days".
McDowell continues to tell Burke that he is "assaulting" him and "preventing me from going about my lawful business".
He then says: "If you keep assaulting me, I am going to report you to the police."
Another member of the church tells Burke "you are in the grounds of a cathedral at a funeral".
A Church of Ireland spokesperson said it was a matter of "deep concern and sadness" that the Burke family had confronted the archbishop in a "particularly hostile and aggressive manner" following the funeral service for a rector of the diocese who died last week.
"No respect was shown for the occasion or the sanctity of the cathedral grounds," they continued.
"Entry onto the See House property, which is a private residence, is a further concern."
The Church said it would assist police with their enquiries and would make no further comment until the investigation was complete.

title: Oleshky ceasefire: Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied town in Ukraine
text:
Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
Hundreds of residents of the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have been evacuated, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have said, following a humanitarian ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
"Everything unfolded without any incidents, and both sides noted the high level of organisation," Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova said.
Planes carrying Oleshky residents landed in the city of Gomel, Belarus on Saturday morning, Belarusian state media and a senior Ukrainian official said.
The evacuees are expected to board buses to drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region later on Saturday.
Speaking to journalists on Friday evening, Lantratova put out a joint request with her Ukrainian counterpart "to the US First Lady... that humanitarian missions such as this one, delivering aid to residents in need, be conducted on a regular basis under the coordination of Mrs Melania Trump".
Melania Trump said that "all elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders".
A ceasefire - the longest and most widespread since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.
Residents who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so on Friday. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
The Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power, which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.
In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."
The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.
On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.
A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.
Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

title: Red rainbow: Extremely rare phenomenon spotted in County Antrim
text:
Extremely rare red rainbow spotted in County Antrim
An extremely rare red rainbow has been captured on camera in County Antrim.
Pete Kirk spotted the sight in Mallusk on Friday morning and sent the photos to the BBC.
Rainbows form when sunlight is bent and reflected by water droplets in the air, splitting the light into different colours.
Red rainbows form in the same way, but appear at sunrise or sunset when the sun is low in the sky.
At these times, sunlight travels through more of the atmosphere.
Colours such as blue and green are scattered away, leaving mostly reds and yellows, giving the rainbow a reddish glow.
It is essentially the same phenomenon that causes red sunsets.
Unlike a red sunset, red rainbows are uncommon, people who study the skies may only ever be lucky enough to see a red rainbow once or twice in their lifetime.

title: Northumberland A1 dualling petition delivered to Downing Street
text:
A1 dualling petition delivered to Downing Street
A petition calling for the dualling of a stretch of the A1 in Northumberland has been handed in to Downing Street.
There have long been calls for the single carriageway stretch to be upgraded but it has been reignited following the deaths of eight people this year.
Almost 15,000 signed the petition, organised by campaign group Northumberland A1 Safety Alliance, which also organised a five-day walk from Berwick to Newcastle city centre to highlight the issue.
The government scrapped a previous dualling scheme due to spiralling costs, but Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on a recent visit to Newcastle his government would look for an "alternative way" to fund the scheme.
It has also committed to safety improvements.
The petition calls for ministers to commit to a continuous dualling of the A1 all the way to the Scottish border.
It also seeks immediate, interim upgrades, including to junction visibility and hazard warnings, to prevent yet more deadly crashes.
70-mile hike
Alliance co-founder Kezz Petronelli-Stone said he hoped it could reach 100,000 names by next February to trigger a debate in Parliament and has invited Burnham to arrange a visit to see the problems on the A1 first hand.
He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "We've cultivated a very strong following.
"I think though it started with the road it quickly came to symbolise the neglect we feel we're suffering.
"Our farmers, our small businesses, particularly our hospitality sector are absolutely on their knees.
"Hard working people are flogging themselves to bits with less and less to show for it."
He handed in the petition alongside Scottish Conservative MP John Lamont, who represents the borders constituency of Berwickshire, Roxburgh and Selkirk.
Before handing over the petition, campaigners hiked along a 70-mile (112km) route, taking in towns and villages including Alnwick, Ellingham, Felton and Morpeth.
Conservative council cabinet member Guy Renner-Thompson, who completed the first leg from Berwick to Belford, said: "The walk may look like a bit of fun but it's about raising awareness for a very serious issue we all face here in north Northumberland.
"We need people in London to take this seriously."
An upgrade to 13 miles (21km) between Morpeth and Ellingham was planned by previous Conservative government, but the cost spiralled to more than £500m and the current government scrapped the project in October 2024, calling it "unfunded and unaffordable".
However, it has committed to carrying out junction improvements on known accident blackspots, with a scheme announced for the Guyzance junction focusing on safety improvements on the southbound carriageway.
In August, Burnham admitted the level of transport infrastructure in the region was "not fair" compared with other parts of the country and officials would work alongside North East Mayor Kim McGuinness to look into whether a funding package could be put together.

title: Keep clear markings painted at Flintshire school that shut in 2016
text:
Gaffe sees 'keep clear' lines painted on road outside school that shut 10 years ago
Bright yellow "keep clear" school markings have been mistakenly painted on a road outside a school that has been closed for 10 years.
The 30ft-long (9.1m) markings in English and Welsh were painted outside Ysgol y Fron in Holywell after Welsh Water dug up the road for the sewer network and was told to reinstate the carriageway "on a like-for-like basis" by Flintshire council.
Holywell resident Russell Price said the error was "the talk of the town", adding: "It's a bit daft, the school has been closed since 2016."
Flintshire council admitted the "school-specific markings were no longer appropriate" and said it was "rectifying" the problem.
Price described it as a "classic case of departments not talking to each other".
He thought Welsh Water would have been asked to reinstate the road "like for like" by the council and took it literally, replacing the faded old markings.
The old school is now overgrown, but there is a nursery next door, leading him to wonder if there had been some confusion.
But, he added, the work took eight weeks "so it would have been apparent the school was not in use".
Tamsin Prichard, who works nearby, branded it "a bit silly".
She walks past regularly and initially thought the markings were for the daycare next door before realising they stopped short of the premises.
Katie Wilby, the council's chief officer for streetscene and transportation, said: "Following the installation and a review of this, the council recognises that the school-specific markings including the school keep clear zigzags and associated school no-parking markings are no longer appropriate given that the school has been closed for a number of years.
"The council is therefore rectifying this and following a review of the road markings outside the former school the council intends to remove the school-specific zigzag and no-parking markings while retaining the existing yellow lines."
Welsh Water said: "Following some works to improve the sewer network in Halkyn Street, Holywell, we reinstated the carriageway.
"The markings were repainted on the instruction of the council."

title: Uttarakhand's Joshimath: Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state
text:
Six dead after helicopter crashes in northern Indian state
Five pilgrims and a pilot have died after their helicopter crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.
The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
The cause of the crash is not yet known but there had been reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.
Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.
Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.
Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter came down near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district.
The local civil aviation authority later confirmed to Indian media that six bodies had been located.
Helicopter services have become increasingly popular among pilgrims seeking to avoid difficult mountain journeys, but their safety has come under scrutiny following a series of accidents.
Before Friday's crash, India's weather department had issued an orange alert for the area, warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds.
In June 2025, seven people were killed when a helicopter carrying pilgrims crashed near Kedarnath. Another seven died in a crash on the same pilgrimage route in October 2022.
Several other helicopter accidents were reported during the 2025 pilgrimage season, prompting aviation authorities to tighten safety checks and restrict some operations.

title: A38 traffic: New speed limit on key route amid safety concerns

The affected road includes the junction with Comeytrowe Lane, which has been shut until 23 December to allow for the delivery of a bus gate as part of the Orchard Grove development.
First approved in 2018, the bus gate is designed to improve public transport links between the new 2,000-home Orchard Grove development and the town centre.

title: Plans to turn former Derby Grand Theatre and nightclub into college
text:
Plans to turn former nightclub into college
Plans to turn a former city centre theatre and nightclub into a new college have been submitted.
UK Management College Ltd, which already has a campus in Derby's Cornmarket, want to turn the former Derby Grand Theatre building, on Babington Lane, into a site with 10 classrooms, an IT lab, board meeting room, learning hub, cafe and lounge.
The site, which was once home to McClusky's nightclub and most recently House of Holes indoor crazy golf, could hold a capacity of 250 people, documents said.
The Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) said Derby City Council could make a final decision on the plans as soon as December.
'Underutilised building'
As well as being McClusky's, the site was the home of Locarno Ballroom in 1959, Tiffany's in the 1970s to 1984, and nightclubs including Confettis, Ritzy, Eclipse, and McClusky's in the 1980s and 90s.
UK Management College Ltd hopes the change will boost Derby's learning offer, employment rates and subsequently the city's economy.
A planning statement on behalf of UK Management College said the site will support the "growth of Derby's education sector" and will create jobs "improve employment rates through the education and upskilling of the community".
"The re-use of the historic building to ensure it enhances the character of the site and surrounding area and the provision of increase choice in education will have a positive social impact," documents added.
"With regard to the environmental objective, reusing the underutilised building and bringing the heritage asset back into a viable use will have significant positive impacts."
No dedicated parking spaces are proposed, but bus stops are located nearby.

title: DUP leader 'hopes' Carla Lockhart will not leave party
text:
DUP leader 'hopes' Carla Lockhart will not leave the party
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson has said he does not want to see Upper Bann MP Carla Lockhart leave the party.
Lockhart has called for the DUP to remove First Minister Michelle O'Neill from office by having Emma Little-Pengelly resign from her role as deputy first minister.
However, on Thursday the DUP confirmed that Little-Pengelly would not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission would not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.
Sinn Féin MP John Finucane called the move "an example of economic sabotage, of self-harm, by the DUP, all because they struggle with internal party cohesion".
It follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order parade in Portadown, County Armagh, from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
In a letter to party colleagues on Thursday, Lockhart said she would "take her own course" if O'Neill was not removed as first minister.
Other DUP politicians, including assembly member Diane Forsythe, have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be removed from office.
Assembly member Maurice Bradley also said that removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the assembly to collapse".
A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held on Thursday.
Party leader Robinson said the decision among DUP assembly members to cease engagement between the first minister and the deputy first minister was "unanimous".
Lockhart is expected to resign from the party, the Belfast Telegraph has reported.
Robinson said he "hopes" that Lockhart would not leave the party, adding: "We all share the same view that there needs to be political sanctions for the behaviour of Michelle O'Neill."
On Friday, in a post on social media, Lockhart said she will "set out the path ahead early next week".
"My principles and my commitment to the people who put me here will guide that path. I will continue to represent Upper Bann and serve my constituents with every bit of the energy, commitment and vigour I always have," she added.
She said "party political calculations are not my concern" and that "this was a moment for unionism".
Last week, Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.
Police have said they have built cases against 60 suspects in connection with the Drumcree and Garvaghy Road protests.
Eighteen of those suspects have been interviewed and case files are being prepared before being submitted to the Public Prosecution Service.
On Thursday the DUP blocked O'Neill from attending the National Economic Council.
The meeting was due to be attended by Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the leaders of the UK's devolved nations.
"If anybody steps back and thinks about the pressures on our political institutions, the fragility of our political institutions and would they tolerate it in Scotland, Wales and England - I think the honest answer to that is: no, they would not," Robinson told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme.
He said his party "will not take steps that will punish the people of Northern Ireland".
"I've been very clear that there is a job of work to do that can only be achieved through the executive and my colleagues will be absolutely, fundamentally principled and absolutely, fundamentally robust in dealing with and for the people of Northern Ireland."
He said the halting of engagements with O'Neill was a consequence of the first minister "stepping outside her pledge of office".
Burnham has said he does not want to see Northern Ireland "left behind" as he expressed disappointment over the first and deputy first ministers being absent from the UK-wide National Economic Council.
Burnham described the absence of the first and deputy first ministers from the summit as "disappointing" but said there was "some representation" in the form of Stormont civil servants.
Burnham said his push for "regional devolution" across England was "moving quickly" and he did not want to see other areas "left behind".
"I don't want to see Scotland left behind, I don't want to see Wales left behind but also crucially I don't want to see Northern Ireland left behind.
"So it's really important that we move at the same pace together and I won't allow anything to delay that growth.
"It can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Sinn Féin's Finucane said: "Yet again we are dealing with the DUP that is mired in scandal and mired in internal division and the unfortunate reality is that everybody has to suffer as a result of this drama playing out in front of all of us.
"This was a very important meeting that the first minister and deputy first minister should have been at."
'Petulant stunt'
Other parties in the Northern Ireland Assembly have been critical of the DUP's move.
Alliance Party assembly member Kate Nicholl said Northern Ireland not being represented at Friday's meeting of the NEC was "so disappointing" and "completely baffling".
Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic", adding: "The DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle."
Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows said the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences".
The move would "probably galvanise Sinn Féin further at the ballot box," he added.
Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) assembly member Matthew O'Toole said: "Plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism."

title: Suffolk councils will know result of government shake-up by March
text:
March deadline for council shake-up, says minister
The government has said it will make a final decision on local government reorganisation (LGR) for Suffolk by March next year.
Jim McMahon, the minister for local government, devolution and regional growth, told Parliament on Thursday the government was reviewing decisions for 15 councils, including Suffolk.
McMahon said: "All options and proposals in these areas will remain under consideration and I'll approach all those with an open mind."
In March ministers had backed a plan to split Suffolk into three unitary authorities, but a legal challenge by Reform UK forced a delay.
The government wants to shake up local authorities by having just one council to provide services over a geographic area.
What has happened in the past?
In June, Reform launched legal proceedings against the government to review the plan for three unitary authorities in Suffolk.
The government responded by withdrawing the plan in September, along with plans for Norfolk, Essex and Hampshire.
McMahon told MPs on Thursday, he was now satisfied the criteria the government had set to make its decision was "robust".
He would conclude the review of LGR plans for 15 areas, including Suffolk, by spring of next year at the latest, he added.
He did caution, however, that "it should be not assumed that the same proposal will be automatically selected".
Michael Hadwen, the leader of Reform-led Suffolk County Council, welcomed the government's stance.
He said: "It seems they are willing to listen. Possibly in December, more likely in the new year, the minister will sit down, review the business cases for Suffolk, talk to us about it, and then a decision will be made."
When asked what plan would be acceptable for Suffolk, Hadwen responded: "I know the three unitaries won't work for Suffolk.
"What I now need to work out is, was the one Suffolk business case the right one? I don't know. I need to look at the detail."
How do councillors feel?
The district and borough councils in Suffolk had supported the plan for three unitary authorities.
Andy Mellen, the leader of the Green Party which runs Mid Suffolk District Council, said: "Given the twists and turns there have been on this journey, I'm not going to accept what we're told until it actually happens.
"We've been down this road before, and the government has pulled the plug."
Cliff Waterman, the Labour leader of West Suffolk Council, which is led by a coalition with West Suffolk Alliance and Independents, said: "It's a good announcement today. It moves things and it shows us that the government is still serious about rebuilding trust, confidence and efficiency into the local government system."
He said he still supported the three unitary plans for Suffolk, adding: "I'm confident the arguments we put forward in our submission still hold true.
"When the minister re-examines the proposals, I hope he'll agree that our proposal is still the best one."
The Conservative Group ran the previous administration at Suffolk County Council, which supported a one unitary bid for the county that was rejected by the government.
Richard Rout, the leader of the Conservative group, said he was hopeful this review may lead to a different outcome.
"It would seem strange for the secretary of state to remake exactly the same decision next year, particularly with many of the flaws in the prior decision being highlighted and then judicially reviewed," he said.
The government's announcement also confirmed elections would go ahead for district and borough councils in May next year along their current boundaries.
In May 2028, depending on the outcome of the review, elections will go ahead for the new authority or authorities in shadow form, with the new councils expected to be fully up and running by 2029.

title: Gloucestershire's 'super council' set to go ahead after pause
text:
'Super council' set to go ahead after pause
Seven county and district councils are to be merged into one unitary authority after the government announced it was reinstating plans for a "super council".
Currently the six local councils are responsible for services like waste collection, with Gloucestershire County Council looking after things like adult social care.
In September, ministers paused proposed local government reorganisation (LGR) plans in 14 areas while a review was carried out. The government has now confirmed Gloucestershire's "super council" can go ahead, with the first elections due in 2028.
Councillor Lisa Spivey, leader of the county council, welcomed the news, but said "the delay has consequences".
"We are already facing extremely difficult financial choices, and it would be wrong for Gloucestershire taxpayers to pick up the costs of LGR," Spivey said.
The new council will be formed following shadow elections in 2028 - a year later than originally planned.
As the new authority is set up, local councils and the county council will keep operating, before being abolished in 2029.
Elections for Forest of Dean and Cotswold District Councils will go ahead next May, along with Tewkesbury Borough Council.
Speaking in the Commons, Conservative MP for the North Cotswolds Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown questioned why the shadow elections are delayed by a year.
"Why [are we] having an election next May on the existing councils?" he said.
The Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said they "have to have a programme that is consistent".
"What we can't do is say because there seems to be a bit more local consensus in one place than the other and the legal risk is a bit less we can shortcut the process," he added.
Devolution delays
In response to the government's announcement more questions were raised about devolution.
Local authorities are clubbing together to create a mayor who then has more devolved powers and money to spend in the local areas.
Gloucestershire was not named in the chancellor's budget speech for extra funding as it still needs to go through the process of abolishing its local councils.
"We cannot allow Gloucestershire to become the forgotten county when it comes to devolution," Spivey said.
Six of Gloucestershire's seven councils have backed a proposal to join the West of England Combined Authority, which covers Bristol, North Somerset and Bath and North East Somerset.
Councillors from Tewkesbury Borough Council want the option of joining a Three Counties or Mercia combined authority to be kept open.
As does Reform UK councillors in Gloucestershire who want to team up with Worcestershire and Herefordshire.

title: Manchester United Munich air disaster memorial items stolen
text:
Items stolen from Man Utd Munich air disaster memorial
A glass sculpture and medals have been stolen from a memorial to the 23 people killed in the Munich air disaster, including eight Manchester United players.
The items were taken from a display case at Manchesterplatz in Munich, where the plane crashed on take-off on 6 February 1958 after refuelling on its return from a European Cup match in Belgrade.
Munich Police said the glass case around the memorial was smashed with a rock when the items were taken between 08:00 and 13:00 local time on Monday 26 October.
The Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF) said it was "deeply saddened", while its chair, Ifty Ahmed, said the theft had caused emotional harm to families.
"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ahmed told BBC News.
He said the memorial had provided solace for families who lost loved ones in the crash.
"And whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories," he said.
Mark Salzmann, chairman of Red Docs Munich, a Bayern Munich supporters' group which helps care for the memorial, said his mother discovered the damage while driving past.
Salzmann said a glass sculpture originally presented to Munich's former mayor, Dieter Reiter, was among the stolen items.
His group collects tributes left by visitors from around the world and places some of them in the display case.
He said the objects were unique and could not easily be replaced, but the group was discussing possible replacements with the foundation.
Ahmed said it was still unclear exactly how many medals were missing.
He said Manchester United had offered to pay for repairs, but the foundation had already agreed to cover the costs itself.
The broken glass was replaced on the same day, according to the foundation.
Ahmed said supporters of Liverpool, Manchester City and Leeds had also sent messages of support.
A memorial stone was installed in 2004, while the display case was added in 2020 and officially inaugurated in 2023.
About 1,500 people from around the world attended the annual remembrance service at Manchesterplatz in February, according to the foundation.
Salzmann said the messages of support he had received showed how important the memorial was, adding that the connection between Manchester and Munich "will never go away".
Police said no suspects had been arrested and appealed for witnesses or anyone with information to come forward.
The BBC has contacted Manchester United for comment.

title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
text:
Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

title: Celebrity Traitors: 'Seeing Claudia and James Blunt wearing my suits was ridiculously exciting'
text:
Seeing Claudia in my suit was ridiculously exciting
A tailor described seeing Claudia Winkleman and singer James Blunt both wearing his bespoke three-piece tweed suits on Celebrity Traitors as "ridiculously exciting".
Claudia's stylist contacted Gloucestershire tailor and shirtmaker, Tom Wharton, after he posted some outfit ideas for the presenter on social media in 2024.
On 22 October, his brown Cotswold country tweed suit was worn by Claudia in episode seven of the hit BBC series, while James Blunt also sported one of his suits in the opening episode.
Wharton said: "No-one tells you. We had James wearing it in the first episode, which was pretty epic and then it's, 'Is it this episode' and suddenly it was."
Cut and tailored by Barrington Ayre in their showrooms in Cirencester, Claudia's brown, herringbone tweed suit, which sells for about £1,600, made its debut in The Traitors' castle last Thursday.
Wharton said they have "always loved The Traitors" and the clothing Claudia wears, so seeing her wearing one of their creations was "huge".
"It's ridiculously exciting," he said.
"It's something we've been working on for going on two years.
"So, actually when you finally get to see it on TV and you're finally allowed to talk about it, it's brilliant."
He was contacted by Claudia's stylist after posting outfit ideas for the host's headline-making wardrobe on Instagram.
"We tried to have a chat and get everything sorted for the last series but with timings and with Claudia's diary we couldn't meet up, so I thought the moment had gone," he said.
"But [her stylist] got in contact again late last year and so, we were making it from there and it popped up on this series."
Despite not getting to meet Claudia in person, he still described the experience as incredible.
Not knowing which episode their creation would appear on, Wharton said he and his staff were glued to every episode of the show watching and waiting.
"You keep an eye on Instagram for them to pop out those little teasers of what she's wearing and suddenly it was like, 'this is it, this is it. We're on, we're on'.
"The worst thing is, you're not allowed to talk about it. There was a complete embargo. So yeah, it's lovely to be able to finally talk about it."
Stalwart faithful, James Blunt also chose the Gloucestershire tailor to kit him out in a suit for the show.
Wharton said he did become a bit suspicious about where his new "rather dashing bespoke three-piece" was going to be worn by the local singer and ex-military man.
"He wanted some clothes made and wanted to keep it local, [in the] Cotswolds," he said.
"And as we were making them, he [dropped some] hints, 'Oh, this would be lovely for me to wear up in Scotland', and I was like, 'who goes to Scotland in June, when you're a popstar?'."
Unsure if the singer was going to be a contestant or not, Wharton decided he could not tell him he had also "made stuff for Claudia".
"I didn't say anything and suddenly I was like, 'hold on, that's my suit', as he popped up on the first episode of Traitors," he said.
"Seeing something you have made being worn on television by some of the most influential celebrities is an epic buzz."

title: Concerns as monkey used in Birmingham restaurant's online videos
text:
Concern as monkey used on restaurant's social media
The use of a baby monkey in a restaurant's social media video has sparked concerns from primate charities.
Eastern Jam, a restaurant in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter, posted a video of a woman holding a young marmoset called Pablo, which was captioned: "Even the monkey had to see what the hype was about."
When people on social media expressed concern about the use of the animal in the video, the restaurant replied that the video was AI-generated.
However, the restaurant later told the BBC that the video was not AI-generated but had been filmed by external social media company without their consent.
Influenceable, the external social media company used by the restaurant, told the BBC they had not authorised the involvement of the monkey in the shoot and had "no prior knowledge" it would be brought to set.
"We do not condone animal cruelty or any behaviour that compromises animal welfare," they said, adding: "We have taken appropriate internal action following the incident."
The video features a woman initially holding the baby monkey in a towel outside the restaurant, who says: "Guys, I bought my friend to try Eastern Jam for the first time."
It then shows the woman inside the restaurant with a table full of food and the monkey placed on her shoulder, before she holds him up in the air while talking about the restaurant's food.
The video sparked several comments from people concerned about the use of the monkey in a commercial video, with the restaurant responding that it had been created by AI.
However, BBC Verify carried out visual checks and concluded that the video did not appear to be AI-generated.
In a statement, a spokesperson for Eastern Jam said they "did not authorise or commission a shoot involving a live monkey".
"Our understanding was that the content being produced featured our approved model and food, and we had incorrectly assumed that any unusual elements were usually AI-generated," they added.
"Due to online feedback from social media users, and in particular someone with experience in AI we started an internal investigation... and we have established that a real monkey was used during part of the shoot, which does not belong to Eastern Jam.
"This particular element was arranged without the knowledge or specific authorisation of Eastern Jam's management."
The spokesperson also explained they had outsourced their social media management to an external company in Willenhall called Influenceable.
Eastern Jam told the BBC that it had now ended its contract with Influenceable "with immediate effect".
"We would also like to offer our sincere apologies for the initial confusion on our part," a spokesperson said.
Welfare charity concerns
The Primate Society of Great Britain said it was "fundamentally opposed to the use of living primates to produce online content for private or commercial gain".
They told the BBC that the primate featured in the video was an immature marmoset monkey, estimated to be between the age of six and 10 weeks old.
A spokesperson said "It is likely that the animal in this video is experiencing significant stress, given the absence of its family members, and through being handled by unfamiliar individuals in a loud and overstimulating environment.
"Additionally, videos like this, whether real or AI generated, can lead to the perception that primates are appropriate pets and suitable for possession in a domestic setting. This is not the case.
"Primates are undomesticated wild animals, which if housed in human-made environments require specialised professional care (e.g., within zoos or sanctuaries).
"The perception that primates are suitable pets is a key driver of illegal pet trades, which is a critical conservation threat for many primates (including marmosets), alongside broader habitat destruction."
Veterinary adviser for the charity Action for Primates, Nedim C Buyukmihci, said: "Using this infant marmoset for entertainment and as a prop for financial gain to advertise a restaurant is cruel and totally inappropriate.
"The monkey is being subjected to a frightening and stressful situation and susceptible to the risk of disease transmission from human customers.
"Monkeys are sentient, intelligent, highly social and complex animals and they do not belong in this kind of domestic setting or in captivity to entertain people."
In January, the government introduced more stringent legislation regarding the ownership of monkeys, estimating that between 3,000 and 9,000 primates were being kept privately in the UK.
The legislation means it has been illegal to keep monkeys, chimpanzees, lemurs and other primates in England without a licence since April, and that they must be kept in "zoo-like" conditions.
Eastern Jam said: "We have been advised that the primate is licensed and well looked after. However, as we aren't the owners, we can't confirm this information ourselves."

title: Parking fine for nurse comforting bereaved family in Birmingham
text:
Parking fine for nurse comforting bereaved family
A nurse who was given a £100 parking fine while comforting a bereaved family has called for greater protections against fines for fellow nurses.
Varanica Whinfield, a community nurse from Oldbury, was giving care while parked at Perry Barr Village, the same location where fellow nurse Lisa Smith was recently fined after getting stuck in a lift while trying to treat a sick baby.
"I'm providing care [at] the last minute, which is like life and death," Whinfield told BBC Radio WM.
The BBC have contacted the company which issued the Penalty Charge Notice (PCN) about the fine.
Whinfield added: "When it comes to health, you just can't say, oh, I'm going to wait. A sick or poorly person can't wait."
She said the nearest place she could find to park was a half an hour walk away, which was not practical because of the equipment she has to carry.
The community nurse had to visit Perry Barr village twice that day and is dreading the prospect of a second fine she cannot afford.
'Can't just walk off'
"I had to make sure the medication is given and is correct, and the other [visit], make sure I stay with the grieving family," she said.
"I can't just walk off. It's care."
While she said she would debate it in court if she had to, she was concerned about the number of her colleagues with similar parking fines, with many given for parking at Perry Barr Village.
"In the future, what happens if you just pay this one off? It's not fair. It shouldn't be like this," she said.
The issue of parking fines related to healthcare was also raised by Joe Lycett earlier this year, when he complained about receiving a fine after not paying for parking immediately while taking his son to Birmingham Children's Hospital's A&E.
Speaking on fellow comedian Katherine Ryan's podcast, What's My Age Again?, Lycett said: "They must be making so much money from people rushing into A&E, not paying for parking straight away. I think that's morally wrong."
Whinfield tried to appeal the parking fine through Popla, an independent appeals service for parking fines issued on private land, but it was refused.
A spokesperson for the organisation said the charge had been "validly issued by the operator".
"The appeals charter does allow charges to be cancelled for health workers on emergency calls, but only if the vehicle displays a British Medical Association (BMA) badge or authorised Health Emergency badge," they added.
"No badge was displayed, and nothing indicated she was a health worker, so the operator had no reason not to issue the charge."
They also said the operator had reduced the charge "beyond its obligations" to £20 after learning Whinfield was a nurse on duty, though Whinfield told the BBC she was not aware of any reduction to her parking fine.
Whinfield believes there should be parking protection in place for community nurses and emergency service workers so they are not fined for providing care.
"No nurse is actually looking out to go park illegally because that's one of the things that we actually do take into consideration," she said.
'Fear of becoming victim'
"And even if someone paid for this one what happens in the future? I'm a community nurse. I'll always be in the community."
A spokesperson for Birmingham Community Healthcare NHS Trust said they were aware of "wider interest in issues at this location" and were "following developments".
A spokesperson from the Royal College of Nursing in the West Midlands pointed to the approach taken in Worcestershire, where they said councils had introduced a permit scheme to stop healthcare workers from receiving fines.
"Unfortunately this approach is far from universal," they added.
"We would urge more of our local councils, working with their local NHS trusts, to follow suit to enable community nurses to carry out their vital work without fear of becoming victim to a parking fine."

title: Yorkshire Water chief Nicola Shaw resigns after firm downgraded
text:
Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency.
Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.
In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was the "right time" to leave her post.
Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.9m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2026, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.
The payments were made by Yorkshire Water's parent company, Kelda Holdings, for what the firm said was "investor engagement" and "financial oversight".
On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".
The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.
'Extremely proud'
In her statement, Shaw said: "It has been a privilege to lead Yorkshire Water and serve the people of Yorkshire.
"Although there remains a huge amount of work to do, I am extremely proud of what our colleagues have achieved, putting the business on a stronger footing for delivery across all aspects of its work."
Yorkshire Water said Medalova, who is a former non-executive director of the company's board, would join the firm on Monday as part of a transition period before assuming the chief executive officer role full time in the new year.
She said: "I am delighted to be joining Yorkshire Water and grateful to the board for the opportunity to lead the business through its next chapter.
"Yorkshire Water faces huge challenges but also great opportunities for continued improvement and I look forward to working with Nicola Shaw, the leadership team and colleagues across the business as I get up to speed."
In December last year Shaw said "not being transparent" about receiving £1.3m in shareholder-funded payments across two instalments had been a "mistake", but had insisted those amounts were "not for me to decide".
She received a further £660,000 earlier this year. Ofwat said the payments were not performance-related.
The previously undisclosed payments had come to light the previous August when the government banned Yorkshire Water and five other water companies from paying "unfair" bonuses to bosses.
Reaction from MPs and campaigners
Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, said Shaw should have stepped down "much earlier".
"Good riddance. Nicola Shaw oversaw abysmal management of our precious natural resources, trashing our rivers while receiving an eye-watering salary," he said.
"Her replacement needs to understand that residents are at their wits' end, paying ever-rising bills for polluted rivers and threats of hosepipe bans while someone at the top rakes in millions."
Meanwhile, Judith Cummins, Labour MP for Bradford South, said Yorkshire Water needed "more than a change of leadership" but a "complete change of direction".
"A new face at the top cannot wash away years of Yorkshire Water failing to put customers first," she said.
"Nicola Shaw's time as Yorkshire Water boss saw customers frustrated by poor service, skyrocketing bills, record pollution incidents, and a plummet from 'good' to the worst possible one-star environment rating.
"There must be a wholesale shift in culture that finally prioritises customers. Only then can the company begin to restore public trust."
Robbie Moore, Conservative MP for Keighley and Ilkley, said Shaw's resignation "could not have come quick enough".
He added: "I have therefore already requested an urgent meeting with the new CEO Designate Nicola Medalova to understand how she plans to improve Yorkshire Water's performance at speed.
"The status quo cannot continue."
Chris Stewart at York campaign group Ouse It Lose It said the new CEO's priority had to be looking at "failures in the system".
"There's been a continual decline in the operation of this business," he said.
"Clearly things are going wrong."
Stewart said he was not surprised by Shaw's resignation but it was a "shocking indictment of the way the company has been performing, while making loud noises about how much they're putting into improving".
Naomi Tilley, campaigns manager at protest group Surfers Against Sewage, said "systematic change" was needed to fix the company.
"Regardless of who the CEO is, there's sewage entering the sea and the water companies are failing. Yorkshire Water is not an outlier," said Tilley.
"The whole system and every water company is failing in different ways and we are seeing that the system is broken and we need fundamental change.
"While these companies are set up for a profit, we're never going to see pollution curbed and stopped."

title: Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
text:
Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years' prison in Pakistan
A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.
The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.
Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.
This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.
Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.
They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.
The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (£541:$723).
In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.
"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.
The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".
Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.
"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.
"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.
The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.
They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".
Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.
Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.
The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

title: South East hospitals urge patients to avoid A&E amid pressures
text:
Hospitals warn of 'extremely busy' A&E amid pressures
Hospitals across the South East have warned that A&E services are "extremely busy" and urged patients to consider alternative services for non-urgent care.
East Surrey Hospital in Redhill has asked patients to "only come to us for life-threatening emergencies" while Royal Surrey County Hospital in Guildford has warned people that they are "currently experiencing long waiting times".
Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust also said in a statement on social media that less urgent conditions "may wait longer than usual" amid the pressures.
It comes as senior health leaders warned in October of "ominous signs" pointing to the beginning of winter pressures.
Non-urgent patients have been advised to use the 111 non-emergency service where possible, as well as to go to minor injuries units rather than the emergency department, if necessary.
Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust also directed patients towards their local pharmacy or GP, 111 service, or the Sevenoaks urgent treatment centre.
Chinyama Okunuga, chief executive at Epsom & St Helier University Hospitals, says its emergency departments are "really feeling the strain, and this will only get worse as we head into winter".
The hospitals are "working hard to prioritise our sickest patients" and urges people to get a flu vaccination "before the virus starts to spike, which will pile more pressure on to our services".
An estimated 7.37 million treatments across the UK were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.
The numbers are the highest since October 2025 and raise questions over whether the NHS will meet a government target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.
Both A&Es and ambulance services in the UK also saw a record number of patients for the month of September.

title: How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
text:
How video game remakes tap the power of nostalgia
The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.
"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.
Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.
It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.
Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."
This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.
The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.
While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.
Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.
"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.
Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.
Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.
Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.
"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.
Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.
But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.
Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.
Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.
Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote, "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."
Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious.
"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.
Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."
Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.
This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.
Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some, is not possible for everyone.
"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."
Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.
Indie developers often lean on retro games aesthetics not just because people respond well to them – but also because they are easier to achieve. "You can't compete with billion dollar budgets, super high-fidelity, Triple A graphics," he says.
One question remains. The visual difference, today, between games released years apart is, arguably, negligible. So will there be any point in remaking a game from 2026 in, say, 2038? Will technology have moved on so much by then that it's actually worth it?
Harding-Rolls predicts that games companies will still seek to connect new audiences with classic titles by offering updates.
Remakes might become less about graphical improvements and more about editorial adjustments. "Reinterpretations," he says. "Or versions with additional content."
It's never really "game over", is it?
description: Video games are good at triggering nostalgia, a key reason why classic games keep getting remade.

title: Jersey dad to run three marathons in memory of son
text:
Dad to run three marathons in memory of son
A man is set to run three marathons in three weeks to raise money in memory of his young son who died from a brain tumour.
Jax was diagnosed with the cancer in January 2021 just before he turned three years old.
After having the tumour removed in Southampton, Jax had treatments in Manchester and London but the cancer kept coming back and in April 2026 he died aged six.
His dad Dave Watson will run the Southampton, Manchester and London marathons to raise money for the Brain Tumour Charity.
Dave said his son started displaying symptoms including headaches, sore eyes and morning sickness.
"He ended up having a scan then diagnosed with a brain tumour, which was a shock, and that was on my birthday, so not a date I'll ever forget," he said.
"Me and my wife Sarah were obviously struggling a little bit, we didn't really know what was going on and it felt like we were in a bad film."
Despite going through surgeries and different forms of treatment, Dave said his son stayed positive.
"He was amazing, fun, kind and thoughtful," he said.
"He got a lot of presents during the time, he wasn't very well, but he always made sure his brothers and sisters got presents as well.
"It was tough when Jax died and we went through some bad, bad times and went to some bad places.
"My wife was amazing... she's kept everything together for us."
Dave has so far raised more than £7,000 for the Brain Tumour charity as he continues his training.
"I want to take on these marathons in memory of Jax and for the Brain Tumour charity to help people who are in the same situation, even if it's only a little bit," he said.
"The support's brilliant and it means so much to me, to my family and Jax - he'd be massively proud.
"It's going to be massively emotional when I finish because I wear my heart on my sleeve."
Brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer death in children and adults under the age of 40 in the British Isles, according to the charity Brain Tumour Research.
Kate Vousden, from the charity, said: "Unfortunately we hear these kinds of stories all the time.
"I think what Dave is doing with his fundraising actually really raises awareness of what a family goes through when something like this happens.
"Dave taking on this, quite frankly, unbelievable, amazing challenge and we're really, really pleased to support him with it.
"Hopefully this will mean other families don't have to go through what his family did."

title: M2 reopens from Chatham to Sittingbourne after overnight works
text:
M2 reopens after emergency works and days of disruption
Part of the M2 that was closed overnight for emergency repair works after days of disruption has reopened on Friday.
Sections of the motorway between Chatham and Sittingbourne had been closed since Tuesday evening after an incident in which a pedestrian died.
They were closed again on Thursday evening for what a National Highways spokesperson called "emergency resurfacing works".
All lanes of the coastbound carriageway reopened at 05:00 GMT following the overnight works, after the motorway closed at 20:00 GMT on Thursday.
Kent Police said a man in his 50s had died after he was struck by several vehicles near Medway Services.
It is understood that police investigation work at the site has concluded, but detectives said they wanted witnesses to the crash, including anyone with dashcam footage, to get in contact.
The man's next of kin has been informed, Kent Police added.

title: King Mojo Club mural celebrates famous 1960s Sheffield venue
text:
New mural 'keeps alive' 1960s nightclub memories
A new mural has been unveiled to celebrate a former Sheffield nightclub's place in Yorkshire's cultural landscape.
Opened by Peter Stringfellow and his brother Geoff in 1964, the King Mojo club hosted celebrities such as Tina Turner, Stevie Wonder, Pink Floyd and Jimi Hendrix, before closing in 1967.
The artwork was commissioned as part of the Mojo Rising project to mark the club's 60th anniversary, and celebrates some of its most memorable moments.
Artist Angie Hardwick said the mural celebrated "the music heritage of Sheffield", adding: "It's really important to show Sheffield now, what it was like then, that it was a vibrant city."
Mojo Rising - Celebrating 60 Years of Music and Community is a National Lottery Heritage funded project.
It received a £114,300 grant to bring the club back into the spotlight through oral history collection, exhibitions, podcasts, a documentary and a book.
Project manager Neil Anderson said: "Most of the ex-club goers are now in their 70s and 80s.
"For me it's so important to record their memories while they are still here, it so important that we do it now."
The mural, which was unveiled at The Old Library in Attercliffe by musician Dave Berry, comprises four canvases painted in a "pop art style".
Phil Barnes and Paul Norton, Mojo fans since the 1960s, painted alongside Hardwick and shared their memories during their creative sessions.
Norton, who helped paint psychedelic colours and Buddha images at the original club, said painting the mural felt "weird, but good, because it was a great time of my life and the love of music has stayed with me".
For Barnes the Mojo years never feel far away.
"Even though it's 60 years ago you can remember it like it was yesterday, it deserves to be remembered, it deserves something like this to keep the memory alive," he said.
Hardwick said it had been a "privilege" to work with Norton and Barnes.
"It's been fabulous to get to know Phil and Paul, they've talked my ears off," she said.
It is hoped that the mural finds a permanent home next year, but first it will visit the former Mojo Club area of Sheffield, Pitsmoor, and the city's Moor Market, gathering further memories of Sheffield's 1960s music scene along the way.

title: First minister claims step forward over Welsh finances after meeting with Burnham
text:
First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting
Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth says there has been a "significant step forward" with regards to his country's spending and borrowing powers after meeting the prime minister.
Andy Burnham held a meeting of his National Economic Council with the first ministers of Wales and Scotland on Friday, after which ap Iorwerth said it was a matter of "how and when" a loosening of financial restrictions will take place.
At the summit in Glasgow, Burnham lobbied the government leaders to devolve "deeper" to the regions of Wales and Scotland.
The prime minister said the two first ministers had agreed to work with him on "regional empowerment".
No timescales were announced for changes to Wales' finances.
Friday's meeting followed rows between the Welsh and UK government over the chancellor's Budget on Wednesday, which ap Iorwerth had said was "not serious about Wales".
His party Plaid Cymru said the budget left the Welsh government with a real-terms cut in funding, which the UK government denied.
Ap Iorwerth had set out a range of demands to the prime minister in a letter sent at the start of October.
As well as calling for powers over policing and justice, and for more funding for rail projects, he called for an end to restrictions on access to the Wales reserve - spare funding that the Welsh government can store in one year to use in another.
It is capped at £385m, and the Welsh government can only draw down £137.5m and £55m for resource and capital spend respectively per year.
The Welsh government can also borrow up to £1.1bn for infrastructure, with a limit of £165m a year.
Ap Iorwerth said: "There were some real positives here.
"On fiscal flexibility, the ability for us to use our funding better in Wales, use our reserves better in Wales - and on borrowing powers, I was told clearly that its now was a matter of how and when. That is a significant step forward."
He said there was "clearly an interest" for the prime minister to "really understand that sheer injustice of underfunding of rail in Wales that we have seen for many years".
"That is a particular issue we will be taking forward now between my office and his," he said.
On policing, the first minister said: "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there and there's still work to do."
At a speech this month the first minister called for "practical agreement" on how the two governments could work together on the economy, calling for Westminster to avoid duplication in areas that are devolved already to the Welsh government.
Burnham said Friday's meeting was "positive", and that both first ministers had agreed to "work together jointly on regional empowerment in Scotland and Wales as well".
"We now have a process where we have detailed work by officials on both sides to see if we can come to a set of arrangements that are right for Scotland and right for Wales," Burnham said.
"We had a good discussion today on two fronts, one around reindustrialisation and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level."
He said it was for Scotland and Wales to decide how that looks.
Burnham also said the UK government will now look at arrangements for further devolution of employment support.
Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said fiscal flexibilities and borrowing was on the agenda for future Welsh government discussions with No 10 North.
"It is going to take some conversations on how that would work in practice.
"I can't give you a specific time frame as things stand," he said.
Following Wednesday's Budget, which saw an extra £450m announced for Wales over the next three years as well as funding for individual projects, the Welsh government claimed the extra money would represent a real-terms cut to its own finances.
A £30m funding pledge for a new railway station in Cardiff was also described as "an insult" by Wales' transport minister.
On Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday before the summit, ap Iorwerth said there were "paltry sums of money coming on rail, when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".
"The Budget was not serious about Wales," he said.
He said in another interview he could "only assume that the prime minister is holding something back".
After the meeting, Downing Street said ap Iorwerth had "agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode".
"This would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from each government, to take this agenda forward," they said.
Ap Iorwerth said in a statement: "There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency.
"I welcome the prime minister's comments that this is now a matter of how and when."
Welsh ministers had called for changes to their borrowing rules and assurances that child poverty payments it wants to introduce would leave recipients' tax and benefits allowances unaffected.
None of that was addressed in the Budget, although Kinnock said "positive" talks were continuing regarding the child poverty payments.
Friday's meeting of the National Economic Council - a summit to help boost the UK economy - was due to be attended by the prime minister and all the devolved leaders.
However, it emerged on Thursday that Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill would not be there after her attendance was blocked by her Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).
Since he became prime minister, Burnham has consistently spoken in favour of devolution.
He has said he is "open" to transferring powers over policing and justice to Wales and, during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he said he was "ready to make an offer" on the devolution of employment support.
