title: From green card to fraud: Kenyans arrested in $130m US ghost student scam
text:
How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

title: Tributes paid to 'Mirfield's finest' actor Sir Patrick Stewart
text:
Sir Patrick Stewart remembered as 'Mirfield's finest'
Sir Patrick Stewart once said he had to drop his Yorkshire accent for Hollywood, but he never forgot his roots.
The Mirfield-born actor, best known for his roles in Star Trek and the X-Men films, died at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.
His death has prompted an outpouring of love from the community he proudly called home, along with his beloved Huddersfield Town - the club he followed from childhood.
Stewart's friend and fellow legendary actor Sir Ian McKellen said Stewart "never forsook his origins".
He added: "Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end."
Referencing a trait often associated with people from the region McKellen said Stewart "told you what he thought and felt".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "very sad" to hear about Stewart's death, describing him as "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".
In a TV interview with fellow Yorkshireman Michael Parkinson, Stewart said "we did toy" with using his regional accent when playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek franchise.
But he added: "It was incomprehensible to the producers."
South Yorkshire-born actor Brian Blessed also paid tribute to Stewart who he first met as "young lads in Yorkshire, on a drama course in Calder Valley".
Posting on Facebook, he said that although Stewart was two years younger, he had "maturity beyond his years."
"His mysterious eyes and reserved demeanour broke open when he smiled, and lit the room," he wrote.
"Art was woven into his huge heart, and the shared passion bonded us at an early age."
Blessed, who hails from Mexborough, added: "Our bond never waned, and whenever we met, he would hug me as hard as when we were boys, never afraid to weep at the enormity of his emotions.
"We have always been connected, and always shall be.
"I'll see you up in space, my dearest friend. Patrick is not gone but merely on another journey."
In 2004 he became chancellor of the University of Huddersfield - a role he filled until 2015. A year later the university's drama building was named after him.
Speaking at the time, he said: "I'm thrilled. It still makes me a little self conscious to think there's a building named after me."
Bob Cryan, the Vice Chancellor of the university, said Stewart was "very proud" of being chancellor and his success never changed him.
"It's something he took very personally," he said.
"He saw it as a way of paying back to Yorkshire because he was very proud of the fact that he was given a scholarship from what was then the West Riding of Yorkshire, but he felt he had never paid back."
Born in Mirfield in 1940, Stewart attended Crowlees Church of England Junior and Infant School before moving onto Mirfield Secondary Modern School.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment, whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had badly affected his mental health.
Stewart's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a reporter and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He later won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School launching a career that would take him from Yorkshire to the world stage.
Although he became one of Britain's most celebrated actors through roles including in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, Stewart spoke of his pride in being from West Yorkshire.
Childhood friend David Pinder described him as a "thoroughly nice man" and said the pair would meet up when they were both in Mirfield.
"I came back here when I retired from the Foreign Office and got into local politics," he said.
"We couldn't have been more different. He was very firmly old Labour and I at the time was Conservative, verging on Independent so we kept off politics."
Pinder said the men would have lunch in the town and added: "People would come and go.
"They'd know it was Patrick and of course by then he was internationally famous, but people were very good. They'd just say hello and not pester him."
Mirfield Free Grammar, which Stewart attended as a child, said he held a "special place" in its history.
The school said he had last visited in 2011, when he was presented with a commemorative plaque "made out of the very stage boards on which he made his first theatrical appearance".
In a tribute, the school said: "Staff and students who met him during his visit remember him as a warm, friendly, compassionate and charismatic gentleman who left a last impression.
"We feel privileged to have been part of his story."
Spen Valley MP Kim Leadbeater described Stewart as "Mirfield's finest".
Posting on X, the Labour MP described him as "an outstanding talent and someone who came across as a thoroughly decent and lovely".
Leadbeater said she had met the actor at Huddersfield Town football matches and corresponded with him several times, adding: "He was incredibly kind and he will be greatly missed."
A lifelong Huddersfield Town supporter, Stewart attended games when his schedule allowed and celebrated the Terriers' promotion to the Premier League at Wembley in 2017.
The club's chief operating officer David Threlfall-Sykes said: "Obviously it was Sir Patrick Stewart walking around so people would get star-struck, but he would get star-struck by seeing the players and the manager because they were his heroes.
"It was a weird dichotomy but it just shows how much this place meant to him, just like it does to everyone that comes here every weekend to fill the ground. He was no different in that respect."
For many, it was the combination of worldwide fame and his down-to-earth Yorkshire roots that made him such a star across the world.
Reflecting on his sense of humour, Cryan, of the University of Huddersfield, said: "He had a great sense of fun.
"I remember saying to him we were hosting a dinner for staff at the university to say thank you for all their hard work and we decided he and I were going to be waiters.
"You can imagine peoples' faces when Patrick served them their meal."
The statement announcing Stewart's death, which was shared on his Instagram account, ended with a quote from his memoirs: "Like me, Jean-Luc has lived an unusual life that has taken him far beyond the bounds of normal human experience.
"But he is also someone who remains true to his earthbound roots, for they are what gave him his identity. In the end, he feels the call of home, as do I."

title: Bride goes to Tameside Hospital to dance with Dad on wedding day
text:
Heartbroken bride visited Dad in hospital on wedding day
A bride who was "completely heartbroken" when her dad was admitted to hospital with heart problems just two days before her wedding decided to spend part of her big day on his ward.
Sinèad Jackson was set to marry her partner of 19 years Stephen on 10 October at the Village Hotel in Hyde, Greater Manchester when her dad, Leslie Healy, was admitted to Tameside General Hospital.
The 36-year-old, from Dukinfield, said she had always dreamed of having her father walking her down the aisle.
"I was completely heartbroken when I found out my dad couldn't attend my wedding," Sinèad said.
"All I wanted was to see him before I walked down the aisle. So I came to him in hospital.
"I'd do it all over again if I could."
After arriving at the hospital an hour before her ceremony, Sinèad was able to show her dress to Leslie and be with him to share their father-daughter dance.
Footage of the tender moment shows Sinèad in her dress and Leslie in his wedding suit slow dancing to This Dance, by Scott Thomas Laughridge.
"I just fought back my tears for my Dad because I thought I can't cry," she said. "He kept saying sorry to me."
Sinèad said she met her now-husband Stephen at college when they were both 17.
The couple have been engaged since 2015 - and after finally deciding to tie the knot earlier this year, Sinèad said they could not wait for their big day to arrive.
Sinèad said she "couldn't believe it" when Leslie was taken to hospital on 8 October.
"My mum rang me [and] told me my Dad was really not well," Sinèad recalled.
"She said he was in hospital and I was crying, she was crying.
"I felt really upset."
After visiting her dad the following day, Sinèad said she knew he was not going to be able to leave his ward.
"The nurse explained to me how bad he was and said he shouldn't be allowed out - even for an hour - because it was such a high risk," Sinèad said.
"It was very sad.
"I could see it in him as well - and he was a bit like breathless, which is unusual."
Leslie told his daughter to continue on with the day despite him not being able to attend.
"But Dad being Dad - he's just stubborn," said his daughter.
"He told me not to postpone it.
"He kept telling me not to worry and to just get on with the day.
"He said he would see the pictures and videos."
Sinèad said she knew she had to bring her big day to her dad as much as possible.
And so, after a quick chat with the nurses, she organised to visit the next day - just before the ceremony - along with her mum and wedding photographer Jen.
"I've got four brothers and I'm the only daughter," she said. "So it was a big deal for him to see me."
Sinèad arrived at the hospital at 15:00 GMT, only one hour before her ceremony.
"I didn't even look in a mirror at myself, walked straight out of the hotel with one thing on my mind - my Dad," she said.
"I stood outside the ward as he got dressed, and then my mum ushered us in, and then obviously I just walked down to him.
"I know it wasn't the ideal place, but it was really nice to to see him and see his reaction."
Sinèad said the hospital staff helped to make the day even better.
"It was nice - I had two or three of them going 'Oh my gosh, can I take a picture of you?'
"And all of a sudden we're taking pictures and videos as we went into the ward.
"I think some of the patients got some pictures as well.
"I definitely got a few extra looks.
"But I just concentrated on Dad."
Sinèad said her big day went smoothly from there on in, despite being "a bit late" to the ceremony.
"I felt really happy we finally did it," Sinèad said of her wedding, and that she "was able to relax after seeing my Dad."
She added: "My little man, Maxie, gave me away on behalf of his Grandad.
"All my brothers were there for me and everyone who needed to be there for me were there."
Leslie has since been discharged from hospital and is now recovering at home.
"He is so pleased with the photos," Sinèad said.
"Sometimes looking at them now makes me feel sad.
"But I am so grateful we got them in the circumstances."
Leslie added: "It was a very emotional day for us all.
"Happiness for my daughter Sinèad, as well as sadness at not being able to attend.
"We're all really grateful for the [hospital staff's] kind efforts in arranging this visit which allowed us to all celebrate together."

title: Ex-Traitors players talk tactics and celebrity final predictions
text:
Ex-Traitors players talk tactics and celebrity final predictions
- Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
From shock slip-ups to a murder by yawning - and a whole host of Jerry Hall one-liners along the way - the current series of Celebrity Traitors has gripped the nation. But ahead of Friday's finale, what do former contestants make of this season's crop of stars and who are they tipping to win?
"Maya has played a damn good game", 61-year-old Judy Wilson says.
Judy, from Doncaster, took home the unwanted title of the first player to be banished from the castle in series four.
She told the BBC while it was a shame people didn't get to see more of her personality, she knew her daughter and fellow player, Roxy, would be "fighting for both of us".
"Roxy had warned me a few people were coming for me, and then my back got up... but I just tried to play the game.
"The thing is, they've got nothing to go off, so obviously people are all going to jump on the same bandwagon... I had to go down gracefully."
Roxy was adopted by Judy aged five, and said it was important for her and her mum to show viewers "if you're adopted or from an adverse background, you can still achieve things and be as regular as everyone else".
Roxy, 33, had been rooting for comedian and faithful Joanne McNally in the latest celebrity series, before she was banished by her fellow faithful on Thursday.
"She's wrong and strong, like me," Roxy jokes.
"When you're in there, your version of the truth becomes the truth, and nobody can tell you otherwise. You're in your own echo chamber."
Roxy said the game was "super intense, more intense than I expected".
After surviving for 11 episodes she was eventually murdered by the traitors, though said she could see it coming.
"After being there for some time, you just expect it more and more every night. You're just kind of waiting."
Roxy had her own memorable moment on the show, when she clashed with crime writer and former barrister Harriet Tyce, whose sights were – correctly – set on traitor Rachel Duffy.
Tyce voiced her theory at breakfast, but turned her frustrations to Roxy, who felt Tyce had interrupted Duffy when defending herself.
It was then Tyce produced the now-iconic line: "The benefit is to set the cat amongst the pigeons, Roxy."
"That moment itself I think has gone down in TV history, so I'm glad to be a part of it," Roxy laughs.
Leeds-born Theo Mayne has only watched clips of the latest series, but said, judging by those, he thinks Maya "will go all the way".
Mayne, 31, played the role of a faithful in the first ever UK series in 2022. Little was known about the show when it first graced our screens, but it has since exploded in popularity.
"I had no expectations – it just taught me to expect the unexpected," he said.
Mayne feels viewers "don't realise how hard the game is", with players' minds constantly in overdrive.
"It's hard to use your brain because you're just always thinking about, am I going to be murdered? Who is a traitor? Who is a faithful?
"There are so many different moving parts and the game is like a big turning cog."
He added: "You're always thinking, right, I need to survive the day, I need to look good, I need to not say this, I need to not do that... But I just went in there, was myself 100%... I mean, I told a few lies, but that's it!"
Mayne told the BBC he would do the show again in a heartbeat - and largely puts its success down to the first ever cast.
"I think if it wasn't for our guinea pig cast, it wouldn't be as big as it is."
Like her fellow veteran players, Jessie Roux, from Hull, is "rooting" for Maya.
"Come on, Maya!", she laughs.
Roux was - and always was - a faithful during her time on series four, until she was eliminated.
"It's hard because all of us aren't going off much, it's just trying to pick at random bits... as hard as it is, it's good vibes, even though it's stressful."
She added: "All of us got on and just hit it off, but when all of us had our different rules, the air just went cold.
"It was like, oh, all of us are in this now, and it did hit me then... I was just so on edge about being murdered."
A Traitors superfan, the 30-year-old was known not only for her bright make-up and outfits, but also for speaking openly about her stammer.
"I didn't have expectations because every game is a different game and I just wanted to do my best, but I guess my aim was to raise awareness of stammering.
"I had people reach out about how I'd helped them, I had mums reach out about their kids and how it's helped them... it was just good to educate others."
Series three's Alex Oleksy originally hails from Scotland, but lives in Whitby.
Although he admits the traitors are "playing it really well" this season, Oleksy is a true faithful and hopes they can defeat the traitors.
"James Acaster is such a reluctant traitor! We've seen all different kinds of traitors, but I don't think we've seen one that played quite like James."
Oleksy, 32, watched the show with his mother-in-law before signing up, and expected to "breeze right through it and win the money".
"I don't think I expected it to be quite so mentally taxing... it turns you so paranoid, it's unreal," he said.
"Everything is heightened; you're making friendships in the blink of an eye, you're deciding who your allies are...everything is just so heightened.
"It's like having a pot on the boil and as soon as these factors come into play, you're just constantly bubbling over."
He does caveat that by saying how much he loved being part of the show and how much it "taught him" about himself.
Oleksy was eventually banished by his fellow players, and says by that point, he was "desperate for a moment of vindication".
"I couldn't wait to get up there and be like, 'haha, told you'."
Watch parties
The final of Celebrity Traitors will air on BBC One at 20:00 GMT, and while many people will be glued to their sofas, venues across the region are hosting dedicated watch parties.
Headrow House in Leeds is hosting a screening of the final, as well as a repeat of the semi-final for those who missed it on Thursday, from 18:00.
The event is ticketed but free to attend.
Two Thirds Beer Co in Sheffield is also showing the final.

title: Traders' tools stolen every 20 minutes in UK
text:
Traders' tools stolen every 20 minutes in UK
Traders' tools worth thousands of pounds were stolen somewhere in the UK every 20 minutes last year, figures show.
At least 26,164 tool thefts were recorded in 2025, based on responses from 30 police forces who shared data. The true figure is likely to be higher as a further 15 forces could not respond.
Gangs and "chancers" are behind the crimes, according to Labour MP Amanda Martin, who is calling for her government to do more to help.
The Home Office said it was "working with the police to tackle and prevent tool theft to protect more hardworking tradespeople", including increasing neighbourhood policing, investing in police and working with industry and AI to tackle the sale of stolen goods.
Lulzim Pjetri owns Alliance Refrigeration Group, a commercial refrigeration business in Aston, Birmingham, from which tools were stolen six times in a year.
On one occasion, thieves broke into a parked van while two staff sat in its cab eating their lunch.
Those responsible were not wearing masks, held up crowbars and told the workers it was not worth them trying to stop it, Pjetri said.
Pjetri said: "Unless they choke the second-hand tool market, this problem will always be there."
"I'm concerned for my guys' safety," said Pjetri, who employs seven people.
"It is our living. It is the emotional trauma that you get from it. It's happening again and again and again and no one out there can see this."
Replacing the tools stolen from each van can cost Pjetri up to £7,000, with a further £4000-£5000 for repairs, and that is before counting the cost of missed work while the vans are off the road - sometimes for weeks at a time.
"You've got to remember these vehicles are supporting the hardest working class of the UK," said Pjetri, who is also known as Mike.
The average value of an insurance claim for tool theft in 2025 was £4,206.60, according to insurers Direct Line for Business.
The biggest cost from multiple tool theft incidents faced by Kerry Field, owner of Change It Homes based in Norton Lindsey, Warwickshire, was £10,000 worth of tools and motorbikes stolen in a break-in.
The BBC has seen CCTV footage showing the thieves making offensive gestures directly at the cameras during the crime.
Field spent a further £10,000 improving security, including new electric gates, cameras and taking on a rescue dog to help keep his headquarters safe.
His staff found one of their stolen saws advertised for sale online, but Field was advised to go to collect it himself when he reported it to police.
The force later apologised and told him the member of staff should not have suggested this, Field said.
"I think it's definitely got worse," he said. "I think a lot of it isn't notified to the police because people know it's not going to make any difference; they're not going to get any tools back.
"It's always been classed as very low level. If you take away someone's livelihood, it has an impact on the whole of society."
He added the lack of consequences for thieves or action by police did not instil confidence, but he understood forces were overstretched.
Warwickshire Police said it took all reports of tool theft "very seriously", but a suspect could not be identified in this case.
A spokesperson added: "Following concerns raised by the victim, the case was re-opened and thoroughly reviewed. No further lines of enquiry were identified."
The Home Office said it had boosted neighbourhood policing, with more than 3,800 additional neighbourhood officers in roles, and was investing "a historic £18.5bn in police force funding".
Martin - whose father was a plumber - has campaigned for tougher sentencing for tool thefts.
"We, as a government, have to do more," said the MP for Portsmouth North.
She said better regulation of the secondhand market was needed, including for pawnbrokers and well-known online retailers and auctioneers.
"It's making sure if you're selling some tools, you've got to have proof that you've owned it," she said.
Businesses with physical stores often require anyone selling goods to provide ID and for transactions to be recorded on CCTV, with other measures including signed undertakings to confirm they can legally sell an item and staff making checks for missing, removed or obscured serial numbers.
Online retailers have published terms and conditions saying they do not accept stolen goods and encourage users to report suspicions if they believe items listed for sale are stolen.
The Home Office said it continued to work with police, industry bodies and online sites to look at the issue of unregulated tool sales and what more could be done.
A common complaint among traders at a conference organised by Fix Radio in Birmingham last week was that when they made insurance claims for stolen tools, the amount repaid would not cover buying new replacements or the business missed out on while waiting for repairs.
Gareth Powley, a senior technical underwriter at Aviva and Direct Line for Business insurance, said it had a "new for old" basis policy.
He said: "The worst thing you want when you have to claim is to be trying to find secondhand tools or to have that shortfall. It's really important to look at the underlying cover you're buying.
"Maybe a cheap policy isn't as good as one providing more full cover."
Businesses can also add a liquid DNA watermark to their tools - which is not clear to the naked eye but glows brightly under UV light - to help trace them and prove their ownership if they are stolen.
Sgt Dave Catlow from the National Business Crime Centre is overseeing a clampdown on tool theft and said organised crime groups were responsible for a large proportion.
Stolen tools were being moved around the UK for resale, as well as abroad, he said.
A five-strong rural gang was jailed last month after a Lincolnshire Police investigation revealed the men frequently used older 4x4 vehicles fitted with cloned registration plates and typically travelled at night, wearing gloves, heavy clothing and face coverings in a bid to conceal their identities.
The Metropolitan Police has now begun to issue notices to car boot sale organisers, warning they could face criminal liability if they knowingly facilitate or ignore the sale of stolen, counterfeit and illicit goods. The warnings are made under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.
Catlow believes this has led to a reduction in stalls selling tools at car boot sales that police have since revisited.
His role is to make sure best practice is shared across different police forces to avoid "displacement" - when one force has success driving down one type of crime locally but culprits move elsewhere.
Bonzer Car Boot Sale in Romford, east London, was visited by The Met earlier this month as part of its operations to deter the resale of stolen tools.
Sniffer dog Kaiser, a two-year-old Alsatian rescue from the company SelectaDNA, joined officers for the operation. He is trained to detect forensic marking or liquid DNA on tools.
The owner of the land where Bonzer Car Boot Sale is held, who did not wish to be named, said: "We don't want to be on the wrong side of the law.
"We don't want individuals who have their power tools stolen not being able to go to work on top of losing the value of those power tools, so we will do whatever we need, whatever we're advised to do, to cut that out."

title: Chathill rail station plea over waiting room shut for five years
text:
Passengers plead over shelter shut for five years
Shivering rail passengers at a station where the waiting room has been closed for five years have pleaded for shelters to be installed this winter.
The Grade-II listed structure at Chathill Station in Northumberland was damaged during Storm Arwen in November 2021 and has not reopened since.
Network Rail estimated the cost of repair at £1.4m, double the allocated budget, as it must be dismantled and rebuilt like-for-like using original materials.
A frustrated John Holwell, of Chathill Rail Action Group (CRAG), said: "Anybody joining a train to Newcastle has to wait in the open air, which is wonderful on a sunny June morning but not so good in December when it's raining and it's dark."
He said he understood the difficulties in repairing the original building, but there was a "desperate need" to find alternative waiting accommodation for "significantly less" than the £1.4m quoted.
The closest station to tourist destinations such as Bamburgh, Seahouses and Beadnell, Chathill is served by just two of the 140 trains which pass each day on the East Coast Main Line.
Since 2022, CRAG has been campaigning for eight trains to stop daily but, despite backing from some local politicians, nothing has moved.
Holwell said: "It's great to have support, but support must be translated into action and sadly so far that hasn't happened."
North East Mayor Kim McGuinness trumpeted the "North East Rail Vision" that aimed to improve rail connectivity to rural communities.
A spokesperson said the mayoral authority was "aware of aspirations to increase the number of services calling at Chathill", but the final decision on changes to the East Coast Main Line lie with the Office of Road and Rail.
description: Passengers face a sixth year of no shelter at Chathill Station where the waiting room closed in 2021.

title: Middlesbrough Empire owners 'put town on map for dance music'
text:
'We put Middlesbrough on the map for dance music'
The departing owners of one of Middlesbrough's most famous nightclubs say they put the town "on the map with dance music".
Father and son Barry Faulkner Sr and Barry Faulkner Jr are handing over the keys to The Middlesbrough Empire next month after 33 years in charge.
The Empire has hosted renowned DJs and acts including Pete Tong, the Arctic Monkeys and James Arthur, with Faulkner Jr saying he hoped the new owner would bring back some of the "glory days".
"At the time, I took a big chance with that place," Faulkner Sr said of taking the former bingo hall and turning it into a club, adding: "I think it cleared me out of money when I first got it."
He told BBC Radio Tees he was selling for health reasons, adding: "There's no use crying over spilt milk, you know what I mean? But it's our choice."
Faulkner Jr said they did not know what the new owners' intentions with the building were, but they were told it would close for about 18 months to "reinvent it".
The club said its events after 17 November would no longer take place at the Empire and would be relocated.
Faulkner Sr said the best night he had seen was when 2,000 people "crammed into the place" to see Paul Oakenfold.
"The place was just running with sweat," he said.
Meanwhile, Faulker Jr remembered people climbing on the roof and bonnet of the Bentley that brought DJ Sasha from Leeds to perform.
"You'd never seen anything like it," he said, adding: "Our life revolved around the Friday night.
"It was a family, we had a really good team."
The announcement sparked shock and sadness, with some saying the venue was their "second home" and their departure being the "end of an era".
Middlesbrough musician Finn Forster said headlining at the venue last year had been an "absolute dream" of his.
"Growing up, and seeing different artists from all over place come through and play Middlesbrough Empire, it shows you what's possible," Forster told BBC Radio Tees.
"I think, without it, there's a huge missing piece there."
He said the venue attracted "such a high calibre of artists".
Forster said: "It doesn't matter how small we are, or what we look like in comparison to the rest of the world, I think we can still have just as much of an important impact.
"And with the Empire, it's been a place that shines a light on the town as a place that can be trusted, whatever level of artist comes through."
Faulkner Sr and Faulkner Jr said they were looking forward to seeing "all the old faces" on their final night.

title: Wiltshire farmers and NFU want quieter fireworks to protect animals
text:
Firework noise 'control' needed to protect animals
Farmers have called for better management of private fireworks displays after their frightened cattle damaged fences and injured themselves on barbed wire during past shows.
Ross Follett said he would use "the best part of a day" to move 350 cows into a barn because he did not want to risk a repeat of his herd "running wild" and getting hurt.
Follett said more needed to be done about private fireworks, which comes as the National Farmers' Union (NFU) called for tougher regulation, the development of quieter fireworks and advance notice of displays.
A government spokesperson said it was assessing feedback to a consultation on fireworks.
Follett said he had needed to treat cuts sustained by his herd in Berwick Saint John, after a large firework display.
"They're not used to it, all the lights and banging...they don't know what to do," he said.
The Wiltshire farmer added he would only bring his herd in for the weekend as the dry summer meant straw supplies were low and grass grazing was a bonus.
Tisbury dairy farmer Peter Shallcross said he was also concerned about fireworks panicking his cattle as it could cause them to "stampede, run through fences, damage farm equipment and damage themselves".
"I think we need greater public awareness so these ad hoc displays don't happen or, if they do, they are managed much more professionally - the private ones are completely uncontrolled," he said.
"I think you've got to balance it. A lot of people enjoy the big bangs of the fireworks. I enjoy going to see a display, but there's probably a place for more lasers," Shallcross added.
What is the NFU calling for?
- Reduced noise levels, encouraging the development of quieter fireworks
- Advance notification of private as well as public displays
- Recognition of both animal welfare risk and fire risk to standing crops, straw and farm buildings
- A balanced, risk-based approach to protect rural businesses and traditional celebrations - the NFU does not support an outright ban on consumer fireworks
An NFU spokesperson said it wanted the government to ensure any future regulations "explicitly consider the welfare of farm animals" and the risks faced by agricultural businesses.
The government said it was assessing feedback on a consultation on fireworks which ended earlier in the month.
A spokesperson added: "We know loud fireworks can have a real impact on farmers and their livestock.
"That's why we've launched a campaign encouraging people to consider the impact fireworks can have on those around them.
"We are also looking at limiting the sale of the loudest fireworks to consumers and banning any additional high-risk products from public sale to protect pets and wildlife."
Abi and Gavin Atterton, who farm 1,000 ewes near Wilton, said they had often "gone and stood with the animals" during firework displays to keep an eye on them.
The couple said the biggest issue they had experienced was with one of their working collie dogs, who was just one week away from giving birth during a large private firework display.
"She actually clawed herself out of a kennel and ripped the hinges off the door coming out, bearing in mind she was eight weeks pregnant...thankfully, she was OK and the pups were fine, but she was petrified," Gavin said.
"I've got no problem with people celebrating weddings, birthdays, but it's just when it comes from nowhere and nobody knows anything about it," he added.

title: Halloween beats Christmas for neighbours behind huge spooky display
text:
Halloween beats Christmas for spooky display pair
Two neighbours who team up to transform their homes into one big Halloween display say they find the occasion more entertaining than Christmas.
Eddie Wood, from Grimsby, has decorated his house for 12 years, while neighbour Gay Hodgson followed suit about seven years ago when she moved in next door.
Visitors are invited to explore the display in return for a donation to Macmillan Cancer Support.
Gay said: "When my daughter was young, I used to always decorate the porch where we lived. And then when I moved here, he [Eddie] definitely got me hooked on Halloween."
She added: "I just love it. I love to see the kids' faces. They just light up when they see it all, it's brilliant."
Eddie said he had spent about £4,000 this year alone updating his collection. Over the past 12 years, he thinks he has spent about £20,000.
"It's about getting a good reaction from other people, and seeing them enjoy themselves.
"Halloween's better [than Christmas]. I enjoy it more, it's more entertaining. I get a buzz out of it," he added.
Gay agreed: "[I prefer] Halloween, definitely. I love it."
Gay said the occasion was at the front of their mind when the pair had their driveways resurfaced, making sure they were at the same height so their spooky decorations would not fall over.
This year, their display has been split into six zones - including a skeleton graveyard, a scarecrow tent and a witches' coven. There will also be activities for children, such as hook-a-duck and lucky dips.
People are able to visit until Sunday 1 November.

title: Darlington Free Toy Exchange looking for new home for Christmas
text:
Free Christmas toy exchange looking for new home
A group is looking for a new venue to host its free toy exchange in time for Christmas.
The Darlington Toy Exchange was started by Macauley Macdonald and his partner last year with hundreds of items donated and taken from their stall in the town's covered market.
Darlington Market, which gave the group the space for free, ended its arrangement earlier this month, saying it could no longer accommodate the enhanced security needed for the unmanned stall.
Macdonald said they were making their "last cry for help" and if a new venue was not found in the next couple of weeks, they would have to cancel this year's Christmas toy exchange.
Macdonald said: "We saved thousands of pounds worth of toys from going to waste last year.
"And it's all due to the community, we hardly did anything, all we did was go down every day or so, make sure the toys were acceptable and just put them on display and everyone else did all the hard work," he said.
"It just makes a lot of sense for little kids to just get it for free, because they don't get a lot for free, do they?"
Macdonald said they would be "forever grateful" to the market but having to find somewhere new was "a little bit of a let-down".
The market said the space used by the exchange would be refurbished ahead of a commercial lettings campaign which would "support the continued use of this building".
The group were looking for a dry space to store donated toys, plus a space in the town centre for the exchange.
"I want it to be a magical little shop where kids can come in and get toys and it doesn't feel like a charity case, it needs to feel like a proper shop," Macdonald said.
He said he approached some shopping complexes but was told they would have to pay taxes.
"It's not about money, it's just a toy exchange, it's as simple as that, so for us to be able to pay £1,000 for business rates for a month, it's just not possible," Macdonald said.
Darlington Council said a venture such as theirs may qualify for tax relief.

title: Drivers disgusted by human waste in Hull's George Street car park
text:
Drivers disgusted by human waste in car park
Drivers who use a Hull city centre car park are urging the council that owns it to do more to prevent anti-social behaviour after human faeces and evidence of drug use were found.
Over the past month, human excrement has been found at the George Street car park multiple times near the doorway to the main stairwell on the fourth floor.
Hull City Council leader Mike Ross said: "Behaviour like this is unacceptable and the council condemns it strongly. My message to anyone experiencing it, or seeing it, is do report it."
The incidents come months after the reopening of the car park, which was closed to the public in April following a car fire.
Jack Lidgett, 25, said he had seen what he believed to be human faeces.
"It was there for a good few days. I could not be certain whose it was, but it was brown and stinky, I will say that."
He said he now parks on the road using a permit, because "it is safer and obviously cleaner".
"£3 a day is quite a lot for somewhere that is not the best. The best way to describe it [George Street] is dodgy," he added.
"There was a fella sleeping at the bottom of the stairs a couple of times."
It costs £3 per 24 hours to park at George Street, with season passes available for £12.50 weekly, £50 monthly, £150 quarterly and £600 for an annual one.
On Wednesday, the BBC counted 369 cars in the car park around midday. It has a capacity of 549.
The "vast majority" of income generated by the car park goes back in to running it, Ross said.
"There are staff that patrol the car park at the moment, but the level of patrols are being examined to review a way of increasing them and more patrols taking place," he added.
"It is important that there is that on-site presence."
Car park user Matilda Wolfe, 25, said: "There are homeless people in there a lot. It stinks. But, they are homeless.
"The council should maybe address homeless problems before people cry about a car park. It is winter.
"I get a permit anyway, but £3 is nothing."
Claire Woodard, 52, said she no longer parks in George Street because it has a "bad rep" and is "scary".
Phoebe Bevan, 18, and Evelyn Spencer, 18, said they use the car park because it is "cheap and nearby" their workplace. They said they had seen "vomit" there before.
"It should definitely be getting cleaned on a regular basis. There are no bins, it is always dirty, always stinks of cannabis," Spencer said. "There are needles on the balcony."
"It is really dark," Bevan said. Spencer added that they sometimes ask their male colleagues to walk them to the car park "because it is kind of scary in there".
The pair were also worried about a "lack of CCTV" and Spencer said: "If something were to happen, people would know where to do it."
Karina Wilkinson, of the All For One charity, which supports homeless people, said she could empathise with car park users, but added the situation with rough sleeping in Hull was "pretty dire".
She said the reasons people sleep rough vary from wanting to stay with their pets, to disliking staying in hostels, to being institutionalised to being on the streets after many years of homelessness.
Describing the conditions in George Street car park, she said: "Clearly, there's no sanitation facilities; they're not going to be warm when it gets cold.
"It's sad, because it's someone's son, someone's daughter, someone's dad. It's just appalling and it shouldn't be happening."
Hull City Council works with the police and other bodies to tackle anti-social behaviour, according to Ross.
Ross also said the income generated by the car park "goes into the running of the car park itself" - including £120,000 on cleaning costs.
He said council car parks were reviewed about every five years and there were no plans to demolish George Street but the authority was looking at making "electrical improvements".

title: Bid to split Staffordshire into two supercouncils dropped
text:
Bid to split county into two supercouncils dropped
Plans to split Staffordshire into two 'supercouncils' have been withdrawn by the government but reorganisation will still go ahead, it has been confirmed.
Ministers said on Thursday that the plan for the new council boundaries would be announced in early 2027.
It was announced in July that Staffordshire's ten councils were due to be scrapped and replaced with new northern and southern unitary authorities, but plans were put on hold in September.
Local government minister Jim McMahon said he would look at the options for each area with an "open mind" and would not be drawn on whether the controversial north-south split would be adopted.
"It should not be assumed that the same proposal will be automatically selected," he said. "It's important to allow the process to run its course and to allow full and proper consideration"
Local elections will go ahead in May according to existing council boundaries.
It is hoped the new councils will be established for 2029, with elections to fill the new local authorities in May 2028.
Why is the reorganisation still going ahead?
At the moment, local services in Staffordshire are divided between the county and district councils, while Stoke-on-Trent has a single unitary council.
The government said that scrapping and replacing them under it's devolution bill, would help streamline and simplify services, and could save money.
It has been a political hot potato in Staffordshire and beyond, with concerns raised about how 'merging' authorities would affect council finances.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told BBC News on a visit to Derby he knew it was not a popular policy.
"I know people don't like this type of change," he said. "It's about getting the best services for the public and that's why we're sticking to this path."
So whilst other areas have been given the green light on reorganisation, it's back to to the drawing board on plans for how Stoke and Staffordshire will be split.
How have politicians reacted?
The news that the council shake-up plans had been withdrawn were welcomed by some, but raised questions of an uncertain future.
Speaking in the House of Commons, Newcastle-under-Lyme's Labour MP Adam Jogee, called on the government to focus on devolution in Staffordshire:
"I welcome the announcement that the minister has scrapped what I would call the disgraceful and discourteous announcement made in July," he said. "He's right to throw it out.
"But my constituents in Newcastle-under-Lyme want and deserve certainty and clarity, and I didn't hear much of it in the statement."
For Reform-led Staffordshire County Council, acting leader Hayley Coles said the decision left staff and communities "facing uncertainty".
"Withdrawing a decision is not a substitute for explaining it," she said. "Our confidence in this process is wearing thin."
Mayor for Staffordshire the 'big prize'
The government is also in the final stages of confirming a new strategic mayoral authority for Stoke-on-Trent and Staffordshire, it was announced in Wednesday's Autumn Budget.
Once approved, elections for a Staffordshire mayor would happen in May 2028.
Stuart Elford, the director of Staffordshire Chambers of Commerce, described this as the "big prize" to come out of the budget and the area was "crying out" for growth and investment.
The area's Labour MPs have written a joint statement describing a mayoral authority as "new powers" that will put the county "in the driving seat".
Councillor Jane Ashworth, Labour leader of Stoke-on-Trent City Council said a mayor would "put us at the head of the pack".
"We know this city and county have huge potential - and the key to unlocking that is putting the power in the hands of the people who live and work here, not bureaucrats in Westminster," she said.
"This is an important step towards making sure our area has a stronger voice and can shape its own future."
The news was also welcomed by Reform leader of Newcastle-under-Lyme Borough Council Jonathan Gullis.
"It has to be genuine devolved power from Westminster to Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent with serious funding behind it, similar to the mayors that we see in the West Midlands and Greater Manchester," he said.

title: St Bees road closures during pavement works
text:
Adverse weather may prolong village road closures
Planned road closures set to bring disruption to the main route through a village could last longer if weather conditions worsen, council chiefs have warned.
Work is set to start on Monday to resurface pavements in St Bees, west Cumbria, with round-the-clock closures planned for at least two weeks.
But Cumberland Council said the work along the B5345 Main Street and Egremont Road may carry on beyond that depending on weather conditions.
While the closures will be in place round the clock, access will be permitted for residents between 18:00 GMT and 06:00 and at weekends, but only where it is deemed possible.
The first phase of work is set to last just a single day and affect the stretch from Egremont Road to Nethertown Road.
It will then move to a section from Nethertown Road to Outrigg junction for four days before a planned five-day operation between Outrigg junction and Finkle Street.
Bus services face diversions via Outrigg Close during the first week and, while the final phase is being completed, will terminate at St Bees Beach before returning to Whitehaven.
The council said access would continue for emergency services, pedestrians and waste collections.

title: Guernsey pet owners share concerns over new winter ferry schedule
text:
Pet owners frustrated with winter ferry schedule
Pet owners in Guernsey say they are frustrated by this year's winter ferry schedule, claiming it is adding hundreds of pounds in extra costs for travel to the UK.
From 1 November, five of the seven weekly Brittany Ferries sailings from Guernsey to the UK will travel via Cherbourg, France.
As the route leaves the Common Travel Area, pet owners are now required to have a valid Animal Health Certificate (AHC), even if they do not intend to disembark in France.
A Brittany Ferries spokesperson said the need for AHC is required by UK's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) and added that pets can still travel without additional paperwork on direct Guernsey-Portsmouth sailings.
Local dog owner Jeanette Brache said the new requirement added extra hurdles for pet owners whose animals compete in events in the UK or abroad.
The AHC is valid for a single entry into the EU and cannot be reused.
Costing about £200 per dog, per trip "it's another added cost, it's added time", Brache said.
Brache has two Finnish Lapphunds who regularly compete in international dog shows, and said the lack of direct sailings and the additional requirements had already put her off competing in two shows.
"Why should we have to do this where two weeks before you could book a ferry and go?"
According to the winter schedule, there are only two direct sailings between Guernsey and Portsmouth, which are scheduled on Monday and Tuesday.
Brache said it was not convenient if they wanted to travel for a weekend competition.
David Chamberlain, States Veterinary Officer, said: "Work is ongoing to explore the possibility of an exemption for those pets remaining on board at Cherbourg to make this journey easier and cheaper for pet owners."
Megan Burns, a qualified clinical canine massage therapist, said the new requirement could also affect animals needing specialist treatment off-island.
She said: "I've had two dogs previously that have both needed to travel to England for their medical issues.
"One was an epileptic dog, he needed an MRI scan, which cannot be provided in Guernsey and the other one had a muscular injury which needed treatment and diagnosis which couldn't be done here."
Burns said it was a widespread issue: "It isn't just dogs, it could be cats, it could be horses... there's hardly anything for horses on the island at the moment. If they need to go to England I don't think they should need the extra expense for that."

title: Hourly chime artwork aims to celebrate Sunderland
text:
Hourly chime artwork aims to celebrate city
An artwork which changes every hour will be aiming to celebrate a city's identity and bring back memories of its past, the creators have said.
Timepiece will see different 50-second long collages made from archive film, photos and audio chime on the hour through Sunderland's newly opened Culture House from 16 November.
Artist Jeremy Bradfield said he hoped the pieces, which would be accompanied by an original soundtrack from The Futureheads' Ross Millard, would "stir" a lot of memories.
A total of 72 chimes were created and Millard said each celebrated a different element of Sunderland's past, present and future.
"They're like these little moments that last for 50 seconds," Millard said.
"We had so much material to work with that we feel like we've got a good spread of Sunderland's identity.
"I'd like to think that people would see one or two in the building and try and time their visits so they can see more."
Themes include a 1950s bus ride through the city, the building and launching of a Hindustan Shipping Co ship at Doxford shipyard and glassblowing in the 1960s.
Brewing beer at Vaux Breweries, football at Roker Park and the Stadium of Light, and city landmarks such as the clock on Joplings department store and Penshaw Monument have also been featured.
The first chime will sound at 10:00 GMT on 16 November, with a different time signal playing every hour on the hour thereafter.
The team, which also included artist Ben Lawrence, used glass instruments and sounds which capture the atmosphere of the city, including the sea and the roar of the football stadium.
Archive material was also provided by the University of Sunderland, The Bunker, Ashbrooke Sports Club, Friends of Roker Pier and Lighthouse, Ryhope Engine Museum, Sunderland Libraries and the North East Film Archive.
Bradfield said the oldest photo used in the artwork dated back to about 1913.
"I hope it will stir lots of memories and nostalgic reflections on the city," he said.
"There's a lot of change happening in the city at the moment but there's also lots of constants as well.
"It's a chance to to experience lots of memories and beautiful artefacts from the history of the city."
Timepiece will run for a year.
Culture House Director Leanne Littlewood said the venue was "incredibly proud" one of the first major artworks in the building "draws so deeply on the people, places and history that make Sunderland what it is".
The multi-purpose venue, which opened in September, features a library, exhibition and events spaces, bar and podcast studio.

title: Southport survivor Leanne Lucas 'violated' by 'morbid curiosity'
text:
Southport survivor 'violated' by 'morbid curiosity'
A yoga teacher who was seriously injured in the Southport knife attack has said she feels "violated" by the "inexcusable morbid curiosity" of NHS staff who allegedly accessed her medical records inappropriately.
Leanne Lucas was helping to run a Taylor Swift-themed dance class when Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and nine-year-old Alice Da Silva Aguiar were fatally attacked in the Merseyside town on 29 July 2024.
Lucas, who was one of two adults hurt along with eight other children, spoke out after news emerged that two more NHS staff were under investigation over allegations they inappropriately accessed Southport victims' medical records.
The latest cases were identified by Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital in a "retrospective audit".
In May, the University Hospitals of Liverpool Group (UHLG) admitted that nearly 50 of its staff had wrongly looked at victims' medical files.
The group runs Aintree Hospital in Liverpool, where some of the survivors of the attack were taken.
Lucas said: "What happened to me was already traumatic enough, but to discover that the very people entrusted with my care have violated my privacy causes further distress and secondary trauma.
"I should not have to fight for answers or accountability from a hospital where I was at my most vulnerable.
"Time and time again I've been placed in this position, driven by what I can only assume is an inexcusable morbid curiosity by medical staff trained and employed to care [for] and protect patients."
Lucas's solicitors confirmed that they had asked for an audit to be conducted by the hospital in September.
Elaine Macdonald, a solicitor at Broudie Jackson Canter, is representing Lucas.
She said: "Leanne has already suffered the indignity of at least 40 members of medical staff inappropriately accessing her medical records during her care at a hospital under the same trust.
"She is now being told that it may not have ended there. Each breach erodes her trust and is a clear violation of her privacy, when she was at her most vulnerable. This is a systemic issue that needs to be addressed urgently."
A separate investigation is also being held at North West Ambulance Service Trust in relation to staff looking up the victims of the attack without authorisation.
Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital said it was "carrying out an investigation into two potential instances of inappropriate access connected to the Southport incident".
It added: "The cases were detected as part of retrospective audit and two members of staff have been placed on precautionary suspension whilst an investigation is concluded."
It said the case had been reported to the Information Commissioner's Office and the health regulator the Care Quality Commission.
The trust's medical director Manoj Kuduvalli said: "We are deeply sorry that this has happened.
"Our patients trust us with their most personal information at some of the most vulnerable moments in their lives, and any inappropriate access to those records is a serious violation of that trust.
"We have been clear with all colleagues that patient records must only ever be accessed for legitimate reasons connected to their role and the patient's care.
"We will not accept behaviour that compromises patient confidentiality or undermines the trust our patients place in us.
"We have spoken to those that are affected and will keep them informed as our investigation continues."
The data breach at UHLG happened at Aintree Hospital in Liverpool, where some of those injured were treated, in the days after the 29 July 2024 attack.
The BBC understands the three patients affected included Leanne Lucas and a 13-year-old girl who had been helping to supervise the dance class.
In May, UHLG described the breach as "inexcusable" and stressed that changes had been made, although no-one had been sacked.

title: P&R urged to speed up review of Guernsey relocation grants
text:
P&R urged to speed up review of relocation grants
Guernsey's top political committee is being urged to prioritise a review of relocation allowances amid concerns it is putting pressure on rental prices.
Policy and Resources (P&R) said in June last year the review was "on track" to be finished by the end of September 2025.
Deputy Tom Rylatt, from Forward Guernsey, said the review should "be a priority for P&R" and the delay was disappointing.
P&R President Lindsay de Sausmarez said "several stages of work on the review have been completed" and the committee was due to consider it again shortly.
She blamed the delay on how busy the committee had been recently including delivering reforms to the island's tax system and a budget for 2027.
A recent report from the Scutiny Management Committee linked the relocation allowances to the current high price of renting a home in Guernsey.
The current policy entitles people relocating to Guernsey for jobs with the States of Guernsey to a £5,000 grant (£6,600 for Alderney) alongside help with rental costs for up to four years, storage costs and, in some cases, support with an unsold home's mortgage.
In the last decade rents have risen by 65% to on average £2,138 per month, according to the States of Guernsey.
A freedom of information request earlier this year revealed more than £5m was spent by the States on relocation packages in 2025, the most since the support was introduced.
Deputy Rylatt said: "It is disappointing that the review has still not been completed, having originally been due in September 2025.
"With housing costs continuing to place enormous pressure on islanders, it needs to be a priority for P&R that we understand the impact these packages may be having, particularly on the rental market.
"I hope the committee will now bring this work to a conclusion and set out what changes, if any, it intends to make."
Relocation grants 'excessive'
Those buying a home in Guernsey can also qualify for a £8,750 house purchase grant, while short-term recruits could receive smaller payments towards travel and moving costs.
Scrutiny Management Committee President Andy Sloan said the current policy was "excessive" and believes "such a subsidy is likely to have an upward impact on local market rents".
In June 2025 P&R said the review of these grants would look at different options for relocation support, including possible alternatives, using workforce data and financial analysis.
It said any changes would need to balance potential savings against the need to recruit and retain staff in essential public services such as health, education, social care and law enforcement.
Officials said the review was unlikely to be made public as it was looking at an internal policy but any changes would be clearly communicated by P&R.

title: Pressure grows over plans for more homes in Shifnal
text:
Pressure grows over plans for more homes in town
Residents concerned about the pace of housing development in Shifnal are being invited to a public meeting amid claims the town's infrastructure is struggling to keep up with growth.
MP Mark Pritchard said people have raised concerns about issues including water pressure, sewerage capacity, schools and health services.
Shropshire Council figures show Shifnal's population grew by 43.5% between 2011 and 2021 to 9,725, making it the county's fastest-growing town.
The Conservative MP for The Wrekin said the meeting would focus on what he described as a growing number of speculative development applications in the town and surrounding area.
He said Shifnal and nearby communities have already "taken more than their fair share of housing" in recent years and argued future development should not come at the expense of green spaces.
"There is a sustainable limit on the number of houses Shifnal can take," he said.
The Labour government has pledged to build 1.5 million new homes in England over the course of this Parliament.
Earlier this year, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK was in the grip of a "housing crisis" and he wanted to deliver "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period"
Several significant housing schemes are currently being considered or prepared for Shifnal.
They include proposals for up to 500 homes and employment land to the east of the town, up to 200 homes south of Lamledge Lane and a separate 57-home development off Windmill View that has already been approved.
Supporters of new housing argue it is needed to meet demand, including for affordable homes, while the government has set councils targets aimed at increasing housebuilding.
Last year, Shropshire Council was told it would need to oversee the delivery of 1,994 homes a year by 2029 as part of plans to increase housing supply.
The authority has also found it more difficult to resist some developments since its draft local plan was withdrawn in 2025 following concerns raised by planning inspectors. A replacement plan is now being prepared.
Such a local plan is the document councils use to identify where future housing and other development should take place.
The public meeting is due to take place at Shifnal Village Hall on Friday from 19:00 GMT.

title: 'Flood roadshow won't help us,' say Boston residents
text:
'Flood roadshow won't help us,' say residents
An advice roadshow has paid a visit to a Lincolnshire town recently hit by flooding – but some affected residents say it will do little to stop the problem happening again.
The Environment Agency's FloodMobile roadshow was in Boston on Wednesday in the wake of a flood in January last year caused by heavy rainfall.
But some residents said there had been little progress on implementing the recommendations made following an investigation into that flood, with campaigner Andy Robinson calling for the necessary infrastructure improvements to be made.
At the roadshow, the agency's Peter Reilly said: "There is always what we call residual risk, however well protected people are."
The flood affected 38 homes in Wyberton West Road and Park Road when water from South Forty Foot Drain breached the flood defence wall, which a Lincolnshire County Council report said was about a quarter of a metre too low.
A recommendation suggested raising the flood wall to the same level as the adjacent bank.
There were also recommendations for how people could improve the flood resilience of their homes.
But Robinson said that while those measures could help, they were costly and would not necessarily protect homes from the scale of flooding previously seen.
He claimed the only work done to the wall since the flood had been the resealing of its joints.
"I understand that these things take time and obviously they take money, but we really need to see the wheels moving quickly on this," he said.
Fellow resident Kelly Saunby said she had been woken up by the fire service banging on her door on the night of the flooding.
Saunby, who was looking after 12 dogs at the time as well as her own children, said it was "carnage", and she said her house insurance had not covered the flooding damage.
"I've had two years of this, and it is still stressful because nothing's changed or majorly been done about it since," she said.
"So when you have wet weather, you're looking at the river and wondering if it's going to happen again.
"Nothing really has changed. Nothing has been put in place to stop it."
Kane Arathoon, 21, recalled how the flooding happened so quickly.
He said his home insurance premiums had subsequently increased 10-fold to more than £77 a month.
Reilly, from the Environment Agency, said the biggest issue in Wyberton West Road was seepage through the bank.
He said the agency had carried out some remedial repairs and was planning to carry out further work, if it could secure national funding.
"If we are successful, we will raise that bank to design height if it's not at design height at the moment," he said.
But he added: "I will reiterate that whatever the level of that bank, there is always the risk of it being overtopped."
The agency said it had invested more than £200m in flood prevention schemes in Lincolnshire over the past decade and was prioritising funding for areas with the highest number of properties at risk.

title: Wildlife trusts secure £30m Rothbury Estate purchase
text:
Attenborough-backed appeal secures £30m estate
Conservationists have completed the purchase of a huge upland estate following a two-year £30m public appeal backed by the likes of Sir David Attenborough.
The Wildlife Trusts - a federation of 47 conservation charities - and Northumberland Wildlife Trust (NWT) plan to "enhance the rich natural heritage" of the Rothbury Estate, a 9,500-acre stretch of former grouse moor, woodland and farmland - having headed off fears it could be split among multiple owners.
Broadcaster Sir David described it as an opportunity "to create something very special for generations to come".
Not everyone supported the campaign, though, with some local farmers having warned the purchase would be "a folly".
Owned by Lord Max Percy, the Duke of Northumberland's youngest son, the estate had been in the family for about 700 years and was understood to be the largest area of land put up for sale in England in decades.
Worried public access could become more difficult if it was divided between owners, the wildlife organisations bought an initial tract in 2024 covering the Simonside Hills and a mixture of lowland, woods, riverside and farmland.
That also saw them strike a deal to purchase the remainder of the estate if they could raise the £30m in two years with ambitions for it to become a 40-mile (64km) "wild" corridor, stretching from the North East coast to Kielder and the Scottish border.
It has now been announced they have taken out a "low-interest loan to bridge the short-term funding gap between pledged monies still to be received and the fundraising target, ensuring completion of the entire estate".
'Extraordinary landscape'
NWT chief executive Mike Pratt said the campaign had been "remarkable".
"Opportunities of this scale and significance are incredibly rare.
"By securing this extraordinary landscape, we've the potential to create a flagship for nature recovery supported by sustainable farming whilst delivering lasting benefits for wildlife, local people and the rural economy."
Backing last year by Sir David, who serves as president emeritus of the Wildlife Trusts, led to a surge in donations with more than £1m being brought in from across the globe in a week.
Commenting on the appeal's success, he said: "Now the opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality.
"This will be a place where nature, community, farming and heritage can combine to create something very special."
More than 25,000 people donated, NWT said, with other major contributions including a £5m grant from the National Lottery Heritage Fund in March this year.
This week it was announced the government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) had pledged £1.94m, taking the appeal to within touching distance of its target.
Why is the area so coveted?
The estate has a number of important wildlife habitats, conservationists say, with some already designated as Sites of Special Scientific Interest.
Species such as curlew, mountain bumblebee, lapwing and other wading birds have made it their home with endangered red squirrels finding safety in the woods.
Harebell, wild thyme and mountain pansy flower colourfully in summer months, with salmon and under-threat eels spotted in the rivers.
The wildlife trusts believe "this rich tapestry of wildlife could be richer still" if more species return over the next 10 years.
There are also hopes pine marten, beavers and ancient breeds of cattle could become common sights.
Duncan Hutt, director of conservation at NWT, said he envisaged "subtle" change in the years ahead including a landscape with more trees and wetlands, and with nature "allowed to lead what we do".
Meanwhile, Sophie Bulgin, projects manager Rothbury at the Wildlife Trusts, said ownership of the site was a "massive responsibility", adding: "Now it's about honouring that support and doing what we said we'd do."
The plan is not universally popular though.
Chris Armstrong, a tenant farmer overseeing 1,000 acres close to the site, has been among those questioning it.
He told the BBC earlier this year the community was split over the issue: "The most recent strapline seems to be 'time is running out to save the Rothbury Estate'.
"The Rothbury Estate doesn't need saving. Saving from what?"
"I would put it very much akin to the Brexit vote, I would think it would be that finely split.
"I think the majority of the farming community see this as a folly."
Meanwhile, Defra's contribution has come under fire from Councillor Guy Renner-Thompson, chairman of Northumberland Conservatives.
He said the pledge showed the government "has its priorities wrong" in light of difficulties people across the country have faced securing sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding.
"Farmers were left scrambling in an application window that opened and closed the same day," Renner-Thompson said.
"Yet ministers can find nearly £2m to help a charity buy an estate."
In response, Nature Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter said the government was "stepping in to help" having seen thousands of members of the public give their support for a "once-in-a-generation opportunity".
