title: PSNI: Police to reduce non-emergency mental health call-outs
text:
How major policy shift is changing police response to mental health call-outs
Police in Northern Ireland handle 30,000 mental health calls every year, or about 80 a day on average - but a major new policy will see a significant change in how those calls are answered.
From the start of November, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) will no longer carry out concern-for-welfare checks unless there's a risk to life or harm or a crime involved.
The public will still phone 999, but calls will be assessed and handlers may pass them onto other emergency services or health and social care staff.
While reaction to the policy has been mixed, the PSNI says it is about ensuring individuals receive care from the most appropriate professional or service.
Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson previously told a Stormont committee that the number of mental health contacts received by police had reached "unprecedented levels".
He said thousands of calls about a person potentially in danger were received by the PSNI - with just 3% of those related to crime.
What is the new 999 policy?
The policy, Right Care Right Person, is being introduced in phases in Northern Ireland.
It has been in place among some forces in England and Wales since 2023 and means police no longer attend calls where no crime has been committed, or where there is no risk of harm or risk to life.
Instead, health, social care, or community services may attend calls for help rather than the police.
Calls to 999 will be triaged and if there is any risk of harm or to life, or if a crime is involved, the police will still attend.
However, calls that require a response like a welfare check may now fall to another part of the emergency service system as opposed to the police.
The public's approach remains the same - they are asked to phone 999 in case of emergency.
One campaigner in favour of the policy is Charles Little, the son-in-law of Michael and Marjorie Cawdery who were killed in a "frenzied attack" in their home in 2017.
Thomas Scott McEntee, who was suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, was sentenced to a minimum of 10 years in prison.
Their murders prompted a review into how the PSNI and the Southern Health and Social Care Trust had "missed opportunities" to detain McEntee for mental health care in the days leading up to the attack.
Little told BBC News NI that if the Right Care Right Person policy was in place at that time it may have "saved the day".
"If you're in a mental health crisis you might find a policeman turning up extremely frightening and it might worsen the situation," he said.
"So you don't always want the police to go first, even though at the moment the police are effectively the mental health front line."
Little said people "need to be looked after properly, they need to get the right care and they need to get it from the right person".
'Health services are currently at crisis point'
There have been some concerns raised about the impact the new policy may have on Northern Ireland's health and social care sector.
Dr Ross Irvine from the Royal College of Psychiatrists in Northern Ireland said "our mental health services are currently at crisis point".
"Thirty per cent of posts across the province are sitting vacant, and that has real-world implications," he said.
"A policy which removes the safety net that the PSNI are currently providing, and transfers that onto services that are already struggling to stand still, does give us cause for concern."
George Hannah, from the NI branch of the British Association of Social Workers, said: "What we're hearing from our members is this is too quick, there aren't sufficient resources in the system to do it safely at the moment.
"Most social workers would tell you that they don't want to be with the police all the time because of the potential for escalation, but I think not knowing that you have access to additional support when it's needed will increase concerns.
"This is about making sure that the right person gets the right care, but if the care isn't available in the system, then we're just moving people around."
'This needs to happen'
The mental health champion for Northern Ireland, Prof Siobhan O'Neill, said she believes that the policy is an important step forward.
"This is something that needs to happen. The police were attending calls where there really wasn't a policing issue," she said.
"I think the systems are working together really well to make sure that anyone who is in crisis and is in need will receive a response."
Funding issues remain a concern for O'Neill, who has previously called for a regional crisis intervention service for Northern Ireland.
"I'm disappointed that there hasn't been the investment in the health services and mental health services to ensure that there's a backfill, alternative service," she added.
The PSNI told BBC News NI it currently responds to approximately 30,000 mental health calls each year, with a "significant proportion" of these calls coming from health workers.
"The approach is about ensuring that individuals receive care from the most appropriate professional or service.
"This will help reduce avoidable delays, improve consistency in decision-making, and support safe and lawful practice across Northern Ireland."

title: Chester pumpkin carver's 'terrifying' Donald Trump portrait
text:
Pumpkin carver's 'terrifying' Trump portrait goes viral
A pumpkin carver who creates portraits of "terrifying people" has become a viral hit for depicting the likes of Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.
Jamie Jones, 42, from Capenhurst, Chester, started pumpkin carving 12 years ago and honed his skills by practising on 30 to 40 pumpkins each year "until his fingers bled".
Jamie creates three-dimensional designs by shaving layers off the pumpkin's surface rather than cutting shapes out of it.
Despite working full-time as an events and media sales manager, he can earn up to £20,000 a year from his Halloween side-hustle, and launched his business, Pumpkin Freak, in 2020, going on to work with brands including Pets at Home and Warner Bros.
His designs have also featured horror icons such as Pennywise, Freddy Krueger, as well as notorious figures including Jeffrey Dahmer and Ed Gein.
His business typically turns over between £10,000 and £20,000 a year, with each commission taking six to 20 hours to complete.
However, this year, he decided to take on no paid work so he could "have fun" with his designs, carving characters including Michael Myers from Halloween and Uncle Fester from The Addams Family, as well as prominent political figures he finds to be "terrifying".
The father of two said: "I wanted to practise carving a face and, quite frankly, I found them both - Putin and Trump - terrifying people so I thought: 'I'm going to stick them on a pumpkin'."
Jamie's designs have become increasingly intricate over the years, and his technique involves starting with a stencil of an image or a drawing before using lino cutters and chisels of different sizes to carve varying depths into the pumpkin.
Jamie also films videos of his carvings on social media, many of which have gone viral – such as his Ozzy Osbourne pumpkin clip gaining more than 1.5 million views on Facebook.
In 2024, he first carved political figures including Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump.
However, he was "not happy" with his Trump design and felt he could improve, prompting him to focus on creating more portraits.
"This sometimes happens and I always feel like I need to revisit certain people. Trump has been at the top of that list for a while."
He also received commissions to create pumpkins featuring a haunted supermarket for Morrisons, Greek vases for the Hercules musical and the logo of Stranger Things: The First Shadow stage show.
He has experimented with artificial intelligence (AI) to speed up his creative process.
He explained: "It's been a game changer for me this year – it's allowed me to make stencils a lot quicker than Photoshop – and with much more precision.
"I'm now able to use AI and manipulate images, changing face expressions, smooth textures, and more importantly change the lighting on a subject.
He said: "It's simply another tool, automates time-consuming tasks, and has given me more time to be creative."
Jamie displays his finished pumpkins on his front lawn, washing them with bleach and water to help them last as long as possible.
Around Halloween, "a lot" of locals drive past his house to admire his creations, and he even judges the local pumpkin carving competition.
His children also get "stuck in" with the carving, with Jamie letting his two daughters "loose" with his tools.
He added: "My eldest gets really into it, and really concentrates when she's doing the carving – I think she's definitely a budding professional pumpkin carver!"

title: Girl raises money for Shrewsbury and Telford Hospitals trust after death of sisters
text:
Girl, 6, wants to 'help other families' after losing twin sisters
A six-year-old girl has spoken of how she wants to make "a massive difference for people who've lost their babies".
Daisy, from Edgmond in Shropshire, cycled 25 miles to Stafford to raise nearly £2,000 for local maternity services.
She set up the ride after her sisters, twins Aurora and Seren died after pregnancy complications, in January 2023, and her family got support from Shrewsbury and Telford Hospitals NHS Trust's maternity bereavement team.
Daisy said she hopes her fundraising efforts "will really help" other families experiencing the same kind of loss.
The maternity bereavement team have "done lots of things to help mummy". Daisy explained, including memory boxes to remember the twins.
"There's candles to remember their birthdays, and certificates. There's little angels as well," she said.
The fundraising challenge was "really good," said Daisy, adding she was a "really big fan" of cycling.
"It was quite hard. I thought it was quite hard, but then it was okay in the end," she added.
Her mum Ella explained that while she was pregnant with Aurora and Seren, she "unfortunately met some complications and had an infection", resulting in her waters breaking early.
"I spontaneously gave birth to one of them and then had to go into hospital and be induced to have the other one," Ella explained.
The support from the maternity bereavement team was "fantastic," she said.
"They talked us through all of our options and supported us in the weeks and years afterwards."
Since then, Daisy's sister Ruby was born, with the team continuing to support Ella during that pregnancy.
"They were just incredible," she said, adding that "we couldn't have done it without them."
Having raised £1,870 for the bereavement team, Daisy said she is "really, really proud".
"It will really help [other families] when they've lost their babies," she added.
Daisy's family had "absolutely no doubts" about her ability to complete the challenge, Ella said.
"I am very, very proud."
The six-year-old's passion for cycling was sparked by Newport Shropshire Cycling Club.
"I go to bike club," she explained, adding "it really makes me feel excited and happy because it's just what I want to do - cycling."
Daisy's answer to whether another challenge is on the cards?
"We might cycle 50 miles next time," she added.

title: The Gloucestershire man who chooses to sleep with bedbugs
text:
The man who chooses to sleep with bedbugs
A scientist has chosen to sleep with bedbugs for the past five years - and says the bites "don't bother him at all".
Entomologist Dr Richard Naylor breeds thousands of bedbugs to test pest control products from all over the world and allows himself to be the test subject.
On a "feeding day", which happens around twice a week, he straps some of his 50-60,000 bugs to his arm and gets on with his work. He then sleeps with them on nights when he needs to test out new devices or repellents.
"I must have been bitten millions of times by now, so I stopped reacting a long time ago. I get a red patch on my arm after the bugs have fed, but it disappears after about half an hour," he said.
Naylor explained that he needed to sleep with the bugs to test if new sprays and repellents worked.
"If there is no-one sleeping in a bed, the bedbugs just sleep, they just go on standby. And so I can't test anything in the test bedrooms without there being a host in there," he added.
Naylor runs a not-for-profit called the Bed Bug Foundation and has a research laboratory set up in a self-contained two-bedroom suite in his garden in the Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire.
He breeds the bugs and sends them all over the world, often to canine detection teams who help hotels spot infestations.
Naylor also uses the insects to help businesses test products before they come to market.
Bedbugs have become resistant to modern insecticide sprays, which makes them very difficult to kill and having an infestation can have long-lasting effects, according to Naylor.
"I don't know of any other pest that has the same level of emotional and psychological impact on people.
"It can leave people with lasting PTSD-type symptoms," he added.
Naylor said it could be difficult to deal with infestations and he advised anyone who suspected they had one to contact a professional.
"A key sign you have bedbugs is the inky black spots the bugs leave behind, often in the shape of an x.
"They don't hide in the bedding, they want to hide nearby in a little dark crevice. It would probably be somewhere down the back of the bed or around zips and the piping around the edge of a mattress," he said.
The Bed Bug Foundation gives the following advice to anyone who suspects they may have bed bugs:
- Declutter around the bed (helps you to spot bedbugs that try to run away)
- Remove bedding and other soft furnishings and put in bin bags for washing
- Inspect the mattress and bed frame, especially near the head of the bed
- Use silica dust and vacuum thoroughly
- Fit bed isolation devices to stop the bedbugs coming back
Ade Williams, lead pharmacist at Bedminster Pharmacy in Bristol, said bedbug bites tended to be clustered in a group, or be spread out in a line.
"Outside of the immense discomfort they cause by itching, they don't usually carry any health risks", he said.
However, Williams advised people to try not to itch bites as they could become infected, and said antihistamine tablets and emollient creams could help.
It advises putting something cool, like a clean, damp cloth, on the affected area to help with the itching and any swelling and to keep the affected area clean.

title: Litherland mother sets up women's group to help tackle loneliness
text:
Mum sets up women's group to help fight loneliness
A Merseyside mother who set up a community group for women experiencing anxiety and loneliness said the response had been "a miracle".
Becky Saunders, 39, from Litherland, said she set up the group Girls Who Gather, after experiencing 14 months of severe anxiety.
"I just couldn't get away from it," she said.
"I went to therapy, on walks, read books, listened to podcasts.
"I tried to look into why I felt that way, and I tried to overcome it. I got to the point where I just didn't think there was going to be a way out," she said.
The mum-of-two said it was only when she decided to reach out to other women that things changed.
"I thought, I don't want to be living like this forever. I need to get myself out of this," she said.
"I thought I don't want to be sat in all the time - there must be other ladies in the area feeling the way I am."
After reaching out on social media, Becky arranged for a small group to meet.
"I thought, I can't be the only one. So that's what made me think, maybe I should put something out there - to see if girls in the area want to get together.
"Even if one person turned up, that was good for me."
Becky said she was amazed when 11 women attended the first meeting.
"It was a miracle," she said.
'No pressure'
"Honestly it's brilliant," Becky said.
The group has since grown, and now Becky arranges regular gatherings of about 20 women each month.
Meetings can include anything from meeting for a coffee, to walks in the park, cake decorating and painting classes.
"People are out there, wanting to do it," she said.
"All of these women are going through the things that I've gone through.
"I think sometimes people are embarrassed to go to therapy, or go to counselling."
She said the group was about "getting out and just talking to other ladies".
"There's no pressure to share anything. You haven't got to tell us why you're there, what you're doing there. You haven't got to tell anything.
"Just come and enjoy yourself. Get yourself away from your kids, away from your partner, away from your dog - away from everything.
"I think it's important to be yourself.
"As well as being a mum... being a partner... it's important to be you."

title: Cotswold tourism, is it a blessing or a burden?
text:
Cotswold tourism, is it a blessing or a burden?
With autumn in full swing, the West of England is a popular region for tourists to make cosy getaways, with the chocolate box villages of the Cotswolds proving particularly popular.
But, with the post-pandemic rise in visitors in some areas, tensions have risen in villages such as Bibury.
The village is home to about 600 people but can see up to 20,000 visitors a day, with fences having to be installed to stop tourists paddling in the river.
Twenty-four miles away, in Painswick, Carol Maxwell said that while there are an "awful lot" of tourists in the village, there is a balance with most "really nice and appreciative".
Victoria Summerley, who has lived in Bibury for 14 years, told the BBC last week that the behaviour of some tourists had become worse since Covid, with "unbelievable" amounts of litter ending up in the stream.
Meanwhile, Maxwell said that while Painswick had seen an increase in visitors, they were "not exactly loud and they don't create a bad atmosphere".
She said she did not think anyone felt that tourists were a "nuisance or an imposition or anything like that" and that they spent money in the village having cups of tea.
"They're not causing problems at all," she added.
Cotswolds Lavender near Snowshill, sees thousands of visitors every summer.
Farm director Hannah Webb said tourists and influencers coming, taking and sharing photographs have driven business, but it can cause problems.
"We're very lucky to have something people want to see and want to tell people that they've been to us," said Webb.
The field has paths that have been mown between rows of lavender and wildflowers to create the illusion of visitors standing in the flower beds in photographs, but some have been sitting and laying down to get the perfect picture which has led to a lot of "squashed plants".
A few years ago, they decided to put up signs to warn people to be more careful which Webb said "completely changed" people's behaviour and now they are "so much more respectful".
She said they took a similar approach to people disobeying their dogs on lead policy, which is in place to protect insects and mammals that nest among the flowers, and that has also led to "more positive results".
In Wiltshire, Castle Combe is among the most popular Cotswolds locations to visit.
It was the backdrop to films such as Stardust and War Horse, and a bridge which stretches over the River Bybrook is often packed with people taking photos.
Most visitors to Castle Combe "enjoy the village respectfully", said local councillor Jon Atkey.
However, the village can struggle to cope with the volume of vehicles and people during busy spells.
Atkey said: "Castle Combe's roads and infrastructure were never designed to accommodate the levels of traffic we now see.
"During busy periods, traffic can become heavily congested, with cars circulating in search of parking spaces and spending long periods queuing through the village.
"Residents are understandably concerned about the impact this has on both safety and air quality.
"The vast majority of visitors simply want to enjoy one of England's most beautiful villages, and they should continue to be welcomed.
"The challenge for all of us is finding a better balance that enables people to visit while ensuring Castle Combe remains a thriving community and a good place for residents to live."
Dr Amir Gohar, University of West England, has worked on tourism policies in environmentally sensitive areas with rapid tourism development.
He said the phrase "overtourism" is when the "tourist get the attention of the government and transforms cities and villages to serve the tourists more than serving the local community or the people".
In areas popular with tourists in the South West, including the Cotswolds, Somerset and Wiltshire, it can mean more pressure on infrastructure like parking, water, sewage and waste collection as high tourist numbers are "not accounted for when planning the town or village".
Dr Gohar said having lots of visitors can also impact "housing affordability" as businesses or development companies start to cater more for the tourists with short stays or Airbnb's which means the "prices get high and the local residents pay that price".
Finding a balance between visitor experience and the residents wellbeing is a "challenge" that "it needs to be regulated", he said.

title: How a Hereford dad became a Timbersports athlete
text:
How one email turned a dad into an international athlete
One email changed everything for George Spencer.
Eight years after asking how he could get involved in a sport he had watched as a spectator, the 30-year-old is preparing to represent Great Britain at a world championship for the third time.
This weekend, he will travel to Germany to compete against some of the world's best athletes in a sport that involves chopping and sawing through wood with axes, chainsaws and crosscut saws.
What started with a simple email after watching an event in Liverpool in 2018 soon became what Spencer describes as an "obsession".
"My friend said I should see about getting involved so I emailed them and got invited to a newcomers' taster day," he said.
Within a few years, Spencer had joined the Welsh Axemen club and worked his way into the Great Britain team.
Now, he is preparing to take on some of the world's elite competitors at the STIHL TIMBERSPORTS World Championship in Stuttgart.
"The quickest way to explain it, timber sports are lumberjack sports," he said.
"It's basically how quick you can chop through wood with chainsaws and axes."
Spencer, who works in forestry and estate management and lives in Hereford, is set to compete in the team relay event, where four athletes complete a series of chopping and sawing disciplines in succession.
He is also most likely to compete in either the stock saw or standing block events.
Great Britain will go head-to-head with six-time defending champions Australia, who Spencer believes remain the team to beat.
"We're not quite at their level yet but we're getting better each year," he said.
"The difference with Australia is they started wood chopping when they were three and they've been doing it for 20-odd years.
"They're one with the axe, let's say."
To many people, the sight of athletes swinging axes and operating chainsaws at speed might seem dangerous.
But Spencer insists the sport is much safer than it appears.
Competitors wear specialist protective equipment, including chain-mail protection around their lower legs and feet.
"With the chopping events you've got to wear chain-mail shin-pads and chain-mail socks underneath your trousers and your shoes," he said.
"It's pretty safe. If anything, you won't cut your toes off, you'll just break them."
His unusual sporting passion has also become a talking point at home.
Spencer said his wife, Amber, and six-year-old son have embraced the sport, despite most people having never heard of it.
"It starts with them asking what sort of stuff I do and then it turns into about one hundred questions because no-one's really heard about it," he said.
"It's really good to watch. It's fast, it's pretty crazy."
Asked whether his son might one day follow him into the sport, Spencer laughed.
"I've tried to get him on the axe already and he goes, 'Yeah, let's do it, let's do it', but when it actually comes to it, he chickens out.
"We'll keep it going, we'll keep the pressure on."

title: Hull woman turns 100 as royal birthday cards surge
text:
Are more people learning the secret to turning 100?
"We are pleased to know you are celebrating your 100th birthday," says Marie Stothard.
She is reading a message from King Charles III and Queen Camilla in a card which she holds in her delicate hands.
A smiling photograph of the King and Queen is displayed on the front.
Marie is surrounded by her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren in a function room on the top floor of the care home where she lives in Hull.
Photographs and mementoes from the last century are scattered around the room.
"I never thought I'd live to be 100," she says with a chuckle.
However, living to 100 appears to be becoming increasingly common in the UK.
Figures from Buckingham Palace show the number of congratulatory cards sent to centenarians has almost doubled over the past 20 years.
In 2005, 4,623 cards were sent to people celebrating their 100th birthday, the Palace said. By 2025, that figure had risen to 8,394.
When asked about the secret to a long life, Marie grins and looks around the room before giving a simple answer: "Family."
She adds: "They've made me happy. They're wonderful. Nothing is too much trouble and I'm very lucky."
Also at the party is Marie's son, Peter Stothard, 69. Pointing towards his mother, he says: "My mum's an amazing woman."
Peter says he believes the secret to a long life is having "a strong work ethic and resilience".
"My mum worked every day. She's still as sharp as a razor," he says.
"When you've worked all your life, like my mum has, it keeps you going. It keeps you motivated.
"I always knew she'd make it to 100."
Having grown up during World War Two, Marie became a familiar face to pub-goers across Hull, pulling pints and managing several alehouses with her late husband.
Another guest at the party is Maria Anson, the manager of Wilton Lodge care home in Hull.
"Marie is not actually our oldest resident," she says with a smile.
"Our oldest resident is 102 and we've got quite a few residents in their late 90s heading towards 100. It's amazing."
Despite being surrounded by several people who have reached the milestone birthday, Maria admits she does not know the secret to a long life.
"I do think it's got something to do with wellness and keeping active, not just physically but mentally as well," she says.
Peter Byers, from Pocklington, East Yorkshire, who celebrated his 100th birthday earlier this year, said the secret to a long and active life was to "keep happy, keep walking and keep breathing".
In August, Peter said he still walked a mile every day because it helped him "escape the four walls".
More people than ever are reaching their 100th birthday in the UK.
According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), there were 16,600 centenarians in the UK in 2024. This had doubled from 8,300 in 2004.
Kerry Gadsdon, a spokesperson for the ONS, said: "Since 2024, the number of 105-year-olds in the UK has increased by nearly a third, meaning there are now more semi-super centenarians than ever before.
"This is the result of the large generation born after the First World War beginning to reach this age."
Mike Padgham, whose own mother recently celebrated her 100th birthday, chairs the Independent Care Group, which supports care providers across Yorkshire.
He said longer life spans should be celebrated, but warned further support would be needed for the social care sector to cope with growing numbers.
"We've got to recruit more people into social care. By 2040, we will need nearly half a million more workers, and currently we're around 100,000 short," he said.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged a major reform of social care in England to create "a system that works on NHS principles" and where "everyone contributes, and everyone is covered".
Anja Hazebroek, executive director of Insight and Commissioning Strategy at the NHS Humber and North Yorkshire Integrated Care Board (ICB) said an ageing population would "undoubtedly change demand for health and care".
"The challenge is making sure more of those extra years are lived in good health and with independence," she said.
"Our response needs to be proactive and preventative, helping people stay well and independent for longer, while ensuring hospital and specialist care is available when it is needed."
For Marie, though, the secret to a long life is much simpler.
Looking around a room filled with four generations of her family as she celebrates her 100th birthday, her answer remains unchanged:
"Family."

title: Mums of autistic girls create special app for parents
text:
Mums of autistic girls create special app for parents
Two mothers who created an app to help parents of children with special needs connect hope it means no one will feel alone.
Kate Dunn, whose daughter Ophelia has non-verbal autism and ADHD, met the mother of Sophia, also diagnosed with autism, Nisha Warburton, in a carpark outside their specialist nursery in Bolton, Greater Manchester.
Nisha said: "You go from feeling like the only person who is dealing with such a situation to recognising that actually a lot of people are."
In their free time, or while their children were asleep, the pair decided to make the app, called SEN2gether, to create a community as well as to share information and tools for parents.
With almost 2,000 sign-ups within its first month, the pair have created a growing private community of parents and carers where they can share what works, ask questions as well as find local connections and guidance.
"We are just mums. We do not have a background in business or digital app making but what we notice is people love it and recognise it, and we are growing and developing it everyday," Nisha said.
'Be strong'
Kate said: "There's not one family that we speak to, who is not going through something."
Speaking of her daughter Ophelia's diagnosis, she said: "We were told that she was deaf, we were given a hearing aid and then we finally got her autism diagnosis.
"You try to be strong for your child even though mentally you are falling apart."
A recent government review found that there is a risk of people being over-diagnosed with ADHD and autism in England.
But, for Kate and Nisha, the findings make them feel more isolated.
"It does feel disappointing because a lot of our families then may question is this valid, do the public think this is a valid diagnosis when we know the daily struggles," Nisha said.
"So regardless of the actual diagnosis label we know that the daily challenges don't just disappear with or without a label."

title: Phone box at centre of Great Britain gets listed status
text:
Phone box at centre of Great Britain listed
A telephone box that stands at the geographic centre of Great Britain has been given Grade II-listed status.
The KX100 kiosk at Dunsop Bridge, in Ribble Valley in Lancashire, was the 100,000th telephone kiosk to be installed in the country.
It was officially opened in June 1992 by explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, who was joined by children from nearby Thornleyholme RC Primary School as he made the first call from the kiosk.
Historic England's (HE) Jayne Rimmer said as part of "the last generation of the public telephone box", it was a "nationally significant kiosk".
The Twentieth Century Society (TCS), which champions outstanding examples of modern design, had applied for it to be listed.
Campaigns director Oli Marshall said he was "absolutely delighted" by their success.
"There's no small irony that it was the arrival of the KX100 that first spurred the Society into action back in 1985 - once the slayer of traditional red telephone boxes, that we fought vigorously to repel, now itself being given heritage protection," he said.
"While widely unloved and underappreciated in comparison to the classic red telephone boxes, the ugly duckling KX100 model has developed a cult following in recent years."
He added that with the Tour de France "passing through Dunsop Bridge next July, we hope the kiosk will form the centrepiece of the village's celebrations, as well as being the centre of Great Britain".
Ribble Valley Borough Council leader Simon Hore said the phone box had "a special place in local people's hearts".
First introduced in 1985, the KX100 design has large glass panels and was designed to be easier to clean and more accessible than the previous red model.
In the HE listing, it is described as having both architectural and historic interest.
The organisation stated it was both a "good and largely intact example... which illustrates all the standard features and branding of this newly introduced type of telephone kiosk" and an "exemplar of the last generation of the 'public telephone box', which makes an important contribution to our understanding of the historic development of the telecommunications industry in England".
TCS said the kiosk was of particular importance as it featured "a bespoke, site-specific design" featuring "key places in Britain radiating from the BT 'Piper' marque and Dunsop Bridge".
The Lancashire village was named as the nearest settlement to the geographical centre of Great Britain following work by national mapping agency Ordnance Survey (OS).
Its calculations put the centre at Whitendale Hanging Stones, about 4.3 miles (7km) north-west of Dunsop Bridge.
The title has been disputed, with other places also making a claim, including Haltwhistle in Northumberland.
OS later stated there could be "no absolute centre for a three-dimensional land mass sitting on the surface of a sphere and surrounded by the ebb and flow of sea water" and "different projections, scales and methods of calculation will all produce different results".
Dunsop Bridge was the result of defining Britain as "the mainland and the 401 associated islands", a spokesperson said in 2014.
They added that "looking only at the mainland of Great Britain", the location was a little further south, lying about 2.5 miles (4km) north-west of Whalley.

title: Youth Olympics call-up a 'dream birthday present' for Warwick boxer
text:
Youth Olympics call-up a 'dream birthday present'
The day before her 17th birthday, Jaya Kalsi received a phone call with the kind of news that every young boxer dreams of.
The athlete, from Warwick, had been selected to represent Team GB at the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, in what she described as an "amazing present to get".
With the Games getting under way on 31 October, Kalsi is preparing to fly out for what will be the highest-level competition of her career so far.
"I'm looking forward to it, it's a great honour to represent Team GB and my country," she said.
Speaking to BBC CWR, Kalsi said she had been training with Team GB in recent weeks in the gym and her preparations had gone "really well".
The Sikh fighter, who is ranked third in the world at her level and is a European gold medallist, will compete in the 54kg weight category and will find out who she is up against next month.
"The draw will happen when we're out there," she said. "It will be an amazing experience."
Kalsi hopes a strong performance can also be another step towards her long-term goal of competing at the 2028 and 2032 Olympic Games, before eventually turning professional.
She said she was looking to bring home a gold medal.
"I aim to make it to the top, I'm looking to hopefully get a place on the 2028 Olympic squad and hopefully the 2032 Olympics and then go pro after that," she explained.
The boxer, who has trained at Cleary Boxing Gym in Leamington Spa since she was young, explained how she took up the sport from the age of seven, after being influenced by her father.
"I loved doing sports before that, I did swimming and karate but my dad, he was a massive fan of boxing so he got me into the sport," she said.
"He looked up to Ricky Hatton and Floyd Mayweather, and he basically took me to the gym."
Irish boxer Katie Taylor, who recently ended her career as a three-time and two-weight undisputed champion, was a "massive inspiration" to her, Kalsi said, highlighting her impact on women's boxing.
She added that she was also inspired by former world champion Mayweather, with his "hard work and dedication".
"I look to achieve something like him in the future," she said.
The athlete will also be joined in Senegal by her mother, who she said had supported her all the way.
"I'm looking to bring back the Youth Olympic gold medal and get a step up," the boxer said.

title: AI makes Britain's largest woodland bat survey possible, scientists say
text:
Largest woodland bat survey a 'nice story of AI for good'
Britain's largest ever woodland survey of bats would "simply not have been feasible" without AI, scientists say.
Researchers left devices on poles among the trees of 310 woodlands across Britain, recording 98 million bat calls over three years, which would have taken more than 30 years to analyse without AI.
Some of Britain's rarest and most threatened bats, including the red-listed Barbastelle, have been recorded in the south-west of England, including Somerset, Devon, Cornwall and Dorset.
Kate Jones, from University College London, said: "AI has fundamentally changed the scale at which we can monitor wildlife." She added the survey was a "nice story of AI for good".
Allow Google YouTube content?
Jones added: "Previously, analysing this volume of acoustic data would simply not have been feasible.
"These efficient open-source AI tools allow us to identify millions of bat calls across thousands of nights of recordings, identify patterns and flag species at a national scale."
The Barbastelle roams ancient forests but its elusive nature has made it challenging to track.
Hotspots of Barbastelle activity detected in the survey were concentrated across the South West.
Lia Gilmour, of the Bat Conservation Trust, which was involved in the survey alongside Forest Research, said the project was "unprecedented".
"We're getting some really good bat activity in the south-west area of Somerset," Gilmour said.
"Somerset is generally a really good stronghold for the bat species we have across the UK.
"It's been quite exciting some of the rarest species popping up in Somerset as part of the survey.
"In biodiversity monitoring, we view AI as a powerful tool," Gilmour added.
"We were looking at huge volumes of data and 90,000 hours of recording, there was no way we would be able to do this manually."

title: Severe drought: How close are we to running out of water?
text:
How close are we to running out of water?
Reservoirs have hit record lows, severe drought has been declared in parts of England and large areas of the country face hosepipe bans. The government says more than £100bn is being invested in water infrastructure, with nine new reservoirs in the pipeline. But, after the hottest summer on record for the UK, are we prepared for a future of more extreme weather? And how close are we to running out of water?
Wimbleball reservoir on Exmoor attracts visitors not only to sail and row, but also so admire the scenery and take a walk.
These days the lake is getting visitors for another reason - to marvel at how empty the Somerset landmark is, even after storms of the past week.
"It's shocking looking at it," said Michael Bertulis. "You can see where the water level should be.
"We need some rain."
The reservoir can hold more than 21 billion litres and provides drinking water to around 400,000 people across Devon, parts of Somerset and Dorset.
Earlier this month it hit a record low of being 12.5% full.
"It's never been as low and it's worrying", said Andrea Worley of Wimbleball Rowing Club. "But we don't know how long the water is going to last."
On 15 October severe drought was declared across parts of Southern England, including Sussex and the South West.
Has recent rain made a difference?
Storm Austen and Storm Boelo - the first named storms of the year - brought heavy rain to much of the country last week.
It led to a slight increase in the level of the South West's reservoirs, including Wimbleball. It rose from being 12.5% full on the 22 October to 14% four days later, on 26 October.
Other reservoirs considered "critically low" have also seen levels rise slightly, including Stithians and Drift in Cornwall, and Venford in Devon.
The Environment Agency (EA) has said England needs 120% of its typical rainfall, for the country to be out of drought by spring next year.
Mark Rice, area director for the EA in Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly said the drought could extend to next summer if rainfall does not reach this level.
He said: "If we get average or below average rainfall, we're potentially going to be in a prolonged drought situation going into next summer.
"It means we're going to have to work really closely with the water companies to ensure we can manage water supplies sensibly and ensure there is no disruption to supply, either this winter or into next summer."
"We need to be really clear with the public, our water resources are reduced but they are not under threat," added Rice, referring to the area he covers in the South West.
"We won't run out of water this winter," he added.
'We were close'
"We were concerned" Richard Stanbrook, South West Water's drought programme director, said after reservoirs dropped to "incredibly low" levels.
The company was granted drought permits by the EA that allows it to abstract more water from some rivers and discharge less into the environment from reservoirs.
Asked how close the South West came to running out of water, Standbrook said: "We were close but every step we took meant that it wasn't something that was very likely to happen."
"We worked closely with the Environment Agency, with everyone involved in water to improve our capability to supply water to customers," he added.
"We did, in the very unlikely event of running out of water, we were working with the EA and other stakeholders on any emergency plans."
According to the Met Office, the summer of 2026 was the hottest on record.
There was persistent heat throughout the spring and summer, with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F), smashing the previous record of 34 days.
A study by the Met Office said that the heat experienced this summer was made 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change.
Professor Liz Bentley, chief executive at the Royal Meteorological Society said this drought - although similar in severity to those seen in 1995 and 1976 - was different.
She said: "We started 2026 on a particularly wet note, with one of the wettest winters on record but we then went into that exceptionally hot, dry period.
"It was more of a flash drought, it happened really quickly.
"And I think that's very much a signal of climate change."
Bentley added: "We need to be much better at capturing rainfall during the wetter winters, to use during the drier summers.
"This is the climate we are going to have to get used to, it's becoming the new norm."
How long will the hosepipe ban last?
Water restrictions are in place across large parts of England, with residents and businesses being urged to be careful with the amount they are using.
A partial hosepipe ban was initially introduced by South West Water in July, and it was then extended to cover the whole of the area covered by the utility company in August.
Stanbrook said the hosepipe ban was likely to be in place for a "significant period", adding that reservoirs needed "a strong recharge over the course of the winter".
Stanbrook also said he hoped customers would "lean in" and continue to be careful with water.
The company has also applied to the government to potentially bring in a non-essential use ban, a restriction that would impact some businesses, including car washes and window cleaners.
Water UK represents water companies across the UK and said it was "incredibly grateful" to customers attempting to protect water supplies by limiting usage.
It repeated the need for significant rain in the coming months to "refill reservoirs and replenish groundwater".
"After being blocked from building a new reservoir for more than 30 years, water companies have finally been given approval to build nine, plus a 10th already under construction at Havant Thicket.
"We need planning hurdles cleared so we can build reservoirs quickly and we need major reform to ensure we are not in this situation again."
The government has said the measures being taken to tackle severe drought "sit alongside long-term measures" it is taking with water companies to "strengthen the UK's water resilience after decades of underinvestment".
"This includes investing £104bn to upgrade water infrastructure, building nine new reservoirs across the country to increase water supply, and changing planning rules to make it easier to build reservoirs".

title: Crowd backs popular singer in Carlton after welfare check
text:
Crowd backs popular singer after welfare check
Dozens of people gathered outside a convenience store to show support for a beloved local singer after a police welfare check left him fearing he would no longer be able to perform.
Miles Green, 28, who has Down's syndrome, has been a familiar sight for the last 10 years, singing on a street corner outside the One Stop store in Gedling Road, Carlton, where passing motorists regularly sound their horns in encouragement.
But after officers were called over concerns for his welfare, customers and supportive strangers rallied round on Thursday for a singalong, encouraging the local star to "shine brighter".
He told the BBC seeing the support made him emotional, and vowed to not stop singing.
Miles said he had been standing on the street corner, singing, as he usually did, when the police arrived and asked for his name and address.
"Obviously, I was upset," he said.
A spokesperson for Nottinghamshire Police said: "We were called by a member of the public who had concerns for the welfare of a man in Gedling Road, Gedling.
"Officers attended and carried out checks to ensure he was safe and well, with no issues identified."
After the "knock" to Miles's confidence, he was greeted on Thursday morning by a crowd of supporters who sang along with one of his favourite songs, Elton John's Don't Let the Sun Go Down on Me.
"I can't believe it. I am a bit emotional obviously," he said. "I just love [singing] and I want it to keep going."
His mother Shirley Green said he had been singing on the corner since 2015 and it was often difficult to get him to come home.
"Everywhere we go, someone will say 'oh look it's Miles off the corner'," she said.
"Everybody knows him."
Deborah Bradley, Miles's manager, said Miles had always loved singing to the public and to customers.
"They absolutely love him," she said. "If he's not there and on holiday, some of the older people come and in and they ask me where he is.
"He's just a general all-rounder for the community, he keeps everyone jolly. It's just his spirit."
On the recent setback, she said: "He came in on Wednesday morning and told me about it and he got quite upset. He said 'I'm not going to be able to sing anymore'.
"I said, 'we're not going to dim your light Miles', and we haven't, we've made it shine even brighter."

title: 'Witch marks' revealed at 17th Century East Riddlesden Hall
text:
Mysterious 'witch marks' revealed at 17th Century manor
In the hills west of Bradford is a 17th Century manor house where residents once feared evil spirits so much that they made special marks to protect themselves - and they made these marks so permanent that they are still being discovered to this very day.
Previously a medieval estate, East Riddlesden Hall near Keighley was built by Halifax wool merchant James Murgatroyd in the 1640s for his eldest son, John.
Now a National Trust property, historians at the site continue to uncover a series of these mysterious marks left behind by previous residents in an effort to ward off unwelcome spirits.
"These are things that have been around for many centuries and were what people who were building the house put in there to protect themselves from evil or witches or bad spirits entering the home," explains Amy Gregory, collections and house officer at East Riddlesden.
"They are things we've known about for quite a while, although we do keep finding more and more, which is quite exciting."
Some of the marks at East Riddlesden can be found on what were known as the "thresholds", places where it was thought evil spirits might enter the home.
For example, on the windowsill of an upstairs bedroom is a daisy wheel, also known as a hexafoil or a witch mark.
Carved into the wood with a needle or compass, the unbroken loop was believed to catch and trap wandering or malevolent spirits in an infinite maze, keeping the household safe.
"It's meant to protect the inhabitants inside from any evil spirits trying to come in, so they put them on their thresholds," explains Gregory.
"This windowsill until about two years ago was completely covered in thick brown paint.
"So we had a furniture conserver remove it because we just wanted it to go back to the wood again - then he came and told us he'd found a daisy wheel on there.
"It's something he thought we might have here because of the age of the building, so he was looking out for them."
Gregory says that another windowsill on the ground floor of the hall, which is still covered in thick brown paint, may well prove to be another location for witch marks.
"Maybe at a future point we'd quite like to remove that to see if there are any more daisy wheels inside the house," she says.
It is not only mysterious marks which can be found at East Riddlesden Hall.
Three strange carved heads above the fireplace in the Great Hall are not just there for decoration, says Gregory.
Known as archaic heads, the figures have been found on field walls, bridges and houses across West Yorkshire – with one even found on the Hebden Bridge aqueduct.
They are thought to have been used as a protection against bad luck.
"They were quite a prevalent thing in Calderdale and James Murgatroyd was from Calderdale," says Gregory.
"They were supposedly put either on the outside buildings or inside buildings to protect the inhabitants from misfortune.
"Murgatroyd had about £2,000 a year, which in today's money is probably several hundred thousands of pounds
"He was quite wealthy and he built at least seven houses, most of them in the Halifax area."
Meanwhile, as well as daisy wheels, there are also further odd marks and markings to be spotted around East Riddlesden.
Deliberate burns can be found along wood panelling which it is thought were put there to protect from fire, and graffiti can be seen in the medieval tithe barn calling for the protection of the Virgin Mary.
"These are called Marion marks and they are Christian protection symbols," Gregory says.
"They're meant to be invocations of the Virgin Mary, so through religious inhabitants they would have put these marks on as a way to protect themselves.
"It's often thought they put them in barns to maybe protect the harvest in here.
"These marks still remain there today, so they've kind of stood the test of time."
Gregory insists the marks must have worked because, despite rumours spread at the end of the last century, there are no reported ghosts at the hall.
"There are ghost stories of the house, but they were all invented in the 1990s, so we think that at the time the house steward was quite interested in ghost stories.
"But I'm in the house quite a lot and I don't see anything."

A motorway will be closed overnight while its central safety barrier is replaced.

A 50mph speed limit will be in place and lane three will be closed for the safety of workers.
Between March and July, three narrow lanes will be running in both directions on that stretch, with the 50mph speed limit remaining in place.

There will be lane closures overnight between 21:00 and 06:00 GMT on the affected stretch of motorway from Monday to Sunday next week.
On 9 November, the M5 will be closed southbound overnight.
Between 10-13 November and on 16 November, the M5 will be closed in both directions overnight.

title: Residents surveyed about part of Guildford with sinking homes
text:
Neighbours to help shape sinking homes plans
The future of part of Guildford where properties began sinking into the ground is the subject of a council survey.
Guildford Borough Council is consulting residents and businesses in the west of the town about "opportunities for future improvements" in the neighbourhoods.
The authority's Better Homes Programme has already launched with the aim of improving public spaces and council-owned homes in the Westborough and Park Barn area.
Several council-owned houses in the neighbourhood, some of which were later demolished, had been left empty due to subsidence problems.
The council previously said the condition issues were related to the properties' shallow foundations and age.
Officials said architects had been appointed but no decisions had been made yet on the programme of works and resident feedback "will help shape any future proposals".
A panel of 15 local people will be created to help shape proposals, according to the council.
Members of the public can answer the survey on the Guildford Borough Council website or at The Hive community centre on 11 November.
Council leader Julia McShane said views from the survey would "help us understand local priorities".
"This is the beginning of a conversation, and we encourage everyone to get involved and share their views," she said.

title: Devolution: Lancashire has 'never been nearer' to having a mayor
text:
Lancashire 'never been nearer' to having a mayor
Leaders in Lancashire say the county has "never been nearer" to having a mayor, after the government confirmed it was one of 10 areas in the final stages of a new devolution agreement.
A devolution deal for Lancashire was first agreed in 2023, but it did not involve a mayor at that time, with a combined authority launched in 2025.
Phil Riley, the Labour leader of Blackburn with Darwen Council, said the government go-ahead was "a good thing", which would put Lancashire on a par with Greater Manchester and the Liverpool City Region.
Stephen Atkinson, Reform leader of Lancashire County Council, also welcomed the move but called for more details: "We need to see it in black and white," he said.
As part of the Budget - announced on Wednesday - the government said it was in the final stages of agreeing 10 new devolution agreements, including Lancashire.
"The converse of having a mayor, would be that Lancashire will be the only place in the north of England that doesn't have a mayor," Riley told BBC Radio Lancashire.
"It's not the right place to be.
"All the direction of travel of government - not just Labour, but previously the Conservatives - all the direction of travel has been about devolution."
Lynn Williams, Labour leader of Blackpool Council, agreed a mayor for Lancashire was something the area "should be ambitious about".
However, Reform's Atkinson stressed the county had two red lines in terms of agreeing a deal - capacity funding and a guarantee that any investment would be greater than the cost entailed.
"We don't have the details," he warned. "We've got the vibe, we've got the mood music - but we need to see it in black and white."
Nonetheless, he acknowledged, "the sound is much better than where we've been".
Shoppers at Ormskirk Market had mixed views on the plans.
"I'm open-minded, but I'm not really sure," one man told BBC Politics North West.
"It might end up like the police commissioners, where it was a big waste of money in the end," he cautioned.
Another, who said he lived in a more rural area, felt mayors were better suited to cities, but other shoppers viewed the move in a more positive light, highlighting how mayors had been beneficial in the Liverpool City Region and Greater Manchester.
"It's not done Liverpool any harm - and it's done Manchester a lot better," said one trader.
"It's nice to have somebody represent the place," another shopper added.
However, one woman, who said she had lived in Ormskirk all her life, felt there were "enough people at the top" already.
Focus on devolution
Lancashire had also been set to undergo local government reorganisation, which would have seen the county council and 14 district councils and unitary authorities replaced with four new unitary authorities.
But the shake-up of local government - which would have impacted 14 areas across the country - was put on hold by the government in September.
Local government minister Jim McMahon has now confirmed only five of the original proposals will go ahead - not including Lancashire.
In a letter to the leaders in the nine areas where the plans have been withdrawn, McMahon said the decision was "not a reflection of the quality of the proposals submitted by councils in your area, but rather the need to give each decision of such significance the careful consideration it deserves".
"All options and proposals in your area will remain under consideration as part of the review," he said.
Atkinson said the government was trying to do too much simultaneously and needed to be clearer about its aims.
He said trying to implement devolution was "a big ask on its own".
"If it's trying to reorganise local government at the same time that puts a real strain on the capacity, because many of the officers that will be working on devolution will be working on local government reorganisation," he said.
"If devolution is what they really care about, they're not helping devolution by trying to do these two things at the same time."

title: Committee approves Melton solar farm despite concerns
text:
Solar farm approved despite councillors' concerns
Councillors have unanimously approved plans for a solar farm in Leicestershire despite voicing concerns it was "not the right place" for it.
At a planning committee meeting on Thursday councillors at Melton Borough Council discussed proposals for the solar farm on land east of Waltham Road, Freeby.
Previously the applicant, Downing Renewable Developments, said the development would produce up to 42 MW of renewable energy and could provide enough electricity to power about 10,000 homes.
Members of the planning committee said changes to the National Planning Policy Framework meant they now had their hands "tied behind their back" when it came to decisions about solar farms.
Under changes to the policy framework, published in August 2026, the government said "substantial weight should be given to benefits for energy security, economic development and net zero".
Planning officers from the council had recommended the plans be approved subject to a section 106 agreement, but five members of the planning committee gave the plans the green light "with reluctance", councillor Ian Atherton said.
The applicant says the project, which would be built on a site spanning 81 hectares (200.2 acres), would be decommissioned in approximately 42 years time.
'Ludicrous' situation
David Chubb, representing the Wymondham ward, said there had been "consistent opposition" to the development from local residents and highlighted concerns about the "industrialisation" of the "historic undisturbed landscape" which had "exceptional character".
Peter Barnett, from Freeby Parish Council, spoke at the meeting to raise the council's "continued objection" to the plans.
James Mason, who represents Bottesford and voted to approve the plans, said: "What we are doing as a council and what this government is doing is industrialising this whole corridor and I find that very distressing.
"But having read through the NPPF, I can find nothing that would defeat this and particularly if it went to appeal."
Allen Thwaites, representing the Melton Warwick ward, said the council was "tied so far with our hands behind our backs" on debates surrounding solar farms.
"The pressure is increasing to find reasons for refusal," he added. "There doesn't seem to be any chink of light in any door.
"I cannot find anything and we've discussed this endlessly for a reason to say no or either abstain."
Thwaites also raised the issue of "industrialisation" of the eastern side of Melton as applications have been submitted for solar farms in Brentingby and Burton Lazars in recent months.
Margaret Glancy, representing Melton Newport, said the committee had been given a "fait accompli" with the application because of policy framework rules and called the situation "ludicrous".
Ian Atherton, representing Melton Craven, said he was "concerned that this is not the right place" for the solar farm.
"It is with some regret that I am unable to find based on the constraints of the debate tonight and the rulings in the new NPPF, anything substantial that would stand up in court as a reason for rejection.
"I find I have no choice but to support the application."

title: How Poundland grew from Wolverhampton market to retail giant
text:
How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant
"When I told people what I wanted to do, open shops on the high street selling things for one pound, they said, 'how will you find products to sell for a pound, what about inflation, it will never work.'"
That is how Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, describes the genesis of the budget giant - which went on to employ thousands of people and see over a million customers a week - on his own website.
But now the West Midlands-based retailer is teetering on the edge, after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group.
Having spent time on his parents stall since the age of two Wolverhampton-born businessman Smith started out in the very same place - selling items for £1 from his own stall.
After a £50,000 loan from his parents he opened the first Poundland shop, in The Octagon Shopping Centre in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, on 13 December 1990.
That first day, with a range of 624 products, the store took more than £13,000 - "and Poundland was born," Smith said.
Smith and his wife, Tracy, now based in Shropshire, owned the company for 16 years.
In 2006, he decided the time had come and he sold his final shares in the business for £250m, but later said the sale felt it was "as though somebody had died".
But by 2025, the Walsall-based company was itself sold for just £1.
Its owner, Polish firm Pepco, confirmed it had sold the brand for a "nominal" sum to US investment firm Gordon Brothers.
At the time Poundland had more than 800 stores across the UK and Ireland and employed around 16,000 staff.
"I did pick up the phone when I heard it was for sale but I was a bit too late," Smith said after the sale.
Now, the retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
A protest was held outside the Poundland HQ on Thursday, Claire Sutcliffe - who has been at the company for nearly a decade - among those demonstrating.
Questioned about how she felt, the 49-year-old replied she was "very sad", adding: "Nine years is a lot working for Poundland and they've been really good to me as a Poundland family, really supportive."
Sutcliffe added that some had worked for the business for 20 years and "it's just very sad for us all".
Asked what her message was to owners Gordon Brothers, she replied: "Please just sell.
"Save our jobs, we've all got families to feed and it's... near Christmas."
Professor Sarah Montano, a retail expert from the University of Birmingham, said: "The real problem for Poundland is, when they first started it was really great because everything was £1, that was a really unique selling point for them.
"[Today] there's competitors which are offering very similar prices and for quite a lot of products they're offering them cheaper."
She added that some competitors had "really got their finger on the key trends".
In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".
"The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs," they said.
"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."
They also thanked "staff, suppliers and customers for their continued support".

title: Hope for stranded canal boats in Bath with tunnel repair plan
text:
Hope for stranded canal boats with tunnel repair plan
A temporary repair could allow stranded canal boats to move again after a road tunnel over the waterway was damaged during roadworks.
The damage happened at the 200-year-old tunnel on the Kennet and Avon Canal in Bath, beneath the A36 Beckford Road.
Bath and North East Somerset Council is proposing a "temporary shield" to let boats pass safely while a permanent repair is designed.
The Canal and River Trust said the design was being worked on and the canal section and towpath would "remain closed until further notice".
Contractors broke through the tunnel's brick roof on 9 October while carrying out roadworks for the council.
The closure has cut off the final mile (about 1.96km) of the canal from the rest of the network, leaving boaters unable to continue their journeys.
The timing has added to the problem, with boaters who usually spend the summer on the River Avon moving onto the canal to avoid flooding.
Boats are now crowding into the short stretch, with no way out except back onto the river.
The tunnel and towpath have been closed on safety grounds since the damage, while a one-lane closure remains in place on Beckford Road.
The road restrictions have caused long queues and prompted safety concerns.
Almost 1,000 people have signed a petition calling for nearby Sydney Road to be reopened to give drivers an alternative route. The road was turned into a liveable neighbourhood in 2024.
A Bath and North East Somerset Council spokesperson said: "Safety is our first priority and engineers are closely monitoring the bridge."
The council said the eastbound one-lane closure on Beckford Road would remain in place, along with the closure of the canal and adjacent towpath at the north end of Sydney Gardens.
The Canal and River Trust said it would provide another update when it had more information about the proposed temporary shield.

title: Thunderbirds-inspired house sells at auction for £375,000
text:
Thunderbirds-inspired house sells for £375,000
A house with an "extensive" network of tunnels, rooms and a railway more than 50ft (15m) underground has been sold at auction for £375,000.
The property in Long Lane, Tilehurst, was inspired by Tracy Island, the secret headquarters featured in 1960s TV series Thunderbirds.
Beginning more than two decades ago, the tunnels were the passion-project of civil engineer Tony Deane.
The site also features a garden, swimming pool, workshop and a model space rocket in the garden measuring at about 23ft (7m) tall.
There are now plans to convert the 2,500 sq ft (232.2 sq m) workshop, which spans three floors, into a three-bedroom house.
Richard Worrall, auctioneer and consultant at BTG Eddisons Property Auctions, said: "It represents a really unique opportunity for somebody to either develop it or to live there and enjoy it.
"To say it's a workshop is doing it down a little bit, it's constructed better than 95% of houses, to be honest."
West Berkshire Council also granted planning consent in December 2024 for a 5,000 sq ft (464.5 sq m) five-bedroom, two-storey house to be built on the site of the swimming pool.
Before the sale, Worrall said: "I think by its very nature it is going to attract a lot of interest from people who have got an idea of what they might want to use the tunnelling network for.
"Whether they be preppers, or people who've got sensitive material they want to keep below ground, it keeps a constant temperature down there and would make a fantastic wine cellar.
"The options are kind of endless."

Fire service celebrates 'fantastic' station reopening
Residents have been invited to celebrate the reopening of a town's fire station.

Quin added: "We can't wait to welcome people to the new Reigate fire station and celebrate this milestone with them.

title: Extra police on Halloween and Bonfire Night in Leeds and Bradford
text:
Extra police out for Halloween and Bonfire Night
Extra police will be on the streets of West Yorkshire for Halloween and Bonfire Night, the county's force has said.
A spokesperson said the two dates, 31 October and 5 November, were among the busiest times of the years for officers and urged those out and about to be considerate.
In other years, the force has had to deal with dozens of motorcycles being used dangerously in a group "ride-out", serious disorder which saw riot police being supported by the force helicopter and also helping fire crews when they have been attacked.
The force also said anyone using Halloween and Bonfire Night as an "excuse for disorder" would be prosecuted.
A spokesperson urged trick-or-treaters to be mindful of those who do not want people knocking on their doors and said it was also providing downloadable signs to put off callers.
Ch Supt Sareth Humpage said: "Halloween isn't an enjoyable time for everyone as we recognise that things that might seem like harmless fun to some can cause a lot of anxiety, stress and worry for some people.
"I would ask that parents keep an eye on their children out trick or treating and encourage them to only visit the homes of friends and neighbours, rather than strangers."
West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service (WYFRS) also urged residents to use LED candles instead of real ones to prevent fires.
District Commander Dale Gardiner said: "Candles can help create a Halloween atmosphere, but it's important to use them safely."
He added: "If you do use real candles, keep them well away from curtains, Halloween decorations, and any other flammable materials, and never leave them unattended and always make sure candles are fully extinguished before you leave the house or go to bed."

title: Leicester mayor hopeful for festive event despite rink doubt
text:
Mayor hopeful for festive event despite rink doubt
Leicester's mayor has said he is "determined" to ensure a festive attraction takes place in Jubilee Square this year despite uncertainty over the future of the city's Christmas ice rink.
The annual ice rink is in doubt after the rink's previous operator pulled out of this year's event amid an ongoing dispute with Leicester City Council.
Sir Peter Soulsby said an ongoing court case meant there was a limit to what he could say publicly.
However, he told the BBC another company could potentially be found to run an ice rink.
"It may even be possible to find a way of doing this, to have a different operator doing an ice rink," he said.
The ice rink has been a festive feature of Jubilee Square since shortly after the public space opened.
Soulsby said the attraction, along with the Christmas big wheel, had "worked incredibly well" and helped establish Jubilee Square as a key venue for city centre events.
"It may be that we have to do something different this year," he said.
"Continuing to make things happen, particularly over the Christmas period in the city centre, is something that I'm absolutely determined to do."
He said future festive attractions could also make use of Leicester's revamped market place.
"There's an exciting future, it's a bit of a problem at the moment, but we're determined to make something happen, if not an ice rink," he said.
A Leicester City Council spokesperson said the authority was "currently looking at other options available" and hoped to provide an update soon.

title: Post Office suspends sending goods to the EU
text:
Post Office suspends sending goods to the EU
The Isle of Man Post Office has stopped accepting goods for delivery to European Union countries until further notice.
It said third-party systems used to process international parcels were being updated ahead of changes to EU customs requirements, but were not yet ready.
Documents can still be sent to EU addresses, and goods can still be posted to the rest of the world, including the USA.
The Post Office said it had been preparing for the changes, but "an unexpected change in approach by one of our UK partners" meant further work was needed.
The suspension covers goods sent from Post Office counters and through its online postage, click & dispatch and franking services.
The Post Office said it was working with its suppliers to fix the problem and would give a further update when a solution was available.
Asked when the service would resume, the Post Office said it would be "as soon as possible but we are dependent on one of our UK partners for that".
It thanked customers "for your patience while we work to restore EU goods services".

title: Vintage Bristol: Photographs show history of city's changes
text:
Bristol then and now: Trams, barges and rugby
In the second of our interactive galleries showing how Bristol has changed over the years we head to the edge of what is now Castle Park and then up to the other side of the centre to see how the roads looked with trams on them.
Finally we take a trip back to the home of Bristol Rugby. Not the Memorial Stadium, but nearby.
Swipe left and right to reveal how each location has changed over the decades.
There remains much debate about a possible light rail or tram system returning to Bristol. Well as this picture from June 1935 shows, it is possible to have a tram network despite the many hills of Bristol.
In 1941 the trams stopped running. Now it's just cars and other vehicle trundling up Upper Maudlin Street, where these pictures were taken.
As war in Europe was looming once again, a photographer snapped this picture of a barge being towed to Bristol Docks on 29 July, 1939, about to go under Bristol Bridge.
That section of waterway looks very different now, with modern bars and restaurants on Finzel's Reach facing across to Castle Park, and even a new pedestrian crossing – just out of shot.
It's long been the home of Gloucestershire County Cricket Club, but the stadium off Nevil Road once hosted rugby, not cricket. The ground was Bristol Rugby's home from the club's foundation right up to the start of the First World War.
In this image the players were taking on a New Zealand side in 1905. The Memorial Stadium, the rugby club's home for nearly a century, was not opened until 1921.
The groundstaff at the cricket club might not be too pleased if anyone tried having a scrum on their playing surface these days.

title: Sompting and Rye farms pumpkin crop exceeds growers' expectations
text:
Pumpkin crop exceeds growers' expectations
Pumpkin growers in Sussex say they have produced a strong Halloween harvest despite the UK's hottest summer on record.
Farms in Sompting near Lancing and Rye are welcoming visitors picking pumpkins in the run-up to Halloween.
At Sompting Pumpkins, tenant farmer Caroline Harriott said growers had been concerned repeated heatwaves would affect the crop.
She said the farm's pumpkins had "exceeded all our expectations" despite the challenging growing conditions.
Harriott said 70,000 seeds were planted in the first week of June and were left to grow in a field which "followed cattle and sheep grazing it".
They "naturally fed the soil with their manure", she explained, adding that the crop included 20 different varieties of pumpkin.
At Tibbs Farm near Rye, partner Phil Wheeler said growers also took steps to help the crop cope with the dry weather.
He said the pumpkins were planted on south-facing land which had not previously been ploughed.
Wheeler said avoiding weeds was an important factor in achieving a strong crop.
He said rain during the first two weeks after planting around 35,000 seeds also helped the pumpkins establish.
Although the pumpkins did not grow as large as in some years, Wheeler said most ripened successfully.
"It was good because we don't always get that," he said. "They weren't big but they were ripened."

title: Mr Potato Head returns to Belper after 'spud-batical'
text:
Mr Potato Head returns to town after 'spud-batical'
He may have been away on a "spud-batical", but a giant Mr Potato Head statue has now returned to a market town in Derbyshire after repairs and a lick of paint.
The 7ft (2.1m) spud was gifted in 2000 by Belper's US twin town of Pawtucket, Rhode Island, the birthplace of the Hasbro toy.
Joshua Grimshaw, from Belper Town Council, said it was "great to have him back" and admitted it was a shame he was in hiding during the release of Toy Story 5 in June.
"I wish we could have tied it all in together," he added. "The stars didn't align, unfortunately, so we were stuck with the timing we had."
"This is just the beginning of his story. We're hoping he can do a tour around Belper and, who knows, he might have some outfits coming out over the next few seasons," he added.
In 2000, there were 48 Mr Potato Head statues made, designed to boost tourism in Rhode Island, and one was shipped across the Atlantic to Derbyshire.
It was decorated in a grey suit and hat to resemble William Blackstone, one of the first English settlers in Rhode Island in 1635.
"People immediately either loved him or they hated him," Belper historian Adrian Farmer said.
Mr Potato Head was positioned outside the town's McDonald's restaurant, then relocated to numerous spaces across Belper, including being chained to the Safeway supermarket in 2002.
On 1 April that year, students posing as the "Potato Liberation Army" moved the Toy Story character into an island in the middle of the road and wrapped him in tinfoil in an April Fools' "spud-nap" stunt.
"That was Mr Potato Head's greatest moment, he made front page of the Belper News that week," said Farmer, former editor of the local paper.
The larger-than-life toy version underwent a decorative makeover in 2015 by a local youth group, painting him in the colours of the recognisable Hasbro toy.
In June, his hand, arm and hat were found to be broken, which the town council said posed a risk of injury to the public and about £1,200 was paid for him to be restored.
"He's looking great again," said Farmer. "We've got our Mr Potato Head back. We couldn't be happier."
Families gathered in the courtyard of the De Bradelei Mill Shopping Village to welcome back the much-loved potato.
"I've been really missing Mr Potato Head and I'm so glad that he's back," said nine-year-old Charlotte.
"He looks like he is almost real, like a big giant version of Mr Potato Head from Toy Story," she added.
"He's unique and a big part of Belper," said 10-year-old Heidi.
"It's nice to have him back and it's nice to see everyone enjoying him," said Anaiya, who is eight.
"We're hoping he'll be very comfortable where he is, loved and looked after," said Belper mayor Katie Harris, who is confident the character will be a boost to local businesses.
"It's a bit different - nobody else has got a potato head," she added.
