title: Sudden closure of Leweston School 'outrageous', MP says
text:
Sudden school closure 'outrageous', MP says
An MP has said he is "shocked and appalled" by the sudden closure of a 135-year-old private school during half term.
Leweston School, near Sherborne, Dorset, announced on its website on Tuesday that it would "not reopen after half term, and will close".
In a letter to staff, Concept Education, whose subsidiary bought the school in December 2025, said wages owed in October would not be paid.
Edward Morello, MP for West Dorset, said staff were given no warning and nearly 600 children had been left without school places.
The Catholic day and boarding school has a 46-acre campus with facilities including an indoor heated swimming pool, a theatre and a purpose-built equestrian centre.
Its alumni include actress Dame Kristin Scott Thomas and Baroness Dido Harding, who headed the NHS test and trace programme during the pandemic.
The school's former head of physics, Robert Nejako, said: "I literally got an email with a screen cap [capture] of a letter that wasn't even on letterhead.
"It was poorly written, misspelled, all of it. Shambles doesn't begin to describe what this was."
Parent Stuart Hamon said the news came as a "complete shock", in an email that was sent to parents 30 minutes after staff were told.
"People thought that it was a joke initially," he said.
"Then the realisation started to set in that actually this was a real event so people were shocked, horrified."
Another parent, Zara, said she had lost two years of a midwife's salary in upfront school fees.
A third, Dr Shobhana Marathe, said: "All of the Leweston community is really struggling – we are just trying to figure out ways a miracle happens and we can keep the school open."
The letter from Concept Education chief executive Hugh Dickinson told staff: "The school cannot pay the salaries due on Friday 30 October... I am very sorry."
It blamed a "cash shortfall caused by falling pupil numbers".
The letter also cited pressures including the introduction of VAT on school fees, the loss of business rates relief, higher employment costs and a decline in boarding demand.
Amy Brinsden, from the National Education Union, said: "Staff are looking for answers.
"Less than a year ago, they were being told that a new partnership with Concept Education and the Catholic Schools' Trust would help secure the school's future.
"That leaves some very obvious questions about what changed, when concerns first emerged, and whether everything that could have been done to avoid this outcome was actually done."
Morello said: "The regulators, the authorities, Dorset Council weren't informed so nobody could prepare, no-one could plan.
"It really is just an outrageous way for Concept Education to act."
The Liberal Democrat said he had heard of one family who had paid four years of school fees in advance.
Simon Hoare, Conservative MP for North Dorset, posted on Facebook: "I am increasingly concerned to hear that prepaid fees will not be refunded and that staff have not been paid."
Dorset Council said it was "working urgently" to support children, young people and families affected by the closure.
Paul Dempsey, the council's executive director for children's services, said: "We know this news has come as a significant shock for many children, young people, families and staff connected to Leweston School.
"Our immediate focus is on supporting those affected and helping families understand the options available to them.
"Teams across the council are working closely with schools, early years providers and other partners to help children continue their education and childcare arrangements with as little disruption as possible."
Dempsey encouraged anyone who needed support to get in touch with the council's teams.
Concept Education has been approached for comment.
description: Leweston School gave no warning of Tuesday's shock announcement, Edward Morello MP says.

title: Worthing Football Club backs suicide prevention charity Olly's Future
text:
Charity partnership helping football fans open up
Linking up with a suicide prevention charity has helped Worthing Football Club fans open up about their mental health, its supporters' association has said.
This season the club has partnered with Olly's Future, founded by Ann Feloy in 2020 after son Olly Hare, who grew up in Worthing, died by suicide at the age of 22.
Feloy believes that "everyone involved in football can get behind this message of looking out for someone they might be worried about".
Natalie Lunn, secretary for the supporters' association, said "people have come up and said things to us that wouldn't have happened if we hadn't been supporting this charity".
Olly Hare died at home on February 14, 2017, just two days before his 23rd birthday.
An accomplished linguist and high-achieving student, Feloy said a combination of factors led to her son becoming "a bit lost" before spiralling into depression "very suddenly".
Since its creation, Olly's Future has provided suicide prevention training to more than 12,000 people, said the charity.
Feloy said: "To think that Worthing Football Club knows about Oliver, and is raising money for our charity, it's phenomenal."
The profits from the 50/50 draw at this weekend's game versus Sutton United will go to the charity.
Nathan Bowen, the club's sporting director, said working with Olly's Future "really resonates with us".
"We see ourselves as a bit of a community hub, so we like to provide an environment hopefully where people can come and be open, and share any issues that they have," he said.
Lunn said the decision to support a suicide prevention charity, particularly one which is "more local", was made with fans in mind.
She said: "We have a predominantly male fanbase, and it is an at-risk group, a hard to reach group, especially men of a certain age that maybe are a little bit socially isolated."
According to the Campaign Against Living Miserably, suicide is currently the leading cause of death in men under the age of 50 across the UK.
Lunn said the partnership had "been really helpful for people to talk about their experiences".
- If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.
Acknowledging the "stigma" associated with opening up, particularly for men in a competitive environment, goalkeeper Harrison Foulkes said there was support within this "tight-knit group".
"If anyone did have any sort of issues, they would be able to speak about it, maybe not to everyone, but there's probably at least one person at the club that they can speak to," he said. "I know that's definitely the case for me."
Flying high in fifth place in the National League, Feloy has no doubt that Olly would relish this period of success for the Rebels.
She said: "He'd have been here watching, so it's a great loss...but I'm sure he's delighted, I'm sure he's looking on. He'll be with us in spirit."

title: World Cup dream win for Derby footballer with cerebral palsy
text:
World Cup dream win for cerebral palsy footballer
Freddie Lamb always dreamed of winning a World Cup.
On Saturday, he saw that happen when the England squad won the Cerebral Palsy World Cup in the US.
The Para Lions, as they are known, beat the hosts the US 2-1 in extra time in Atlanta to win the trophy for the first time.
Lamb, one of the squad's goalkeepers, who lives in Derby, said: "It's been a whirlwind last month, last couple of months, so all the training over the last 15 years made it work."
According to the NHS, cerebral palsy, is the name for a group of lifelong conditions that affect movement and coordination caused by a brain condition before, during or soon after birth.
Lamb, who grew up in Melbourne in Derbyshire, said the Cerebral Palsy World Cup was his first senior tournament and he made his debut in a game against Ireland.
"It's been an absolute amazing opportunity, an amazing time over there."
He added: "I think the last two-and-a-half weeks have shown that nothing is impossible and if you want to achieve something and you put your mind to it, you can achieve it."
The 25-year-old, who said he played grassroots football for the Melbourne Dynamos, said it was "life-changing" to play in a squad of players with cerebral palsy and it had "a brought everyone together".
Lamb said this was also the case locally as he played for a cerebral palsy team at Burton Albion Community Trust.
Talking about the condition, Lamb, who was born at 24 weeks old, said: "For me, it affects my lower legs.
"Everyone is different - it generally affects your balance, your coordination and stability, but for me, it's both my legs.
"For others, it's one side and it's more mild - there's no cure for it at all but physio and treatments do help."
He added: "My brain registers it all and what I want to do, it's just my body sometimes can't do it, to put it in the simplest terms.
"So for me, stopping over the short, quick distances is what I struggle with, to then get set to generate the power, to then make the saves."
During the final of the World Cup, where Lamb was on the bench, the hosts had taken a late lead in Atlanta from a corner with three minutes left of normal time, before England responded with a late equaliser in added time.
Early in extra time, David Porcher, who had come on as a substitute, fired home the winner - crowning England as champions for the first time in their history.
Porcher told the BBC the win was "unbelievable".
Lamb added: "For us as players, it's more a disbelief of what we've achieved and I don't think it's quite set in for everyone yet."

title: Kent pensioner pays £3k for cataract surgery to avoid NHS wait
text:
Pensioner pays £3k to avoid NHS eye surgery wait
A pensioner says he plans to pay nearly £3,000 for private cataract surgery after being told he faces a minimum 16-week NHS wait.
Duncan Robertson, 70, from Kent, said he was "desperate" for the treatment as he feared delays would affect his independence and quality of life.
He said the situation created a "two-tier system" in which people who can afford private treatment are seen sooner.
NHS Kent and Medway said routine cataract patients across the area could expect surgery no sooner than 16 weeks after referral and that those with the greatest clinical need continued to be prioritised.
Robertson, from near Maidstone, said he was referred by his optician on 9 October and received confirmation from the NHS five days later.
He said he was then told routine cataract surgery would not take place for at least 16 weeks.
"It's an absolute disaster," he said.
"If I wanted the surgery sooner, I would have to pay for it myself but I'm retired and disposable income is limited."
Robertson, who has not yet had the surgery, said his deteriorating eyesight had affected his ability to drive safely.
"Being able to drive means my wife and I can go about our daily business," he said.
"I also help a friend, who is blind, to run errands."
He said the NHS should take greater account of the impact delays have on patients' lives, particularly those who could not afford private surgery.
NHS Kent and Medway said cataract services had expanded significantly but waiting times had become inconsistent.
The organisation said a more consistent approach would provide fairer access to planned care while ensuring those needing surgery most urgently were treated first.
A spokesperson said: "We have a responsibility to use NHS funding as fairly and effectively as possible for the two million people we serve."
The organisation said 70% of patients were seen within 18 weeks of referral in July 2025, compared with 65% a year earlier.
'Extremely concerning'
Robert Cooper, director of strategic engagement at the Royal Institute of Blind People (RNIB), said long waits for cataract surgery were "extremely concerning" for patients.
"Some NHS boards are imposing a minimum 14-week wait," he said.
"People become anxious, particularly those with cataracts, as their sight deteriorates over time and it can affect their quality of life."
He said the charity provides support services, including liaison officers in hospital trusts, for patients.
He added there was no clear guidance on "acceptable" waiting times for cataract treatment and called for better support for patients.
"It's about prioritising patients and identifying who should receive timely care, support and surgery," he said.

title: Work to cut sewage spills nears completion in Sheffield
text:
Work to cut sewage spills nears completion
A giant underground tank designed to cut sewage spills into a local watercourse is taking shape as a major infrastructure project reaches a key milestone.
Yorkshire Water said work beneath the Brushes allotment site on Vickers Road in Sheffield, was about two-thirds finished and remained on track for completion in summer 2027.
The £3.2m scheme sparked concern in January when a community charity feared it could struggle to survive after being forced to leave the site while construction took place.
Yorkshire Water said it had worked with Sheffield City Council to relocate allotment tenants where possible, while storing equipment for others until the site could be handed back.
In January the Friends of Firth Park Community Allotments warned its future was uncertain after Yorkshire Water announced plans to build a storm overflow storage tank on the allotment occupied by the charity.
The charity, which has worked from the site for about 20 years, raised concerns over compensation, funding and the impact of an 18-month break in its activities.
The tank, which measures 15m (49ft) in diameter and extends 17m (56ft) below ground, will be capable of holding 1.5 million litres of wastewater and rainfall during periods of heavy flows.
Yorkshire Water said the scheme would reduce discharges into Firth Park stream by 90% and stop sewage water from flooding homes in the area.
Head of Alliance Delivery, Jon Stokes, said: "This tank will take the rain that ends up in our sewers so that we can then return it to our sewage treatment works and clean it before discharging it safely back into the environment."
Once construction is complete, Yorkshire Water said the allotments would be reinstated, with three previously unusable plots upgraded and brought back into use.
"We'll return this site to how it was when we found it and we'll make it a little bit better as well," Stokes said.
The charity's allotment coordinator, Saskia Peet, said the group had adapted after being displaced from the site by continuing projects in schools and other community growing spaces, helping to safeguard funding and create new opportunities for local families.
While she accepted the work to reduce sewage flooding "needed to be done", Peet said she remained concerned about the loss of mature fruit trees, established growing areas and uncertainty over compensation and restoration.
"It's going to take us five to 10 years to get those [trees] back to how they were," she said.
Despite the concerns, she said the group hoped the redeveloped site could attract more users and provide a fresh start for the community allotment.
"We're hoping this could be a good news story for everyone," she said.
The project is part of 470 across the county and forms part of Yorkshire Water's £1.5bn programme to reduce storm overflows across the region by 2030.
Yorkshire Water said it would work through any outstanding compensation claims.

title: Community raises thousands for Portland farm hit by Storm Austen
text:
Community raises thousands for storm-hit family farm
The co-owner of a storm-hit farm says the community's response to a fundraiser has been "completely overwhelming".
The pony shelter, play area and hutches at Porter's Farm in Portland, Dorset, were damaged by Storm Austen, which brought gusts of 75mph to the island, last Friday.
A fundraiser set up by a family friend has raised more than £5,000, which will be used to replace the pony shelter and build a new play area.
Lee Porter, who runs the farm with his wife, Charlotte, said: "We never dreamt that we would get anywhere near the amount that's raised.
"We're completely overwhelmed and humbled by the generosity."
The farm, which offers Highland Cow meet and greets and has a cafe, has been open for about four months.
Charlotte and Lee work full time alongside running it.
Lee said the couple "poured our absolute blood sweat tears, all of our savings, everything" into the farm to get it open.
"We knew it was going to be really, really tough this winter and then obviously [the storm] happened and we just thought, God, what are we going to do?
"There's nothing really that we could do. You've just got to let the storm obviously pass by and then reassess and see what we can do."
Porter said the main damage was to the shelter that houses four miniature Shetland ponies, which he estimated would cost about £2,000 to repair.
"I haven't actually punched any figures yet but the price of timber at the minute is through the roof," he said.
The rest of the money raised will go towards building a new children's play area.
The previous play area was temporary and the couple had already planned to replace it next year with a purpose-built play area, securely fixed into the ground.
Porter said the money raised will give them "a good start on it".
Porter said the couple had been "absolutely blown away" by the support.
"I think within 48 hours it was up to nearly four thousand pounds," he said.
"It was unbelievable - the first day, the first couple of hours, someone donated a thousand pounds.
"We don't know this guy, he's a customer of ours, he's been up here, his wife loves the Highland cows, but to donate a thousand pounds is something else really."

title: Smokers offered free lung cancer screening pilot in West Kent
text:
Smokers offered free lung cancer screening
Smokers and ex-smokers in parts of Kent are being invited to take part in a free lung screening pilot scheme.
Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS Trust is encouraging those aged between 55 and 74 to attend, with checks being offered at the Royal Victoria Shopping Centre on Friday.
The aim of the service, in Tunbridge Wells, Tonbridge and surrounding areas, is to save lives by catching cancer early, the trust said.
Dr Stefano Santini, clinical director for the lung cancer screening programme for the trust, said: "Lung cancer is often difficult to detect early, and many people do not realise anything is wrong until the disease is more advanced. That's why this programme is so important."
NHS Kent and Medway Cancer Alliance is responsible for the expansion of the programme across Kent and Medway.
Clinical lead Dr Jonathan Bryant said: "Lung cancer is one of the most common and serious types of cancer, so it's very important that people attend their lung cancer screening appointment.
"The earlier the diagnosis, the more treatment options there are."
From now, patients in West Kent will be screened at the Fordcombe site.
The scheme started in November 2022 and has been rolled out so far across the south Kent coast, Canterbury, Whitstable, Faversham and Herne Bay.
It is also in place in Dartford, with Medway and Swale to follow by the beginning of 2028.
Since the targeted lung health check programme launched, now called the lung cancer screening programme, more than 120 lung cancers have been diagnosed so far in East Kent - with the vast majority at stages one or two.
Ken Boorman, from Dymchurch, got invited for a lung health check in May 2024 and lung cancer was detected in August 2025 at an early stage.
He said: "I would 100% recommend people to go for their checks, it saved my life."
People diagnosed with lung cancer at the earliest stages are nearly 13 times more likely to survive for five years than those whose cancer is caught late, according to NHS England.
Lung cancer is the third most common type of cancer in the UK and about 26,000 people die from the disease every year. Seven out of 10 cases of lung cancer are caused by smoking.

title: Community asset application for Wighill pub rejected
text:
Community asset application for pub rejected
A bid to protect a village's only pub has been rejected but the venue's new landlord said it had "a bright future anyway".
Wighill Parish Council had applied for The White Swan in Wighill, near Tadcaster, to be registered as an asset of community value, which would give villagers an opportunity to bid for the property if it was put up for sale.
However, a council assessment concluded that while the pub had hosted numerous community events there was not enough evidence to demonstrate significant community use.
The pub closed in June following the retirement of its former publicans and reopened earlier this month under new ownership.
Landlord Tom Brown said they had taken on a long lease to secure the pub's future.
"We've got a good chef in the kitchen, letting bedrooms and some big plans for the place," said Brown.
"We already run several pubs in York, but this is going to be our big site. The pub is here to stay and it's definitely not being turned into housing."
In its application in September, the parish council had described the pub as a vital social hub, pointing out that the village has no community centre, village hall or school.
According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, the application listed 27 activities and events associated with the pub, including Christmas celebrations, bonfire nights, beer festivals, quiz nights, book clubs, film clubs, knitting groups, parish council meetings and elections.
However, council officers said that while some of the activities had demonstrated community involvement, about half were commonly associated with running a traditional rural pub.
The report added that no community interest group or similar organisation had been established with an expressed interest in acquiring or operating the pub.

title: Hempstead couple create Halloween display with handmade props
text:
Halloween lovers build spooky garden graveyard
A couple have created a spooky Halloween scene outside their home using handmade decorations after spending about two months building the attraction.
Nico Slatter and Ashleigh Feveyear have transformed their garden in Hempstead, near Gillingham, with props including gravestones, sound effects, smoke and animated figures.
The graveyard they have created in Birch Grove uses headstones that were made out of polystyrene by Nico, and then painted by Ashleigh.
Ashleigh said: "It was fun. I mean, it gave us something to do over two months, basically, and we did it because we just really enjoy creating stuff and we like spooky and we like Halloween. So it just all kind of made sense."
Ashleigh said the spooky scene had been popular with visitors adding: "People have been coming with their children and taking photos, and their dogs as well, so it's been fun seeing everyone enjoy it."
She said Nico cut out the headstones.
Ashleigh then painted them and filled in the letters in dark grey.
She said: "I would look at inspirations online of real gravestones and just pick out parts of them that I really liked."
The couple, who have posted pictures on Facebook, have said people are welcome to walk through the graveyard, and all the sound and light effects will be turned on each night up to Halloween.
"I'm very excited for people to come and see our display," Ashleigh said, adding that they both just wanted to people to enjoy it with them.
She said: "We come out here most nights and just experience the front garden, so we're looking forward to people seeing it and feeling it too."

title: 'A stroke aged 43 changed my sense of who I was,' says Oxford man
text:
'A stroke aged 43 changed my sense of who I was'
"The stroke didn't just change my body. It changed my mind, my confidence, my sense of who I was."
Darren Dickenson from Headington, in Oxford, had just become a granddad in October 2024 when, at the age of 43, he suffered a stroke while at home.
He was forced to undergo life-saving emergency surgery, before complications followed - leading to a lengthy recovery.
Dickenson and his wife Sophie are now sharing their story as part of a new campaign by The Stroke Association called Survival is Not Enough.
"I was at work, it was a normal day and he had come home from a night shift, ready to get the children ready," Sophie said.
"My daughter said, around about 10 o'clock, he was spinning in the kitchen with very split speech and acting very strange."
Moments later, Darren collapsed after managing to get himself upstairs. Sophie later found out this had been because he "felt he was gonna die in front of the children and he didn't wanna scare them".
His daughter, then aged 16, instantly called an ambulance, which Sophie said "definitely" saved his life.
"He wouldn't be here today if it wasn't for her," she said.
The stroke had come entirely out of the blue for a healthy and active man who worked five nights a week at a local supermarket.
Darren was rushed to hospital, where initial thoughts that the incident could have been related to meningitis were shelved after a blood clot was found on the 43-year-old's brain.
He had suffered a rare basal ganglia stroke with brainstem involvement.
"Life changes in just a second," Sophie said.
"Your life is just shattered just by the word stroke - when you actually see the effects of it, the word is shattering."
Return and rehab
Darren spent nine weeks in hospital recovering from the stroke and its complications, which at times left his life hanging in the balance.
He returned home to be cared for after declining a place in a long-term rehabilitation centre because "he just wanted to get home to his young family".
But him being back at home was not easy, Sophie said, with her husband unable to walk unaided or verbally communicate.
"We were speaking through the Jabber, which is a text-type computer to enable communications," she said.
"He learnt how to talk with the children and how to be at home again."
Just over two years on from his stroke, Darren now lives with attention, memory and cognitive difficulties, can only walk short distances and still struggles to speak.
He is now looking to set up a stroke survivors group for people around his age, after he found that meeting others with similar experiences had been "the first time I felt truly understood" during his recovery.
"When you see what you need to pull through for, then you pull through, and he's found his inner strength from the children," Sophie said.
"It's a big change for the whole family, and the person from going from the breadwinner to the person that then needs help is a huge emotional rollercoaster.
"But there is hope and light at the end of the tunnel."
description: Darren Dickenson has spent the past two years recovering after he suffered a stroke when he was 43.

title: Petition to offer ADHD education in schools reaches 10,000 signatures
text:
ADHD education petition reaches 10,000 signatures
A petition to make ADHD education in schools mandatory has reached 10,000 signatures in just two weeks.
Ryan Swain, from Malton, launched the campaign in a bid to reduce the stigma around neurodiversity and encourage earlier support.
The 36-year-old said he grew up with undiagnosed ADHD and Tourette's syndrome and was permanently excluded from mainstream education when he was 14 years old.
He believes that earlier understanding and appropriate support could have made a big difference to his childhood.
ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and is a condition that can affect how a person focuses.
According to the NHS, symptoms of ADHD in children and young people can include inattention, high energy levels and difficulty controlling impulses.
Swain's parliamentary petition calls for age-appropriate teaching that helps pupils, staff and parents recognise and understand neurodivergent differences.
He said: "When I was at school, I was labelled naughty, disruptive and difficult. Nobody explained ADHD to me.
"Nobody helped me understand why I struggled with things that other children seemed to manage.
"I was excluded from mainstream education at 14. It took years for me to understand myself."
As his petition has now reached 10,000 signatures, the government must issue a formal written response.
"Reaching 10,000 signatures is incredibly emotional because this campaign has never been about me," Swain said.
"It's about every child who feels misunderstood, every parent fighting to be heard and every teacher who wants to help but hasn't been given the knowledge or resources."
He added: "We teach young people about physical health, relationships, drugs and alcohol.
"Why shouldn't they receive age-appropriate education about ADHD, autism and other forms of neurodivergence?"
His next aim is to reach 100,000 signatures, which would see the petition considered by the House of Commons Petitions Committee for debate in Parliament.
Swain travels across the country to deliver free ADHD awareness talks to schools, colleges, alternative provision settings and community organisations.
During ADHD Awareness Month in October, he made more than 25 educational visits as part of his You, Me & ADHD initiative.
The BBC has contacted the Department for Education for comment.

title: Oxford-born writer's 'unknown' spy thriller shortlisted for Waterstones award
text:
'Unknown' spy thriller shortlisted for annual award
A best-selling author has described the spy in his latest book as "unlike any I have come across before".
Oxford-born multimillion-selling writer and historian Ben Macintyre says he used never-before-seen material to craft the Cold War thriller Redwood - the "unknown spy" whose work "possibly averted nuclear Armageddon".
It has made the 2026 Waterstones shortlist for Book of the Year, which highlights the books that booksellers have most enjoyed recommending to readers.
Even though Macintyre has written extensively about espionage, including bestseller Operation Mincemeat, he says he "had not realised just how important Redwood was" before writing the book.
"Redwood was a Russian intelligence officer based in Iran who went over to the other side and he agreed to spy for Britain for MI6," he said.
The man behind the codename is Vladimir Kuzichkin, who Macintyre says had a "very private problem".
The author said it was a sexual secret, which if revealed, would have turned his life upside-down, so in his desperation, the agent saw the only solution in the MI6, in return for the KGB's secrets.
"It has been completely covered up - that one person's personal trauma that changed the world in very, very significant ways.
"He revealed the existence of a plot on the part of the Soviet Union to take over Iran to initially have the Communist Party mount a coup backed by the KGB and then to have the Red Army move in to support it," the author added.
"If that had happened then the US would undoubtedly have responded with nuclear weapons because they didn't have enough weapons and enough troops in theatre to deal with it."
But he says that also reinforced the Iranian regime, making it also "partly a story about unintended consequences".
American author John Grisham says that given the current war in Iran, Macintyre's latest book "is certainly his most timely".
Macintyre agrees the story has "very strong modern resonances".
"Some of my main characters in this book were killed in the first Israeli air strike last February - the situation that we face in the Middle East would be very different without this unknown double agent at the centre of it."
Macintyre says he grew up "in a house in north Oxford that was suffused with history".
"I went to Cambridge, as did my siblings - Cambridge is also a nest of spies, in fact probably more so than Oxford."
He says in the spy world truth is "always" stranger than fiction.
"Particularly with this story because it is so unlikely and his motivation for doing what he did is so different from any other spy I've ever come across.
"This is one of those cases that if you wrote it up as a novel, no one would believe you."
Macintyre says it is "a delight" to see his book shortlisted.
The winner will be announced on 26 November.
description: Ben Macintyre speaks of crafting spy thriller Redwood - a true story that is stranger than fiction.

title: Syrians grow frustrated as soaring living costs threaten recovery
text:
Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery
Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago.
Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".
The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war.
Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.
There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.
From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country. "We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".
Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.
In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family. "We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.
Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some.
The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising.
"We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."
As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.
Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said.
The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year. Marwan told me how he made ends meet. "Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".
There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts. Syria has also not been immune to the impact of the US-Iran war. The government said the fuel increase that led to the protests was, in part, due to the pressure on energy markets because of the conflict.
I met another pensioner, Nabil al-Remhein, who is 63. None of his four adult children could find work. "We're now having only one meal a day. It's tragic," he said. His face looked tired. "It isn't only me. It's the entire population. We're all hungry... We're suffocating under rising costs."
Nabil took me to his house, in a poor area of narrow alleys and modest buildings. There, I met his wife. She was doing her chores in the dark. "I'm afraid of the electricity bill," Nabil said. "We've cut back on lighting up the house and we [also] turn off the fridge for about five hours a day". Still, their latest bill was about a third of the family's income. He has not paid it.
Dr Haid Haid, a Syrian columnist and consulting fellow at the London-based think tank Chatham House, said a "significant portion of the population" was worse off than before Assad's fall. The economic crisis, he told me, was "one of the most dangerous issues" for the government, and that some of it was of its own making.
"Part of [the crisis] is related to the lack of [financial] resources and the legacy left by the former regime," he said. "But it's also the direct impact of the new policies that are moving [Syria] towards a liberal and free-market sort of economy, which don't take into account the impact on people".
A spokesman for the Syrian economy and industry ministry told me no-one was available for an interview.
Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains. International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable.
And the president continues to consolidate his power and, earlier this year, retook the resource-rich north-east from a Kurdish-led militia. (The Druze still control areas in the south, where they want to create an autonomous state; Israel occupies parts of the south-west.)
But real economic recovery is yet to happen. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins after a war that killed half a million people and displaced half of the population. Unable to afford rent, many families live in partially destroyed buildings. The World Bank says reconstruction costs are estimated at $216bn and, without foreign help and investment, it will be impossible for Syrians to rebuild.
Samir Aita, a Syrian economist who heads the Circle of Arab Economists, a Paris-based independent think-tank, said the crisis was a "combination of policies with the [government] not managing expectations and creating unrealistic hopes". When I asked him about how he felt about the future, he said: "It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos."
Exhausted after years of conflict, Syrians, left with almost no choice, remain hopeful. Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, told me: "They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."
Additional reporting by Lana Antaki, Samantha Granville and Neha Sharma
description: End of subsidies and rising prices drive discontent, testing support for Ahmed al-Sharaa's government.

title: Former Traitors star from Southampton reviews season before final
text:
Former Traitors star reviews season before final
With millions poised to watch the second Celebrity Traitors final tonight former star Joe Scott looks back on how the series has played out so far.
The series three Faithful and Southampton teacher spoke to BBC Radio Solent's Katie Martin about his highlights and how it compared to last year's season.
He also shared his views on who the winner could be, as well as little things that could give away a contestant's position.
"What a series it's been," he said. "I can't see how the Faithfuls can win, but you never know with this game."
He said a series highlights was the first banishment of a Traitor.
"Obviously Richard [E Grant] helped them with that massive slip up," he said.
"I thought Maya [Jama] and James [Acaster] are just going to keep recruiting people to throw under the bus and that was going to be the gameplan.
"But they decided not to do that, and I thought 'interesting'."
Scott said he found Jama to have been "the best Traitor" so far in the series.
"I do think she's the most at risk," he said. "I think they all know she's a very switched on person so I think people might, as it gets to the very end, start questioning her over the other two."
The teacher also pointed out the contrast in her demeanour with previous season winner and Traitor Alan Carr.
"He was amazing. It's just Alan being Alan, so I think they sort of believed it," he said.
"I think they think when people are more nervous, ironically, they think it's not because they're a traitor. They're just nervous in the game.
"But I think Faithfuls get so nervous and stressed, whereas the Traitors are the ones that are a bit more cool, calm and collected."
Scott said that due to the growing popularity of the show, people "tripped up on the silliest things" as fans gained more insight.
He said: "They said that to Leigh-Anne [Pinnock], she was like touching up her lip gloss and they were like 'Why would she be doing that if she was going home?', so it's little things like that."
He also said "shock" moments in the finale were "always fun" to see.
"That is the joy of the show - when people just genuinely have no idea, there's always the ones they think are the Traitors," he said.
When it came to who would be the last one standing, Scott said he "really can't call it".
"A betting person would have to say there's three Traitors left, surely it's going to go in their favour, but it's difficult - the game can change at any moment," he said.
"I'm team Traitor. I never used to be but I've just gone to the dark side and I've enjoyed the Traitors this year."
The Celebrity Traitors airs at 20:00 GMT on BBC One.

title: Developer left Alton housing estate unfinished, councillors say
text:
Developer left estate unfinished, councillors say
A developer has built a housing estate without delivering promised extras, councillors have said.
Cala Homes built 220 homes on the site of the former Alton Brewery in Hampshire after winning planning permission in 2020.
However, it has not completed the development and has left some elements in an "unacceptable condition", according to members of East Hampshire District Council.
The firm said it was waiting for the council and the Environment Agency to approve revised plans for riverside work and play equipment.
The former Molson Coors brewery closed in May 2015 with the loss of more than 100 jobs after losing a contract with Heineken.
Cala Homes promised to create a landscaped path beside the River Wey, which runs through the site.
It also agreed to provide play equipment before the 160th home was occupied.
Councillor Angela Glass, in charge of regulation and enforcement, said she shared "residents' frustration" about the work.
The Conservative said: "Residents were entitled to expect a development completed to a high standard.
"It is therefore deeply disappointing that parts of the site remain unfinished and elements of the work have been left in an unacceptable condition."
Councillor Emily Young said the missing parts included riverside landscaping, a pedestrianised bridge, play equipment and a heritage trail.
The Liberal Democrat posted on Facebook that Cala Homes had left the site earlier this year.
She said: "I understand how frustrating it is for residents living alongside an unfinished site. I will continue pushing for clarity about when this outstanding work will be delivered."
A spokesperson for Cala Homes said: "We remain committed to completing the communal areas at our Rivermead Gardens development to a high standard.
"During the course of construction, changes became necessary and required us to revise elements of our plans and submit an updated Flood Risk Activity Permit (FRAP) application to the Environment Agency (EA) for works within the riverside area, including the heritage trail.
"We are now in the final stages of the approval process, having received feedback from the EA last week, and are ready to commence works as soon as consent is granted.
"We have also reviewed and submitted a revised proposal for the play equipment to improve the original plan.
"We will continue working closely with all relevant partners to finalise these works as quickly as possible and thank residents for their patience and understanding as we progress to completion."
description: Part of the Alton Brewery development is in an "unacceptable condition", the local authority says.

title: Thames Valley Police has sacked 65 staff for sexual misconduct since 2020
text:
Force has sacked 65 staff for sexual misconduct
A police force says it has sacked 65 officers or staff since 2020 after sexual misconduct was proven against them.
Thames Valley Police (TVP) is the largest non-metropolitan force in England and Wales and has periodically published reports of sexual misconduct relating to its employees since 2024.
It said by the end of September, 129 officers or staff had been sanctioned, with measures varying from dismissal to being told to undertake reflective practice.
The force said the reports had been published to "improve confidence in reporting these matters".
In addition to the 65 employees who have been dismissed since 2020, 15 were given final written warnings. Another 15 were given written warnings.
Two were demoted and 32 officers or staff were told to undertake reflective practice.
John Thirlway, who was a constable in Oxford, was sacked last year after he told a colleague that he would like to have sex with her and made suggestive comments about her and a member of the public.
The force said the number of officers it employed had increased by about a third since April 2020.
It said it had about 4,500 full-time equivalent (FTE) officers then, but had nearly 6,000 in mid-October.
Its number of staff has also increased from about 3,400, six-and-a-half years ago, to 4,130 earlier this month.

title: Funds sought to recast slavery memorial sculptures in bronze
text:
Slave memorial sculptures need recasting in bronze
An artist with planning permission for a memorial to enslaved people in south London is trying to raise the money to make it permanent.
Sokari Douglas Camp's All the World is Now Richer is a set of six steel figures, which Southwark Council has approved for a site near Burgess Park.
To stand outdoors for the long term, the sculptures would need to be recast in bronze so the figures - and the words they carry - do not weather away.
The steel versions were on display at the Flowers Gallery to coincide with Black History Month.
Douglas Camp said the history of the work was "part of our heritage that people should know about", because it explained how England became the rich country it is.
She said she was inspired by William Prescott, a formerly enslaved man who said people would remember that they had been slaves, but not that they had been brave.
"Normally black people are seen cowering in some way or begging in some way," she said.
"We were strong. We were brave. We survived."
School pupils from Southwark who visited the sculptures said: "These might help you understand your background, your history and your ethnicity, and be proud of it."
Another said: "I think it's important because I'm black and it's really good to show our heritage."
Douglas Camp said the borough was home to many people from the Caribbean and across the African continent.
"We have a story to tell about how our people created wealth for this country," she said.
Her search for funding continues.

title: London Fire Brigade has 'limited resources' to protect heritage
text:
Fire service 'limited' to protect heritage sites
The London Fire Brigade (LFB) does not have enough resources to adequately assess and protect London's heritage sites from future blazes, City Hall has been told.
Last year, more than 800 fire incidents happened in or within 50ft (15m) of a heritage site, which generally do not meet the requirements of current fire safety regulations.
In recent years, the capital has seen fires at Somerset House in 2024, Grade II* listed St Mark's church in St John's Wood in 2023 and Battersea Arts Centre in 2015.
The LFB said prevention was the "best way to protect London's historic and culturally significant buildings" and said fire protection was a "shared responsibility".
The London Assembly Fire Committee heard on 21 October that it was "not possible" for the brigade to assess every heritage building across the capital, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Professor José Torero, head of department of civil, environmental and geomatic engineering at University College London (UCL), said: "They are trying the best they can, but the reality is also that the level of complexity and uniqueness of these buildings it is most likely going to escape their level of expertise.
"You are talking about buildings like the Houses of Parliament or Westminster Abbey.
"It is not possible that they can provide this service with the resources that they have," said Torero, who is also a fire safety engineer.
"Pretending that a small group within the LFB, with the modest capacity they have to elevate their training, can handle a problem of that nature, is like trying to cover the sun with your hands."
Torero said that most of the time, heritage buildings were treated "like conventional buildings", with decisions made without considering how to refurbish and retrofit the building safely.
He added: "Generally, we don't necessarily identify the weak points that can result in a disaster."
Current guidance from the LFB and fire heritage experts advises that protecting people from fire while preserving a building's historic character requires "a balanced approach, taking account of both fire safety and heritage conservation."
Charles Harris, national fire adviser at Historic England, suggested to the committee that the LFB's limited resources meant that it was looking at buildings which would present a risk to life if there was a fire, such as care homes and hospitals.
An LFB spokesperson said protecting heritage buildings was a shared responsibility among building owners, premises managers, councils and fire brigades.
They said: "Through our dedicated heritage work, fire safety officers engage with those responsible for historic buildings to promote effective fire safety measures, share specialist guidance and encourage robust emergency and salvage planning.
"We also carry out familiarisation visits and salvage exercises at heritage sites to ensure firefighters are prepared to respond effectively should an incident occur.
"We welcome any measures that help strengthen the protection of these important buildings for future generations."
The London Assembly Fire Committee has launched a call for evidence as part of its investigation into fire risk management in London's heritage buildings.

title: Sizewell C is making our street a rat-run, say Suffolk villagers
text:
Villagers fed up after becoming Sizewell C rat-run
A country road is becoming a rat-run for the construction of a nuclear power station, according to villagers living nearby.
The B1125 in east Suffolk runs between the A12 at Blythburgh and the B1122, passing by the villages of Westleton and Middleton.
Mandy Beaumont, who is part of the B1125 Action Group, said: "After having been promised that Sizewell C would bring improvements to local areas, this particular area is being turned into a race track".
A Sizewell C spokesperson said it was bringing highway improvements to the road.
Sizewell C is being built next to the functional Sizewell B nuclear power station, close to the town of Leiston.
Metal yellow rat sculptures have been placed along the road by residents, unhappy that drivers are using it as a shortcut to get to the Suffolk coast.
Local sculptor Paul Richardson made 150 of the rat figures as a "tongue-in-cheek" way of making their point.
"I thought, what can I do, how can I help this campaign, there are a lot of really upset people," he explained.
Richardson, who lives close to the B1125, said that traffic started to build at around 05:30 each day.
Around 50 of the rats appeared to have been stolen from the roadside, he added.
Philip Wilshere, who lives on the side of the B1125, said: "We can't keep our windows open in the summer because [the traffic] starts too early."
Wife Joyce Wilshere said she counted around 300 cars passing in the same direction in one morning.
"They weren't speeding but it's just the volume that it is now," she said.
Philip Wilshere believes most of the traffic is workers heading to Sizewell C. He hopes the volume will decline once infrastructure has been completed, such as a nearby park and ride that will take people to the construction site.
Sizewell C said it hoped to have two park and ride sites fully operational by the end of 2026, which could accommodate 2,500 vehicles.
Frank Peel, who lives at Westleton, says the road is "extremely busy", especially at rush hour.
Residents understand that people need to use the road, he says, but "the volume of traffic has made it really quite difficult to cross" over.
He fears the increase in the number of heavy vehicles using the street has damaged the road surface in places.
Dilys Hall, who lives in the village, agreed: "The roads are just not well designed and they're definitely not designed for the volume of traffic we're seeing now."
Jenny Riddell-Carpenter, the Labour MP for Suffolk Coastal, said that Suffolk County Council had "failed to engage with residents" over the issue.
"This rural route has become a real rat-run used by drivers trying to avoid roadworks on the A12," she said.
"It really shouldn't be used like this."
The MP called for the council to produce an "action plan" that looked at "what can be done straight away to make that road safer as well as looking at what measures need to be done in the longer term".
A spokesperson for Suffolk County Council said it recognised concerns around traffic levels, although claimed the volume on the B1125 was no greater, and "in many cases lower, than many other B-class roads" in the county.
"There are a number of mitigation measures related to Sizewell C and the B1125 coming forward, including monitoring road safety, traffic speeds and volumes," the spokesperson added.
A Sizewell C spokesperson said as well as "highway improvements" on the B1125, it was "delivering" the Sizewell Link Road and the Two Village Bypass.

title: Gruffalo illustrator considering legal action against AI firms
text:
Gruffalo illustrator considering legal action against AI firms
The illustrator behind the popular children's book The Gruffalo has told BBC London he is "seriously considering" launching legal action against artificial intelligence (AI) firms he says breach copyright in reproducing his work.
Axel Scheffler, whose illustrations have captivated children since 1999, said he wanted AI companies to stop using artists' work without permission.
The Gruffalo, written by London-born children's author Julia Donaldson, tells the story of a mouse who outsmarts a beast.
"I've been in touch with a lawyer in Germany," Scheffler said.
"There have been illustrators taking legal action against AI companies and I'm seriously considering it. I just want them to stop."
The south London-based artist did not name a company his legal team would consider pursuing.
AI firms have previously argued that using copyrighted material to train their models does not necessarily constitute copyright infringement.
Scheffler, who does not own a smartphone, said he tried to ignore AI until someone showed him how his most famous creations had been digitally recreated in locations such as Silicon Valley and Oktoberfest.
"I was quite shocked. It's clearly my mouse, my Gruffalo, as close as they can do it, but the rest of the image is completely created - it's a clear theft of copyright," he told the BBC.
Scheffler is considering launching the legal action in Germany because he believes the European Union is more creator-friendly.
Nick Buckland, an intellectual property lawyer at London firm Lewis Silkin, agreed that Germany could offer a route for creators seeking to protect their work.
"There have been two cases in Germany where music collecting societies have been able to win against AI companies by showing that those AI companies have copied lyrics of songs verbatim and have presented them," he told the BBC.
But proving copyright infringement could be difficult, he said.
While having a distinctive character such as the Gruffalo could help Scheffler's case, he would need to establish that his copyright had been infringed.
"A generative AI machine trains on datasets which contain copies of images taken from the internet," Buckland explained.
"It then learns patterns from those images to create a general 'model'.
"For example, if someone wants a picture of a dog, the AI machine uses that model to predict what a dog picture might look like.
"What gets generated is simply a mathematical prediction of what the machine thinks a 'dog' should look like based on its training."
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, is already being sued by German publishing group Penguin Random House, together with author and illustrator Ingo Siegner.
The allegation is that OpenAI copied the children's book character The Little Dragon Coconut (Der kleine Drache Kokosnuss).
Whether the AI company has breached copyright law will be decided by the Munich Regional Court in spring 2027.
Carina Mathern, children's and young adult books publisher and member of the management board of Penguin Random House publishing group, said: "Through this lawsuit, we... want to help ensure that copyright remains effectively protected in the age of artificial intelligence and that fair conditions are secured for creative professionals."
An OpenAI spokesperson said: "We're having productive conversations with rightsholders around the world about supporting creativity, including fan art, while protecting intellectual property and taking appropriate action in response to copyright complaints."
The California-based firm said its models were trained in various sources and that copyright holders could submit disputes directly with them.
For Scheffler, the issue goes beyond the work of an established illustrator whose Gruffalo books have sold more than 18 million copies worldwide.
He said any legal action would not be about compensation, but about protecting creators now and in the future.
Other artists also fear the possible impact of AI on their livelihoods.
Ivy Deng, who is doing a master's degree in painting at the Royal College of Art, said: "In terms of regulations, I don't feel protected about the fair use of my art."
"In terms of the art industry and the people who support art, I have faith that they understand that there is a difference between the process and the perspiration behind developing an art practice and creating something by hand and replicating something in one moment," she added.
Prof James Coupe, head of the college's Artificial Intelligence & Digital Art programme, welcomed Scheffler's contribution to the debate.
"We tend to frame this debate as a choice between embracing AI and rejecting it, but that misses the more important question of who gets to shape these technologies and whose interests they serve," he said.
"Art has a vital role here, not because artists should become technology developers, but because artistic practice should challenge the assumptions, values and forms of power that technology often asks us to take for granted."
Last June, the UK government announced £2bn of investment in AI by 2030 "to harness the transformative potential".
Buckland said the government needed to strike a balance between protecting creative industries and allowing AI to develop.
"It seems pretty clear that in order for the AI investment to be maximised, you need to open those floodgates," he said.
"The government has a difficult choice to make. It's trying to find a middle ground."
The government said it did not accept that backing the creative industries and supporting the AI sector were mutually exclusive.
A Department for Culture, Media and Sport spokesperson said: "We have engaged extensively with creatives, AI firms, industry bodies, unions, academics and AI adopters.
"Copyright laws must protect the UK's position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation to grow the economy and improve British lives."
Even so, Scheffler and his publishers are still discussing the possibility of legal action in his native Germany.
For the illustrator, the value of the work itself remains central to the debate.
"AI can never replace the hand-drawn image," he said.
"There's always something lacking. I recommend drawing by hand and being old-fashioned, and hopefully that will be more appreciated when AI takes over."

title: Bungay farmer reveals recipe for scarily big Halloween pumpkins
text:
Farmer reveals recipe for scarily big pumpkins
A farmer who has grown a scarily big pumpkin for the second Halloween in a row said she hoped to break the world record for the largest winter squash - as she finally revealed the secret of her ginormous gourds.
Frances Crickmore, from Fen Farm Dairy, near Bungay, Suffolk, competes with her son Jonny to see who can grow the biggest pumpkin.
Last year she won with a 58-stone (368-kg) whopper, compared to his 2.9-stone (19-kg) effort, and this year her 55-stone (349-kg) pumpkin beat his 7-stone (44-kg) attempt.
She says her success in the inter-family grow-off is all down to her granny's green tea recipe of manure and water, which she feeds to her pumpkin twice a week.
But, like last year, she also invested a lot of time and effort into caring for it to ensure it had the best chance of fulfilling its potential.
"I spend so much time with mine - I covered it every night from when it's tiny to when it's finished with blankets, coats and towels," she said.
"If it rained, I would whizz out there and put something on top of it - I just love growing everything. I'm just one of those hands-on people.
"Jonny's was a complete flop, it was tiny, and he's not going to beat me, ever, and now I want to beat the world record."
Earlier this month, American farmer Ron Wallace's pumpkin was declared the heaviest ever, weighing 225.4 stone (1,431kg), according to Guinness World Records.
It came just days after the UK's Ian Paton was told he had grown the biggest pumpkin after it tipped the scales at 204 stone (1,295.8kg).
While Crickmore's fell a little short of the mark in comparison, she said she had "done quite well" and was "very proud".
'We'll need a chainsaw'
"I would love it to be big, a lot bigger, but it's lovely to just see it sitting there and at the moment it is really beautifully round at the front," she added.
"People think it is plastic, but it is as hard as a rock."
Once the season is over, Frances plans to remove the pumpkin's 400-500 seeds and give them out to people so they, too, can have a go at growing their own next year.
And, so as not to waste the fruits of her labour, the rest of it will be fed to the farm's cattle, provided it can actually be cut-up.
"Whether we'll carve it or not, [I don't know], I think we'll need a chainsaw," she said.

title: West Northants Council seeks 'parity' over historic debt
text:
Authority seeks 'parity' over historic council debt
A council said its call for a formal review of historic debt inherited through local government reorganisation was motivated by a duty to seek "parity for our residents".
In a letter to Secretary of State Angela Rayner, West Northamptonshire Council leader Mark Arnull asked the government to write off "substantial legacy liabilities" from the authorities replaced when the county's new unitary councils were created in 2021.
The Reform UK-controlled council pointed the government's decision to write off £500m of Woking Borough Council's historic £2bn debt.
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has been approached for comment.
West Northamptonshire Council said it inherited £316m of the shared debt.
In his letter to Rayner, Arnull said: "Our residents have been paying the price for shouldering the debts of the old councils for far too long.
"We're asking the Government to apply the same principle to Northamptonshire that it is now applying in Surrey.
"We are not asking for preferential treatment, only parity for our residents. This is about fairness, consistency and ensuring our taxpayers are not left carrying a burden that should have been addressed years ago."
He added that Northamptonshire residents "should not be held back by financial difficulties that arose before their current councils even existed" and said the unitary authorities had shown they could "manage our finances responsibly".
Arnull's letter was issued after the proposal received cross-party backing at last month's full council meeting.

title: Community cinema to bring films back to Kettering
text:
Film buff brings community cinema back to town
A film fan wants to restore cinema screenings to a town following the closure of a national chain in the area.
Will Preston, 28, is organising a community cinema event at Corn Market Hall in Kettering, Northamptonshire.
About 75 people are expected to attend a screening of The Rocky Horror Picture Show on 30 October.
Preston said: "We'd like to do [a screening] every month. We're moving around Kettering to all different places to try to keep it accessible and get as many people to enjoy the cinema experience as possible."
The Odeon in Kettering closed in January 2025 following what the building's owner, Augur Group, described as a "significant drop" in attendance over the past five years, making the venue "no longer viable".
Preston said he had fond memories of visiting the cinema with his parents and grandparents.
"It was a big part of the town and of who I am as a person," he said.
He began planning the community cinema in summer 2025 after a social media post attracted strong interest.
The response prompted him and his partner to research the equipment, licences and insurance needed to run screenings.
"We're going to keep it all as cheap as possible for people," he said.
"We're going to have tickets as cheap as possible, the snacks and stuff as cheap as possible, just to make it accessible."
In 2024, more than 2,000 people signed a petition to pledge their support for the Kettering Odeon and prevent its closure.
The cinema opened in 1997 with the James Bond film Tomorrow Never Dies, and its final screening was the Bob Dylan biopic, A Complete Unknown.

title: 380-home scheme in Dereham approved despite bridge concerns
text:
380-home scheme approved despite bridge concerns
Nearly 400 homes have been approved on the edge of a town after a developer sought to reassure councillors that a promised railway bridge would be built.
Parish councillors have asked for confirmation that a new two-way railway bridge would be constructed as part of the Persimmon Homes development on land off Westfield Road in Dereham, Norfolk.
They say the crossing is essential to avoid traffic issues, but there has been little visible progress towards the project.
The developer said it remains committed to delivering the bridge and that discussions are ongoing.
The first 40 houses could be built by next year, with Persimmon Homes saying it will work "at pace" to deliver them.
Persimmon Homes already has outline planning permission for the development, but the scheme has now cleared a final hurdle after councillors approved the design and layout of the properties.
The decision means construction work can begin.
However, concerns were again raised at a Breckland Council meeting this week about whether the new railway bridge would be built. An existing crossing is due to be demolished and replaced with a larger two-way bridge.
Sian Carrel, chairperson of Whinburgh and Westfield Parish Council, said the two-way bridge was "essential" to prevent traffic from becoming gridlocked but currently but that there is "no evidence" to show it was being progressed.
Breckland Council officers said conditions attached to the planning permission would ensure the bridge is built.
Debbie Sherman, representing Persimmon Homes, said the company was in detailed discussions with Norfolk County Council about securing the land needed for the bridge and was "confident" it could be delivered.
Councillors ultimately approved the project, although there are still some matters that need to be resolved.
The development cannot proceed until flood experts and Norfolk County Council highways officers approve changes to the drainage plans and road layout.

title: Norfolk foot artist's work chosen for Christmas card collection
text:
Foot artist's work chosen for Christmas card collection
For most of his life, Peter Longstaff has used his feet to paint scenic landscapes.
The 65-year-old from Marsham, Norfolk, was born without arms after his mother, Brenda Longstaff, was prescribed thalidomide, a drug used to treat morning sickness that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies.
She encouraged her son to use his feet as a child and he taught himself how to paint. He later gained a number of art qualifications.
Longstaff joined the Mouth and Foot Painting Artists (MFPA) 24 years ago and, for the first time, one of his paintings has been selected for the organisation's 2026 Christmas card collection.
Longstaff was one of thousands of babies around the world affected by the thalidomide scandal.
The drug was prescribed to mothers in the late 1950s and early 1960s and, according to the Thalidomide Trust, more than 100,000 babies were affected by it.
"From being born with no arms, my mum encouraged me to use my feet," Longstaff explained.
"I just started to pick things up and then she got me some paper and colouring pencils... so in a sense I don't know any different.
"From then on I've used my foot - it's my right hand."
At school, Longstaff excelled at art but, as an adult, spent 20 years running a pig farm.
"When I wanted a pig unit, nobody thought I could do it, even my mum and dad were hesitant," he continued.
"I actually started with breeding rabbits, which didn't work out because I didn't enjoy it.
"I went to Norwich Market and I bought two young pigs and that's where it started. I ended up with 200."
Longstaff sold his pig farm in the 1990s to gain various art qualifications and joined the MFPA.
While he stills look after rare pigs, much of his time is now devoted to painting landscapes. It can take him a week or two, sometimes longer, to paint one piece.
This year, his painting Winter Landscape was chosen for the festive card collection, it is the first time one of his artworks has been selected.
"I was astonished... it makes me proud because I've done a lot of work with this," Longstaff said.
"I've had some tuition, I've done the A-level Fine Art to make myself better, so with that, I've conquered my [goals].
"Hopefully, I can keep going and get a few more."

title: Council calls for faster action on unadopted Hertfordshire roads
text:
Calls for action over unadopted roads
A Hertfordshire county councillor has called on the government to require roads on all new housing developments to be built to "adoptable" standards.
Currently unadopted roads must meet particular design and construction standards before they can be adopted by councils.
At a development in Hatfield where roads have remained unadopted for 20 years, councillors said residents are plagued by issues around maintenance and fly-tipping.
Liberal Democrat councillor Paul Zukowskyj has written to the Secretary of State to call for a national common planning requirement. However, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing said local authorities were best placed to make decisions on the matter.
Labour councillor for Hatfield North, Beth Kelly, presented a motion to the latest meeting of the county council's environment, transport and growth cabinet panel on 22 October.
According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, councillors at the meeting heard how there are currently 99 roads across the county that remain unadopted.
Hatfield's Salisbury Village development was highlighted, where some roads have remained unadopted by the county council for more than two decades.
Kelly said persistent issues such as fly-tipping, poor lighting maintenance, anti-social behaviour and lack of clarity over maintenance and enforcement had left "residents in a state of confusion and frustration".
A spokesperson for developers Taylor Wimpey and Vistry said a route to adoption had now been agreed.
They said the companies "continue to work closely together, and with Hertfordshire County Council, to secure adoption of the Salisbury Village development as efficiently and swiftly as possible."
Zukowskyj said that legislation is needed for councils to compel developers to "do what the developer is supposed to do."
The spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing said that the government has consulted on "setting common standards for roads and mandatory adoption of certain amenities - and will set out next steps in due course."

title: Essex mental health failings led to my family's deaths, says mum
text:
I buried my son and partner - I want answers
A woman whose son and partner both died following failures in their care under NHS services in Essex has said she will not stop fighting for answers.
An inquest concluded there were several missed opportunities to assess 81-year-old Colin Flatt's mental capacity before he fell from height at hospital in July 2021.
His partner, Melanie Leahy, told the BBC: "I haven't just been let down, my family has been wiped out." Her son Matthew Leahy died at a mental health unit in 2012.
A spokesperson for the NHS mental health trust in Essex said it would take a "careful note" of the recent inquest conclusions.
Melanie Leahy spearheaded the successful campaign to launch England's first independent statutory public inquiry into mental health services, which has been ongoing since 2024.
It is examining the deaths of more than 2,000 people who died while under the care of NHS mental health services in Essex between 2000 and the end of 2023.
"Both of my boys, I've buried - my life is destroyed [and] I'm having to rebuild it," said Leahy.
Colin Flatt was described during the recent inquest as a fit and active man, who played football professionally, which included stints at Cambridge United, Leyton Orient and Southend United.
In May 2021, he was suffering from memory loss and was admitted to Broomfield Hospital in Chelmsford with a low heart rate.
He was assessed by the Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT) and was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease.
Flatt was transferred to Goodmayes Hospital in Ilford, east London - after incidents of "violence and aggression" - and was detained under the Mental Health Act.
On Wednesday, the 10-person jury at Essex Coroner's Court concluded there was a missed opportunity when a mental health tribunal approved his discharge from Goodmayes in June 2021.
The following month, after being admitted to Basildon Hospital, Flatt stabbed himself with scissors in the abdomen and climbed over a landing.
He fell about 5m (16ft) on to a glass table and died in the September.
Jurors concluded there were other failures, including the lack of referral to a specialist mental health team and a handover failure when he was admitted to Basildon Hospital.
"Colin was poorly, Colin was confused, Colin was absolutely petrified and I don't think for once he was treated as a person," said Melanie Leahy.
She said not all her questions were answered at the two-week inquest.
"I don't want to hear recommendations and lessons learnt. I want to know who is going to take responsibility," she said.
Melanie Leahy's son died while he was an inpatient at the Linden Centre in Chelmsford.
A health ombudsman concluded there were a long list of failures in Matthew Leahy's care and EPUT said his care "fell below acceptable standards".
The campaigner said the Lampard Inquiry was her last chance for answers.
"I don't want this to happen to another family," she said.
"I have to do it - Colin fought with me and stood beside me and saw what Matthew's death did to me - not knowing that he would also be part of his fight.
"For me to stop now, would be an insult to both of them."
An EPUT spokesperson said: "All of us across healthcare have a responsibility to work together to improve care and treatment for all, and to take careful note of the coroner's conclusions."
Former EPUT chief executive Paul Scott has previously apologised for the failings in Flatt's care.
Christine Blanshard, the chief medical officer at the Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Basildon Hospital, said it had acted on recommendations made following Flatt's death.

text:
Passengers warned of November rail disruption
Passengers are being urged to plan ahead for their journeys this November while essential upgrades are made to the rail network.
Parts of the Great Eastern Main Line in Essex and Suffolk will be affected, as well as the branches to Harwich, Braintree and Sudbury.
The work - to improve reliability and prepare for major track renewals over Christmas - will also affect the lines to Southend Victoria and Southminster.
It means buses will replace trains over the course of three weekends.
Network Rail said the planned engineering work included:
• Replacing wheel timbers, general maintenance, vegetation management and tamping on the Harwich Town branch line
• Platform upgrade work at Bures railway station, part of a £1m investment
• Rerail and track maintenance at Marks Tey and Kelvedon
Martin Beable, chief operating officer for GBR Anglia, thanked passengers for their patience and said: "We're working together to minimise disruption wherever possible."
The final three weekends of November are affected by the engineering works, and Network Rail has provided more information on its website.
Passengers are advised to check information online before travelling.
