title: RSPCA rescuers find more than100 guinea pigs in one home
text:
Rescuers find 100 guinea pigs in one home
An animal charity has rescued more than 100 newborn and adult guinea pigs from a home.
The RSPCA said the number of guinea pigs "rapidly grew out of control, leaving an owner unable to cope".
About 70 of the animals are being cared for at the charity's Cambridge branch, 21 in Milton Keynes, and 10 at the South Buckinghamshire branch, with more sent to other centres. Some have also been allowed to stay with the owner.
The RSPCA has put out a "desperate" plea for foster carers as it expected the numbers to increase, as many of the rescued females were pregnant.
The charity said its branches had "taken on the large number of small furries at short notice" and were under pressure.
They said 120 were removed from the property, and while most were in good health, four had to be put to sleep, and those that remained with the owner had been put into same-sex pairs to ensure no further breeding.
Some of those being cared for at the charity's branches had already given birth.
The mass rescue, supported by Woodgreen Pets Charity in Cambridgeshire, was dubbed "Operation Guinea Pig".
Rosemary Rodd, treasurer at RSPCA Cambridge and District Branch, said: "We are so grateful to our amazing team of volunteers and fosterers who all rallied to our cry for help and enabled us to help so many of these little ones.
"Our branch took 69 in total, but the numbers are already starting to increase as one foster carer has already reported the birth of some babies."
Louise Norman, who runs a small animal sanctuary and volunteers at the RSPCA in Buckinghamshire, said: "On the day they arrived, one baby was born and she weighed 100 grams (3.5oz) - thankfully she was mum's only baby.
"We do, however, strongly suspect that all the females are pregnant - and some of the girls are only eight to 10 weeks old."
RSPCA Animal Rescue Officer Maya Thakrar said she was "blown away by the support of my colleagues at our branches and centres who all offered to help take on these little ones at such short notice".
"This rescue is just one of those multi-animal rescues we are having to deal with, and we are struggling and need help," she said.
"As with many multi-animal rescues, this was not a case of deliberate cruelty - but something we are seeing far too often when people are overwhelmed unintentionally by not neutering early enough."
The RSPCA said it was dealing with an average of 410 "multi-animal" incidents involving 10 or more animals every month, an increase on 2025 - which it said was already a record-breaking year.

title: Further delay in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough council shake-up
text:
Council shake-up plans face further delay
Plans to replace the seven councils in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough with either two or three new authorities are facing a further delay.
The new councils would oversee services including planning and social care. Five options were put forward for consideration, with elections to any new unitary authorities scheduled for May 2028.
Jim McMahon MP, minister for local government, devolution and regional growth, told the House of Commons on Thursday proposals submitted for the area "will remain under consideration".
He said a final decision would be made early next year at the latest.
The government is abolishing two-tier council systems across England, saying the changes will save money by streamlining services.
It also hopes it will make it easier for residents to understand who is responsible for local services.
McMahon also announced the region would receive £500,000 in transition funding to support work on reorganisation.
It comes after the government had previously announced all areas would receive £900,000 in transition funding for each new unitary authority.
"After final decisions, we will pay any remaining balance, depending on how many councils are chosen," McMahon added.
Liberal Democrat councillor and leader of Cambridgeshire County Council, Lucy Nethsingha, said the decision was "a bitter disappointment".
"Cambridgeshire and Peterborough were already stuck in 'LGR limbo' and to simply extend that further beggars belief," said Nethsingha.
She said "continued uncertainty" would prevent authorities from making long-term plans.
"In particular, the anxiety and uncertainty that this creates for the hard-working staff in the seven councils in this area is intolerable."
Cambridge City Council said local elections planned for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough in May 2027 would still go ahead for the existing authorities.
Katie Thornburrow, Labour councillor and leader of Cambridge City Council, said she welcomed the update.
"Having more certainty around the nature of future arrangements for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough by early 2027 will mean we will then be able to start work in earnest on shaping a new unitary authority, which will come into being from April 2029," she said.
Labour leader of Peterborough City Council Shabina Qayyum said: "It is right that any changes and their implications are closely examined before a final decision is made.
"However, I remain convinced that Option D is our preferred option for Peterborough."
Paul Bristow, Conservative mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said: "Other parts of the country are getting certainty about their future.
"There is no good reason why Cambridgeshire and Peterborough should be left behind."

title: Peterborough councillor used Snapchat to catfish army cadets
text:
How a councillor used Snapchat to catfish army cadets
Councillor, cadet, carer. Rylan Ray built a reputation as a young volunteer committed to public service. However, beneath the respectable veneer was a man who was using social media apps such as Snapchat to groom and deceive teenagers.
On Thursday, the 26-year-old former Conservative politician was convicted of 28 sexual offences including sexual assault and making indecent photographs of children.
Victims included children he met through his role with the Cambridgeshire Army Cadet Force. Jurors also found him guilty of raping a man.
How did a man trusted by young people and elected to represent thousands of residents come to commit such serious crimes?
It is 2022 and Ray is standing for election in Peterborough, the city he was born and raised in. One of his promises: To fight for improved safeguarding services.
With more than half of the votes, he becomes the new city councillor for Eye, Thorney and Newborough.
What residents do not know, though, is that he has already broken the safeguarding rules at the heart of his campaign – something that would ultimately lead to his downfall.
Ray, who was born Rylan Fowler, was no stranger to the Army Cadets.
He joined as a child, and was quick to return as a volunteer as an adult, rising to the rank of detachment commander.
The organisation's approach to safeguarding is clear. During Ray's trial, the jury was read a statement from head of safeguarding Nathan Ditton who said volunteers "must not send personal contact communications to a cadet in any form outside of a family relationship".
Despite that, Ray was part of a WhatsApp group for the young people in his detachment, which he said was to deter bullying.
Having access to cadets' phone numbers meant he could, and did, contact them privately.
Conversations would start professionally – praise for their good work, for example.
But he encouraged some of those conversations to move to Snapchat where they would become increasingly personal and sexual.
The app is popular with young people and messages are automatically deleted within 24 hours.
For some of the boys, they spoke to him on the app without even realising.
Catfishing
"Who are you?" one boy asked when a Snapchat account he did not recognise reached out to him.
"Chelsie," they responded.
It was a story echoed by other young people. Chelsie would make contact, introducing herself as a young woman from Peterborough. Some recalled her saying she was a teenager who attended a local school; others a woman in her 20s.
Chelsie would send explicit photos and videos of a woman and request similar images in return.
"That," pointing at Ray in the dock on the first day of his trial, "was Chelsie," said prosecutor Claire Matthews.
How was she so sure?
One young man grew suspicious of Chelsie and made a telephone call to a number associated with the account. The voice at the end of the phone answered: "Hello, Rylan Ray."
The court also heard how the devices linked to the account were traced back to Ray's home address in Westgate, Peterborough.
Ray's barrister Rhodri James described him as someone who "struggled to make friends and saw friendship in the wrong places".
He began caring for his mum, who attended the court for some of the trial, when he was 12.
Matthews described his behaviour as "grooming" and said he had used his fake persona to "catfish" his victims.
Catfishing, according to the Oxford English Dictionary, is the act of deceiving someone online using a fictional persona, often with the intent of luring them into a relationship.
One man, who had been contacted by Chelsie as a child, was later contacted by an account using the same name and pictures on the dating app Tinder.
Cambridgeshire Police became aware of Ray's offending after two boys made complaints at school. Three mobile phones and one laptop were seized.
A total of 704 indecent images of children were found on Ray's devices, including 73 of the most serious Category A classification.
At least five children were contacted by the Chelsie account. Not all of the children in the images found on Ray's devices have yet been identified.
Ray appeared to have deleted them from his phones but digital forensics specialists managed to extract them.
He claimed Chelsie was actually an Army cadet who he became aware was taking advantage of their colleagues and that he sent the images to his own phone so he could confront them about it.
When asked, he refused to reveal the true identity of who he believed was Chelsie.
'Gay in everyone'
Some boys exchanged nude photos with Ray directly.
One victim said he felt he had no choice but to comply with Ray's requests because he feared his own progression within the cadets would otherwise be hindered.
Another, who did not return images, told Ray he was not gay in an attempt to get the messages to stop. The response was: "There's a little bit of gay in everyone."
The abuse was not conducted exclusively online. Ray sexually assaulted three young people he met through the cadets and raped a man he met on a night out.
Ray also used his role as a councillor to further his relationships with teenage boys.
He had been the chairman of Peterborough City Council's licensing committee.
During the trial, one man said that while he was underage, the councillor took him on nights out in the city and that Ray's presence meant he was not asked to prove his age.
The parent of another victim said in a statement Ray took her son to parties that were attended by Ray's "acquaintances from the council".
He was removed from the council's Conservative group in February, becoming an independent member, and in May's local election he did not contest his position.
Ray also had jobs at HM Courts and Tribunals Service, the Ministry of Justice, and two schools in the Peterborough area.
At Ipswich Crown Court, it took the jury of four men and eight women about 11 hours to find Ray guilty of 23 offences. He had already pleaded guilty to five offences against one of his teenage victims.
Sentencing will be on 8 January.

title: New York police will investigate all sex crimes at Cornell, governor says
text:
New York police will now investigate Cornell sex complaints, governor says
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has announced that state police will now investigate all future sexual offence complaints at Cornell University after the fallout from a gang rape accusation at the institution.
It follows the handling of a 2024 alleged campus rape incident, where a student, known anonymously as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit against Cornell after she was allegedly drugged and gang raped at a fraternity.
The university, after initially defending its disciplinary measures, acknowledged it fell short in its handling of her case.
The fallout has continued to rile the university. Cornell's administration - including its president - is facing a no-confidence vote by its faculty.
Hochul said New York State Police signed an agreement with Cornell University so that all sexual offence complaints, which had historically fallen under the jurisdiction of university police, will be immediately referred to state police instead.
"When someone reports sexual assault," Hochul said on Thursday, they deserve "to know their allegations will be taken seriously and thoroughly investigated by law enforcement trained to support survivors".
"Survivors should be able to trust the institutions responsible for protecting them," the governor added.
Backlash against the Ivy League university has been intense since Jane Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September.
On Wednesday, the institution's Faculty Senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff, met behind closed-doors and decided to move forward with voting on a resolution of no-confidence against the administration and the university's President Michael Kotlikoff.
The vote will be open for faculty starting on Friday and run until 6 November. The vote is largely symbolic but could intensify pressure on changing the university's leadership.
Earlier this month, the university announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including adding sexual assault investigators to its police force.
Hochul had said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She appointed a special prosecutor, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, earlier this month to oversee a reopened investigation into whether criminal charges are warranted.
The woman at the centre of the case filed a civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.

title: Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
text:
Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
Three people have died after two helicopters collided midair near a small airport in Oregon, officials said.
The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred near McMinnville Municipal Airport on Thursday afternoon. Both aircraft crashed in a field adjacent to a highway, the sheriff's office said.
Authorities identified the victims as a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, who were aboard one of the helicopters. The sole occupant of the other aircraft - a 38-year-old from Oregon - was also killed.
It was not immediately clear what caused the crash.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) responded to the scene and are leading the ongoing investigation.
The flight instructor on the Robinson R22 was identified Maddie Aasbo.
The student pilot from the UK was identified on Friday as 31-year-old Christopher James Joughin.
Authorities did not initially name Joughin on Thursday as they had not notified his family. The family was said to be in Zimbabwe, according to the Statesman Journal.
The sole occupant of the Airbus was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.
The Airbus was on a post-maintenance check flight and the Robinson R22 was on a flying lesson with two aboard, the NTSB said on Friday.
Grant Mills, an investigator with the NTSB, said that his agency and the FAA are still investigating the crash.
He was unable to provide a cause or comment on weather conditions at the time of the crash, but confirmed that it occurred midair.
He added that witnesses reported the collision occurred about 500ft (152.4m) off the ground about a mile east of the airport.
Mills noted that the McMinnville Airport does not have an air traffic control tower, which means pilots need to self-report their whereabouts and intentions to take off and land over a shared frequency.
description: The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred on Thursday afternoon, with both aircraft crashing in a field adjacent to a highway.

title: Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
text:
Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.
His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.
Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.
"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.
The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.
Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour – Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.
And yet despite those circumstances, the Democratic Party is also unpopular nationwide. The Real Clear Politics polling average shows the American public sees the Democrats as only marginally better than the Republicans. Recent polls show the Democratic Party still has a net unfavourability rating among Americans. Political analysts say that if the Republicans manage to buck the trend and survive these midterms, one key reason is that the Democratic Party (or the Democratic brand) is disliked by a majority of American voters too.
Behind the headlines of which party or which candidates win this Tuesday, there's also a story this election season about Democratic identity. This is a fight between institutionalists and reformists, of people who want incremental change and those who demand root-and-branch transformation. The question is, who will win out in the long run?
The not-Trump party?
I've covered every national US election in the past dozen years and this is an unusual one. When I was out interviewing voters ahead of the 2018 midterms during Donald Trump's first term, I was struck by how united many Democratic voters were in their opposition to the president. This time, I've noticed that under the facade of unity, there's a brewing fight.
There are persistent questions about what the Democratic Party stands for, and these divides erupted during the primaries this midterm cycle. "The identity of the party is pretty cloudy," said Ruy Teixeira, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a centre-right think tank. "It's all centred on reaction to the Trump administration and taking advantage of what is a thermostatic reaction against the administration... Beyond that, there's all these different factions in the party."
Part of the reason for this Democratic infighting is that the party never had a chance to have this fight during the 2024 presidential race, with the sudden departure of Joe Biden months before the election and nomination of Kamala Harris.
Analysts agree that if Democrats make big wins on election night, it still won't answer deeper, unresolved questions as they try to keep their big tent together to corral votes in Congress or eye the 2028 presidency.
In simplistic terms, the divide is between the centrist, more moderate wing of the party and its left flank. But operatives and analysts say it's also a divide between institutionalists and those who want to completely upend the existing institution. Both feel they have a better read on what voters genuinely want.
Usamah Andrabi, of the Justice Democrats, a prominent left-wing group, blames the Democratic establishment for ushering in a Republican Congress and president. "And so I think the people who led us into this mess are simply not gonna be the ones who lead us out of it," he told me.
"The affordability crisis… is a massive one, and it's not going to be resolved by tinkering at the margins," he added. Instead, he insists, it'll be solved through policies like universal healthcare and childcare, and redistributing money by cutting the Pentagon's budget to stop "endless wars". His organisation sprang up in 2017 to recruit and support the congressional members who became known as "the Squad", the furthest-left faction in the House, which includes members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar.
Healthcare will be one of the main arenas in which this fight is likely to play out, says Carrie Dann, managing editor of the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter that forecasts the competitiveness of races.
"There is a lot of appetite for, at the very least, more transparency, more understanding of why healthcare costs are so high," said Dann. " Take a bad step, break your leg, and a huge swathe of Americans would see their worlds turned upside down by that because of the healthcare system as it is."
Several Democratic candidates this election cycle have outlined ideas to lower "out-of-pocket" costs for those who already have health insurance - being hit with additional costs on top of regular insurance payments is a common feature of the American healthcare system. But there's another flank of the party that is fed up with incremental changes and wants a national healthcare system that is free at the point of use - Medicare for All.
Recent polling suggests a majority of Democrats favour this kind of healthcare system, but a majority of Republicans oppose it.
But some Democrats say there's nuance in the issue.
"People want to have universal healthcare, and they also want to be able to keep their health insurance," says Neera Tanden, Joe Biden's former domestic policy adviser, now CEO of the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.
Mainstream establishment Democrats acknowledge that many people see healthcare as a right, but they insist that others strongly oppose a fully government-run programme, fearing lower standards of care, and insist on having the option of keeping their private health insurance.
Healthcare costs have gone up across the board - health insurance and out-of-pocket healthcare expenses, hospital expenses and prescription drug costs have all surged in recent years, rising faster than the rate of inflation. As medical expenses have increased, polls suggest the idea of universal healthcare isn't as outlandish as it once seemed, and this campaign cycle has shown that it's far less taboo for politicians to openly call for it.
Back in Georgia, it's an issue on which Tamara and James agree - they want universal healthcare.
But their most fundamental disagreement is over Israel. Tamara calls herself a Zionist. "My kids get mad at me for saying that," she said.
And they're hardly the only Democrats having this debate.
Dann, from the Cook Political Report, says one of the biggest lessons from this election cycle is that Democratic voters weren't just looking for candidates willing to fight Trump, but candidates willing to take on the establishment. Dann points to the key swing state of Michigan, where in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed - a fierce critic of Israel and its actions in Gaza - came out on top over the objections of the Democratic establishment.
"I think one reason for that was that he was not only talking about taking on Donald Trump, but taking on the Democratic establishment… the establishment in Washington writ large," she said. And part of that anti-establishment attitude is about US support for Israel.
The Israel question
Some who left the party in 2024 because they believe Biden was too supportive of Israel's actions in Gaza are now returning, energised by El-Sayed's tough tone.
"My red line has been Gaza," said Samraa Luqman, an Arab-American activist in Michigan who voted for Trump in the last presidential election, feeling betrayed by Democrats that year.
"2023 and 2024 have really taught this community a lesson that we are no longer going to be wishy-washy about the issue. It's Gaza or bust," she told me. "If you're not good on Gaza, on Israel, on Palestine, then we don't need you. We don't need you in office, and we don't need to vote for you, no matter what your party affiliation is."
But as El-Sayed has energised voters, he's also alienated others, particularly some who see support for Israel as connected to Jewish safety in the US and feel that antisemitism in their party has grown after the deadly Hamas attacks of October 7.
Zach Nessel is one of those Democrats. And he's increasingly worried about becoming politically homeless.
"We have people who don't think Zionists should have a place in our party, that they should be removed from the party," Nessel told me. "And as a proud Zionist, I don't want to be removed from the Democratic coalition just over this one issue in the Middle East."
Support for Israel became a litmus test in some Democratic primaries this season, leading to mounting resistance to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the longtime influential lobbying group.
Ideological test
But Dann tells me that it's not just Israel that's a litmus test, it's El-Sayed's race itself.
"Abdul El-Sayed's theory of the case is that he can run as an unabashed progressive in a purple state [a state that swings between the 'red' Republican party and 'blue' Democrats] and win because progressive ideas are not only popular if they're communicated correctly, but also activate voters who are not necessarily a normal part of the political process, particularly young people," she said.
If he wins, left-wing candidates will see it as a model, she adds. And if he loses, Democrats in the more centrist wing of the party will see it as evidence that left-wing ideas are out of touch with mainstream voters.
But there are others, like Jim Kessler with Third Way, a centrist think tank, who think Michigan shouldn't be the focus. He pointed out that if Democrats take control of the Senate it'll be because of more centrist candidates: Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Mary Peltola in Alaska, James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas. They, he said, are the ones expanding Democrats' odds this cycle. " So the bigger the Democratic victory, the more it seems like the centrist Democrats came through, not the DSA candidates," he said.
DSA-endorsed candidates made gains during the primaries this election cycle, but their ideas are still controversial to many.
" I don't think… the vast majority of working-class people in America are kind of mini socialists," Tanden told me, pointing to reporting that suggests the majority of people who support the DSA are college-educated voters.
" Working-class people are pretty moderate on issues like crime and immigration," she added.
Nonetheless, if Democrats gain the majority, their congressional leaders will have to navigate a group of Democrats in which there will likely be an increase in the loudest and most left-wing voices.
" The Democrats' biggest challenge is to figure out how to actually deliver on running the economy better and making things more affordable, because they've said over and over again and very loudly that's what they're going to do," said Teixeira.
Seizing the momentum
In all likelihood, people will start thinking seriously about the next presidential candidate the day after the midterms.
So, who actually has the momentum: the left flank or the centre?
"I think after the election we'll see a lot of fighting between the factions to claim credit," Teixeira said. " And that will of course feed into the jostling for the presidential nomination for 2028."
Back in Georgia, Tamara and James may disagree on some things, but they both want Democrats to win big on Tuesday.
"I'm a very pragmatic person when it comes to progressive politics," James said. He wants to make it clear he doesn't agree with everything DSA members espouse.
So much of this midterm cycle has also come down to candidate quality - not just the message but the messenger. So I asked both mother and son who their "ideal" Democrat is.
Tamara instantly answered Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator running for re-election in Georgia.
It's a point of agreement. They both really like their Georgia senator.
Ossoff is seen by many as a rising star of his party. The seat he is contesting is characterised by the Cook Political Report as "likely Democratic" - considered by analysts to be an impressive achievement in a swing state that voted for Trump in 2024.
"He knows how to speak to moderate Republicans, moderate Democrats, and members of the DSA," Tamara said. "He's not afraid to pull any punches… I appreciate how much he talks about corruption."
On Wednesday night, she joined thousands of people just outside Atlanta for a rally to cheer on the senator as former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats.
And when Ossoff took the mic, he spoke at length about what he sees as "corruption" in the Trump administration and in American politics, healthcare and corporate money.
And I heard this concern from voters in Georgia this past week, not just at the campaign rally, but at early voting sites in both Republican and Democratic counties.
"We have a corruption crisis," said Richard Schosky as he walked out of the voting booth in north Atlanta, after casting his ballot early. It's an issue that seems to be resonating deeply with voters, although the White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.
In fact, Dann with the Cook Political Report says "corruption has become one of the central issues of this election".
Still, she added, "Democrats would be foolish to believe that a very good night for them in November is a mandate for the Democratic Party," said Dann.
"They are as almost as unpopular as Republicans and the president."

title: Erin Patterson: Australian mushroom murderer loses appeal to overturn convictions
text:
Mushroom murderer fails to overturn convictions in Australian court challenge
Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.
Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.
In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.
Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said.
"We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.
After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.
Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.
Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.
She promptly launched an appeal against her convictions, with her legal team in August arguing seven grounds for her appeal.
They claimed a hotel booking mishap - which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media - was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial.
They also argued certain pieces of evidence shown to the jury were irrelevant and prejudicial - such as cell tower data suggesting Patterson visited areas where death cap mushrooms might be found and Facebook posts where she complained about her in-laws.
Meanwhile, the judge wrongly blocked other evidence that would have demonstrated the mother-of-two's long-time hobby of mushroom foraging, they said.
The defence team also asserted that the prosecution's five-day cross-examination of Patterson was "unfair and oppressive", and that the Crown was inconsistent in its arguments about a motive.
On Friday, the appeal judges dismissed all seven grounds.
Patterson has 28 days to decide if she will seek to convince the High Court of Australia to hear another appeal over the case.
description: Erin Patterson argued her trial was unfair due to seven grounds but three appeal judges dismissed them all.

title: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
text:
We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
Rachel Stone was five and her brother Ian was 10 when their mum and dad took them on a caravan holiday to Wales with the family next door.
They spent two fun-filled weeks together - but when they got home, each family split in half and swapped houses.
Rachel and her mother Kay moved in with the neighbour Eddie and his daughter Alison. Eddie's wife Irene and their daughter Dawn moved in with Rachel's dad Rex and her brother Ian.
Rachel tells Dr Sian Williams, host of Radio 4's Life Changing podcast, of the trauma of her family being torn apart, the chaos that unfolded and how she has come to forgive her parents.
Rachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together.
Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Snowdon (officially known as Yr Wyddfa).
But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.
Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister.
"And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."
Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.
As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.
That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.
Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."
Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".
She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.
Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."
She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother.
"I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler."
Rachel was seven when the two couples went to court together and got divorced. They later married their new partners in separate low-key registry office ceremonies.
Rachel did not even know her dad had married Irene until she saw the wedding photo. Her visits to her old home tailed off when she was about 11 or 12. She says she found it difficult to go and visit her dad and did not get along with Irene.
Meanwhile, life with her mum Kay and Eddie was chaotic.
"[He] was quite possessive and controlling. By the time we got to 13, she [Mum] said, 'it's not sustainable, [we] can't live like this".
Rachel said school was her "escape". She got good grades and became a teacher. She got married and had two sons but is now separated and works as a business coach.
Throughout her life, Rachel's mother would never talk about the swap. "I asked a lot of questions. She told me it was complicated."
Decades later, on a family holiday with her own sons, Rachel asked again.
"I said to my mum, 'Oh, Joseph's 10 now... Ian was 10 when you let him go with Dad and Irene.'"
She says her mum was "beside herself with guilt and the shame... for her selfish decisions."
"Years later she actually said to me - the words I almost wanted to hear all my life - 'I'm so sorry I let you down and I want to try and make it up to you.'"
Rachel says it was the start of her rebuilding a "wonderful" relationship with her mum.
Rachel never had a close relationship with her dad. "He told me he had a choice between his wife and his children. Unfortunately for me, he chose his wife."
He and Irene stayed together until his death aged 81.
But when she spoke at her dad's funeral, Rachel said she felt she owed him an apology.
"I imagined a character of a perfect dad that had been taken away from me... I created this superhuman being that could be everything.
"And I wanted him to be like that. But I also think you have to accept people for who they are.
"I think that parents do the best they can... You can't hope for your parents to be something they're not."

title: Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
text:
Biggest fibre boost could be scraps in your bin, experts say
Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers.
They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.
Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.
Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer.
Stalks, pips and rind on
As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.
Eating a kiwi with the skin on provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.
For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.
They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.
For example:
- watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal bread
- butternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakes
- pineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the flesh
- broccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the florets
Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.
Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.
"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one - you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."
Banana peel curry?
King's College London has been experimenting in its canteen, offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.
At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.
While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.
Steaming, microwaving or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best.
Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."
She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it.
Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.
Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.
Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.
Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.
She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.
Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.
"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.
She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.
And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.
Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.
description: Chomping on vegtable skins, seeds and stalks could give us vital fibre, say food scientists.

title: Crypto giant Binance hit by hack suspected to be largest in history
text:
Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, also said it has "high confidence" that the North Korean group are linked to the hack.
For the last few years North Korea-linked operatives have focussed on attacking cryptocurrency companies for large thefts of digital tokens.
Western security agencies have previously said stolen funds are used to finance North Korea's nuclear weapons and missile development programs.
The regime has denied any involvement in hacks in the past.
Eric Jardine, Chainalysis' Head of Research, urged every exchange to remain vigilant as the platforms are attractive targets for hackers due to the sheer value of assets.
Binance did not directly respond to BBC questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea but said: "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."
The incident concerns Binance.com - while much smaller crypto platform Binance.US, which provides trading services specifically for American residents - said its platform is not affected by the issue.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the company's initial investigation suggested the hack started with a compromised engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions," he said in a statement.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak."
He said a detailed "post-mortem" would be shared once the investigation was complete.
In an update, the company said in a statement on X that another investigation found there had been other breach points: "We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
Check Point's Dave said this attack also resembled a hack on crypto exchange platform Bitget in September in which $388m (£289m) was lost: "This implies that attackers no longer need the vault keys. They target the systems and people with authority to use them."
In a series of posts, Yi He, Binance's co-chief executive, thanked various cryptocurrency issuers for freezing the assets.
"Safety first: withdrawals are currently disabled until the environment is confirmed to be secure," she said.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they had frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it has worked with its partners to freeze stolen funds.
Crypto exchange Coinbase said it was unaffected by the incident and was monitoring the situation.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the security issue.
Bitcoin dropped by more than 4% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.
description: Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.

title: I didn't know when I collapsed at work - it was low vitamin D
text:
I didn't know I was lacking in vitamin D until I collapsed at work
Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.
"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.
Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy. While her symptoms are not directly linked to vitamin D deficiency - she realised something was wrong.
Blood tests later showed her level was so low - it was "next to nothing".
In the UK, low vitamin D rates are increasing in some age groups - particularly in girls and young women.
According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.
Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.
But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.
Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.
Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.
Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.
What are the symptoms - and their daily impact?
Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia.
"They call it the silent disease," says Dr Suma Uday, a paediatric endocrinologist who wants to raise awareness of the problem.
She warns that vitamin D deficiency in young people and adults is difficult to spot and can be missed or misdiagnosed. Symptoms include fatigue and joint and bone pain.
Uday says: "It's basically silently eating away at the bones, leaving them softened and prone to breaks."
Amaka was in the middle of making dinner at her university house in Liverpool when she started shaking.
"I couldn't really see in front of me," she says. Her housemate took her to A&E - later she too would be diagnosed as vitamin D deficient.
Other than feeling tired, she says she had no symptoms: "I'm a 21-year-old student. I've got work and uni - I'm always feeling tired."
She remembers her mother suffering from low vitamin D but says she did not realise it could happen to her.
After taking supplements, Amaka feels a lot better, but she is anxious in case it happens again. "It was scary and I don't want to experience that again."
Lifelong deficit in girls
Uday joins other clinicians and academics who have formed a group - ACT NOW Vitamin D - calling for the threshold at which you are classified as deficient to be raised.
She says that would "catch" more people with low vitamin D and give a more accurate picture of how widespread the issue is. It would also mean they can treat the deficiency earlier, she says.
Uday warns of "a lifelong deficit" in women - in adolescence, then pregnancy, and then the newborn is affected.
"If you don't correct it from the very beginning," she says, "this is going to affect multiple generations."
"It's shocking," says Prof Martin Hewison, from the University of Birmingham.
He tells me that despite being 100 years on from the discovery of vitamin D "rickets hasn't gone away".
"If we have rickets in the community, there are going to be many more people who are vitamin D deficient."
He says the government should look into wider fortification of food in which vitamins are added to foods during production. Countries like Canada and Sweden have mandatory policies.
In the UK, some foods such as breakfast cereals and spreads are already fortified with vitamin D, but it is voluntary.
During the winter months, people start to lose their vitamin D levels.
"We might have to accept that for certain groups vitamin D supplementation is a matter of course," says Hewison.
Saskia is now taking vitamin D supplements regularly - and is back in goal.

description: Doctors are finding vitamin D deficiency is increasingly widespread in the UK, especially in young people. But the symptoms are difficult to spot and can be missed.

title: Cubans in Florida waver on Trump and Republicans over immigration
text:
Many Cubans voted for Trump - now they're turning on Republican immigration policies
Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ismael Labrador, in Miami is never empty. His appointment book is packed with relatives of detained immigrants trying to secure their release before they're deported back to their countries of origin.
Although business is booming, Labrador wishes it wasn't.
"We have relatives living in fear right now, we've had relatives who have been deported back to Cuba, unfortunately," he explains.
Cubans have traditionally enjoyed favoured immigration status in the United States under provisions enshrined in 1960s-era legislation called the Cuban Adjustment Act. But widespread arrests across Florida by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have left the Cuban American community more vulnerable in the US than they'd ever imagined, says Labrador.
"The way I put it is that if you don't have a Green Card in the United States, you may be a target."
Countless mobile phone videos have recorded such arrests in places previously considered off-limits: parents detained outside schoolyards, at bus stops, youth sporting events and even inside courthouses at pre-arranged immigration hearings.
Few have had the impact of the footage of 39-year-old Ecuadorean immigrant, Grace Calero, and her 19-year-old daughter, Giulianna Carriel, being arrested in a hospital ward.
Two months ago, the pair were driving to work in Kissimmee, central Florida when they were hit by another car and taken to hospital in an ambulance. While they were being treated for their injuries, ICE agents burst in and arrested them. They were deported back to Ecuador within days.
Labrador's cousin has also been caught up in the dragnet of ICE detentions. Despite his best efforts, the immigration lawyer was unable to prevent his own relative from being deported back to Cuba.
"It's hard when you're fighting against a lot of resources," he laments.
The Trump administration has repeatedly said the president was elected on a promise to deliver mass deportations and is delivering on that. "He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," a White House spokeswoman told the BBC last week.
ICE, meanwhile, has said it is targeting anyone who has broken American immigration law and is in the country illegally.
Labrador was among the 68% of Cuban Americans in Florida who voted for Donald Trump two years ago, a decision he roundly regrets today.
Few could accuse Trump of hiding his plans on immigration. On the campaign trail in 2024, he touted his policy of mass deportations of undocumented migrants.
"On Day One, I will launch the largest deportation programme in American history", he said repeatedly at rallies, including in Florida.
Labrador – and many thousands of disillusioned Latino voters like him – thought the administration would only deport people with criminal records.
"I think we got blindsided by the administration," he argues.
"Personally, I voted for Trump because I wanted to get criminals out of the country," he says, alleging that "communists came in from Cuba under Biden."
"We wanted to have a safe America. We never thought that he was going to go after everybody."
"This isn't what I voted for," he insists.
Labrador is far from the only Cuban American in Florida to experience buyer's remorse over President Trump.
Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents Florida's 27th Congressional district, recently released a video filmed outside the White House in which she distanced herself from his deportation policy saying it had gone "too far".
"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said, addressing President Trump.
Salazar is locked in a tight race against another Cuban American, the Democratic Party's candidate, Eliott Rodríguez. Her close association with Trump on immigration could potentially cost Salazar her congressional seat.
Florida remains a Trump stronghold. At a recent gathering of Cuban American entrepreneurs in Miami, the atmosphere remained staunchly pro-Trump. "Miami loves Trump, Cuban Americans love Trump," says real estate businessman, Juan Omar Sixto, motioning at the other guests behind him.
"They agree with Trump that anyone who crossed the border illegally should be out," he says, despite acknowledging he illegally entered the US himself six decades earlier.
A poll released on Thursday by Florida International University found that not all South Florida Cubans agree - 76% said they disapprove of the Trump administration's deportations of Cubans with no criminal record. But their support for the Republican Party remains steadfast, with 68% saying they plan to vote Republican in November.
In other parts of the country, support amongst Latinos is declining.
In the last election, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 56.1% to 43% - the biggest margin of victory for a candidate in the state since 1988 - in part because of the support of Latino communities. But a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll of 8,000 registered Latino voters showed nearly 60% favour seeing Congress come under Democratic Party control to just 35% wanting a Republican victory.
The high cost of living is a big factor for people's discontent, as residents feel supermarket and petrol prices are impossibly high for working families.
But for many Hispanics, it's also partly because of stories like Heydi Sanchez's.
Sanchez left Cuba in 2019 as the island spiralled into economic collapse and illegally crossed the border from Mexico into the US. After nine months in a detention centre, she was released under an i-220B Order of Supervision which grants the right to remain in the US but carries the constant threat of deportation.
Sanchez settled in Tampa where she worked with autistic children and the elderly. After a complex and expensive fertility struggle, she and her husband had a baby girl called Kailyn.
Most i-220B holders try to normalise their immigration status via 'humanitarian parole' and must check in with ICE agents at regular scheduled appointments. Last year, President Trump revoked temporary humanitarian parole to about 300,000 Cubans. Sanchez knew something was wrong in her case when her regular ICE meeting was brought forward without warning.
At the appointment, she was detained. Kailyn was taken from her arms and passed to her father, a US citizen. Within a day, Sanchez was on a deportation flight back to Havana in shackles with no recourse to appeal.
I met her in Cuba where she now lives in a one-bed apartment in Mayabeque, a rural province outside Havana.
"It's like the sky fell in and crushed me", she says of being separated from her daughter.
"When we have video calls, she says: 'Mummy, come home.' And I say: 'darling, Mummy is away working.' What else can I tell her? How can I explain it?'", Sanchez asks, unable to hold back the tears.
Despite expressions of support from several US politicians, including Maria Elvira Salazar, more than a year has passed since her deportation and Sanchez remains in limbo in Cuba.
In a statement, ICE said that "in this case, the parent stated they wanted to be removed without the child and left the child in the care of a safe relative in the United States".
While the Trump Administration has rolled back Cubans' special immigration privileges, it has sent thousands of people back to an island Washington itself describes as a "failed state". Cuba is in the grip of its worst ever energy crisis amid a months-long fuel blockade imposed by the US.
Since overwhelmingly voting for Trump in 2024, Cubans in Florida now realise they are just as vulnerable to deportation as any other diaspora. His Republican colleagues may feel the brunt of their frustration at the ballot box.

description: President Trump's fellow Republicans might feel the brunt of frustration among Cubans at the ballot box, writes the BBC's Will Grant.

title: Serbia: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations
text:
Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.
Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.
It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.
But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.
Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.
Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.
"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.
The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.
Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.
They have made some bold promises.
Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".
The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.
Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.
The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.
Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".
But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.
"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.
By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.
That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.
Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".
All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.
That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.
Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade.
"While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC.
"Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.
Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.
Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.
The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.
But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".
For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.
That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list.
"Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.
The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.
Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."
description: Days after ousting Aleksandar Vučić's party from power, Student List MPs call for top figures to stand down.

title: Irish Travellers' nomadic life 'is at risk', says support committee
text:
Nomadic life for Irish Travellers 'at risk' over site shortages
The nomadic life of Irish Travellers is "at risk" in Northern Ireland with members of the community feeling pressured to move into "bricks and mortar" housing, a support group has said.
The number of sites and pitches in Northern Ireland has "reduced drastically" in the past 20 years, according to the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee.
It added that the issue was "compounded" by "well below par" provisions on remaining sites.
The Northern Ireland Housing Executive (NIHE), which is responsible for the accommodation needs of travellers, said it is investing in and future-proofing their way of life.
It is currently consulting the public on a draft strategy for the next five years on traveller accommodation.
Meanwhile, the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee also criticised Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly for contacting the police over roadside travellers during the summer, suggesting she should have found them somewhere suitable to stay instead.
One traveller at a site in Craigavon, who wanted to remain anonymous, told BBC News NI that "no one cares" about them.
They added: "It's got to the point where we just put up with it.
"We feel pressured to move into a house but that isn't our way of life. That would be horrific for mental health.
"Personally I feel no one improves it because we're travelling people."
Lisa Hogg, from the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee, described some families using shower units on sites with sewage coming up from under the shower tray.
She added that provisions have led to families becoming homeless or displaced.
"It has been frustrating, it has impacted health and mental health. We've seen a huge number of families moving off, out of the area because of the provision here, they just can't do it.
"I think there's a huge misconception that travellers don't pay rent and rates if they're in social housing. They are liable for rents and rates and it is claimed for and paid in the way that all social housing is."
Hogg added that nomadic traveller families were having their ability to maintain that lifestyle "slowly eradicated".
"The right to travel is a protected characteristic of Irish travellers, but there are no provisions in the north to allow that to happen."
Who is responsible for Irish Traveller sites?
The Housing Executive oversees accommodation needs for that community, as well as providing, managing or leasing caravan sites for travellers, who pay rent like social housing tenants.
As of June 2026, the NIHE provided and managed a range of sites including two transit/emergency halting sites, two serviced/permanent sites and seven grouped, social housing sites.
Three sites - based in Londonderry, Strabane and Belfast - have closed in the last decade.
In a statement, the NIHE explained this was due to "specific circumstances" in those locations including health and safety concerns, site viability issues and the proposed acquisition of land for major infrastructure projects such as the A5.
"We recognise that every site matters. When a site is lost, it can reduce accommodation choice for Irish Traveller families and communities," the NIHE said.
Currently under consultation, the draft Irish Traveller Accommodation Strategy 2026–2031 sets out the NIHE's objectives, including "to improve the provision and standard" of sites.
"The Housing Executive remains committed to exploring opportunities to maintain and increase accommodation choice for Irish Travellers where feasible and where needs are identified," NIHE added.
"Our ambition is not simply to provide accommodation. It is to support the Irish Traveller way of life by ensuring that accommodation choice, cultural identity and community connections are recognised and respected."
In a response to the consultation, the Equality Commission said the strategy was an important opportunity "against a backdrop of declining traveller-specific accommodation and evidence of poor conditions on existing sites".
It said that at the time of writing only four Housing Executive sites were operational compared to seven in 2018 and 16 in 2009.
The Equality Commission also called on "stronger commitments" around Irish Traveller accommodation as well as "clear targets, timescales and resource commitments".
Meanwhile, the Craigavon Travellers Support Committee has criticised Northern Ireland's deputy first minister over her comments she made during the summer.
In August, Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly posted a video on social media to say she had contacted the police over travellers parked at Sprucefield Centre, outside Lisburn.
In the video, she said: "Just to reassure people we have been in contact already with the PSNI and Translink who operate the site, raising those concerns about what is happening.
"It is not legal to camp here overnight," the Lagan Valley assembly member added.
While she said in the video she had contacted Translink and the PSNI, it is not known whether she also took steps to find alternative accommodation for the travellers.
Speaking to BBC News NI, Kelly Laverty from Craigavon Travellers Support Committee was critical of this, and said "she should have contacted the statutory authority to highlight these people have nowhere to go".
BBC News NI has approached Emma Little-Pengelly through both the Executive Office and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) for a response.
Are Irish Travellers moving into houses?
Prof Michelle Norris, from University College Dublin, has been on an expert panel for the Irish government looking at accommodation in the Republic of Ireland. She said accommodation is central to Irish Travellers' "identity as an ethnic group".
"So having access to accommodation that will facilitate their nomadic tradition is central to their identity as a traveller," she added.
Norris said it's not just about having "adequate" accommodation.
"It's also about accommodation that's appropriate for their ethnic identity and traditions.
"Demand for traveller specific accommodation, halting sites and group housing schemes, is falling."
Each year, local authorities in the Republic of Ireland undertake an assessment of social housing need, which are then compiled into a nationwide report.
"We found in the latest figures from 2025 that around 95% of travellers actually want standard housing in a housing estate," Norris said.
"I think that reflects changing aspirations among younger households.
"But that doesn't mean that travellers who want traveller-specific accommodation shouldn't be facilitated and we know that lots of households who do want that type of accommodation can't get access to it."
description: Craigavon Travellers Support Committee says members of the community feel pressured to move into "bricks and mortar".

title: Dramatic clifftop rescue of bride and groom-to-be
text:
Dramatic clifftop rescue of bride and groom-to-be
A couple who went for a beach walk shortly after getting engaged had to be rescued by the Irish Coast Guard after an incoming tide trapped them against a coastal cliff.
The bride and groom-to-be were hauled approximately 150m (490 ft) to the top of the cliff to safety because rescuers could not reach them by boat or by helicopter.
The dramatic rescue took place during gale-force winds on Achill Island, off the west coast of Ireland, on Monday afternoon.
Coast Guard volunteer Peter McManamon, who coordinated the operation, told BBC News NI: "They were two very lucky people."
It is believed the pair are originally from overseas but live in Ireland and were on a visit to Achill Island, off the County Mayo coast, when the incident happened.
McManamon said the couple had gone for a walk along Keel Beach when the tide began to come in behind them - at one point reaching above knee-level.
"They got engaged in Achill and they were just walking along [the beach] and they went out too far on the rocks," he explained.
"The weather conditions were atrocious there, and in that particular area the tide has come in very quick."
Unable to get off the sand because of the towering cliff behind them, the couple called 999 and asked for a coast guard rescue.
"It was too rough for a rib (rigid inflatable boat) to be tasked - it was blowing Force 8 to 10 at the time and the wave conditions wouldn't let us," McManamon said.
"We tried to walk out along the rocks to them but... the waves were just coming in and it was just too dangerous to put the crew in, so the helicopter was tasked."
'Hypothermia was beginning to set in'
Coast Guard helicopter R118, based in County Sligo, flew to the scene but the force of the winds meant its crew were unable to help the stranded couple.
"When the helicopter came, they tried to move in to winch them but there was too much down draft off the mountain for it to happen," McManamon explained.
So he then deployed climbers from Achill Island Coast Guard's cliff rescue team who abseiled down the cliff to pluck the couple out of the rising tide.
"The water was coming in around them - the water was roughly just above their knees," McManamon recalled.
The couple were taken to safety in stages. The woman was brought to higher ground first while her fiance waited with "waves crashing" around his legs.
Once they were both out of immediate risk, the climbers used ropes to separately haul both casualties a further 150m to the clifftop.
"They were very cold - hypothermia was beginning to set in," McManamon said.
However, the remote beauty spot could not be reached by vehicle so the casualties then faced a 2km (1.2 mile) walk down the hill to a waiting ambulance.
There, they were treated by paramedics before being taken to hospital for checks, but they did not need to be admitted.
McManamon said it is never a safe decision to walk along coastal cliffs in such weather conditions.
"It can be a dangerous spot, the locals don't really go near it at all," he said, explaining that other parts of the beach are more suitable for walking or swimming.
McManamon has been a member of the Irish Coast Guard for 20 years, the last seven of which he has spent at "officer in charge" at Achill Island Coast Guard Unit.
The role is voluntary.
Monday's rescue operation took more than seven hours, with his crew finally leaving cliff at about 21:30 local time.
"I didn't get a chance to talk to them [the couple] properly, I was too busy organising my own team," McManamon said.
"We were that wet and hungry, we just wanted to get tidied up and get our equipment back and to get to our own homes and families."
Popular site to pop the question?
McManamon agreed that it was one of the most dramatic engagement stories that he had come across.
Having celebrated his own 25th wedding anniversary earlier this month, he has some affinity with the couple - in fact Keel Beach was the setting for his own marriage proposal.
However, he was quick to point out that he popped the question "on the safe side of the beach".
description: A romantic walk after agreeing to tie the knot turns into a 150m rope rescue off the Irish coast.
